continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Fix $n\ge1$, $p\ge1$, a finite design matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with rows $x_i^\mathsf T$, a dispersion value $\phi$, and an open parameter domain $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$. A **generalized linear model (GLM)** on this design consists of the response family in [[def-glm-observation-family]], a differentiable one-to-one link $g:\mathcal M\to g(\mathcal M)$ on a specified mean domain $\mathcal M$, and a specified map $\tau:\mathcal M\to J$ satisfying $b'(\tau(\mu))=\mu$. For $\beta\in\Theta$, put

$$\eta_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta,\qquad \mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i),\qquad \theta_i=\tau(\mu_i),$$

and require $\eta_i\in g(\mathcal M)$ and $\theta_i\in J$ for every $i$. The **canonical link** is the choice $g=\tau$, equivalently $\theta_i=\eta_i$. When $\theta_i=\eta_i$ and the component scales are common, write $a_i(\phi)=a(\phi)>0$; this common-scale restriction is part of every formula that uses $a(\phi)$.

The joint sampling density is the product density from [[lem-glm-product-density]]. For an observed $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for every $i$, define its log likelihood by

$$\ell(\beta;y,\phi)=\sum_{i=1}^n\left\{\frac{y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)}{a_i(\phi)}+c_i(y_i,\phi)\right\}.$$

For a differentiable log likelihood, the **score** is $U(\beta;y,\phi):=\nabla_\beta\ell(\beta;y,\phi)$. When its entries have finite second moments, the **expected score outer-product information** is $I(\beta,\phi):=\mathbb E_{\beta,\phi}[U U^\mathsf T]$. This page treats $X$ as fixed or conditions on its realized value; it supplies no random-design asymptotic conclusion.

In the setup of [[def-glm-observation-family]], let $P_\theta=\bigotimes_{i=1}^nP_{i,\theta_i,\phi}$ and $\nu=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\nu_i$. Then the joint sampling law has density

$$q_\theta(y_1,\ldots,y_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)$$

relative to $\nu$. At any $y$ for which every factor $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)$ is positive, the log likelihood is $\log q_\theta(y)=\sum_i\log f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

For each coordinate $j$, the chain rule [F4] gives $\partial_{\beta_j}\ell=\sum_i x_{ij}\{y_i-b'(\eta_i)\}/a(\phi)$. By [F3], $b'(\eta_i)=b'(\tau(\mu_i))=\mu_i$, so these entries assemble as $X^\mathsf T(y-\mu)/a(\phi)$.

Differentiating the coordinate expression in step 1.1 with respect to $\beta_k$ gives $\partial_{\beta_k}\partial_{\beta_j}\ell=-\sum_i x_{ij}x_{ik}b''(\eta_i)/a(\phi)$ by [F4]. The sum and matrix-product rules [F5] identify these entries with $-X^\mathsf T\operatorname{diag}(b''(\eta_i))X/a(\phi)$.

Fix a finite integer $n\ge1$ and a dispersion value $\phi$. For each $1\le i\le n$, let $\mathcal Y_i\subseteq\mathbb R$ carry its Borel sigma algebra and let $\nu_i$ be a sigma-finite positive measure on it. Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $b:J\to\mathbb R$ be twice continuously differentiable, let $a_i(\phi)>0$, and let $c_i(\,\cdot\,,\phi)$ be measurable. An **explicit one-parameter exponential-family response contract** supplies, for each $\theta_i\in J$, a density or mass function relative to $\nu_i$,

$$f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)=\exp\!\left\{\frac{y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)}{a_i(\phi)}+c_i(y_i,\phi)\right\}.$$

The contract requires $f_i\ge0$, $\int f_i(\,\cdot\,;\theta_i,\phi)\,d\nu_i=1$ for every $\theta_i\in J$, and a fixed support $S_i\in\mathcal A_i$ such that $f_i>0$ on $S_i$ and $f_i=0$ off $S_i$, up to a $\nu_i$-null set independent of $\theta_i$. Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then

Inputs are an observed response vector $y$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for every $i$, a finite design matrix $X$, an admissible finite current parameter $\beta$, and a GLM with common scale $a(\phi)>0$. Require each $\dot\mu_i=d\mu_i/d\eta_i$ to be finite and nonzero and each $V_i=b''(\theta_i)$ to be finite and positive.

1. Compute $\eta_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta$ and $\mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i)$.
2. Compute the **working response** and positive weight
$$z_i=\eta_i+\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{\dot\mu_i},\qquad w_i=\frac{\dot\mu_i^2}{a(\phi)V_i}.$$
3. Form $W^{1/2}=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w_i})$ using [[thm-of-square-roots]], and put $A=W^{1/2}X$, $r=W^{1/2}z$. By [[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]] and [[thm-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse-exists-and-is-unique]], form $A^+$. Return $\beta_{\mathrm{new}}=A^+r$, the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm member of the nonempty weighted least-squares minimizer set by [[thm-a-plus-b-is-the-unique-minimum-norm-least-squares-solution]].

The Moore--Penrose convention makes the procedure single-valued even when $X$ is rank deficient; the underlying least-squares minimizer need not then be unique. Existence and the minimum-norm property follow from [[thm-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse-exists-and-is-unique]] and [[thm-a-plus-b-is-the-unique-minimum-norm-least-squares-solution]]. The output need not lie in $\Theta$, and this definition makes no claim that repeated updates terminate or converge to a maximizer.

Fix $n\ge1$, $p\ge1$, a finite design matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with rows $x_i^\mathsf T$, a dispersion value $\phi$, and an open parameter domain $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$. A **generalized linear model (GLM)** on this design consists of the response family in [[def-glm-observation-family]], a differentiable one-to-one link $g:\mathcal M\to g(\mathcal M)$ on a specified mean domain $\mathcal M$, and a specified map $\tau:\mathcal M\to J$ satisfying $b'(\tau(\mu))=\mu$. For $\beta\in\Theta$, put

$$\eta_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta,\qquad \mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i),\qquad \theta_i=\tau(\mu_i),$$

and require $\eta_i\in g(\mathcal M)$ and $\theta_i\in J$ for every $i$. The **canonical link** is the choice $g=\tau$, equivalently $\theta_i=\eta_i$. When $\theta_i=\eta_i$ and the component scales are common, write $a_i(\phi)=a(\phi)>0$; this common-scale restriction is part of every formula that uses $a(\phi)$.

The joint sampling density is the product density from [[lem-glm-product-density]]. For an observed $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for every $i$, define its log likelihood by

$$\ell(\beta;y,\phi)=\sum_{i=1}^n\left\{\frac{y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)}{a_i(\phi)}+c_i(y_i,\phi)\right\}.$$

For a differentiable log likelihood, the **score** is $U(\beta;y,\phi):=\nabla_\beta\ell(\beta;y,\phi)$. When its entries have finite second moments, the **expected score outer-product information** is $I(\beta,\phi):=\mathbb E_{\beta,\phi}[U U^\mathsf T]$. This page treats $X$ as fixed or conditions on its realized value; it supplies no random-design asymptotic conclusion.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] and
[[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]].

For every matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or
$\mathbb C$, there exists a unique matrix $A^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$
satisfying the four Penrose equations of
[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]].

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and let $b\in\mathbb F^m$. Then $A^+b$ is
a least-squares solution of $Ax=b$, and among all least-squares solutions it
is the unique one of minimum Euclidean norm.

derivations.claim: Each predictor is a finite sum of products of real design and parameter entries, and each mean is a unique finite real value by [F2]. The observed response coordinates are finite real numbers by [F1]. Thus $z_i=\eta_i+(y_i-\mu_i)/\dot\mu_i$ is finite and uniquely determined because its denominator is nonzero. Likewise $w_i=\dot\mu_i^2/(a(\phi)V_i)$ is finite and strictly positive: its numerator is positive and its denominator is a finite positive real number. These operations refer to real arithmetic, with no floating-point overflow assertion.

By [F3] each $w_i$ has one finite positive square root. Consequently the diagonal matrix $D=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w_i})$, the weighted design $A=DX$, and the target $r=Dz$ are unique finite real matrices or vectors with the specified dimensions. By [F4] the $p\times n$ matrix $A^+$ exists uniquely for every rank of $A$, so the returned $A^+r$ exists uniquely in $\mathbb R^p$. No inverse of $X^\mathsf T W X$ was required at this stage.

For every $\gamma\in\mathbb R^p$, the diagonal construction gives $\|A\gamma-r\|_2^2=\sum_iw_i(x_i^\mathsf T\gamma-z_i)^2$. Since a nonnegative real number and its square have the same minimizing arguments, [F5] makes $A^+r$ a member of the displayed weighted least-squares minimizer set and the unique member of minimum Euclidean norm. In particular that set is nonempty even when $X$ is rank deficient. The minimum-norm property is the conclusion of the supplied theorem, not an extra condition imposed on the algorithm's inputs.

The weighted normal matrix is symmetric, and for every $u\in\mathbb R^p$ one has $u^\mathsf T H u=\sum_iw_i(x_i^\mathsf T u)^2=\|Au\|_2^2\ge0$, so $H$ is positive semidefinite. If $Xu=0$, then $Hu=X^\mathsf T W Xu=0$. Conversely, if $Hu=0$, the displayed sum is zero, and its finitely many nonnegative terms with strictly positive $w_i$ force every $x_i^\mathsf T u=0$; hence $Xu=0$. This proves $\ker H=\ker X$. Steps 2.1–3.1 apply equally when this kernel is nontrivial.

If $X=0$, then $A=0$. The zero matrix satisfies the Penrose equations, so uniqueness in [F4] gives $A^+=0$ and the algorithm returns $0$. The weighted objective is then constant in $\gamma$, so every vector is a minimizer and $0$ is its unique minimum-norm member, consistent with step 3.1. A single response, zero observed responses, and other ranks use the same proof whenever the original admissibility conditions hold. Thus all stated well-definedness claims hold without an invertibility condition or a condition that the returned vector remain in the model domain.

Let $(Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ follow [[def-generalized-linear-model]] with a common scale $a(\phi)>0$, canonical link $\theta_i=\eta_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta$, and twice differentiable $b$. For an observed $y$ with $f_i(y_i;\eta_i,\phi)>0$ for every $i$,

$$\nabla_\beta\ell(\beta;y,\phi)=\frac{X^\mathsf T(y-\mu)}{a(\phi)},\qquad \nabla_\beta^2\ell(\beta;y,\phi)=-\frac{X^\mathsf T\operatorname{diag}(b''(\eta_i))X}{a(\phi)}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Fix distinct $\beta_0,\beta_1\in\Theta$, put $d=\beta_1-\beta_0$, and define $q(t)=\ell(\beta_0+td;y,\phi)$ for $0\le t\le1$. Convexity keeps this segment in $\Theta$. By [F1], $q''(t)=d^\mathsf T\nabla^2\ell(\beta_0+td)d=-a(\phi)^{-1}\sum_i b''(x_i^\mathsf T(\beta_0+td))(x_i^\mathsf Td)^2<0$, because $Xd\ne0$ by full column rank and every displayed $b''$ is positive. The mean value theorem [F2] applied to $q'$ makes $q'$ strictly decreasing. For any $0<t<1$, another application of [F2] gives $(q(t)-q(0))/t=q'(u)$ for some $u\in(0,t)$ and $(q(1)-q(t))/(1-t)=q'(v)$ for some $v\in(t,1)$; strict decrease gives the first secant slope larger than the second, which rearranges to $q(t)>(1-t)q(0)+tq(1)$. Thus every nonconstant segment is strictly concave.

Two distinct stationary points would give $q'(0)=q'(1)=0$ on their connecting segment, contradicting strict decrease. If $\beta_0$ is stationary and $\beta_1\ne\beta_0$, then $q'(0)=0$ and strict decrease gives $q'(t)<0$ for $0<t\le1$; [F2] applied to $q$ yields $\ell(\beta_1;y,\phi)-\ell(\beta_0;y,\phi)=q'(c)<0$ for some $c\in(0,1)$. Thus any stationary point is the unique global maximizer when it exists.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces and let $b\in W$. A vector $x\in V$ minimises $\lVert Tx-b\rVert$ if and only if

$$T^*(Tx-b)=0,$$

equivalently $T^*Tx=T^*b$. Minimisers exist, and if $x_0$ is one minimiser, then the full set of minimisers is $x_0+\ker T$.

derivations.claim: For every $i$, [F2] gives $w_i(z_i-\eta_i)=\{\dot\mu_i^2/(aV_i)\}\{(y_i-\mu_i)/\dot\mu_i\}=\dot\mu_i(y_i-\mu_i)/(aV_i)$. Since $\eta=X\beta$, multiplying by $X^\mathsf T$ and using [F1] yields $X^\mathsf T W(z-X\beta)=U(\beta)$.

Apply [F3] to the weighted least-squares map $T=W^{1/2}X$ and target $W^{1/2}z$. Its normal equation is $X^\mathsf T W(X\beta_{\mathrm{new}}-z)=0$, so $I(\beta)(\beta_{\mathrm{new}}-\beta)=X^\mathsf T W(z-X\beta)=U(\beta)$ by step 1.1. The assumed invertibility of $I(\beta)$ now gives $\beta_{\mathrm{new}}=\beta+I(\beta)^{-1}U(\beta)$.

The joint sampling density is the product density from [[lem-glm-product-density]]. For an observed $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for every $i$, define its log likelihood by

Fix $i$ and $\phi$ in [[def-glm-observation-family]], and write $a=a_i(\phi)$. Under its fixed-support, twice differentiable density, local integrable derivative-envelope, and finite-second-moment hypotheses,

$$\mathbb E_{\theta_i,\phi}[Y_i]=b'(\theta_i),\qquad \operatorname{Var}_{\theta_i,\phi}(Y_i)=a\,b''(\theta_i).$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Fix $n\ge1$, $p\ge1$, a finite design matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with rows $x_i^\mathsf T$, a dispersion value $\phi$, and an open parameter domain $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$. A **generalized linear model (GLM)** on this design consists of the response family in [[def-glm-observation-family]], a differentiable one-to-one link $g:\mathcal M\to g(\mathcal M)$ on a specified mean domain $\mathcal M$, and a specified map $\tau:\mathcal M\to J$ satisfying $b'(\tau(\mu))=\mu$. For $\beta\in\Theta$, put

$$\eta_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta,\qquad \mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i),\qquad \theta_i=\tau(\mu_i),$$

and require $\eta_i\in g(\mathcal M)$ and $\theta_i\in J$ for every $i$. The **canonical link** is the choice $g=\tau$, equivalently $\theta_i=\eta_i$. When $\theta_i=\eta_i$ and the component scales are common, write $a_i(\phi)=a(\phi)>0$; this common-scale restriction is part of every formula that uses $a(\phi)$.

The joint sampling density is the product density from [[lem-glm-product-density]]. For an observed $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for every $i$, define its log likelihood by

$$\ell(\beta;y,\phi)=\sum_{i=1}^n\left\{\frac{y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)}{a_i(\phi)}+c_i(y_i,\phi)\right\}.$$

For a differentiable log likelihood, the **score** is $U(\beta;y,\phi):=\nabla_\beta\ell(\beta;y,\phi)$. When its entries have finite second moments, the **expected score outer-product information** is $I(\beta,\phi):=\mathbb E_{\beta,\phi}[U U^\mathsf T]$. This page treats $X$ as fixed or conditions on its realized value; it supplies no random-design asymptotic conclusion.

Let $(Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ follow [[def-generalized-linear-model]] with a common scale $a(\phi)>0$, canonical link $\theta_i=\eta_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta$, and twice differentiable $b$. For an observed $y$ with $f_i(y_i;\eta_i,\phi)>0$ for every $i$,

$$\nabla_\beta\ell(\beta;y,\phi)=\frac{X^\mathsf T(y-\mu)}{a(\phi)},\qquad \nabla_\beta^2\ell(\beta;y,\phi)=-\frac{X^\mathsf T\operatorname{diag}(b''(\eta_i))X}{a(\phi)}.$$

Suppose the canonical-link GLM has an open convex parameter domain $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, full-column-rank design $X$, common scale $a(\phi)>0$, and $b''(\eta_i)>0$ at every predictor vector in $X\Theta$. For a fixed response vector $y$ whose component densities are positive throughout $\Theta$, $\ell(\,\cdot\,;y,\phi)$ is strictly concave on $\Theta$. It has at most one stationary point; if a stationary point exists, it is the unique global maximizer. This conclusion does not assert that a finite maximizer exists.
For $p\in[0,1]$, a **Bernoulli$(p)$ random variable** takes the value $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability $1-p$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: The column $X=(-1,1)^\mathsf T$ has rank one, and $b''(\eta)=e^\eta/(1+e^\eta)^2>0$ for every finite $\eta$. Thus [F3] applies and the log likelihood is strictly concave on $\mathbb R$.
By [F1], $\ell(\beta)= -b(-\beta)+\beta-b(\beta)=-2\log(1+e^{-\beta})$. The score formula [F2] gives $\ell'(\beta)=2/(1+e^\beta)>0$ at every finite $\beta$.

The log likelihood is strictly negative for every finite $\beta$, while $\ell(\beta)\to0$ as $\beta\to+\infty$. Hence its supremum is $0$ and is not attained at any finite parameter: this separated logistic model has no finite MLE despite strict concavity.

Consider [[def-generalized-linear-model]] at an admissible finite $\beta$ with common scale $a(\phi)>0$. Put

$$w_i=\frac{\dot\mu_i^2}{a(\phi)V_i},\qquad z_i=\eta_i+\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{\dot\mu_i}.$$

For every observed $y$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for each $i$, the score and expected score outer-product information are

$$U(\beta;y,\phi)=X^\mathsf T\left(\frac{\dot\mu_i(y_i-\mu_i)}{a(\phi)V_i}\right)_{i=1}^n,\qquad I(\beta,\phi)=X^\mathsf T\operatorname{diag}(w_i)X.$$

Inputs are an observed response vector $y$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for every $i$, a finite design matrix $X$, an admissible finite current parameter $\beta$, and a GLM with common scale $a(\phi)>0$. Require each $\dot\mu_i=d\mu_i/d\eta_i$ to be finite and nonzero and each $V_i=b''(\theta_i)$ to be finite and positive.

1. Compute $\eta_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta$ and $\mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i)$.
2. Compute the **working response** and positive weight
$$z_i=\eta_i+\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{\dot\mu_i},\qquad w_i=\frac{\dot\mu_i^2}{a(\phi)V_i}.$$
3. Form $W^{1/2}=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w_i})$ using [[thm-of-square-roots]], and put $A=W^{1/2}X$, $r=W^{1/2}z$. By [[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]] and [[thm-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse-exists-and-is-unique]], form $A^+$. Return $\beta_{\mathrm{new}}=A^+r$, the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm member of the nonempty weighted least-squares minimizer set by [[thm-a-plus-b-is-the-unique-minimum-norm-least-squares-solution]].

The Moore--Penrose convention makes the procedure single-valued even when $X$ is rank deficient; the underlying least-squares minimizer need not then be unique. Existence and the minimum-norm property follow from [[thm-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse-exists-and-is-unique]] and [[thm-a-plus-b-is-the-unique-minimum-norm-least-squares-solution]]. The output need not lie in $\Theta$, and this definition makes no claim that repeated updates terminate or converge to a maximizer.

derivations.claim: For Bernoulli, $b'(\theta)=e^\theta/(1+e^\theta)$, so the finite natural parameter corresponding to $\mu\in(0,1)$ is $\theta=\log(\mu/(1-\mu))$. Under the identity link, $\eta=\mu=\beta$; as $\mu\downarrow0$, $\theta\to-\infty$, so $\mu=0$ is outside the finite-natural-parameter interior.

On the interior, $\dot\mu=d\mu/d\eta=1$ and $V(\mu)=b''(\theta)=\mu(1-\mu)$. Hence [F2] gives $w=1/\{\mu(1-\mu)\}\to+\infty$ as $\mu\downarrow0$. The boundary therefore violates the finite-weight admissibility in [F3], even though the limiting Bernoulli law itself is a probability measure.

citations.quote:
Fix $n\ge1$, $p\ge1$, a finite design matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with rows $x_i^\mathsf T$, a dispersion value $\phi$, and an open parameter domain $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$. A **generalized linear model (GLM)** on this design consists of the response family in [[def-glm-observation-family]], a differentiable one-to-one link $g:\mathcal M\to g(\mathcal M)$ on a specified mean domain $\mathcal M$, and a specified map $\tau:\mathcal M\to J$ satisfying $b'(\tau(\mu))=\mu$. For $\beta\in\Theta$, put

$$\eta_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta,\qquad \mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i),\qquad \theta_i=\tau(\mu_i),$$

and require $\eta_i\in g(\mathcal M)$ and $\theta_i\in J$ for every $i$. The **canonical link** is the choice $g=\tau$, equivalently $\theta_i=\eta_i$. When $\theta_i=\eta_i$ and the component scales are common, write $a_i(\phi)=a(\phi)>0$; this common-scale restriction is part of every formula that uses $a(\phi)$.

The joint sampling density is the product density from [[lem-glm-product-density]]. For an observed $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for every $i$, define its log likelihood by

$$\ell(\beta;y,\phi)=\sum_{i=1}^n\left\{\frac{y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)}{a_i(\phi)}+c_i(y_i,\phi)\right\}.$$

For a differentiable log likelihood, the **score** is $U(\beta;y,\phi):=\nabla_\beta\ell(\beta;y,\phi)$. When its entries have finite second moments, the **expected score outer-product information** is $I(\beta,\phi):=\mathbb E_{\beta,\phi}[U U^\mathsf T]$. This page treats $X$ as fixed or conditions on its realized value; it supplies no random-design asymptotic conclusion.

Fix $i$ and $\phi$ in [[def-glm-observation-family]], and write $a=a_i(\phi)$. Under its fixed-support, twice differentiable density, local integrable derivative-envelope, and finite-second-moment hypotheses,

$$\mathbb E_{\theta_i,\phi}[Y_i]=b'(\theta_i),\qquad \operatorname{Var}_{\theta_i,\phi}(Y_i)=a\,b''(\theta_i).$$

Consider [[def-generalized-linear-model]] at an admissible finite $\beta$ with common scale $a(\phi)>0$. Assume each $\eta_i\mapsto\theta_i$ is differentiable, each $\eta_i\mapsto\mu_i$ is differentiable with $\dot\mu_i:=d\mu_i/d\eta_i\ne0$, $V_i:=b''(\theta_i)>0$, the component scores have finite second moments, and the common-support, differentiability, and local integrable derivative-envelope conditions from [[def-glm-observation-family]] hold. Put

$$w_i=\frac{\dot\mu_i^2}{a(\phi)V_i},\qquad z_i=\eta_i+\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{\dot\mu_i}.$$

For every observed $y$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for each $i$, the score and expected score outer-product information are

$$U(\beta;y,\phi)=X^\mathsf T\left(\frac{\dot\mu_i(y_i-\mu_i)}{a(\phi)V_i}\right)_{i=1}^n,\qquad I(\beta,\phi)=X^\mathsf T\operatorname{diag}(w_i)X.$$

In particular, if $X$ has full column rank, then $I$ is positive definite.

Inputs are an observed response vector $y$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for every $i$, a finite design matrix $X$, an admissible finite current parameter $\beta$, and a GLM with common scale $a(\phi)>0$. Require each $\dot\mu_i=d\mu_i/d\eta_i$ to be finite and nonzero and each $V_i=b''(\theta_i)$ to be finite and positive.

1. Compute $\eta_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta$ and $\mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i)$.
2. Compute the **working response** and positive weight
$$z_i=\eta_i+\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{\dot\mu_i},\qquad w_i=\frac{\dot\mu_i^2}{a(\phi)V_i}.$$
3. Form $W^{1/2}=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w_i})$ using [[thm-of-square-roots]], and put $A=W^{1/2}X$, $r=W^{1/2}z$. By [[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]] and [[thm-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse-exists-and-is-unique]], form $A^+$. Return $\beta_{\mathrm{new}}=A^+r$, the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm member of the nonempty weighted least-squares minimizer set by [[thm-a-plus-b-is-the-unique-minimum-norm-least-squares-solution]].

The Moore--Penrose convention makes the procedure single-valued even when $X$ is rank deficient; the underlying least-squares minimizer need not then be unique. Existence and the minimum-norm property follow from [[thm-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse-exists-and-is-unique]] and [[thm-a-plus-b-is-the-unique-minimum-norm-least-squares-solution]]. The output need not lie in $\Theta$, and this definition makes no claim that repeated updates terminate or converge to a maximizer.

Under the admissibility hypotheses of [[alg-fisher-scoring-irls]], assume also that each map $\eta_i\mapsto\theta_i$ is differentiable, each map $\eta_i\mapsto\mu_i$ is differentiable with finite nonzero derivative $\dot\mu_i$, and $V_i:=b''(\theta_i)>0$. Each response has finite second moment, its density has the fixed common support and locally uniform integrable envelopes for its first and second $\theta_i$ derivatives required by [[def-glm-observation-family]], and each component score has finite second moment. If $I(\beta)=X^\mathsf T W X$ is invertible, let $U(\beta)$ and $I(\beta)$ be the score and expected score outer-product information from [[thm-glm-general-link-score-and-information]]. Then the weighted least-squares output satisfies

$$\beta_{\mathrm{new}}=\beta+I(\beta)^{-1}U(\beta).$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $p,m\ge1$ be integers and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $p\times p$ matrix, in the sense of [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. Give $\mathrm{Sym}_p$, the space of real symmetric $p\times p$ matrices, its Euclidean Borel sigma-algebra by identifying a matrix with its upper-triangular entries. The finite product measure $N_p(0,\Sigma)^{\otimes m}$ exists because each factor is a probability measure and hence sigma-finite. Define the **Wishart law** $W_p(\Sigma,m)$ as the pushforward of this product measure by the continuous map $(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^m z_jz_j^T$. Equivalently, it is the law of $\sum_{j=1}^m Z_jZ_j^T$ for independent $Z_j\sim N_p(0,\Sigma)$.

Here $\Sigma$ is the scale matrix and the positive integer $m$ is the degrees of freedom. This definition allows a singular Wishart law when $m<p$ or $\Sigma$ is singular; no Lebesgue density is included in the convention. The usual nonsingular density when $m\ge p$ is not needed below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $1\le p\le m$ and let $G=[G_1|\cdots|G_m]$ be a $p\times m$ matrix whose columns are independent $N_p(0,I_p)$ random vectors. Then the first $p$ columns are linearly independent almost surely. Consequently $GG^T$ is positive definite almost surely.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$ have independent standard-normal coordinates, and let $U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $U^TU=I_n$. Then $UZ$ also has independent $N(0,1)$ coordinates. Here $I_n$ is the identity matrix and $U$ is orthogonal.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$, and let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be an orthogonal projection of rank $r$, where $0\le r\le n$. Then the random vectors $PZ$ and $(I_n-P)Z$ are independent, and
$$
\|PZ\|^2\sim\chi_r^2,\qquad \|(I_n-P)Z\|^2\sim\chi_{n-r}^2.
$$
The two squared norms are independent. The cases $r=0$ and $r=n$ are included, with $\chi_0^2=\delta_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For an integer $k\ge1$, let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_k)$ have law $N_k(0,I_k)$, so its coordinates are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The **chi-square law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $\chi_k^2$, is the law of
$$
Q_k=\sum_{j=1}^k G_j^2=\|G\|^2.
$$
For $k=0$, define $\chi_0^2=\delta_0$, the point mass at zero. This zero-degree law records a rank-zero projection only; it is not used as a denominator in a Student or Fisher ratio. The multivariate-normal characteristic-function theorem makes the definition independent of the chosen realization of $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a positive integer $k$, take the product probability law of an independent standard normal $G$ and an independent $Q_k\sim\chi_k^2$. The **Student t law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $t_k$, is the law of
$$T_k=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{G}{\sqrt{Q_k/k}},&Q_k>0,\\ 0,&Q_k\le0. \end{cases}$$
For positive integers $r,s$, take independent $Q_r\sim\chi_r^2$ and $Q_s\sim\chi_s^2$. The **Fisher F law with degrees $(r,s)$**, denoted $F_{r,s}$, is the law of
$$F_{r,s}=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Q_r/r}{Q_s/s},&Q_s>0,\\ 0,&Q_s\le0. \end{cases}$$
The displayed piecewise maps are defined on all of $\mathbb R^2$ and are Borel measurable: each quotient is continuous on its Borel positive-denominator region, and the value on the complementary Borel nonpositive-denominator region is constant. The positive-degree chi-square lemma proves that the denominators are positive almost surely, so these versions agree almost surely with the usual quotients. Zero degrees are excluded from both definitions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $k\ge1$, the law $\chi_k^2$ has density
$$
f_k(x)=c_k x^{k/2-1}e^{-x/2}\mathbf 1_{\{x>0\}},\qquad c_k=\frac{\sigma_{k-1}(S^{k-1})}{2(2\pi)^{k/2}}>0,
$$
where $\sigma_{k-1}$ is the polar surface measure on the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^k$. Consequently, $Q_k>0$ almost surely, and its cumulative distribution function is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

An endomorphism $P$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space is the orthogonal projection onto some subspace if and only if

$$P^2=P\qquad\text{and}\qquad P^*=P.$$

In that case it is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{im}P$, along $\ker P=(\operatorname{im}P)^\perp$. The cases $P=0$ and $P=I$ are included.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

derivations.claim: By [F1], realize $W=GG^T$ with $G=[g_1|\cdots|g_m]$ and independent $g_j\sim N_p(0,I_p)$. For any square matrix $A$, extend inversion by setting $J(A)=A^{-1}$ when $\det A\ne0$ and $J(A)=0$ otherwise. This is Borel: the invertible matrices form an open set, inversion is continuous there, and the complementary branch is constant; [F11] supplies Euclidean Borel measurability. Thus $J(GG^T)$ is a Borel matrix-valued random element and agrees with $W^{-1}$ whenever $GG^T$ is invertible. Since $m\ge p$, [F2] makes $G$ full row rank almost surely; hence for nonzero $v$, $v^TWv=\|G^Tv\|^2>0$ and $W$ is invertible almost surely.

For $p\ge2$, write the first row of $G$ as $g$ and the remaining $p-1$ rows as $G_2$. The event $E_2=\{\det(G_2G_2^T)\ne0\}$ is Borel. Define $C^\dagger=(G_2G_2^T)^{-1}$ on $E_2$ and $C^\dagger=0$ on $E_2^c$, and put $P=G_2^TC^\dagger G_2$; this is Borel by the same piecewise-inversion argument as in step 1.1. By [F2], $E_2$ has probability one. On $E_2$, direct multiplication gives $P^T=P$ and $P^2=P$, and its image is the row space of $G_2$, of dimension $p-1$; [F9] identifies it as an orthogonal projection. For $p=1$, use the empty-row convention $G_2=0$, $P=0$. In either case define the Borel scalar $Q=g(I_m-P)g^T$ on the whole matrix space. On the full-probability event that $G$ has full row rank, the block matrix $W=GG^T=\begin{pmatrix}gg^T&gG_2^T\\G_2g^T&C\end{pmatrix}$ has invertible lower block $C$ when $p\ge2$, and solving $Wx=e_1$ gives $e_1^TW^{-1}e_1=(gg^T-gG_2^TC^{-1}G_2g^T)^{-1}$. Thus for $p\ge2$ this $Q$ equals $(e_1^TW^{-1}e_1)^{-1}$ on the full-probability event. For $p=1$, $W=gg^T$ and the same identity reads $Q=gg^T=(e_1^TW^{-1}e_1)^{-1}$.

The entries of $G$ are independent standard normals, so its first row $g$ is independent of the remaining rows $G_2$ by [F7]. For each fixed full-row-rank value of $G_2$, $I_m-P$ is an orthogonal projection of rank $m-p+1$. Therefore [F4] gives the section law $Q\sim\chi^2_{m-p+1}$ for every such $G_2$; the $p=1$ case follows from [F5]. The matrix rank event is Borel because it is determined by continuous minors, and the extended map $P(G_2)$ is Borel by step 2.1. The exceptional set has probability zero by [F2]. Applying the product-law identity [F8] to these Borel sections shows that the unconditional law of the Borel extension $Q=g(I_m-P)g^T$ is also $\chi^2_{m-p+1}$.

For any fixed unit vector $u\in\mathbb R^p$, [F10] supplies an orthogonal matrix $U$ with $Uu=e_1$. By [F3] and [F7], applying $U$ to each independent column preserves their joint standard-normal product law; hence $UWU^T$ has the same law as $W$. Let $h(t)=t^{-1}$ for $t>0$ and $h(t)=0$ otherwise. Since $J(W)=W^{-1}$ almost surely by step 1.1 and $W\succ0$ almost surely, $h(u^TJ(W)u)$ has the same law as $Q$ in step 3.1 for every unit $u$, using the orthogonal invariance just proved. Set $U_Z=Z/\|Z\|$ when $Z\ne0$ and let $U_Z=e_1$ when $Z=0$. The map $z\mapsto U_z$ is Borel, and $Q_Z:=h(U_Z^TJ(W)U_Z)$ is Borel because $J$ and $h$ are Borel; $Z=0$ is null by [F5]–[F6]. For Borel sets $A,B$, independence and the product law give $$\mathbb P(\|Z\|^2\in A,Q_Z\in B)=\int_{\{z:\|z\|^2\in A\}}\mathbb P_W\bigl(h(u_z^TJ(W)u_z)\in B\bigr)\,d\mathbb P_Z(z),$$ where $u_z=z/\|z\|$ for $z\ne0$ and $u_0=e_1$. The inner probability is the same for every unit $u_z$, so this factors as $\mathbb P(\|Z\|^2\in A)\mathbb P(Q\in B)$. Thus $Q_Z$ is independent of $\|Z\|^2$ and has the same $\chi^2_{m-p+1}$ law as $Q$ in step 3.1.

By [F5], $\|Z\|^2\sim\chi_p^2$ and it is independent of $Q_Z\sim\chi^2_{m-p+1}$ by step 4.1. Therefore $\frac{m-p+1}{p}Z^TW^{-1}Z=\frac{\|Z\|^2/p}{Q_Z/(m-p+1)}$ has law $F_{p,m-p+1}$ by the defining Fisher ratio; its denominator is positive almost surely by [F6].

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Fix integers $n\ge2$ and $p\ge1$. Let $\mathcal S_{++}^p$ be the set of real symmetric $p\times p$ matrices $\Sigma$ such that $v^T\Sigma v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$. The iid multivariate-normal sampling experiment has data space $\mathcal X=(\mathbb R^p)^n$ with sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^p)^{\otimes n}$, parameter set $\Theta=\mathbb R^p\times\mathcal S_{++}^p$, and sampling law $P_{\mu,\Sigma}=N_p(\mu,\Sigma)^{\otimes n}$. The finite product is a probability measure by [[def-probability-measure]] and [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]. The coordinate projection $X_i$ is the complete vector observation for sampling unit $i$; its $p$ coordinates need not be independent.

For $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathcal X$, define
$$\bar x=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i,\qquad R(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)^T,\qquad S(x)=\frac{R(x)}{n-1},\qquad M(x)=\frac{R(x)}n.$$
The functions $x\mapsto\bar x$, $S(x)$, and $M(x)$ are continuous, hence Borel measurable under AC and [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]]; they are statistics in the experiment by [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. Here $S$ uses the $n-1$ covariance denominator, while $M$ is the $n$-denominator covariance candidate whose maximum-likelihood property is proved separately below.

This item instantiates the mathematical portion of the scientific model contract ([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]) as follows. One sampling and analysis unit is one complete observed vector $X_i$; index $i$ identifies the sampling unit and coordinate $a$ identifies a component within that vector. For fixed parameter label $\theta=(\mu,\Sigma)$, $\mu$ and $\Sigma$ are fixed, every $X_i$ is random, every component of each $X_i$ is observed, and there are no latent quantities, predictors, treatments, or randomization. The target population for this reference experiment is the abstract law $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$ of a vector-valued sampling unit, and the target parameter is $\theta$ itself; no separate scientific estimand or physical setting is asserted. The observation map records the complete vector tuple unchanged, and inference uses the joint product law, with no conditioning convention beyond that law. No topological support or empirical adequacy claim is needed; this is a mathematical reference model, not an assertion that observed scientific data follow it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$ have independent standard-normal coordinates, and let $U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $U^TU=I_n$. Then $UZ$ also has independent $N(0,1)$ coordinates. Here $I_n$ is the identity matrix and $U$ is orthogonal.

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $p,m\ge1$ be integers and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $p\times p$ matrix, in the sense of [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. Give $\mathrm{Sym}_p$, the space of real symmetric $p\times p$ matrices, its Euclidean Borel sigma-algebra by identifying a matrix with its upper-triangular entries. The finite product measure $N_p(0,\Sigma)^{\otimes m}$ exists because each factor is a probability measure and hence sigma-finite. Define the **Wishart law** $W_p(\Sigma,m)$ as the pushforward of this product measure by the continuous map $(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^m z_jz_j^T$. Equivalently, it is the law of $\sum_{j=1}^m Z_jZ_j^T$ for independent $Z_j\sim N_p(0,\Sigma)$.

Here $\Sigma$ is the scale matrix and the positive integer $m$ is the degrees of freedom. This definition allows a singular Wishart law when $m<p$ or $\Sigma$ is singular; no Lebesgue density is included in the convention. The usual nonsingular density when $m\ge p$ is not needed below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $1\le p\le m$ and let $G=[G_1|\cdots|G_m]$ be a $p\times m$ matrix whose columns are independent $N_p(0,I_p)$ random vectors. Then the first $p$ columns are linearly independent almost surely. Consequently $GG^T$ is positive definite almost surely.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

derivations.claim: Define $Y_i=\Sigma^{-1/2}(X_i-\mu)$. The positive root exists by [F10], and if $\Sigma^{1/2}v=0$ then $v^T\Sigma v=\|\Sigma^{1/2}v\|^2=0$, so $\Sigma\succ0$ makes the root invertible. Whitening is a continuous, hence Borel, map by [F9]; [F6] therefore preserves independence of the sample vectors. By [F2], each $Y_i\sim N_p(0,I_p)$ has independent standard-normal coordinates, and [F11] gives the product joint law across $i$. Thus all $np$ entries $Y_{ia}$ are independent standard normals. Let $u=n^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)^T\in\mathbb R^n$. By [F3], complete $u$ to an orthonormal basis $u_1=u,u_2,\ldots,u_n$ of $\mathbb R^n$. For each coordinate $a\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$, the sample-coordinate vector $(Y_{1a},\ldots,Y_{na})^T$ is therefore standard normal in $\mathbb R^n$, and these $p$ vectors are independent.

Let $Y=[Y_1|\cdots|Y_n]$ and, for each $j,a$, define $Y'_{ja}=u_j^T(Y_{1a},\ldots,Y_{na})^T$. Applying the orthogonal invariance [F4] separately to the $p$ independent coordinate vectors gives independent standard-normal entries within each transformed coordinate vector; [F6] preserves independence between those $p$ vectors under their separate orthogonal maps. Thus all $np$ entries $Y'_{ja}$ are independent standard normals, and the $p$-vectors $Y'_1,\ldots,Y'_n$ formed from their coordinates are independent $N_p(0,I_p)$ vectors.

Since $u_1=u$, $Y'_1=\sqrt n\,n^{-1}\sum_iY_i=\sqrt n\,\Sigma^{-1/2}(\bar X-\mu)$. Its law and [F2] give $\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)\sim N_p(0,\Sigma)$. The vector $Y'_1$ is independent of $(Y'_2,\ldots,Y'_n)$ by [F5].

The matrix $U=[u_1|\cdots|u_n]$ is orthogonal and $u_1=u$. Hence $YY^T$ splits as $YY^T=Yuu^TY^T+\sum_{j=2}^nY u_ju_j^TY^T$. The first term is $n\bar Y\bar Y^T$, and the remaining terms are $Y'_jY_j'^T$, so $\sum_i(Y_i-\bar Y)(Y_i-\bar Y)^T=\sum_{j=2}^nY'_jY_j'^T$. Since $X_i-\bar X=\Sigma^{1/2}(Y_i-\bar Y)$, it follows that $(n-1)S=\Sigma^{1/2}(\sum_{j=2}^nY'_jY_j'^T)\Sigma^{1/2}$. The independent vectors in [F5] and Wishart definition [F7] give $(n-1)S\sim W_p(\Sigma,n-1)$. The sample mean is a function of $Y'_1$, while $S$ is a function of $Y'_2,\ldots,Y'_n$; the maps are Borel by [F9], so [F6] gives $\bar X\perp S$.

If $n>p$, then $n-1\ge p$ and the residual vectors $Y'_2,\ldots,Y'_n$ are independent standard-normal columns. By [F8], their $p\times(n-1)$ matrix has row rank $p$ almost surely. Its sum of column outer products is therefore positive definite; the congruence in step 4.1 and $n-1>0$ show $S\succ0$ almost surely.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each

$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$ have independent standard-normal coordinates, and let $U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $U^TU=I_n$. Then $UZ$ also has independent $N(0,1)$ coordinates. Here $I_n$ is the identity matrix and $U$ is orthogonal.

derivations.claim: By [F2] and [F3], one observation has density $\phi_{\mu,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-p/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp[-(x-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)/2]$: the independent-coordinate product density follows from [F4], its continuous Gaussian formula is Borel by [F15], and the invertible affine map $z\mapsto\mu+\Sigma^{1/2}z$ has determinant $|\det\Sigma^{1/2}|=(\det\Sigma)^{1/2}$, so [F5] gives the displayed density. Independence in [F1] then makes the sample density its product over $i=1,\ldots,n$. The finite-dimensional Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite by [F13], so the product law is dominated by it and the displayed function is a likelihood density by [F14].

Under $H_0$, the positive root $\Sigma_0^{1/2}$ is invertible by [F12], so define $Y_i=\Sigma_0^{-1/2}(X_i-\mu)$. By [F1]–[F2] these are iid $N_p(0,I_p)$. Write $C_n=n^{-1}\sum_iY_iY_i^T$ and $A_n=\Sigma_0^{-1/2}M\Sigma_0^{-1/2}=C_n-\bar Y\bar Y^T$. For a symmetric matrix, let $\operatorname{vech}$ list its upper-triangular entries in a fixed order; put $V_i=\operatorname{vech}(Y_iY_i^T-I_p)$. These vectors have mean zero and diagonal covariance: diagonal coordinates have variance $2$, off-diagonal coordinates variance $1$, and distinct coordinates have covariance zero. Indeed, independence and symmetry give zero for any product with an odd coordinate power; integration by parts against [F3]'s density gives $E Z^2=1$ and $E Z^4=3$ (using $\phi'(z)=-z\phi(z)$ and vanishing polynomial-times-Gaussian boundary terms), while independence factors mixed even products. These finite moments make $V_i$ square-integrable, so [F7] yields $\sqrt n\operatorname{vech}(C_n-I_p)\Rightarrow N(0,D)$ with those diagonal variances. Also $\sqrt n\bar Y=O_P(1)$ by [F7]–[F8], whence $\sqrt n\bar Y\bar Y^T=n^{-1/2}(\sqrt n\bar Y)(\sqrt n\bar Y)^T=o_P(1)$ by [F8]. Thus $H_n=\sqrt n(A_n-I_p)$ converges in distribution to a symmetric Gaussian matrix $H$ whose entries on and above the diagonal are independent, with variances $2$ on the diagonal and $1$ off it.

Taking logarithms of that positive product density gives, up to the parameter-free constant $-np\log(2\pi)/2$, $$\ell_n(\mu,\Sigma)=-\frac n2\log\det\Sigma-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(X_i-\mu).$$ Expanding $X_i-\mu=(X_i-\bar X)+(\bar X-\mu)$ and using $\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)=0$ shows the quadratic sum equals $n(\bar X-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(\bar X-\mu)+\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}R)$. Since $\Sigma^{-1}\succ0$, this is minimized uniquely at $\mu=\bar X$ for every fixed $\Sigma$.

By [F6], $M=R/n\succ0$ almost surely. The square root $M^{1/2}$ exists by [F12] and is invertible because $M\succ0$. At $\mu=\bar X$, compare the covariance log likelihood at any $\Sigma\succ0$ with its value at $M$. Let $B=M^{1/2}\Sigma^{-1}M^{1/2}\succ0$. The trace and determinant identities give $$\ell_n(\bar X,\Sigma)-\ell_n(\bar X,M)=-\frac n2\{\operatorname{tr}B-\log\det B-p\}.$$ By [F11], the eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p$ of $B$ are positive and the brace is $\sum_j(\lambda_j-\log\lambda_j-1)\ge0$, since $x-\log x-1\ge0$ for $x>0$ by differentiation and its unique minimum at $1$. Equality holds precisely when all $\lambda_j=1$, hence $B=I$ and $\Sigma=M$. Thus the unrestricted MLE is $(\bar X,M)$; under $H_0$ the maximizing mean remains $\bar X$ by step 2.1.

Substituting the unrestricted and null maxima into [F10], and using $R=nM$, yields $$-2\log\Lambda_n=n\{\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_0^{-1}M)+\log\det\Sigma_0-\log\det M-p\}.$$ Since $\det(\Sigma_0^{-1/2}M\Sigma_0^{-1/2})=\det M/\det\Sigma_0$, this is the asserted finite-sample identity.

Since $H_n=O_P(1)$ by [F8], $E_n=A_n-I_p=H_n/\sqrt n$ has Frobenius norm $\|E_n\|_F=O_P(n^{-1/2})$, where $\|B\|_F=(\sum_{i,j}B_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$. On an event whose probability tends to one, every eigenvalue $e_j$ of the symmetric $E_n$ has $|e_j|\le1/2$. Taylor's theorem on $[-1/2,1/2]$ gives $e-\log(1+e)=e^2/2+O(|e|^3)$ with a uniform finite remainder constant there. Hence the statistic in step 4.1 equals $$n\sum_{j=1}^p(e_j-\log(1+e_j))=\frac12\operatorname{tr}(H_n^2)+O_P(n\|E_n\|_F^3)=\frac12\operatorname{tr}(H_n^2)+o_P(1),$$ because $p$ is fixed and $n\|E_n\|_F^3=O_P(n^{-1/2})$.

The map $H\mapsto\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(H^2)$ is continuous, so [F8] and step 1.2 give convergence to $\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(H^2)$. For the stated independent entries this is $$\sum_{i=1}^p(H_{ii}/\sqrt2)^2+\sum_{1\le i<j\le p}H_{ij}^2,$$ a sum of $p+p(p-1)/2=p(p+1)/2$ independent squared standard normals, which has law $\chi^2_{p(p+1)/2}$ by [F9]. Step 5.1 and Slutsky [F8] prove the asserted limit. When $p=1$, the off-diagonal sum is empty and the same count gives one degree of freedom; $p$ is fixed throughout, and no finite-sample calibration follows from this limit.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and the sample model in [[def-multivariate-normal-sample-model-and-statistics]], with $n\ge2$, $p\ge1$, and $\Sigma\succ0$. Then
$$\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)\sim N_p(0,\Sigma),\qquad \bar X\perp S,\qquad (n-1)S\sim W_p(\Sigma,n-1).$$
If $n>p$, then $S$ is positive definite almost surely. The Wishart scale is $\Sigma$ and its degrees of freedom are $n-1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $p,m\ge1$ be integers and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $p\times p$ matrix, in the sense of [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. Give $\mathrm{Sym}_p$, the space of real symmetric $p\times p$ matrices, its Euclidean Borel sigma-algebra by identifying a matrix with its upper-triangular entries. The finite product measure $N_p(0,\Sigma)^{\otimes m}$ exists because each factor is a probability measure and hence sigma-finite. Define the **Wishart law** $W_p(\Sigma,m)$ as the pushforward of this product measure by the continuous map $(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^m z_jz_j^T$. Equivalently, it is the law of $\sum_{j=1}^m Z_jZ_j^T$ for independent $Z_j\sim N_p(0,\Sigma)$.

Here $\Sigma$ is the scale matrix and the positive integer $m$ is the degrees of freedom. This definition allows a singular Wishart law when $m<p$ or $\Sigma$ is singular; no Lebesgue density is included in the convention. The usual nonsingular density when $m\ge p$ is not needed below.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $m\ge p\ge1$, let $W\sim W_p(I_p,m)$, and let $Z\sim N_p(0,I_p)$ be independent of $W$. Then $W$ is positive definite almost surely and
$$\frac{m-p+1}{p}Z^TW^{-1}Z\sim F_{p,m-p+1}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a positive integer $k$, take the product probability law of an independent standard normal $G$ and an independent $Q_k\sim\chi_k^2$. The **Student t law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $t_k$, is the law of
$$T_k=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{G}{\sqrt{Q_k/k}},&Q_k>0,\\ 0,&Q_k\le0. \end{cases}$$
For positive integers $r,s$, take independent $Q_r\sim\chi_r^2$ and $Q_s\sim\chi_s^2$. The **Fisher F law with degrees $(r,s)$**, denoted $F_{r,s}$, is the law of
$$F_{r,s}=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Q_r/r}{Q_s/s},&Q_s>0,\\ 0,&Q_s\le0. \end{cases}$$
The displayed piecewise maps are defined on all of $\mathbb R^2$ and are Borel measurable: each quotient is continuous on its Borel positive-denominator region, and the value on the complementary Borel nonpositive-denominator region is constant. The positive-degree chi-square lemma proves that the denominators are positive almost surely, so these versions agree almost surely with the usual quotients. Zero degrees are excluded from both definitions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For an integer $k\ge1$, let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_k)$ have law $N_k(0,I_k)$, so its coordinates are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The **chi-square law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $\chi_k^2$, is the law of
$$
Q_k=\sum_{j=1}^k G_j^2=\|G\|^2.
$$
For $k=0$, define $\chi_0^2=\delta_0$, the point mass at zero. This zero-degree law records a rank-zero projection only; it is not used as a denominator in a Student or Fisher ratio. The multivariate-normal characteristic-function theorem makes the definition independent of the chosen realization of $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $k\ge1$, the law $\chi_k^2$ has density
$$
f_k(x)=c_k x^{k/2-1}e^{-x/2}\mathbf 1_{\{x>0\}},\qquad c_k=\frac{\sigma_{k-1}(S^{k-1})}{2(2\pi)^{k/2}}>0,
$$
where $\sigma_{k-1}$ is the polar surface measure on the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^k$. Consequently, $Q_k>0$ almost surely, and its cumulative distribution function is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Assume AC. Fix integers $n\ge2$ and $p\ge1$. Let $\mathcal S_{++}^p$ be the set of real symmetric $p\times p$ matrices $\Sigma$ such that $v^T\Sigma v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$. The iid multivariate-normal sampling experiment has data space $\mathcal X=(\mathbb R^p)^n$ with sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^p)^{\otimes n}$, parameter set $\Theta=\mathbb R^p\times\mathcal S_{++}^p$, and sampling law $P_{\mu,\Sigma}=N_p(\mu,\Sigma)^{\otimes n}$. The finite product is a probability measure by [[def-probability-measure]] and [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]. The coordinate projection $X_i$ is the complete vector observation for sampling unit $i$; its $p$ coordinates need not be independent.

For $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathcal X$, define
$$\bar x=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i,\qquad R(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)^T,\qquad S(x)=\frac{R(x)}{n-1},\qquad M(x)=\frac{R(x)}n.$$
The functions $x\mapsto\bar x$, $S(x)$, and $M(x)$ are continuous, hence Borel measurable under AC and [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]]; they are statistics in the experiment by [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. Here $S$ uses the $n-1$ covariance denominator, while $M$ is the $n$-denominator covariance candidate whose maximum-likelihood property is proved separately below.

This item instantiates the mathematical portion of the scientific model contract ([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]) as follows. One sampling and analysis unit is one complete observed vector $X_i$; index $i$ identifies the sampling unit and coordinate $a$ identifies a component within that vector. For fixed parameter label $\theta=(\mu,\Sigma)$, $\mu$ and $\Sigma$ are fixed, every $X_i$ is random, every component of each $X_i$ is observed, and there are no latent quantities, predictors, treatments, or randomization. The target population for this reference experiment is the abstract law $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$ of a vector-valued sampling unit, and the target parameter is $\theta$ itself; no separate scientific estimand or physical setting is asserted. The observation map records the complete vector tuple unchanged, and inference uses the joint product law, with no conditioning convention beyond that law. No topological support or empirical adequacy claim is needed; this is a mathematical reference model, not an assertion that observed scientific data follow it.

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric, with $n\ge1$, and let $\Delta_k$ be the determinant of its leading $k\times k$ principal submatrix. Then $A$ is positive definite if and only if

$$\Delta_k>0\qquad(1\le k\le n).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

derivations.claim: The statistic $T^2$ in the Statement is a random variable: by [F9], $\{S\succ0\}$ is Borel; on this set inversion is continuous, so the displayed quadratic form is Borel, and setting it to zero on the Borel complement preserves measurability. Let $Z=\sqrt n\,\Sigma^{-1/2}(\bar X-\mu_0)$. The positive root is invertible by [F7]; under the null, [F1] and [F3] therefore give $Z\sim N_p(0,I_p)$. Moreover, $Z$ and $W:=\Sigma^{-1/2}(n-1)S\Sigma^{-1/2}$ are independent: $\bar X$ and $S$ are independent by [F1], and the separate whitening maps are continuous, hence Borel, so [F8] preserves independence. The congruence in [F1] and [F2] gives $W\sim W_p(I_p,n-1)$; it is positive definite almost surely by [F1].

On the event $S\succ0$ (which has probability one by [F1]), substitute $S=\Sigma^{1/2}W\Sigma^{1/2}/(n-1)$ and $\bar X-\mu_0=\Sigma^{1/2}Z/\sqrt n$ into the definition. Cancelling the inverse congruence gives $$T^2=(n-1)Z^TW^{-1}Z.$$

Apply [F4] with $m=n-1\ge p$. It gives $\frac{n-p}{p}Z^TW^{-1}Z\sim F_{p,n-p}$. Multiplying the identity in step 2.1 by $(n-p)/(p(n-1))$ proves the asserted law. Since $S\succ0$ almost surely, the off-domain zero convention affects only a null event.

A **randomized test** is a randomized procedure with binary action space
whose action set is $\{0,1\}$, equipped with its full sigma-algebra
$2^{\{0,1\}}$ (the power set, which is a sigma-algebra by
[[def-sigma-algebra]]), where $1$ means reject and $0$ means do not reject
([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its **test function** is
$$\varphi(x)=K(x,\{1\}),\qquad x\in\mathcal X.$$
Since $K(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure and $\{0\},\{1\}$ partition the
action set, $K(x,\{0\})+K(x,\{1\})=1$. Thus $\varphi(x)\in[0,1]$ and
$1-\varphi(x)=K(x,\{0\})$ is the probability of not rejecting. Give $[0,1]$
the trace of the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,+\infty]$, namely
$\{C\cap[0,1]:C\in\mathcal B([0,+\infty])\}$. By
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], $x\mapsto K(x,\{1\})$ is
measurable; since it has range in $[0,1]$, its preimage of $C\cap[0,1]$ equals
its preimage of $C$ and is measurable for every such $C$. Hence $\varphi$ is a
measurable map in the preimage sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Its value is the
rejection probability after observing $x$.
The convention $1=\text{reject}$ is fixed here. No null or alternative
hypothesis is part of this definition.

parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a positive integer $k$, take the product probability law of an independent standard normal $G$ and an independent $Q_k\sim\chi_k^2$. The **Student t law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $t_k$, is the law of
$$T_k=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{G}{\sqrt{Q_k/k}},&Q_k>0,\\ 0,&Q_k\le0. \end{cases}$$
For positive integers $r,s$, take independent $Q_r\sim\chi_r^2$ and $Q_s\sim\chi_s^2$. The **Fisher F law with degrees $(r,s)$**, denoted $F_{r,s}$, is the law of
$$F_{r,s}=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Q_r/r}{Q_s/s},&Q_s>0,\\ 0,&Q_s\le0. \end{cases}$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $T:V\to V$ be self-adjoint on an $n$-dimensional real inner product space,
and list its eigenvalues in weakly decreasing order:

$$\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n.$$

Then for every $1\le k\le n$,

$$\lambda_k=\min_{\dim W=n-k+1}\ \max_{0\ne v\in W} R_T(v)=\max_{\dim U=k}\ \min_{0\ne v\in U} R_T(v).$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: For every unit vector $x$, [F3] and [F4] give $|x^{\mathsf T}Ex|\le\|x\|_2\|Ex\|_2\le\epsilon$. The top-eigenvalue Rayleigh characterization in [F2] therefore gives $\lambda_1(A+E)\le\lambda_1(A)+\epsilon$, while evaluating the perturbed Rayleigh quotient at $v$ gives $\lambda_1(A+E)\ge v^{\mathsf T}(A+E)v\ge\lambda_1(A)-\epsilon$. This proves the eigenvalue bound.

The minimum--maximum formula in [F2], with the $(p-1)$-dimensional subspace $v^\perp$, gives $\lambda_2(A+E)\le\max_{\|x\|_2=1,\ x\perp v}x^{\mathsf T}(A+E)x \le\lambda_2(A)+\epsilon$, since every such $x$ has $x^{\mathsf T}Ax\le\lambda_2(A)$. Step 1.1 gives $\lambda_1(A+E)\ge\lambda_1(A)-\epsilon$, hence $\lambda_1(A+E)-\lambda_2(A+E)\ge g-2\epsilon>0$; the perturbed leading eigenvalue is simple. Also $\lambda_1(A+E)-\lambda_2(A)\ge g-\epsilon>0$.

Let $P=I-vv^{\mathsf T}$, the orthogonal projection onto $v^\perp$, and write $\widetilde\lambda_1=\lambda_1(A+E)$. Projecting $(A+E)\widetilde v=\widetilde\lambda_1\widetilde v$ onto $v^\perp$ gives $(\widetilde\lambda_1 I-A|_{v^\perp})P\widetilde v=PE\widetilde v$. In an orthonormal eigenbasis of $A|_{v^\perp}$, every eigenvalue of $\widetilde\lambda_1 I-A|_{v^\perp}$ is at least $\widetilde\lambda_1-\lambda_2(A)\ge g-\epsilon$ by step 2.1. Therefore $(g-\epsilon)\|P\widetilde v\|_2\le\|PE\widetilde v\|_2\le\epsilon$. Indeed, $z=Pz+(I-P)z$ is an orthogonal decomposition, so $\|Pz\|_2\le\|z\|_2$; then [F3] and $\|\widetilde v\|_2=1$ give the final inequality. Since $\|P\widetilde v\|_2^2=1-(v^{\mathsf T}\widetilde v)^2$, division by $g-\epsilon>0$ proves the angle bound.
