Fix a finite DAG $G=(V,E)$ and a specified topological ordering
$v_1,\ldots,v_n$ (every arrow points from an earlier to a later vertex).
Partition $V=O\sqcup H$ into **observed** vertices $O$ and **latent** vertices
$H$. For each $v\in V$, specify a measurable state space $(S_v,\mathcal
S_v)$, a measurable exogenous space $(E_v,\mathcal E_v)$, a jointly
measurable structural function
$$f_v:\prod_{u\in\operatorname{pa}(v)}S_u\times E_v\to S_v,$$
and an exogenous random element $U_v$ with values in $E_v$. Here
$\operatorname{pa}(v)=\{u:(u,v)\in E\}$; the empty product is a singleton.
The model is **Markovian** when the finite family $(U_v)_{v\in V}$ is mutually
independent. No parametric form or distributional truth is asserted. Correlated
disturbances may be represented by adding their common causes as latent
vertices, after which the exogenous family in the expanded model is required
to be mutually independent.

Recursion in the topological order defines the endogenous random elements
uniquely by $X_v=f_v(X_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},U_v)$. The full-joint law is the
law of $(X_v)_{v\in V}$; the observed law is its marginal law on $O$. An
observed-only DAG factorization is asserted only when $H=\varnothing$ or when
an additional stated latent-variable condition proves it.

For $I\subseteq V$ and a value $a=(a_v)_{v\in I}\in\prod_{v\in I}S_v$,
**$do(X_I=a)$** means replace only the equations indexed by $I$ by the
constants $X_v=a_v$, leaving every other structural function and every
exogenous law unchanged. Recursion then defines counterfactual values
$X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$; the interventional law is their joint law. The
response map $(a,\omega)\mapsto X_w^a(\omega)$ is jointly measurable, by
induction through the finite topological order and joint measurability of each
$f_v$. This permits evaluation at a random treatment value, such as
$X_w^{M^a}$. When $I=\{A\}$, write $X_w^a$ for the response under
$do(A=a)$. If the factual treatment is $A$, then on $\{A=a\}$ recursion
gives $X_w=X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$.

Let a finite Markovian recursive SCM be as in
[[def-recursive-structural-causal-model-and-dag]], with topological order
$v_1,\ldots,v_n$. For each $v$, let $\nu_v$ be the law of $U_v$ and define
$$K_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},B) :=\nu_v\{u:f_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},u)\in B\},\qquad B\in\mathcal S_v.$$
Then $K_v$ is a probability kernel from the parent-coordinate product to
$(S_v,\mathcal S_v)$. If $n=0$, the full-joint law (and the only possible
interventional law) is the point mass on the empty-product singleton. For
$n\ge1$, the full-joint law is the iterated topological composition
$$\mu(dx_{v_1},\ldots,dx_{v_n}) :=K_{v_1}(dx_{v_1})\prod_{r=2}^n K_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)},dx_{v_r}).$$
For $n\ge1$ and an intervention $do(X_I=a)$, the same formula holds with the factor
$K_v$ replaced by the point mass $\delta_{a_v}$ for each $v\in I$; all other
factors are unchanged. Marginalizing latent coordinates means taking the
pushforward to $\prod_{v\in O}S_v$ and does not in general produce a
factorization on the observed-only induced graph.

Assume AC. Let $(X_v)_{v\in V}$ be random elements in measurable spaces
whose joint law is generated, in a topological order of the finite DAG $G$,
by probability kernels $K_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},dx_v)$. For pairwise
disjoint $A,B,C\subseteq V$, if $C$ d-separates $A$ and $B$ in $G$, then
$$\sigma(X_A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_B)\mid\sigma(X_C).$$
This is the global Markov implication. Its converse is the separate
faithfulness condition in [[def-faithfulness-of-a-dag-model]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

For $S\subseteq V$, its **ancestral set** is
$$\operatorname{An}_G(S):=\{v\in V:\text{there is a directed path from }v\text{ to some }s\in S\},$$
where paths of length zero are allowed, so $S\subseteq\operatorname{An}_G(S)$.
The induced directed subgraph on this set keeps exactly the arrows of $G$
whose two endpoints lie in $\operatorname{An}_G(S)$. Its **moral graph** is
the undirected simple graph obtained by replacing every arrow by an
undirected edge and joining every distinct pair of parents of a common child
by an undirected edge; loops and duplicate edges are discarded. This
undirected graph is the **ancestral moral graph** on $S$ and is denoted
$\operatorname{mor}_G(S)$.

For disjoint $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, $C$ d-separates $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ if and
only if deleting $C$ from $\operatorname{mor}_G(X\cup Y\cup C)$ leaves no
undirected path from $X$ to $Y$.

derivations.claim: Fix finitely many intervention values $F$. Build one finite graph $J$ with the factual ancestors of $T\cup C$ and, for each $t\in F$, the equation ancestors needed for $X_W^t$ after replacing every $T$-input by its constant $t$. Omit those constant treatment nodes from the response graph. Share every nondescendant of $T$ across the factual and response systems; copy every remaining nonintervened response vertex separately for each $t$. Sharing is legitimate because nondescendants have no treatment ancestor and hence their equations and values are unchanged by intervention, by topological induction. Add one root $U_v$ per used original equation, shared by all copies of that equation. Every endogenous graph vertex uses its original structural function, with constants substituted for treatment parents in the response system, so deterministic point-mass kernels together with the independent root laws give a topological kernel factorization of the joint factual/response law by [F1]. The graph is acyclic: roots come first and each endogenous copy follows its original topological rank. Restrict to ancestors in $J$ of factual $T,C$ and response $W$; this retains the same endpoint law.

Write $G'=G_{\underline T}$ and $H=\operatorname{An}_{G'}(T\cup W\cup C)$. Every nonroot vertex retained in $J$ projects to an original vertex in $H$. For a response ancestor, its directed route to $W$ has no treatment vertex, because treatment inputs were constants. For a factual ancestor of $C$, its route has no treatment vertex by the nondescendant hypothesis. For a factual ancestor of $T$, truncate its directed route at the first treatment vertex: this has no outgoing treatment arrow. Each of these gives ancestry in $G'$. Moreover, if a factual retained vertex $v\notin T$ is a descendant of $T$, it cannot be an ancestor of $C$, so there is a directed route from $v$ to a treatment vertex, truncated at its first treatment occurrence. This route lies in $G'$ and avoids $C$, since every vertex on it is a descendant of $T$. Hence $v$ is in a connected component meeting $T$ in the moral graph on $H$ with $C$ deleted.

By the backdoor hypothesis and [F5], no component of that original moral graph meets both $T$ and $W$. Assign each nonroot vertex of $J$ outside $C$ to the component of its projected original vertex. All parent-child and parent-parent moral edges of $J$ outside $C$ preserve the two sides, as follows. A response family has no treatment parent, so its projected nonroot family is a clique already present in the moral graph of $G'[H]$. A factual family without a treatment parent is likewise such a clique. If a factual family has a treatment parent, its child is a factual descendant of $T$ retained as an ancestor of $T$, hence is in a component meeting $T$ by step 2.1. Every nonconditioned nontreatment parent is joined to that child by an arrow retained in $G'$; every treatment parent is itself in a component meeting $T$. These family vertices therefore all lie on the treatment side (although the treatment components need not be the same). This exhausts skeleton edges and moral edges between nonroot vertices.

Assign a root $U_v$ with $v\notin C$ to the side of its projected child $v$: all copies of $v$ have that same projection. Its moral neighbors are its equation children and their other parents, and the family analysis in step 3.1 puts every neighbor outside $C$ on the same side. If $v\in C$, the child is a single shared nondescendant node, not copied, and has no treatment parent. Its nonconditioned original parents form a clique in $G'[H]$. Assign $U_v$ to their common component side when there are any such parents, and arbitrarily otherwise; after $C$ is deleted it has no neighbor on the opposite side. There are no root-root moral edges, since each equation uses one exogenous root. Let the left side consist of the components meeting $T$ and roots assigned to that side, and let the right side be everything else outside $C$. Thus deleting $C$ from the full moral graph of the retained graph $J$ leaves no edge between the sides. Factual $T$ is on the left and every response $W$ is on the right. In particular no ancestral moral path connects these endpoint sets, and [F5] gives their d-separation in $J$. By its kernel factorization and [F2], $X_T$ is conditionally independent of the finite vector $(X_w^t)_{w\in W,t\in F}$ given $X_C$. This argument handles shared roots and shared nondescendants through moral families and does not assume that a projected copied path preserves collider status.

Fix a bounded nonnegative measurable $f(X_T)$. Response events depending on finitely many coordinates form a pi-system generating $\mathcal R_W^T$. Step 4.1 gives the conditional-product identity for their indicators. The response events for which it holds form a lambda-system: complements subtract the identity for the whole space, and disjoint countable unions follow by summing conditional-expectation versions for the pieces and testing the increasing partial sums over events in $\sigma(X_C)$; ordinary monotone convergence gives a version for the union. Dynkin's theorem [F4] gives the identity for every response event. Simple approximation and monotone convergence extend it to all bounded nonnegative response-measurable functions. Decompose bounded real functions into positive and negative parts to obtain all bounded functions on both sides, hence the claimed independence by [F3]. This cylinder argument applies to any cardinality of the intervention-value set, with no common null set chosen across that set. The fixed-value conclusion is a restriction to one response coordinate vector.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement requires T, W, and C to be pairwise disjoint, as required for d-separation. If T is empty, X_T is the singleton-valued empty vector and sigma(X_T) is trivial; if W is empty, the response-family sigma-algebra is trivial. In either case the bounded-function conditional-product criterion used in step 5.1 holds automatically because the trivial side is constant.
The Statement makes no treatment-positivity assumption. Steps 1.1 and 4.1 permit any supplied intervention value, including a zero value in the treatment state space, by constant substitution.
Step 1.1 permits a finite intervention-value collection F with one member; step 4.1 then gives the fixed-response conditional independence, and step 5.1 states the fixed-value restriction.

Step 4.1 invokes the AC-backed global Markov supplier [F2], and step 5.1 uses conditional-expectation versions and their conditional-product meaning [F3]. Assume AC and a finite Markovian recursive SCM on $G$. Let $T,W,C$ be pairwise
disjoint vertex sets, with every vertex of $C$ a nondescendant of $T$. Define the
response-family sigma-algebra
$$\mathcal R_W^T:=\sigma\{X_w^t:w\in W,\ t\in\prod_{v\in T}S_v\}.$$
If $C$ d-separates $T$ and $W$ in $G_{\underline T}$, then
$$\sigma(X_T)\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal R_W^T\mid\sigma(X_C).$$
For each fixed intervention value $t$, this implies
$X_W^t\perp\!\!\!\perp X_T\mid\sigma(X_C)$. No treatment-positivity
condition is needed.

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

Fix a finite DAG $G=(V,E)$ and a specified topological ordering
$v_1,\ldots,v_n$ (every arrow points from an earlier to a later vertex).
Partition $V=O\sqcup H$ into **observed** vertices $O$ and **latent** vertices
$H$. For each $v\in V$, specify a measurable state space $(S_v,\mathcal
S_v)$, a measurable exogenous space $(E_v,\mathcal E_v)$, a jointly
measurable structural function
$$f_v:\prod_{u\in\operatorname{pa}(v)}S_u\times E_v\to S_v,$$
and an exogenous random element $U_v$ with values in $E_v$. Here
$\operatorname{pa}(v)=\{u:(u,v)\in E\}$; the empty product is a singleton.
The model is **Markovian** when the finite family $(U_v)_{v\in V}$ is mutually
independent. No parametric form or distributional truth is asserted. Correlated
disturbances may be represented by adding their common causes as latent

Recursion in the topological order defines the endogenous random elements
uniquely by $X_v=f_v(X_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},U_v)$. The full-joint law is the
law of $(X_v)_{v\in V}$; the observed law is its marginal law on $O$. An
observed-only DAG factorization is asserted only when $H=\varnothing$ or when
an additional stated latent-variable condition proves it.

For $I\subseteq V$ and a value $a=(a_v)_{v\in I}\in\prod_{v\in I}S_v$,
**$do(X_I=a)$** means replace only the equations indexed by $I$ by the
constants $X_v=a_v$, leaving every other structural function and every
exogenous law unchanged. Recursion then defines counterfactual values

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ be an estimand, and set
$\mathcal M:=\mathsf P(\Theta)$, the set of laws in the model. For
$\theta\in\Theta$, write
$$
[\theta]_\sim:=\{\eta\in\Theta:\eta\sim\theta\}.
$$
Then the following are equivalent: **(i)** $\psi$ is identifiable; **(ii)**
$\psi$ is constant on every observational equivalence class $[\theta]_\sim$;
and **(iii)** there is a unique function $\bar\psi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal T_0$
such that $\psi=\bar\psi\circ\mathsf P$.

The factorization is a statement about sets and functions. It asserts no
measurable structure or measurable factor map.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $Y^a$ and $A$ are conditionally independent given $L$. By [F2] take regular conditional laws of $Y^a$ given $L$ and given $(A,L)$. The conditional-independence identity implies that, for $P_{A,L}$-almost every $(a',l)$, the latter law equals the former law at $l$. Since $a$ is an atom with $e_a(l)>0$ for $P_L$-almost every $l$, the measure $P_{L\mid A=a}$ is equivalent to $P_L$: its density with respect to $P_L$ is $e_a(l)/P(A=a)$, which is positive and integrates to one. Hence the conditional-law equality at $A=a$ holds for $P_L$-almost every $l$.

On the event $A=a$, the factual structural recursion and the recursion with the $A$ equation replaced by $a$ agree at $A$. Induction down the fixed topological order shows that they agree at every descendant, in particular $Y=Y^a$. Therefore the conditional law of $Y^a$ given $A=a,L=l$ equals that of $Y$ given $A=a,L=l$ for $P_L$-almost every $l$. Combining with step 1.1 identifies the conditional law of $Y^a$ given $L=l$ with the observed conditional law in the formula.

Disintegrating the joint law of $(Y^a,L)$ by [F2] gives $P(Y^a\in B)=\int P(Y^a\in B\mid L=l)P_L(dl)$. Substitute the equality from step 2.1 to obtain the displayed formula. If two SCM parameter values induce the same observed law, the integrand kernel and $P_L$ agree outside their common null sets; positivity makes those sets null for the target integral. Hence the right side, and so the estimand, is constant on each observational-equivalence class by [F4]. The real-valued expectation formula follows by applying the distribution identity to bounded truncations of $Y$ and using integrability to pass to the limit.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement allows L to be the empty finite covariate tuple. Then sigma(L) is trivial, step 1.1 is marginal exchangeability, and the integral in step 3.1 is over a singleton.

Step 3.1 includes a real integrable zero outcome in its mean corollary; the identified integral and intervention mean are both zero. A zero target propensity is excluded by the Statement, not admitted as a cancellation case.
Step 3.1 permits a one-point covariate law: the adjustment integral is a single conditional law. If treatment is constant at its target atom, its propensity is one and step 1.1 remains valid.
The standard-Borel outcome law in steps 1.1 and 3.1 may be a point mass. Positive propensity and the assumed graph separation, not outcome nondegeneracy or faithfulness, are required.

The Statement requires distinct A and Y and a covariate vertex set disjoint from both endpoints, so the d-separation condition is well-formed. It also restricts the pointwise result to a positive-probability treatment atom with positive propensity almost surely. Step 1.1 uses positivity to transfer conditional-law equality to P_L; continuous-treatment formulas receive only the explicit almost-everywhere qualification in the Statement.

The Statement assumes AC for the regular conditional laws. Step 1.1 invokes the standard-Borel conditional-law suppliers [F2], and step 3.1 uses their disintegration identity; finite consistency recursion in step 2.1 needs no additional choice.

boundaries.reason: The backdoor theorem supplies sufficient graph and propensity hypotheses for an identified intervention law. It does not claim that every identified effect must have a backdoor adjustment set.
No implication from equality of an adjustment functional or identifiability back to the backdoor graph criterion is asserted; the stated theorem is sufficiency only.

citations.quote:
Fix a finite DAG $G=(V,E)$ and a specified topological ordering
$v_1,\ldots,v_n$ (every arrow points from an earlier to a later vertex).
Partition $V=O\sqcup H$ into **observed** vertices $O$ and **latent** vertices
$H$. For each $v\in V$, specify a measurable state space $(S_v,\mathcal
S_v)$, a measurable exogenous space $(E_v,\mathcal E_v)$, a jointly
measurable structural function
$$f_v:\prod_{u\in\operatorname{pa}(v)}S_u\times E_v\to S_v,$$
and an exogenous random element $U_v$ with values in $E_v$. Here
$\operatorname{pa}(v)=\{u:(u,v)\in E\}$; the empty product is a singleton.
The model is **Markovian** when the finite family $(U_v)_{v\in V}$ is mutually
independent. No parametric form or distributional truth is asserted. Correlated
disturbances may be represented by adding their common causes as latent
vertices, after which the exogenous family in the expanded model is required
to be mutually independent.

Recursion in the topological order defines the endogenous random elements
uniquely by $X_v=f_v(X_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},U_v)$. The full-joint law is the
law of $(X_v)_{v\in V}$; the observed law is its marginal law on $O$. An
observed-only DAG factorization is asserted only when $H=\varnothing$ or when
an additional stated latent-variable condition proves it.

For $I\subseteq V$ and a value $a=(a_v)_{v\in I}\in\prod_{v\in I}S_v$,
**$do(X_I=a)$** means replace only the equations indexed by $I$ by the
constants $X_v=a_v$, leaving every other structural function and every
exogenous law unchanged. Recursion then defines counterfactual values
$X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$; the interventional law is their joint law. The
response map $(a,\omega)\mapsto X_w^a(\omega)$ is jointly measurable, by
induction through the finite topological order and joint measurability of each
$f_v$. This permits evaluation at a random treatment value, such as
$X_w^{M^a}$. When $I=\{A\}$, write $X_w^a$ for the response under
$do(A=a)$. If the factual treatment is $A$, then on $\{A=a\}$ recursion
gives $X_w=X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$.

Let a finite Markovian recursive SCM be as in
[[def-recursive-structural-causal-model-and-dag]], with topological order
$v_1,\ldots,v_n$. For each $v$, let $\nu_v$ be the law of $U_v$ and define
$$K_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},B) :=\nu_v\{u:f_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},u)\in B\},\qquad B\in\mathcal S_v.$$
Then $K_v$ is a probability kernel from the parent-coordinate product to
$(S_v,\mathcal S_v)$. If $n=0$, the full-joint law (and the only possible
interventional law) is the point mass on the empty-product singleton. For
$n\ge1$, the full-joint law is the iterated topological composition
$$\mu(dx_{v_1},\ldots,dx_{v_n}) :=K_{v_1}(dx_{v_1})\prod_{r=2}^n K_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)},dx_{v_r}).$$
For $n\ge1$ and an intervention $do(X_I=a)$, the same formula holds with the factor
$K_v$ replaced by the point mass $\delta_{a_v}$ for each $v\in I$; all other
factors are unchanged. Marginalizing latent coordinates means taking the
pushforward to $\prod_{v\in O}S_v$ and does not in general produce a
factorization on the observed-only induced graph.

Assume AC. Let $(X_v)_{v\in V}$ be random elements in measurable spaces
whose joint law is generated, in a topological order of the finite DAG $G$,
by probability kernels $K_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},dx_v)$. For pairwise
disjoint $A,B,C\subseteq V$, if $C$ d-separates $A$ and $B$ in $G$, then
$$\sigma(X_A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_B)\mid\sigma(X_C).$$
This is the global Markov implication. Its converse is the separate
faithfulness condition in [[def-faithfulness-of-a-dag-model]].

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Let $I_A=\operatorname{An}_G(A)$, including $A$. By recursive substitution, $A$ is measurable with respect to $U_{I_A}$; under $do(A=a)$, the equation at $A$ is replaced, so $M^a$ is measurable with respect to $U_{I_M}$. Under $do(M=m)$, the equation at $M$ is replaced, so $Y^m$ is measurable with respect to $U_{I_Y}$. These claims follow by induction in the finite topological order: an endogenous value depends only on the exogenous coordinates at vertices with directed paths to it in the relevant mutilated graph.

Suppose $v\in I_M\cap I_A$. Since $v\ne A$, there are directed paths $v\to\cdots\to A$ in $G$ and $v\to\cdots\to M$ in $G_{\overline A}$; the latter avoids $A$. Take the last common vertex $w$ of these paths in a topological ordering. Their suffixes are disjoint, so they form a simple fork path $A\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow w\to\cdots\to M$ with no internal collider. It is retained in $G_{\underline A}$, because the path uses no arrow out of its endpoint $A$, and is active given the empty set. This contradicts (ii), so $I_M\cap I_A=\varnothing$.

Suppose $v\in I_M\cap I_Y$. There are directed paths $v\to\cdots\to M$ in $G_{\overline A}$ and $v\to\cdots\to Y$ in $G_{\overline M}$. The first path avoids $A$. The second avoids $M$; it also avoids $A$, since otherwise its segment $A\to\cdots\to Y$ would be a directed $A$-to-$Y$ path avoiding $M$, contrary to (i). Take the last common vertex $w$ of the paths. Their suffixes form a simple fork path $M\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow w\to\cdots\to Y$ with no internal collider and no internal $A$. It lies in $G_{\underline M}$ and is active given $\{A\}$, contradicting (iii). Thus $I_M\cap I_Y=\varnothing$.

Fix $v\in I_Y$. There is a directed path $q$ from $v$ to $Y$ in $G_{\overline M}$. It avoids $M$ by definition and avoids $A$, because an occurrence of $A$ would leave a directed $A$-to-$Y$ suffix avoiding $M$, contrary to (i). Thus $q$ is retained in $G_{\underline M}$. If an active path $p$ from $M$ to $v$ given $\{A\}$ existed there, choose the last vertex $w$ of $p$ that also lies on $q$ when $q$ is traversed from $v$ to $Y$. Keep the prefix of $p$ from $M$ to $w$ and append the directed suffix of $q$ from $w$ to $Y$. The suffix after $w$ is disjoint from the prefix by the choice of $w$, so this is a path. Its old internal vertices remain active; $w\notin A$ and the outgoing directed edge makes it a noncollider; all new internal vertices are noncolliders outside $A$. This would be an active path from $M$ to $Y$ given $A$, contradicting (iii). Hence $A$ d-separates $M$ and $v$ in $G_{\underline M}$. In the expanded graph each added root has only one skeleton neighbor, its own equation vertex, so a simple path cannot contain a root internally. An active path ending at $U_v$ would therefore have penultimate vertex $v$; deleting its last edge leaves an active path from $M$ to $v$ (or $v=M$). The latter case is excluded by $M\notin I_Y$, and the former was just excluded. Adding roots does not create new directed descendants of endogenous vertices, so the remaining collider-activity tests are unchanged. Thus $A$ also d-separates $M$ and the whole root set $U_{I_Y}$ in the expanded graph with arrows out of $M$ deleted.
By [F3], the disjoint exogenous vectors $U_{I_M}$ and $U_{I_A}$ are independent. Step 1.1 makes $M^a$ and factual $A$ measurable functions of these respective vectors, so $M^a\perp A$.

The finite vectors $U_{I_M}$ and $U_{I_Y}$ are independent by [F3]. By step 1.1, $M^a$ and the response family $(Y^m)_{m\in S_M}$ are measurable functions of these disjoint vectors; in particular $M^a\perp U_{I_Y}$.

Adjoin all exogenous coordinates as independent root vertices. In the factual law, no strict descendant of $M$ is an ancestor of $(M,A,U_{I_Y})$: it cannot be an ancestor of an exogenous root, and if it were an ancestor of $A$, the directed path from $M$ to $A$ would remain in $G_{\underline A}$ and contradict (ii). Reverse-topological integration therefore marginalizes all other vertices and leaves the joint law of $(M,A,U_{I_Y})$ factored on its ancestral subgraph, which has no outgoing edge from $M$. This is a subgraph of the expanded mutilated graph in step 1.4, so the separation there still holds. The global Markov implication [F2], interpreted by the conditional-independence definition [F4], gives $M\perp U_{I_Y}\mid A$.

In $G_{\overline M}$ there is no directed path from $A$ to $Y$, since every directed $A$-to-$Y$ path in $G$ contains $M$ and arrows into $M$ were deleted. With $M$ fixed, changing the equation at $A$ therefore cannot change $Y$ by recursive substitution: any directed route by which $A$ could affect $Y$ would have to reach the fixed node $M$. Under $do(A=a)$, the mediator equals $M^a$. Replacing the mediator equation by that same realized value leaves every other equation unchanged; the no-directed-path argument shows that leaving $A$ factual has no further effect on $Y$. Thus $Y^a=Y^{M^a}$.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement requires pairwise distinct observed vertices A, M, and Y, as required for its d-separation conditions. It permits any number of latent vertices, including none; steps 1.1 and 2.3 use the full finite observed/latent DAG regardless of the latent count.

boundaries.reason: The frontdoor helper has no real numerical parameter fixed to zero. Its supplied intervention values are arbitrary members of S_A and S_M, and zero is allowed only when it belongs to such a state space.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 and the Statement allow singleton treatment or mediator state spaces; structural substitution and the kernel independence proof in step 2.3 remain valid for constant variables.
Steps 2.1 and 2.2 use independence of finite exogenous coordinate sets, and step 2.3 uses arbitrary probability kernels, so point-mass disturbances and deterministic response maps are allowed.

boundaries.reason: The helper proves identities for supplied intervention values in arbitrary state spaces; it makes no pointwise conditional-regression assertion at a null treatment endpoint.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement assumes AC for the conditional-independence interface [F4]. Step 2.3 invokes the AC-backed global Markov implication [F2] to obtain M independent of U_{I_Y} given A, interpreted through [F4]. Steps 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 use finite recursive substitution and finite path operations without additional arbitrary-index choice.

boundaries.reason: The three frontdoor graph conditions imply the listed response/exogenous-coordinate identities. This helper does not assert those graph conditions are necessary for every model having these identities.

Neither the response composition identity nor conditional independence is used to reconstruct graph separation in this helper; such a converse would require additional structural restrictions not claimed.

risk_review.notes: All eight steps and eight direct suppliers checked. Fork witnesses prove I_M is disjoint from I_A and I_Y; directed paths to Y after fixing M avoid A by condition (i). In step 1.4 the last intersection in the directed q order gives a simple active splice; root leaves introduce no internal shortcuts. Pruning the factual expanded graph is legitimate because M has no descendant ancestor of A (condition ii), or of any exogenous root. Hence the actual factual marginal factors on a subgraph with no outgoing M edge, proving M independent of U_IY given A. Finite exogenous-vector independence proves both unconditional independences. Joint structural measurability and no A-to-Y path after fixing M justify the realized-value composition Y^a=Y^{M^a}, including non-atomic mediators, without diagonal substitution into an a.e. identity. Reader pairwise distinctness makes all three graph conditions well-formed. Current raw hash equals post-reader hash. Accept repair; confidence 1.

citations.quote:
Assume AC and a finite Markovian recursive SCM on a full DAG with pairwise
distinct observed vertices $A,M,Y$ and any number of latent vertices.
Suppose: (i) every
directed path from $A$ to $Y$ contains $M$; (ii) $A$ and $M$ are
d-separated by the empty set in $G_{\underline A}$; and (iii) $A$
d-separates $M$ and $Y$ in $G_{\underline M}$. For each supplied value
$a\in S_A$, let $M^a$ be the response under $do(A=a)$. Define
$$I_M=\operatorname{An}_{G_{\overline A}}(M)\setminus\{A\},\qquad I_Y=\operatorname{An}_{G_{\overline M}}(Y)\setminus\{M\},$$
where ancestry includes the vertex itself and $U_I$ is the finite vector of
exogenous coordinates $(U_v)_{v\in I}$. Then $M^a$ is measurable with
respect to $\sigma(U_{I_M})$, each response $Y^m$ is measurable with
respect to $\sigma(U_{I_Y})$, and
$$M^a\perp\!\!\!\perp A,\qquad I_M\cap I_Y=\varnothing,\qquad M^a\perp\!\!\!\perp U_{I_Y},\qquad M\perp\!\!\!\perp U_{I_Y}\mid A.$$
The recursive responses also satisfy $Y^a=Y^{M^a}$ almost surely. The
conditional independence is for the factual law; it supplies a genuine
conditional product law for the exogenous coordinates used by the outcome
response.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

Assume AC. Let X,Y take values in standard-Borel E,T, and let K be a disintegration kernel giving the conditional law of X given Y. For measurable $f:E\to[0,\infty]$, put $h(y)=\int_E f(x)K(y,dx)$. Then h is measurable and
$$E[f(X)\mid\sigma(Y)]=h(Y)\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

For measurable real f with $E|f(X)|<\infty$, define $D=\{y:\int|f(x)|K(y,dx)<\infty\}$ and use the signed integral for h on D, zero off D. Then $P_Y(D)=1$, h is real measurable, and the same identity holds.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ be an estimand, and set
$\mathcal M:=\mathsf P(\Theta)$, the set of laws in the model. For
$\theta\in\Theta$, write
$$

common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

A **finite directed acyclic graph** (DAG) is a finite vertex set $V$ with an
arrow set $E\subseteq V\times V$ and no directed cycle. A **path** from $u$ to
$v$ is a finite sequence of distinct vertices beginning at $u$ and ending at
$v$ in which each consecutive pair is joined by an arrow in either direction;
the arrows are not required to point along the sequence. An internal vertex of
a path is a **collider on that path** when the two arrows on the path both point
into it, and is a **noncollider** otherwise. A vertex $w$ is a **descendant** of
$v$ if there is a directed path from $v$ to $w$; for this definition
$\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ includes $v$ itself as well as its descendants.

For pairwise disjoint vertex sets $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, a path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is **active given $C$** when every internal noncollider is outside $C$ and
every internal collider has at least one member of $\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ in
$C$. The set $C$ **d-separates** $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ when no path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is active given $C$; write $X\perp_d Y\mid C$ in $G$. The empty set of
vertices is allowed for any of $X,Y,C$; in particular d-separation is vacuous
if either endpoint set is empty.

For $T\subseteq V$, $G_{\underline T}$ is obtained by deleting every arrow
whose tail lies in $T$, and $G_{\overline T}$ by deleting every arrow whose
head lies in $T$. These are graph operations only; they do not by themselves
specify a probability law under intervention.

independent. No parametric form or distributional truth is asserted. Correlated
disturbances may be represented by adding their common causes as latent
vertices, after which the exogenous family in the expanded model is required
to be mutually independent.

derivations.claim: In the confounding model, $P(A=1)=P(U=0,E=1)+P(U=1,E=0)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac14+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac34=\tfrac12$. Thus $P(Y=1\mid A=1)=3/4$ and $P(Y=1\mid A=0)=1/4$, although under $do(A=a)$ the variable $Y=U$ remains Bernoulli$(1/2)$. The difference between the observational conditionals and the intervention law is caused by the open backdoor path through $U$; conditioning on $U$ blocks that path and the adjusted mean is $\sum_{u\in\{0,1\}}P(Y=1\mid A=a,U=u)P(U=u)=1/2$.

For the collider model, $P(B=1,C=1)=1/4=P(B=1)P(C=1)$ by [F1], so the variables are independent before conditioning. But $D=1$ on exactly the three equiprobable pairs $(1,1),(1,0),(0,1)$. For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

If $M=1$, then $Y=1$. If $M=0$, then $Y=U$, so $E(Y\mid M=0,A=1)=3/4$ and $E(Y\mid M=0,A=0)=1/4$. Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Set $I=\mathbf 1_{\{A\in C\}}$, $e=E[I\mid\mathcal G]$, and $U=E[Z\mid\mathcal G]$. These conditional-expectation classes exist under AC, and $0\le e\le1$ almost surely by positivity and preservation of constants.

For each integer $n\ge1$, put $Z_n=\max(-n,\min(Z,n))$. The functions $z\mapsto\max(-n,\min(z,n))$ are bounded and measurable, so [F1] applied to $1_C(A)$ and this truncation of $Z$ gives $E[IZ_n\mid\mathcal G]=eE[Z_n\mid\mathcal G]$.

By [F4], $Z_n\to Z$ in $L^1$. Since $|I|\le1$, $IZ_n\to IZ$ in $L^1$; [F3] then gives $E[IZ_n\mid\mathcal G]\to E[IZ\mid\mathcal G]$ in $L^1$ and $eE[Z_n\mid\mathcal G]\to eU$ in $L^1$, using $0\le e\le1$.
The two sides of step 2.1 are equal for every $n$ and converge in $L^1$ to the two sides claimed in the Statement. Uniqueness of limits in $L^1$ gives $E[IZ\mid\mathcal G]=eU$ almost surely.

Step 2.1 remains valid when e=1; the L1 limit in step 3.1 gives the stated factorization.
Step 3.1 includes Z=0 and other integrable degenerate inputs because the L1 limits remain valid.
Steps 2.1 and 3.1 include C empty or the whole treatment state space.

Fix a target population with probability law $P$, a real outcome, and a nonempty countable discrete set $\mathcal A$ of treatment versions. A treatment version $a\in\mathcal A$ is a specified intervention protocol, not just a treatment label. The **potential outcome** $Y^a$ is the real random variable giving the outcome for a unit in the target population under version $a$. Write $A$ for the observed treatment assignment or receipt, with values in $\mathcal A$, and $Y$ for the observed outcome. The **observed potential outcome** is the measurable random variable

$$Y^A=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}\mathbf 1_{\{A=a\}}Y^a,$$

where the countable sum has at most one nonzero summand at each sample point. **Consistency** is the assumption $Y=Y^A$ $P$-almost surely. It links the observed outcome to the potential outcome for the received version; it does not assert that treatment assignment is unconfounded.

The **full-data law** is the joint law of the potential-outcome family, $A$, any baseline covariate random element $L$, and $Y$. The **observed-data law** is its marginal law of $(A,L,Y)$. A target population, outcome, intervention protocol, and contrast must be fixed before the associated causal target is specified. If interference between units matters, the version or treatment regime must include the relevant assignment or exposure of other units; the notation $Y^a$ by itself does not assert no interference.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $Q$ be a probability law for an observed discrete or atomic treatment $A$, a covariate random element $L$, and a real-valued observed outcome $Y$. Fix an atom $a$ with $Q(A=a)>0$, let $\mathcal G=\sigma(L)$, and define
$$I_a=\mathbf 1_{\{A=a\}},\qquad e_a(L)=E_Q[I_a\mid\mathcal G].$$
Assume $e_a(L)>0$ $Q$-almost surely and $I_aY\in L^1(Q)$. Define
$$q_a(L)=E_Q[I_aY\mid\mathcal G],\qquad m_a(L)=\frac{q_a(L)}{e_a(L)}.$$
The **standardization functional** at $a$ is
$$\Psi_{\mathrm{std}}(Q;a)=E_Q[m_a(L)],$$
provided $m_a(L)$ is integrable. The numerator and denominator are conditional-expectation classes; the ratio is defined almost surely because the denominator is positive. In conventional notation $m_a(L)$ is $E_Q[Y\mid A=a,L]$, and the displayed expectation averages that treatment-specific conditional mean over the target law of $L$.

When $L$ has discrete support, this is $\sum_\ell E_Q[Y\mid A=a,L=\ell]\,Q(L=\ell)$. For general $L$ we use the version-free conditional-expectation class above and integrate it under $Q$; no value of a regression function is chosen at a null covariate stratum.

This is a population functional of the observed law and the true conditional treatment probability. It is not an algorithm for estimating a propensity from a finite sample.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC) for the conditional-expectation existence convention used here. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sub-$\sigma$-algebra, let $A$ be a random element, and let $C$ be a measurable set in its state space. If $Z$ is a real integrable random variable and $Z\perp\!\!\!\perp A\mid\mathcal G$, then, with $I=\mathbf 1_{\{A\in C\}}$,
$$E[IZ\mid\mathcal G]=E[I\mid\mathcal G]E[Z\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
The conclusion holds for every integrable $Z$, not only bounded outcomes.

Assume Choice. For random elements $Y,Z$ and a sigma-algebra $\mathcal G$,
the following are equivalent:

1. $Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$;
2. for every bounded measurable $g$,
   $$ \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G\vee\sigma(Y)] =\mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$

Conditional independence is preserved by measurable maps of either variable.
It is also preserved when a $\mathcal G$-measurable random element is adjoined
to either side.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.
If $Y,Z$ are conditional-expectation versions of the same real integrable $X$ given $\mathcal G$, then $Y=Z$ almost surely.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ be an estimand, and set
$\mathcal M:=\mathsf P(\Theta)$, the set of laws in the model. For
$\theta\in\Theta$, write
$$
[\theta]_\sim:=\{\eta\in\Theta:\eta\sim\theta\}.
$$
Then the following are equivalent: **(i)** $\psi$ is identifiable; **(ii)**
$\psi$ is constant on every observational equivalence class $[\theta]_\sim$;
and **(iii)** there is a unique function $\bar\psi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal T_0$
such that $\psi=\bar\psi\circ\mathsf P$.

The factorization is a statement about sets and functions. It asserts no
measurable structure or measurable factor map.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal A$ be a countable discrete set containing treatment versions $0$ and $1$. On a full-data probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, let $A$ take values in $\mathcal A$, let $L$ take values in a standard-Borel space $\mathcal L$ ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), let $Y$ be the observed real outcome, and let $(Y^b)_{b\in\mathcal A}$ be the potential outcomes of [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]. For each treatment value $a$ under consideration, assume $Y^a\in L^1(P)$, consistency $Y=Y^A$ almost surely, conditional exchangeability $\sigma(Y^b:b\in\mathcal A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(A)\mid\sigma(L)$, and positivity $P(A=a)>0$ and $E[\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}\mid\sigma(L)]>0$ almost surely. These are assumptions on the full-data law; Choice is required for the stated conditional-expectation classes and regular conditional distributions.

Write $P_L(B)=P(L\in B)$ for the target-population law of $L$. For such an $a$, define the treatment-stratum probability $P_a(C)=P(C\cap\{A=a\})/P(A=a)$ for $C\in\mathcal F$. Under $P_a$, let $K_a(l,dy)$ be a regular conditional law of $Y$ given the standard-Borel random element $L$, and put $m_a(l)=\int y\,K_a(l,dy)$ wherever the absolute integral is finite, with value $0$ on the exceptional set. The suppliers [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]], [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]], [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]], and [[thm-conditional-integration-through-a-regular-conditional-law]] give this construction. Then $m_a$ is $P_L$-integrable and is uniquely determined $P_L$-almost everywhere by the observed-data law, and

$$E_P[Y^a]=\int_{\mathcal L}m_a(l)\,P_L(dl).$$

If $L$ is countably discrete, this is

$$E_P[Y^a]=\sum_{l:P(L=l)>0}E_P[Y\mid A=a,L=l]P(L=l).$$

In this sum, $E[Y\mid A=a,L=l]$ denotes $E[Y\mathbf1_{\{A=a,L=l\}}]/P(A=a,L=l)$, whose denominator is positive for each displayed atom.

For the binary contrast, both treatment levels must satisfy positivity. The CATE is then represented $P_L$-almost everywhere by $m_1-m_0$, and the ATE is $\int(m_1-m_0)\,dP_L$. In the model whose parameters are all full-data laws satisfying these assumptions and whose observation map sends a full-data law to its $(A,L,Y)$ marginal, each $E[Y^a]$ is identifiable in the sense of [[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]]: it is constant over full-data laws with the same observed-data law.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $P$ in the stated model class, let $I_a=\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}$, $e_a=E_P[I_a\mid\mathcal G]$, $\mu_a=E_P[Y^a\mid\mathcal G]$, and $q_a=E_P[I_aY\mid\mathcal G]$. By [F4] and [F10], $P(A=a)=E_P[I_a]=E_P[e_a]$. Global consistency, or the stated atom-consistency directly, gives $I_aY=I_aY^a$ almost surely, so $I_aY$ is integrable. By [F3], full-family exchangeability implies $Y^a\perp\!\!\!\perp A\mid\mathcal G$; in the general atom formulation this coordinate independence is assumed directly; [F2] then gives $q_a=E_P[I_aY^a\mid\mathcal G]=e_a\mu_a$.

Let $\lambda=P_L=Q_L$ be the common law of the covariate coordinate. Since $\mathcal G=\sigma(L)=\{L^{-1}(B):B\in\mathcal S\}$, each real $\mathcal G$-measurable version $V$ factors as $v(L)$: for each rational $r$ choose $B_r\in\mathcal S$ with $\{V<r\}=L^{-1}(B_r)$, and put $v(x)=\inf\{r\in\mathbb Q:x\in B_r\}$, replacing nonfinite values by $0$. Its rational sublevel sets make $v$ measurable, and $v(L)=V$. Apply this to the five conditional versions, writing $\widetilde e_a,\widetilde q_a$ for the $Q$-conditional classes in [F1], and $\bar e_a,\bar q_a,\bar\mu_a$ for the $P$-conditional classes $e_a,q_a,\mu_a$ from step 1.1. By [F12], all five functions are integrable under $\lambda$. For each measurable set $B$ in the covariate space, the defining event integrals for $e_a,q_a$ and the fact that $Q$ is the observed-data law give $$\int_B\widetilde e_a\,d\lambda=Q(A=a,L\in B)=E_P[I_a\mathbf1_{\{L\in B\}}]=\int_B\bar e_a\,d\lambda,$$ $$\int_B\widetilde q_a\,d\lambda=E_Q[I_aY\mathbf1_{\{L\in B\}}]=E_P[I_aY\mathbf1_{\{L\in B\}}]=\int_B\bar q_a\,d\lambda.$$ Each difference is integrable and has zero integral over every $B$, so it and zero are conditional-expectation versions of zero given the full sigma-algebra on $(\mathcal L,\mathcal S,\lambda)$. Uniqueness [F5] gives $\widetilde e_a=\bar e_a$ and $\widetilde q_a=\bar q_a$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere. Factoring the a.s. identity in step 1.1 gives $\bar q_a=\bar e_a\bar\mu_a$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere; positivity therefore makes the ratio in [F1] equal to $\bar\mu_a$ $Q_L$-almost everywhere. Thus $m_a$ is integrable and the standardization functional is well-defined.
By [F12] and step 2.1, $E_Q[m_a(L)]=\int m_a\,d\lambda=\int\bar\mu_a\,d\lambda=E_P[\mu_a]$. The tower property [F4] then gives $\Psi_{\mathrm{std}}(Q;a)=E_P[Y^a]$.

For either potential-outcome formulation in the Statement, let $\Theta_a$ be the class of full-data laws on the fixed measurable spaces for its variables that satisfy the stated integrability, consistency, conditional-exchangeability (or atom-specific independence), and positivity assumptions. Define the target by $\psi_a(P)=E_P[Y^a]$ and the observation map by $\mathsf O(P)=\mathcal L_P(A,L,Y)=Q$, the pushforward of $P$ under $(A,L,Y)$. Steps 2.1–3.1 show for every $P\in\Theta_a$ that $\psi_a(P)=\Psi_{\mathrm{std}}(\mathsf O(P);a)$, where the conditional classes in the right-hand side are determined uniquely by that observed law. Hence the target factors through the observation map on this model, and [F7]–[F9] imply identifiability from $Q$.

Under the additional countably discrete treatment and standard-Borel covariate hypotheses of [F11], the earlier theorem's RCD regression evaluated at $L$ equals $\mu_a$ almost surely on the target support, as established in its proof steps 2.1–3.1. Step 2.1 gives the same class for this algorithm's $m_a$. Thus the two standardization functionals coincide. The causal identification on this overlapping domain is the earlier theorem applied to the conditional-class algorithm; steps 1.1–4.1 supply the extension to arbitrary covariate random elements and the general target-atom formulation.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement permits an arbitrary covariate random element L, hence also the singleton-valued empty covariate tuple. In step 1.1 its sigma-algebra is trivial; the conditional-class and expectation identities in steps 2.1 and 3.1 still apply. An empty treatment-version family cannot contain the supplied positive-probability target atom a and is excluded by that premise.
Statement: e_a(L)=0 violates strict positivity; step 2.1 divides only on the full-measure set where e_a>0.
Step 2.1 remains valid at e_a=1, and step 3.1 averages the observed outcome under treatment a.
If L is degenerate, sigma(L) is trivial and step 3.1 is the unconditional expectation identity.
Step 2.1 includes e_a=1 and excludes e_a=0; it assumes no uniform positive lower bound.

AC is explicit for CE existence and for selecting B_r for each rational r in the real-version factorization (standardization step 2.1; IPW step 1.1). The selections are countable; no stronger choice assumption is introduced.

It is not formulated as a two-direction equivalence: a necessity result deriving the causal assumptions from equality of a standardization mean is outside its claimed scope.

A reverse inference would require a necessity result deriving the causal assumptions from equality of a standardization mean. The Statement instead supplies sufficient consistency, exchangeability, integrability and positivity for fixed-atom conditional-class identification, so no such converse is a claimed obligation.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all five steps and all 15 cited dependencies, including the independently reviewed current batch-19 proof/contract/manifest. Consistency makes IY integrable; coordinate independence and factorization yield q=e*mu. Rational-sublevel factorization works for arbitrary measurable L spaces, with countably many B_r choices covered by declared AC. Change of variables puts all five functions in L1 of the common L law; event-integral uniqueness equates P and Q numerator/propensity versions. Positive propensity makes their ratio equal mu, hence integrable without uniform overlap. The common-law integral and tower give the target and identifiability; the RCD comparison is restricted to countable treatments containing 0,1 and standard-Borel L. e=1, zero outcomes, constant L and null strata are handled; there is no continuous-treatment pointwise or converse causal-assumption claim. Batch-19 delayed integrability estimate is immediate nonfatal polish, recorded for its owner, and does not invalidate the overlapping-domain result. Reader repair is sound.
