exists for every sigma-finite $\mu$. For each pattern put
$$\kappa_r(B)=\rho(\pi_r^{-1}(B))$$
for measurable $B\subseteq\mathcal W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r)$, and define the finite
measure on the observed disjoint union by
$$\lambda_O(A)=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\kappa_r(\{x:(r,x)\in A\}).$$

continuous with respect to $\kappa_r$. Choose finite-valued nonnegative
Radon--Nikodym density representatives $q_{\theta,r}$ and
$\ell_{\theta,\psi,r}$ for these measures. Then the observed record
$O=(R,W_{\mathrm{obs}}(R))$ is dominated by $\lambda_O$ and has density
$\ell_{\theta,\psi}(r,x)=\ell_{\theta,\psi,r}(x)$ at $(r,x)$.

$\mu=\nu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^k\nu_j$, each $\nu_j$ is sigma-finite, and the
coordinate reordering $w=(x,z)=(W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r),W_{\mathrm{mis}}(r))$
identifies $\nu$ with
$\nu_r^{\mathrm{obs}}\times\nu_r^{\mathrm{mis}}$, where
$\nu_r^{\mathrm{obs}}=\bigotimes_{j\in I_r}\nu_j$ and
$\nu_r^{\mathrm{mis}}=\bigotimes_{j\in J_r}\nu_j$, one may instead use the
pattern reference $\nu_r^{\mathrm{obs}}$, with disjoint-union reference
$\lambda_O^{\mathrm{prod}}(A)=\sum_r\nu_r^{\mathrm{obs}}(\{x:(r,x)\in A\})$.
The observed record is dominated by this sigma-finite measure, and Tonelli's
theorem gives the density versions
$$\bar q_{\theta,r}(x)=\int p_\theta(x,z)\,\nu_r^{\mathrm{mis}}(dz),\qquad
\ell_{\theta,\psi,r}(x)=\int p_\theta(x,z)g_\psi(r\mid x,z)\,\nu_r^{\mathrm{mis}}(dz).$$
An empty coordinate block is a one-point space with unit mass.

Fix the full-data/observed-data partition of

specified conditional law $g(r\mid w)$ of the pattern $R$ given full data
$W=w$, represented by a probability kernel from the full-data space to the
finite pattern space
([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]],

on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$

$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f : X \to [0,+\infty]$ be measurable. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ define

$$s_k := \sum_{j=0}^{k2^k-1} j2^{-k}\, \mathbf{1}_{\{j2^{-k} \le f < (j+1)2^{-k}\}} + k\,\mathbf{1}_{\{f \ge k\}}.$$

Then each $s_k$ is a simple measurable function,

$$0 \le s_k \le s_{k+1} \le f,$$

and $s_k(x) \to f(x)$ for every $x \in X$. If $E \subseteq X$ is a set on which

$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

$$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$

$$g=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let
$W=(W_1,\ldots,W_k)$, for a finite $k\ge1$, be a random element of the product
measurable space $\mathcal W=\prod_{j=1}^k\mathcal W_j$
([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]],

measure defined in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. Let
$\mathcal R$ be a nonempty finite set of observation patterns with its

For each $r\in\mathcal R$, specify the recorded coordinate set
$I_r\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ and its complement
$J_r=\{1,\ldots,k\}\setminus I_r$. The **observed projection**
$W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r)$ is the coordinate projection into
$\mathcal W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r):=\prod_{j\in I_r}\mathcal W_j$, and the
**missing projection** $W_{\mathrm{mis}}(r)$ is the projection into
$\mathcal W_{\mathrm{mis}}(r):=\prod_{j\in J_r}\mathcal W_j$. An empty
coordinate tuple takes values in a one-point measurable space. The **observed
record** is $O=(R,W_{\mathrm{obs}}(R))$ in the disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_{r\in\mathcal R}(\{r\}\times\mathcal W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r))$,
where a set in the disjoint-union sigma-algebra is measurable exactly when
each pattern section is measurable. The pattern records which coordinates are
available; it does not replace an unrecorded full-data value by zero.

Fix the full-data/observed-data partition of
[[def-full-observed-and-missing-data]]. A **response mechanism** is a
specified conditional law $g(r\mid w)$ of the pattern $R$ given full data
$W=w$, represented by a probability kernel from the full-data space to the
finite pattern space
([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]],
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]). In a parameterized model, write
the response kernel as $g_\psi$; it must be a probability distribution over
patterns for each full-data value.

Relative to a specified full-data law, the mechanism is **missing completely
at random (MCAR)** when, for every pattern $r$, $g(r\mid w)$ is constant in
$w$ almost surely. It is **missing at random (MAR)** when, for every pattern
$r$, there is a measurable function $h_r$ on that pattern's observed-data
space such that
$$g(r\mid w)=h_r(W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r))\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
For a family of full-data laws, the condition is required under each law with
the same response mechanism and observed-coordinate function. It is
**missing not at random (MNAR)** when MAR fails for at least one pattern, for
the declared full-data and observed-data partition. MCAR is a special case of
MAR, since a constant is a function of the observed coordinates.

These conditions concern a supplied version of the conditional law; values
off the full-data model's support do not affect the classification. This
definition does not assert that a response mechanism is empirically true or
that every joint law comes with a selected conditional kernel.

Let $Y,R\in\{0,1\}$, with $R=1$ meaning that $Y$ is observed, and encode the

response kernel specified below when assessing the MAR clause; arbitrary
null-state values do not affect that classification. The full-data mean $m(P)=P(Y=1)$ is an estimand on this
model. Its set of values over $\Theta_{a,b}$ is exactly
$$[b,b+1-a].$$

$a<1$; it is identified as $b$ when $a=1$. If MAR also holds, then for $a>0$

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on

$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$

  **expectation** is again

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Assume AC. Let $X$ take values in a standard-Borel space $\mathcal X$, let $Y$ be real-valued, and let $R\in\{0,1\}$ indicate response in the one-outcome full/observed-data setup of [[def-full-observed-and-missing-data]]. Suppose $P(R=1)>0$, $P(R=0)>0$, and the covariate laws overlap in this direction: for every measurable $A\subseteq\mathcal X$, $P(X\in A\mid R=1)=0$ implies $P(X\in A\mid R=0)=0$. Under the respondent law $P(\cdot\mid R=1)$, choose a conditional law $K_1(x,\cdot)$ of $Y$ given $X=x$; standard-Borel disintegration supplies such a probability kernel under AC ([[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]], [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]). The overlap condition makes the respondent version relevant almost surely under the nonrespondent covariate law.

A **location-shift pattern-mixture sensitivity function** is a measurable $\Delta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ for which the nonrespondent conditional law is specified by
$$K_0^\Delta(x,B)=\int_{\mathbb R}\mathbf1_B(y+\Delta(x))K_1(x,dy)$$
for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, on the covariate support of nonrespondents. This is the full conditional distribution restriction $Y\mid(X=x,R=0)\stackrel d=Y_1+\Delta(x)$ for $Y_1\sim K_1(x,\cdot)$, not merely a restriction on conditional means. For each $x$, $K_0^\Delta(x,\cdot)$ is the pushforward of $K_1(x,\cdot)$ under the measurable translation $y\mapsto y+\Delta(x)$, hence is a probability measure; its evaluations are measurable in $x$ by kernel integration because $(x,y)\mapsto\mathbf1_B(y+\Delta(x))$ is measurable ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]], [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The relation specifies the missing conditional law while leaving the respondent conditional law fixed. A finite mean target additionally requires integrability under the resulting full-data law; the definition alone does not assert that moment condition.

In this specified family, $\Delta=0$ gives equality of the respondent and nonrespondent conditional laws. This does not make equality of conditional means alone equivalent to MAR in a general full-data model; equality of means need not imply equality of distributions. Values where no respondents occur are outside the definition because $K_1$ is unavailable there, and a pattern with no nonrespondents requires no sensitivity function.

The formal one-outcome MCAR/MAR/MNAR taxonomy for this pair is supplied by [[def-mcar-mar-and-mnar]]. The location-shift relation above is the selected sensitivity model within that taxonomy; it does not claim that all MNAR laws are location shifts.

Fix the full-data/observed-data partition of
[[def-full-observed-and-missing-data]]. A **response mechanism** is a
specified conditional law $g(r\mid w)$ of the pattern $R$ given full data
$W=w$, represented by a probability kernel from the full-data space to the
finite pattern space
([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]],
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]). In a parameterized model, write
the response kernel as $g_\psi$; it must be a probability distribution over
patterns for each full-data value.

Relative to a specified full-data law, the mechanism is **missing completely
at random (MCAR)** when, for every pattern $r$, $g(r\mid w)$ is constant in
$w$ almost surely. It is **missing at random (MAR)** when, for every pattern
$r$, there is a measurable function $h_r$ on that pattern's observed-data
space such that
$$g(r\mid w)=h_r(W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r))\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
For a family of full-data laws, the condition is required under each law with
the same response mechanism and observed-coordinate function. It is
**missing not at random (MNAR)** when MAR fails for at least one pattern, for
the declared full-data and observed-data partition. MCAR is a special case of
MAR, since a constant is a function of the observed coordinates.

These conditions concern a supplied version of the conditional law; values
off the full-data model's support do not affect the classification. This
definition does not assert that a response mechanism is empirically true or
that every joint law comes with a selected conditional kernel.

for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded

derivations.claim: The near-positivity law has atom weights $1/2$ at $(X,R,Y)=(0,1,0)$, $\varepsilon/2$ at $(1,1,1)$, and $(1-\varepsilon)/2$ at $(1,0,1)$. By [A1] and [F2], these are nonnegative and sum to one. Given either value $X=x$, $Y=x$ is constant, so for bounded measurable $f(R)$ and $g(Y)$, $E[f(R)g(Y)\mid X=x]=g(x)E[f(R)\mid X=x]=E[f(R)\mid X=x]E[g(Y)\mid X=x]$. Thus this construction is MAR under the assigned conditional-independence formulation [F9]. Hence $V$ equals $1/\varepsilon$ on the responding $X=1$ atom, of probability $\varepsilon/2$, and is zero on the other atoms.

For each $\theta\in\{0,1\}$, the full-data law assigns probability $1/2$ to $(X,R,Y)=(0,1,0)$ and $1/2$ to $(1,0,\theta)$. Mapping these atoms to $O=(X,R,RY)$ gives the same two observed atoms for both values of $\theta$, while [F1] gives $\psi(\theta)=E_\theta[Y]=\theta/2$. Thus the observed sampling laws agree but the estimand values are $0$ and $1/2$.

For each $\Delta\in[0,1/2]$, assign observed-pattern masses $0.3$ to $(R,Y)=(1,0)$, $0.2$ to $(1,1)$, and missing-pattern masses $0.3$ to $(0,\Delta)$, $0.2$ to $(0,1+\Delta)$. These masses sum to one by [F2]. Conditional on $R=1$, the outcome is Bernoulli$(0.4)$; conditional on $R=0$, it has the law of that Bernoulli variable translated by $\Delta$, as required by [F7]. The observed record $(R,RY)$ has masses $0.3,0.2,0.5$ at $(1,0),(1,1),(0,0)$ for every $\Delta$.

By [F1], $E[V]=(\varepsilon/2)(1/\varepsilon)=1/2$ and $E[(V-EV)^2]=(\varepsilon/2)(1/\varepsilon-1/2)^2+(1-\varepsilon/2)(1/2)^2=1/(2\varepsilon)-1/4$. This diverges as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, although $\pi(X)>0$ for each fixed $\varepsilon>0$. At $\varepsilon=0$, $\pi(1)=0$, so positivity fails on an $X$ stratum of probability $1/2$.

By [F5], the two parameters are observationally equivalent; by [F6], the different values of $\psi$ therefore show that the full-data mean is not identifiable from this observed-data model. The response probability is zero at $X=1$, exactly the stratum on which the two full-data laws differ.

By [F1], the target mean is $0.2(1)+0.3\Delta+0.2(1+\Delta)=0.4+0.5\Delta$. At $\Delta=0$ it is $0.4$, and at $\Delta=1/2$ it is $0.65$, while step 1.3 shows that the observed sampling law is unchanged. Thus the target is not identified across this sensitivity family; the interval $[0.4,0.65]$ is only the set of means induced by the stipulated $\Delta$ range and carries no repeated-sampling coverage assertion.

If $\Delta>0$, then $P(R=0\mid Y=0)=0$ whereas $P(R=0\mid Y=\Delta)=1$: both conditioning events have positive probability, and $\Delta\in(0,1/2]$ keeps $\Delta$ distinct from respondent support $\{0,1\}$. With no always-observed covariate, the missing pattern has an empty observed-coordinate vector, so [F8] requires this response probability to be constant in $Y$ for MAR; it is not, hence this member is MNAR. At $\Delta=0$, both response groups have the same Bernoulli$(0.4)$ law and $R$ is independent of $Y$, so the response probability is constant and the member is MAR.

Let $X,W,U$ be real random variables on one probability space, meaning
measurable maps into $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$
([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]). The variable $X$ is the
**latent true value**, $W$ is its **measured value**, and $U$ is an
**error term**. We use the following two additive models:

- **Classical additive error:** $W=X+U$, with $\mathbb E[U]=0$ and $U$
  independent of $X$ in the sense of
  [[def-independent-random-elements]].
- **Berkson additive error:** $X=W+U$, with $\mathbb E[U]=0$ and $U$
  independent of $W$ in that same sense.

The equations have opposite directions and their independence conditions
refer to different variables. They are distinct model assumptions.

For nonempty finite sets $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal W$, a **categorical
misclassification mechanism** is a row-stochastic matrix
$K(w\mid x)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $x\in\mathcal X$ and $w\in\mathcal W$:
for every $x$, $\sum_{w\in\mathcal W}K(w\mid x)=1$. When categorical random
variables $X,W$ have $\mathbb P(X=x)>0$, the entry represents
$$K(w\mid x)=\frac{\mathbb P(W=w,\ X=x)}{\mathbb P(X=x)}.$$
If $\mathbb P(X=x)=0$, the observed joint law determines no conditional row
at that $x$; any row there is an additional part of a specified model, not an
empirical consequence.

The matrix $K(w\mid x)$ describes the conditional law given $X$ alone. If an
outcome or covariate is also named, whether the error is nondifferential must
be stated relative to those variables; the marginal matrix alone does not
settle that question.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(Y_j)_{j\in J}$ be finite families of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space. Then covariance is symmetric, and for real scalars $a_i,b_j$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}a_iX_i,\sum_{j\in J}b_jY_j\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}a_ib_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y_j).$$
This includes empty sums and constant summands. On a finite probability space all real random variables are square-integrable, so the original finite-space case is included with the same centered-product covariance.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be a finite mutually independent family of real random variables on a common probability space, with independence in the sense of [[def-independent-random-elements]].

1. If every $X_i$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i\in I}X_i$ is integrable and
   $$\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{i\in I}X_i\right]=\prod_{i\in I}\mathbb E[X_i]$$
   in $\mathbb R$.
2. If every $X_i$ is nonnegative, the same identity holds in $[0,+\infty]$. A zero factor on the right makes the product zero even if another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise the usual extended nonnegative product is used.

The original finite-probability-space case is included: for a finite family of finite-valued real random variables, mutual atom independence as in [[def-independence-of-finite-random-variables]] suffices, and all expectations are finite. For $I=\varnothing$, both sides equal $1$. The converse is not asserted.

Let $X,Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ be square-integrable real random variables on one
probability space, and write
$$W:=\operatorname{span}\big([1],[Y_1],\dots,[Y_n]\big)\subseteq L^2(\mathbb P),$$
where $[\cdot]$ denotes the almost-everywhere class from
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]].

Then there is a unique class $[Z_*]\in W$ minimizing $\|[X]-[Z]\|_2$ over
$[Z]\in W$. This minimizing class has an affine representative
$Z_*=a_0+\sum_{j=1}^n a_jY_j$, and its coefficients satisfy
$$a_0=\mathbb E[X]-\sum_{j=1}^n a_j\mathbb E[Y_j],$$
$$\sum_{j=1}^n \operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j)a_j=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y_i)\qquad(1\le i\le n).$$

The class $[Z_*]$ is unique. If the covariance matrix
$\Gamma=(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j))_{i,j}$ is singular, the coefficient vector
need not be uniquely determined by the normal equations, but any two solutions
yield the same predictor almost surely.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

derivations.claim: By [F7] the variables are integrable. Independence of $U$ from $(X,\epsilon)$ implies independence of $U$ from each coordinate, because the coordinate sigma-algebras are contained in that of the pair; together with $\epsilon$ independent of $X$, [F4] and [F5] give $\mathbb E[XU]=\mathbb E[\epsilon U]=\mathbb E[X\epsilon]=0$. Centering and [F2] therefore give $\operatorname{Cov}(X,U)=\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,U)=\operatorname{Cov}(X,\epsilon)=0$.

By [F1], $W=X+U$; by bilinearity [F3] and the zero covariances in step 1.1, $$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,W)=\operatorname{Cov}(\alpha+\beta X+\epsilon,X+U)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(X).$$ The same expansion gives $$\operatorname{Var}(W)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+2\operatorname{Cov}(X,U)+\operatorname{Var}(U)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(U).$$
The variance sum is positive by hypothesis, so [F6] determines the unique slope $\gamma=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,W)/\operatorname{Var}(W)$. Substitution from step 2.1 gives the displayed formula.

Nonnegative variances and a positive sum give $0\le\operatorname{Var}(X)/(\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(U))\le1$. Equality at $0$ occurs exactly when $\operatorname{Var}(X)=0$; equality at $1$ occurs exactly when $\operatorname{Var}(U)=0$. When both are positive the factor is strictly between the endpoints, so for $\beta\ne0$ step 3.1 gives a coefficient of the same sign and smaller absolute value; when $\beta=0$, step 3.1 gives $\gamma=0$, so no strict reduction holds. This proves the stated attenuation and boundary cases.

boundaries.reason: A probability space with total mass one is nonempty, and no sample-size-indexed empty data set appears in the Statement.

boundaries.evidence: Step 4.1 treats Var(X)=0, where the factor is 0 and the denominator remains positive by the hypothesis.
The single-predictor case is the Statement; step 3.1 uses its one-dimensional covariance normal equation.
Step 4.1 checks Var(X)=0 and Var(U)=0 separately; the simultaneous zero case is excluded by the positive-sum premise.
Step 4.1 proves that the factor reaches 0 and 1 exactly at the stated zero-variance endpoints.

boundaries.reason: The proof is a finite covariance calculation and selects no element from a nonempty family.

boundaries.evidence: Step 4.1: with the positive denominator from the Statement and step 3.1, an attenuation factor of zero forces Var(X)=0; an attenuation factor of one forces Var(U)=0 by subtracting the numerator from its variance-sum denominator. These are the exact endpoint characterizations of the factor, not of gamma when beta=0.

Step 4.1: Var(X)=0 gives factor zero because the remaining variance is positive; Var(U)=0 gives factor one because Var(X)>0. Step 3.1 then gives gamma=beta times that factor; beta=0 is separately allowed and makes gamma=0 without altering the factor equivalences.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all four steps and seven direct dependency carriers. Independence of U from the pair (X,epsilon) implies independence from each coordinate; the separate epsilon,X hypothesis removes the remaining covariance. L2 ensures integrability; product factorization gives all three cross covariances zero. Cov(Y,W)=beta Var(X), Var(W)=Var(X)+Var(U)>0, and the actual affine-prediction theorem gives the unique slope. Nonnegative variances give factor in [0,1], endpoints at zero component variances, and strict magnitude reduction only for both variances positive and beta nonzero. Beta=0 yields gamma=0, including constant Y when epsilon=0; both predictor-component variances zero is excluded. No choice, conditional-mean linearity or converse is assumed. STRATOS §3.1.1 gives the covariance-ratio argument; current proof handles zero and sign cases explicitly. H&R Fine Point 9.1 is printed p.128, so the reader locator repair is correct. No mathematical defect remains.

$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$

the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

derivations.claim: Let $\Omega=\{-1,1\}^4$ with its full power set and uniform probability, and label its coordinate variables $A,B,C,D$. For any subsets $S_i\subseteq\{-1,1\}$ on $k$ distinct coordinates, counting gives $$\mathbb P(A_i\in S_i\text{ for all selected }i)=\prod_i\frac{|S_i|}{2},$$ where $(A_1,A_2,A_3,A_4)=(A,B,C,D)$. Thus the coordinate sigma-algebras are mutually independent in the sense of [F2]. Each coordinate has mean $0$ and variance $1$; [F3] gives zero expectation for products of distinct coordinates, so [F4] gives their zero covariances.

Define $(X_0,U_0,W_0)=(A+B,C+D,A+B+C+D)$ and $(X_1,U_1,W_1)=(A+B+C,D,A+B+C+D)$. Thus $W_0=W_1$ pointwise. For any Borel $B_0,B_1\subseteq\mathbb R$, the event $X_0\in B_0$ is determined by $(A,B)$ and $U_0\in B_1$ by $(C,D)$; their preimage sets $E,F\subseteq\{-1,1\}^2$ satisfy $\mathbb P((A,B)\in E,(C,D)\in F)=|E||F|/16=(|E|/4)(|F|/4)$. The same count for the three-coordinate block and the last coordinate proves $X_i$ independent of $U_i$ for $i=0,1$. Both errors are centered.

Bilinearity and the zero covariances from step 1.1 give $\operatorname{Var}(X_0)=\operatorname{Var}(A+B)=1+1+2(0)=2$, $\operatorname{Var}(U_0)=\operatorname{Var}(C+D)=1+1+2(0)=2$, $\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=\operatorname{Var}(A+B+C)=1+1+1+2(0+0+0)=3$, and $\operatorname{Var}(U_1)=\operatorname{Var}(D)=1$. The variance pairs $(2,2)$ and $(3,1)$ are different.

Let $\Theta=\{0,1\}$, take sample space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$, and define $P_i$ to be the law of $W_i$. Then $\mathsf P:i\mapsto P_i$ is a parametric model [F5], and $\psi(i)=(\operatorname{Var}(X_i),\operatorname{Var}(U_i))$ is an estimand [F6]. Since $W_0=W_1$, $P_0=P_1$, but step 2.2 gives $\psi(0)\ne\psi(1)$. This violates the defining implication for identifiability [F7], so the split is not identifiable from the observed law of $W$ alone.

citations.quote:
Let $X,W,U$ be real random variables on one probability space, meaning
measurable maps into $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$
([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]). The variable $X$ is the
**latent true value**, $W$ is its **measured value**, and $U$ is an
**error term**. We use the following two additive models:

- **Classical additive error:** $W=X+U$, with $\mathbb E[U]=0$ and $U$
  independent of $X$ in the sense of
  [[def-independent-random-elements]].
- **Berkson additive error:** $X=W+U$, with $\mathbb E[U]=0$ and $U$
  independent of $W$ in that same sense.

The equations have opposite directions and their independence conditions
refer to different variables. They are distinct model assumptions.

For nonempty finite sets $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal W$, a **categorical
misclassification mechanism** is a row-stochastic matrix
$K(w\mid x)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $x\in\mathcal X$ and $w\in\mathcal W$:
for every $x$, $\sum_{w\in\mathcal W}K(w\mid x)=1$. When categorical random
variables $X,W$ have $\mathbb P(X=x)>0$, the entry represents
$$K(w\mid x)=\frac{\mathbb P(W=w,\ X=x)}{\mathbb P(X=x)}.$$
If $\mathbb P(X=x)=0$, the observed joint law determines no conditional row
at that $x$; any row there is an additional part of a specified model, not an
empirical consequence.

The matrix $K(w\mid x)$ describes the conditional law given $X$ alone. If an
outcome or covariate is also named, whether the error is nondifferential must
be stated relative to those variables; the marginal matrix alone does not
settle that question.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(Y_j)_{j\in J}$ be finite families of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space. Then covariance is symmetric, and for real scalars $a_i,b_j$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}a_iX_i,\sum_{j\in J}b_jY_j\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}a_ib_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y_j).$$
This includes empty sums and constant summands. On a finite probability space all real random variables are square-integrable, so the original finite-space case is included with the same centered-product covariance.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be a finite mutually independent family of real random variables on a common probability space, with independence in the sense of [[def-independent-random-elements]].

1. If every $X_i$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i\in I}X_i$ is integrable and
   $$\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{i\in I}X_i\right]=\prod_{i\in I}\mathbb E[X_i]$$
   in $\mathbb R$.
2. If every $X_i$ is nonnegative, the same identity holds in $[0,+\infty]$. A zero factor on the right makes the product zero even if another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise the usual extended nonnegative product is used.

The original finite-probability-space case is included: for a finite family of finite-valued real random variables, mutual atom independence as in [[def-independence-of-finite-random-variables]] suffices, and all expectations are finite. For $I=\varnothing$, both sides equal $1$. The converse is not asserted.

Let $X,U,\epsilon,W,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one
probability space with
$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[U]=\mathbb E[\epsilon]=0$,
$U$ independent of the random element $(X,\epsilon)$, and $\epsilon$
independent of $X$. Set
$$W=X+U,\qquad Y=\alpha+\beta X+\epsilon,\qquad \alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R,$$
so $W$ has classical additive error. If
$\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(U)>0$, the coefficient $\gamma$
of the best affine $L^2$ predictor of $Y$ from $W$ is
$$\gamma=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,W)}{\operatorname{Var}(W)}=\beta\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(U)}.$$
The attenuation factor lies in $[0,1]$. When both variances are positive, it
is strictly between $0$ and $1$, so for $\beta\ne0$ the coefficient has the
same sign as $\beta$ and smaller absolute value; when $\beta=0$, $\gamma=0$.
The boundary cases are: if $\operatorname{Var}(X)=0$, the factor is $0$; if
$\operatorname{Var}(U)=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)>0$, it is $1$.

Let $W,U,\epsilon,X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one
probability space with
$\mathbb E[W]=\mathbb E[U]=\mathbb E[\epsilon]=0$, $U$ independent of $W$,
and $\epsilon$ independent of $W$. Put
$$X=W+U,\qquad Y=\alpha+\beta X+\epsilon,\qquad \alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R,$$
so $X$ has Berkson additive error relative to $W$. If
$\operatorname{Var}(W)>0$, the coefficient of the best affine $L^2$
predictor of $Y$ from $W$ is $\beta$. Independence between $U$ and
$\epsilon$ is not assumed or needed.

Let $X,W,Y,Z$ be real random variables on a common probability space. Let
$\mathcal G$ be the smallest sub-sigma-algebra of the ambient sigma-algebra
that makes both $X$ and $Z$ measurable; when no $Z$ is named, take
$\mathcal G=\sigma(X)$. The error in measuring $X$ by $W$ is
**nondifferential with respect to $Y$ relative to $(X,Z)$** exactly when
$$W\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\mid\mathcal G,$$
using the library definition
[[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. It is
**differential with respect to $Y$ relative to $(X,Z)$** when this conditional
independence fails.

The named variables are part of the definition: changing $Y$ or $Z$ can
change the classification. This condition alone fixes no direction of bias
for a specified estimator or target. Such a direction requires additional
model and target assumptions.

**Axiom:** This definition assumes the Axiom of Choice
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) because the cited
conditional-independence definition is stated using the library's
conditional-expectation classes.

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Within the class of centered, square-integrable classical additive error
models with $U$ independent of $X$, the observed law of $W=X+U$ need not
identify the target
$$\psi(\theta)=(\operatorname{Var}_{\theta}(X_{\theta}),\operatorname{Var}_{\theta}(U_{\theta}))\in[0,+\infty)^2.$$
In particular, there is a two-point parametric model whose two parameter
values give the same law of $W$ but different latent-error variance pairs.

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

derivations.claim: In the first construction, each of the four sign pairs has probability $1/4$ and each coordinate sign has probability $1/2$, so $X$ and $U$ are independent. Each has $\mathbb E[X]=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=1$, and likewise for $U$. Their covariance is $0$ by [F2]–[F4]. The error is classical, $\epsilon=0$, and the response coefficient is $\beta=2$. Applying [F5] gives measured slope $2(1)/(1+1)=1$, while $Y=2X$ gives latent slope $2$.
In the second construction, $W$ and $U$ are independent centered signs with variance $1$, $X=W+U$, and $\epsilon=0$. Thus the distinct Berkson hypotheses hold, and [F6] gives measured slope $2$.

In the third construction $Y=X$. On each positive-probability stratum $X=x$, the variable $Y$ is constant. The conditional-independence definition [F10], applied under the explicit Axiom of Choice premise [F8], therefore gives for all bounded measurable $f,g$, $$\mathbb E[f(W)g(Y)\mid\sigma(X)]=g(X)\mathbb E[f(W)\mid\sigma(X)]=\mathbb E[f(W)\mid\sigma(X)]\mathbb E[g(Y)\mid\sigma(X)].$$
By [F7], the error is nondifferential relative to $Y$ given $X$.

In the fourth construction, $\mathbb E[Y\mid X=1]-\mathbb E[Y\mid X=0]=3/4-1/4=1/2$. Since $W=1-Y$, $\mathbb E[Y\mid W=1]-\mathbb E[Y\mid W=0]=0-1=-1$. On the positive stratum $X=1$, the conditional expectation of $\mathbf 1_{\{W=1\}}\mathbf 1_{\{Y=1\}}$ is $0$, whereas the product of the two conditional expectations is $(1/4)(3/4)=3/16$. The factorization in [F10] fails, so the error is differential relative to $Y$ given $X$.

On the uniform four-sign space, every specified pattern of $k$ distinct signs has probability $2^{-k}$; thus the coordinates are mutually independent, centered, and have variance $1$. For sign-pattern sets $E,F$ on disjoint blocks of sizes $2,2$ or $3,1$, the joint probability is $|E||F|/16$, the product of the two block probabilities; hence $X_i$ is independent of $U_i$ for $i=0,1$. Their distinct-coordinate covariances are zero by [F4]. They satisfy $W_0=W_1=A+B+C+D$ pointwise.

The true contrast is $\mathbb E[Y\mid X=1]-\mathbb E[Y\mid X=0]=1$. The table gives $\mathbb P(W=1)=1/2$, $\mathbb E[Y\mid W=1]=1/5$, and $\mathbb E[Y\mid W=0]=4/5$, so the measured contrast is $1/5-4/5=-3/5$. Thus this nondifferential mechanism reverses the contrast direction.

Bilinearity [F2] and the zero coordinate covariances from step 1.5 give $\operatorname{Var}(X_0)=1+1=2$, $\operatorname{Var}(U_0)=1+1=2$, $\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=1+1+1=3$, and $\operatorname{Var}(U_1)=1$. Thus the same observed $W$ law is compatible with distinct variance pairs, as asserted in [F9].

The event $X_0=0$ requires opposite signs among $A,B$, so has probability $2/4=1/2$. Since $X_1=A+B+C$ is a sum of three signs, it takes values only in $\{-3,-1,1,3\}$, and therefore $\mathbb P(X_1=0)=0$. These unequal marginals show that the joint validation laws of $(X,W)$ differ, so observing $X$ adds information that separates these two candidate laws.

citations.quote:
An **event time** is a measurable real-valued map $T$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. A **covariate** is a measurable map $Z$ into a specified standard-Borel space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal B)$, where standard Borel means measurably isomorphic to a Polish space ([[def-standard-borel-space]]). A **censoring or inspection time** is a measurable real-valued map $C$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. When conditional laws are used, they are probability kernels $K_T(z,\cdot)$ and $K_C(z,\cdot)$ in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]] and [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. They are part of the specified model; their existence for real-valued targets and factorization through standard-Borel $Z$ follow under [[def-axiom-of-choice]] from [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]].

The notation $T\perp\!\!\!\perp C\mid\sigma(Z)$ has the meaning in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: for bounded measurable $a,b$, $\mathbb E[a(T)b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]=\mathbb E[a(T)\mid\sigma(Z)]\mathbb E[b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]$ almost surely. It is a model assumption about the conditional observation law, not a consequence of adjusting for $Z$ and not an empirical conclusion.

Under **right censoring**, the recorded pair is $U=\min(T,C)$ and $\delta=1\{T\le C\}$. Thus $\delta=1$ records an event at $U=T$, including a tie, while $\delta=0$ records censoring at $U=C$ and implies $T>C$. **Left censoring** at a known threshold $L$ records only $T\le L$. **Interval censoring** at known endpoints $L<R$ records $L<T\le R$. **Current-status observation** at an inspection time $C$ records only $\delta_C=1\{T\le C\}$.

**Left truncation**, also called delayed entry at $L$, selects a unit into the sample only when $T>L$; observation begins after that selection. **Right truncation** at $R$ selects a unit only when $T<R$. These are selection rules before the observed sample is formed, whereas censoring coarsens an event time after sampling. The strict and weak inequalities in these definitions fix the endpoint conventions. A random observation endpoint is called noninformative here only when it is fixed by design or is generated independently of $T$ conditional on the stated covariates under a parameter-distinct law; otherwise its joint observation law must be modeled.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

Let
$$\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). When the model is
parametric, write $\mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). A **scientific statistical model
contract** is an explicit record of the following fields for a specified
analysis.

1. **Observation space and record.** Give $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and say
   which values form one recorded data object. A response and each predictor
   used as a function of the data must be a specified measurable map from this
   space to a named measurable target. This is the map convention for a
   statistic in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; it does not make a predictor
   causal or the response law correct.

2. **Scientific, sampling, assignment, and analysis units.** Name the
   biological or physical unit about which the scientific question is asked,
   the sample unit selected for observation when sampling occurs, the
   assignment unit receiving a randomized treatment when randomization occurs,
   and the analysis unit represented in each data record. These roles may
   differ. A technical replicate is a repeated reading or assay of the same
   specimen; a biological replicate is a distinct biological unit. Neither
   term asserts independence. State whether enrollment is a probability
   sample or a specified convenience/design cohort.

3. **Indices and time.** Give every unit, treatment, visit, and repeated
   measurement index, the object each index identifies, and the time origin.
   In particular, do not identify a participant index with a visit or assay
   index merely because all are written as rows in a data array.

4. **Quantity status.** Mark each model quantity as **fixed** (held
   nonrandom under the declared law), **random** (a measurable random element
   with its law specified, using [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]
   and [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]), **observed** (recorded
   in the data object), or **latent** (part of a fuller model state but not
   recorded). A latent quantity must separately be declared fixed or random.
   If inference conditions on a design value or event, name it and state the
   conditional law being used.

5. **Target and estimand.** Name the target population of units, settings,
   and time period, and distinguish it from the enrolled or observed sample.
   Specify the target as a function $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T$ when it is an
   estimand in the parametric model, as in
   [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]. The contract alone does not show
   that the target is identifiable. Identifiability means that equality of
   sampling laws forces equality of target values
   ([[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]]).

6. **Observation mechanism.** State how a fuller scientific state becomes
   the recorded data. A deterministic mechanism is a specified measurable map
   $O:(\mathcal W,\mathcal G)\to(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. A stochastic
   mechanism is specified by $K:\mathcal W\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ such that,
   for each $w$, $A\mapsto K(w,A)$ is a probability measure and, for each
   $A\in\mathcal A$, $w\mapsto K(w,A)$ is measurable. These clauses define the
   mechanism supplied by the contract; they do not assert that a conditional
   version exists for an arbitrary joint law.

7. **Support and law.** State the sampling law $P_\theta$ on
   $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. For an asserted support set, give a measurable
   $S_\theta\subseteq\mathcal X$ with $P_\theta(S_\theta)=1$. If “support”
   instead means topological support, name the topology and the conditions
   under which that convention is being used. If densities are used, name the
   dominating measure and state whether their positive sets agree across
   parameter values. For a randomized design, also state its assignment law;
   if inference averages over assignments, give the resulting joint law.

8. **Conditioning convention.** Say whether inference uses the joint law,
   averaging over the declared randomization, or a specified conditional law
   given the realized design. A conditional law at an event of probability
   zero must be supplied as a specified version with its existence
   hypotheses; it is not defined by an ordinary probability ratio.

9. **Adequacy assumptions.** List each scientific adequacy assumption and
   classify it as **design-controlled** (imposed by protocol and checked
   against implementation records), **empirically assessable** (data or
   validation measurements can challenge it, without proving it true), or
   **substantively untestable** from the declared observed-data law (external
   domain evidence or additional assumptions are needed). Split an assumption
   that has different parts into separate entries and justify each label.

These are bookkeeping and interpretation requirements. They do not assert that
an empirical law equals a proposed model, that a design was implemented as
specified, that calibration is valid, or that any scientific or physical
application is adequate. No independence, exchangeability, missingness,
causal-identification, or common-support assumption follows from the indexing
or the classification labels. This definition uses no axiom of choice.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$

An **event time** is a measurable real-valued map $T$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. A **covariate** is a measurable map $Z$ into a specified standard-Borel space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal B)$, where standard Borel means measurably isomorphic to a Polish space ([[def-standard-borel-space]]). A **censoring or inspection time** is a measurable real-valued map $C$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. When conditional laws are used, they are probability kernels $K_T(z,\cdot)$ and $K_C(z,\cdot)$ in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]] and [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. They are part of the specified model; their existence for real-valued targets and factorization through standard-Borel $Z$ follow under [[def-axiom-of-choice]] from [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]].

The notation $T\perp\!\!\!\perp C\mid\sigma(Z)$ has the meaning in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: for bounded measurable $a,b$, $\mathbb E[a(T)b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]=\mathbb E[a(T)\mid\sigma(Z)]\mathbb E[b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]$ almost surely. It is a model assumption about the conditional observation law, not a consequence of adjusting for $Z$ and not an empirical conclusion.

Under **right censoring**, the recorded pair is $U=\min(T,C)$ and $\delta=1\{T\le C\}$. Thus $\delta=1$ records an event at $U=T$, including a tie, while $\delta=0$ records censoring at $U=C$ and implies $T>C$. **Left censoring** at a known threshold $L$ records only $T\le L$. **Interval censoring** at known endpoints $L<R$ records $L<T\le R$. **Current-status observation** at an inspection time $C$ records only $\delta_C=1\{T\le C\}$.

**Left truncation**, also called delayed entry at $L$, selects a unit into the sample only when $T>L$; observation begins after that selection. **Right truncation** at $R$ selects a unit only when $T<R$. These are selection rules before the observed sample is formed, whereas censoring coarsens an event time after sampling. The strict and weak inequalities in these definitions fix the endpoint conventions. A random observation endpoint is called noninformative here only when it is fixed by design or is generated independently of $T$ conditional on the stated covariates under a parameter-distinct law; otherwise its joint observation law must be modeled.

All displayed conditional identities hold for $P_{Z;\theta,\eta}$-almost every $z$ under each fixed parameter pair $(\theta,\eta)$, where $P_{Z;\theta,\eta}$ is the marginal law of $Z$ under that pair as in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. All density equalities are in their almost-everywhere versions for that pair; no common exceptional set over an uncountable parameter set is asserted.

For right-censored data $(U,\delta)$, define the reference measure $\rho$ on $[0,\infty)\times\{0,1\}$ by $\rho(B\times\{1\})=\operatorname{Leb}(B)$ and $\rho(B\times\{0\})=\nu(B)$. Put $S_\theta(u\mid z)=K^T_\theta(z,(u,\infty))$ and $G_\eta(u\mid z)=K^C_\eta(z,[u,\infty))$. In the scientific model contract of [[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]], one analysis unit is one subject; the full-data random quantities are $T,C$, and the observation map records $(Z,U,\delta)=(Z,\min(T,C),1\{T\le C\})$, so the record contains the minimum and status rather than both full times. This theorem conditions on observed $Z$ and asserts no target-population estimand or empirical adequacy. The conditional density of $(U,\delta)$ with respect to $\rho$ is

$$h_{\theta,\eta}(u,1\mid z)=f_\theta(u\mid z)G_\eta(u\mid z),\qquad h_{\theta,\eta}(u,0\mid z)=S_\theta(u\mid z)g_\eta(z,u).$$

Consequently, up to the censor-only factor, the event-model likelihood contribution is $f_\theta(U\mid Z)^\delta S_\theta(U\mid Z)^{1-\delta}$, where the two cases mean $f_\theta(U\mid Z)$ when $\delta=1$ and $S_\theta(U\mid Z)$ when $\delta=0$. This is a conditional likelihood given $Z$; a parameter-dependent marginal law of $Z$ would supply a separate factor.

For an arbitrary conditional event-time law $\mu_{\theta,z}$ on $[0,\infty)$ with distribution function $F_\theta(t\mid z)=\mu_{\theta,z}((-\infty,t])$, for $0\le L\le R<\infty$,

$$P(L<T\le R\mid Z=z)=F_\theta(R\mid z)-F_\theta(L\mid z),\qquad P(T\le L\mid Z=z)=F_\theta(L\mid z),$$

and $P(T=t\mid Z=z)=F_\theta(t\mid z)-F_\theta(t^-\mid z)$. For fixed inspection endpoints, or endpoints conditionally independent of $T$ given $Z$ under a law with no event parameter $\theta$, these are the event factors for interval and left-censored observations. In current-status observation at a fixed inspection time $c$, the event contribution is $F_\theta(c\mid z)^\delta S_\theta(c\mid z)^{1-\delta}$, with $S_\theta(c\mid z)=P(T>c\mid Z=z)$ and $\delta=1\{T\le c\}$. An informative inspection process requires its own joint model.

For delayed entry at $L$, let $W$ denote all pre-entry covariates; take $Z=W$ when $L$ is fixed by design and $Z=(W,L)$ when random $L$ is observed. In the random-entry case, assume that before selection the conditional joint law of $(T,L)$ given $W=w$ factors as $K^T_\theta(w,dt)Q_\eta(w,d\ell)$, where the entry kernel $Q_\eta$ does not depend on the event parameter $\theta$. Thus $L\perp\!\!\!\perp T\mid W$ under this parameter-distinct entry model, and the event law given $Z=(W,L)$ remains $K^T_\theta(W,\cdot)$. For each parameter pair, require $S_\theta(L\mid W)>0$ for almost every $(W,L)$ under its pre-selection law, select only units with $T>L$, and assume post-entry right censoring satisfies $T\perp\!\!\!\perp C\mid\sigma(Z)$ with $C\ge L$. Conditional on inclusion $T>L$, the event density and survivor terms are $f_\theta(u\mid W)/S_\theta(L\mid W)$ for an event and $S_\theta(u\mid W)/S_\theta(L\mid W)$ for censoring, for $u>L$. Thus the right-censored event contribution is divided by $S_\theta(L\mid W)$. An event branch has $u>L$, while a censoring branch may have $u=L$ when the censoring law has an atom at entry; the survivor ratio $S_\theta(u\mid W)/S_\theta(L\mid W)$ applies for every $u\ge L$.

For right truncation at fixed $R$, or at an observed threshold conditionally independent of $T$ given $Z$ under a law with no event parameter $\theta$, inclusion is conditional on $T<R$ with $P(T<R\mid Z=z)>0$. Its conditional event-time law is $\mu_{\theta,z}(A\cap(-\infty,R))/P(T<R\mid Z=z)$; in the continuous-density case the selected-sample density is $f_\theta(t\mid z)/F_\theta(R^-\mid z)$ for $t<R$. This selection likelihood is distinct from the right-censoring likelihood. Independence of censoring, inspection, or entry is a model assumption, not a theorem about an empirical study.

derivations.claim: Integrating the density gives $F_\lambda(t)=1-e^{-\lambda t}$ and $S_\lambda(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t\ge0$; in particular $F_\lambda(0)=0$ and $S_\lambda(0)=1$.

With fixed censoring time $C=2$, an event observed at $U=1$ has event factor $f_\lambda(1)=\lambda e^{-\lambda}$ and censor factor $1$. A censored observation at $U=2$ has event factor $S_\lambda(2)=e^{-2\lambda}$ and censor factor $1$ relative to the point-mass censoring law.
An interval observation $1<T\le2$ has probability $F_\lambda(2)-F_\lambda(1)=(1-e^{-2\lambda})-(1-e^{-\lambda})=e^{-\lambda}-e^{-2\lambda}$.
At fixed inspection time $C=1$, current status $\delta=1$ has event factor $F_\lambda(1)=1-e^{-\lambda}$, and $\delta=0$ has event factor $S_\lambda(1)=e^{-\lambda}$.

After delayed entry $L=1$, with fixed censoring time $C=3$, an event observed at $U=2$ has conditional event factor $f_\lambda(2)/S_\lambda(1)=\lambda e^{-2\lambda}/e^{-\lambda}=\lambda e^{-\lambda}$. A censored observation at $U=3$ has conditional event factor $S_\lambda(3)/S_\lambda(1)=e^{-2\lambda}$.

If instead the sample is right-truncated at $R=2$, the selected-sample density is $\lambda e^{-\lambda t}/(1-e^{-2\lambda})$ for $0\le t<2$, since $P(T<2)=F_\lambda(2)=1-e^{-2\lambda}$. This is a conditional event-time density, not a right-censoring contribution.

The censoring and truncation examples use different event factors: ordinary right censoring uses $f_\lambda(u)$ or $S_\lambda(u)$, delayed entry divides by $S_\lambda(1)$, and right truncation divides by $P(T<2)$.

citations.quote:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

For every $M\in\mathbb R$ there are $a,b>0$ such that

$$L(a)<M<L(b).$$

In particular, $L$ is unbounded both below and above.

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $X$ be a real random variable. Its **cumulative distribution function** is
the function
$$F_X:\mathbb R\to[0,1],\qquad F_X(x):=\mathbb P(X\le x)=\mathbb P_X((-\infty,x]).$$

The second expression is the same quantity written in terms of the law
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] of $X$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

1. Let $X$ be a real random variable, let $\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let
   $F_X(x)=\mathbb P(X\le x)$. Then $F_X$ is nondecreasing and right-continuous,
   satisfies
   $$\lim_{x\to-\infty}F_X(x)=0,\qquad \lim_{x\to+\infty}F_X(x)=1,$$
   and obeys
   $$\mathbb P_X((a,b])=F_X(b)-F_X(a)\qquad(a<b).$$
2. Conversely, if $F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is nondecreasing and
   right-continuous with
   $$\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0,\qquad \lim_{x\to+\infty}F(x)=1,$$
   then there is a unique Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$ such
   that
   $$\mu((a,b])=F(b)-F(a)\qquad(a<b),$$
   equivalently
   $$F(x)=\mu((-\infty,x])\qquad(x\in\mathbb R).$$

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Define $F_\lambda(t)=0$ for $t<0$ and $F_\lambda(t)=1-e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t\ge0$; define $F_{k,\eta}(t)=0$ for $t<0$ and $F_{k,\eta}(t)=1-e^{-(t/\eta)^k}$ for $t\ge0$. Both are continuous at $0$ by [F2], [F4], and [F5]. On $t>0$ their derivatives are the displayed densities and are positive by [F2]. The piecewise densities are Borel measurable: on $(0,\infty)$ they are products of continuous functions, and on $(-\infty,0]$ they vanish; both domains are Borel by [F11]. The mean value theorem in [F3] makes each increasing on $(0,\infty)$. For $t>0$, both $a=\lambda t$ and $a=(t/\eta)^k$ are positive, so strict increase of the exponential gives $e^{-a}<e^0=1$; hence both candidate CDFs are positive there; thus their value $0$ at $0$ is consistent with monotonicity. Their limits are $0$ at $-\infty$ and $1$ at $+\infty$, so each is a CDF on $\mathbb R$.

Fix $0<a<b$. Each CDF is differentiable on $[a,b]$ with the continuous derivative $f$ from the Statement. By [F6] its Riemann integral is $F(b)-F(a)$; by [F7] this equals its Lebesgue integral with respect to the measure in [F10]. Letting $a=1/n\downarrow0$ for integers $n$ large enough that $1/n<b$, [F8] and continuity at $0$ give $$\int_{(0,b]}f(u)\,du=F(b).$$ This applies separately to the exponential and Weibull formulas.

For either displayed nonnegative density $f$, [F1] defines the measure $
u_f=f\,dt$ on Lebesgue-measurable sets. By [F12], its restriction to Borel sets is a measure. Step 2.1 gives $
u_f((0,t])=F(t)$ for every $t>0$. Since $f=0$ on $(-\infty,0]$, this part has $
u_f$-measure zero, so $
u_f((-\infty,t])=F(t)$; for $t\le0$ both sides are $0$. Also $$
u_f(\mathbb R)=\lim_{n	o\infty}
u_f((-\infty,n])=\lim_{n	o\infty}F(n)=1$$ by [F8] and step 1.1. Thus $
u_f$ is a probability law with CDF $F$, and [F9] identifies it with the unique law specified by the survival formula. Consequently $f$ is the stated density.
Dividing the exponential density by its positive survival gives hazard $\lambda$. Dividing the Weibull density by its positive survival gives $\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}$ for $t>0$.
Steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, and 4.1 establish CDF validity, density-law existence, survival formulas, uniqueness, and the density hazards for both parameter families.
