citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes in
this definition are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$; the filtration is
neither assumed complete nor right-continuous. The Axiom of Choice is declared
because the conditional-expectation classes used in clause 3 are supplied by
the Radon--Nikodym interface of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]],
which assumes it; the countable-choice obligations inherited from that
interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

1. **Adapted.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when $X_t$
   is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$. This is exactly the notion
   of [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

2. **Stopped process.** For a stopping time $\tau$ for $(\mathcal F_t)$
   [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] the **stopped process** is
   $$X^{\tau}_t(\omega):=X_{t\wedge\tau(\omega)}(\omega),\qquad t\ge0,$$
   with the convention $t\wedge\infty:=t$, so no value $X_\infty$ is ever
   required and $X^\tau_0=X_0$ identically. This formula defines a pathwise
   family; adaptedness of $X$ alone does not assert measurability or
   adaptedness of its stopped values. If in addition $\tau\le c$ for a
   deterministic constant $c$, then $X^\tau_t=X_{t\wedge\tau}$, and only the
   values of $X$ on $[0,c]$ enter. Stopping at a stopping time is not the same
   as replacing a process by a modification; it is a pathwise operation.

3. **Martingale.** $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **martingale** (an all-pairs
   continuous-time martingale) relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted,
   $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$, and for all $0\le s\le t$
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
   The equality is an equality of the almost-everywhere classes of
   [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; equivalently, every version
   of the conditional expectation on the left equals $M_s$ off one null set.
   At $s=t$ the identity reduces to the known-variable case. The word
   "continuous-time" refers to the index set only and does not assert path
   continuity.

4. **Local martingale.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **local martingale** relative
   to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted, $E|X_0|<\infty$, and there exist stopping times
   $(\tau_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\tau_0\le\tau_1\le\cdots$ and
   $\tau_n\uparrow\infty$ almost surely such that for every $n\ge0$ the stopped process
   $$X^{\tau_n}-X_0=(X_{t\wedge\tau_n}-X_0)_{t\ge0}$$
   is a martingale in the sense of clause 3. The sequence $(\tau_n)$ is called
   a **localizing sequence**. Equivalently, every $X^{\tau_n}$ is a
   martingale: adaptedness makes the integrable variable $X_0$ measurable with
   respect to every $\mathcal F_t$, so the constant process with value $X_0$
   is a martingale and may be added to, or subtracted from, each stopped
   process. The centering merely makes every localized process start at $0$;
   apart from the required integrability of $X_0$, no claim is made that $X$
   is integrable at a positive deterministic time, and no claim is made that
   $X$ has continuous paths.

5. **Path and integrability attributes.** A process has **continuous paths**
   when $t\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega$
   in an event of probability one; the usual almost-sure path conventions of
   [[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]] apply. A
   martingale $M$ is **square-integrable** when $EM_t^2<\infty$ for every
   $t\ge0$, and **$L^2$-bounded** when $\sup_{t\ge0}EM_t^2<\infty$. These are
   properties of the single process under consideration, not of its versions:
   a modification of a martingale need not be adapted, so every later statement
   names the adapted versions it uses.

The following remarks specify what follows directly from this vocabulary.

1. **A martingale is a local martingale.** If $M$ is a martingale, the constant
   sequence $\tau_n:=n$, $n\ge0$, localizes it: the stopped process $M^{n}-M_0$ is again
   a martingale by the martingale identity applied at the deterministic times
   $s\wedge n\le t\wedge n$. The converse fails; a local martingale need not be
   a martingale, and no such implication is used in this development.
2. **Localization after a separately justified stopping operation.** Suppose
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X$, $\sigma$ is a stopping time, $X^\sigma$ is
   adapted, and each $(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$ is a martingale. Then
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X^\sigma$. Indeed it still increases to infinity,
   $(X^\sigma)_0=X_0$, and the pathwise identity
   $$(X^\sigma)^{\tau_n}-(X^\sigma)_0=X^{\sigma\wedge\tau_n}-X_0=(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$$
   verifies exactly clause 4. The stopped-piece martingale assertion and
   adaptedness are hypotheses here, not consequences of the unrestricted
   all-pairs definition. They must be established in each application.
   The sequence $(\sigma\wedge\tau_n)$ is not a substitute for $(\tau_n)$:
   its almost-sure limit is $\sigma$, which need not be infinity.

No path continuity, no right continuity of the filtration, and no completeness
of the underlying probability space is imposed by this definition. Choice
enters only through the conditional-expectation interface named above,
whose countable-choice obligations are declared as dependencies of this item.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a continuous-time filtration
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

1. A map $\tau:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ (infinite values allowed) is a **stopping
   time** for $(\mathcal F_t)$ when
   $$\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0 .$$
2. For a stopping time $\tau$ its **stopped sigma-algebra** is
   $$\mathcal F_\tau:=\{A\in\mathcal F:A\cap\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t \text{ for every }t\ge0\}.$$

The following facts are used below, and each is a direct set computation.

(a) $\mathcal F_\tau$ is a sigma-algebra: $\emptyset\cap\{\tau\le
    t\}=\emptyset\in\mathcal F_t$; for $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ one has
    $A^c\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\{\tau\le t\}\setminus(A\cap\{\tau\le t\})\in\mathcal
    F_t$; and for a sequence $A_n\in\mathcal F_\tau$ the union satisfies
    $\bigl(\bigcup_nA_n\bigr)\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcup_n(A_n\cap\{\tau\le
    t\})\in\mathcal F_t$. All operations are literal, not modulo null sets, and
    no completeness of the filtration is assumed.
(b) If $\tau\equiv t_0<\infty$ is deterministic, then
    $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}$ is $A$ for $t\ge t_0$ and $\emptyset$ for $t<t_0$, so
    $\mathcal F_\tau=\bigcap_{t\ge t_0}\mathcal F_t=\mathcal F_{t_0}$, where
    the last equality follows because the intersection includes its least
    member $\mathcal F_{t_0}$. If $\tau\equiv\infty$, then every test event
    $\{\tau\le t\}$ is empty and $\mathcal F_\tau=\mathcal F$.
(c) Suppose the filtration is right-continuous. Then $\tau$ is a stopping time
    if and only if $\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for every $t>0$. Indeed
    $$\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\}$$
    (with the terms for $t-\tfrac1n<0$ read as the empty set, since
    $\tau\ge0$), which gives the forward implication; conversely
    $$\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\},$$
    and $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\bigcap_{s>t}\mathcal F_s=\mathcal F_t$ by
    right-continuity together with monotonicity of the filtration.
(d) Under the same right-continuity assumption, for $A\in\mathcal F$ one has
    $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ if and only if $A\cap\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for
    every $t>0$: the forward implication follows from
    $A\cap\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_n(A\cap\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\})$ and the converse
    from $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_n(A\cap\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\})$ together with
    $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\mathcal F_t$.

Because the two versions of each test are interchangeable exactly when the
filtration is right-continuous, the convention is recorded here once: the
Brownian strong Markov theorem is stated for the usual augmentation, which is
right-continuous, and the raw-filtration statements use the non-strict test
directly. No choice principle is used by this definition.
Assume AC. If $M$ is a martingale then $(|M_n|)$ is a submartingale. More generally, for real $p\ge1$, if $E|M_n|^p<\infty$ for every $n\ge0$, then $(|M_n|^p)$ is a submartingale. We use $0^p=0$.

Assume AC. Let $N\in\mathbb N_0$, $p>1$, and $q=p/(p-1)$. If $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a nonnegative submartingale and $X_N\in L^p$, then
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}X_k\right\|_p\le q\|X_N\|_p.$$
In particular, for a martingale $M$ with $M_N\in L^p$,
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}|M_k|\right\|_p\le q\|M_N\|_p.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Let $\pi_n$ be nested finite partitions of $[0,T]$ containing any fixed $s,t$ with mesh tending to zero. For each $\pi_n$, the values of $|M|$ on its grid form a discrete-time nonnegative submartingale by [F1, F3]. The Doob bound gives $\mathbb E\max_{u\in\pi_n}|M_u|^2\le4\mathbb E|M_T|^2$. Càdlàg paths and the nested dense grids imply $\sup_{u\le T}|M_u|=\sup_{u\in\cup_n\pi_n}|M_u|$; [F5] then gives $\mathbb E\sup_{u\le T}|M_u|^2<\infty$.

For a finite partition $\pi_n=\{r_0<\cdots<r_m\}$, round $\tau$ up to the first grid point $\tau_n\ge\tau$. This is a finite-valued stopping time because $\{\tau_n\le r_j\}=\{\tau\le r_j\}\in\mathcal F_{r_j}$. At adjacent grid points, $M_{r_k\wedge\tau_n}-M_{r_{k-1}\wedge\tau_n}=\mathbf1_{\{\tau_n>r_{k-1}\}}(M_{r_k}-M_{r_{k-1}})$; the indicator is $\mathcal F_{r_{k-1}}$-measurable. Conditioning each increment on its left endpoint proves the stopped grid values have the martingale identity at grid times, in particular at $s,t$.

Refine the partitions while keeping $s,t$ as grid points. Then $\tau_n\downarrow\tau$, and pathwise right continuity gives $M_{s\wedge\tau_n}\to M_{s\wedge\tau}$ and $M_{t\wedge\tau_n}\to M_{t\wedge\tau}$. For $u=s$ or $u=t$, the events $\{\tau_n=r_j\}$ with grid value $r_j<u$ lie in $\mathcal F_{r_j}\subseteq\mathcal F_u$, and their complement $\{\tau_n\ge u\}$ is also in $\mathcal F_u$; expressing $M_{u\wedge\tau_n}$ over these finitely many events proves $\mathcal F_u$-measurability. The pointwise limits are then measurable there without completing the filtration. Both are dominated by $\sup_{u\le T}|M_u|$, integrable by step 1.1. For each $B\in\mathcal F_s$, apply [F4] to the event-integral martingale identity from step 1.2; it yields $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B(M_{t\wedge\tau}-M_{s\wedge\tau})]=0$, hence the stopped process satisfies the all-pairs martingale identity. Also $|M_{t\wedge\tau}|\le\sup_{u\le T}|M_u|$ gives square integrability.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.

indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,

$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1 \le p < \infty$. Then

filtration $(\mathcal F_t)$, with $D_0=0$. Suppose each path has finite total

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes in
this definition are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$; the filtration is
neither assumed complete nor right-continuous. The Axiom of Choice is declared
because the conditional-expectation classes used in clause 3 are supplied by
the Radon--Nikodym interface of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]],
which assumes it; the countable-choice obligations inherited from that
interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

1. **Adapted.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when $X_t$
   is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$. This is exactly the notion
   of [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

2. **Stopped process.** For a stopping time $\tau$ for $(\mathcal F_t)$
   [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] the **stopped process** is
   $$X^{\tau}_t(\omega):=X_{t\wedge\tau(\omega)}(\omega),\qquad t\ge0,$$
   with the convention $t\wedge\infty:=t$, so no value $X_\infty$ is ever
   required and $X^\tau_0=X_0$ identically. This formula defines a pathwise
   family; adaptedness of $X$ alone does not assert measurability or
   adaptedness of its stopped values. If in addition $\tau\le c$ for a
   deterministic constant $c$, then $X^\tau_t=X_{t\wedge\tau}$, and only the
   values of $X$ on $[0,c]$ enter. Stopping at a stopping time is not the same
   as replacing a process by a modification; it is a pathwise operation.

3. **Martingale.** $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **martingale** (an all-pairs
   continuous-time martingale) relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted,
   $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$, and for all $0\le s\le t$
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
   The equality is an equality of the almost-everywhere classes of
   [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; equivalently, every version
   of the conditional expectation on the left equals $M_s$ off one null set.
   At $s=t$ the identity reduces to the known-variable case. The word
   "continuous-time" refers to the index set only and does not assert path
   continuity.

4. **Local martingale.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **local martingale** relative
   to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted, $E|X_0|<\infty$, and there exist stopping times
   $(\tau_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\tau_0\le\tau_1\le\cdots$ and
   $\tau_n\uparrow\infty$ almost surely such that for every $n\ge0$ the stopped process
   $$X^{\tau_n}-X_0=(X_{t\wedge\tau_n}-X_0)_{t\ge0}$$
   is a martingale in the sense of clause 3. The sequence $(\tau_n)$ is called
   a **localizing sequence**. Equivalently, every $X^{\tau_n}$ is a
   martingale: adaptedness makes the integrable variable $X_0$ measurable with
   respect to every $\mathcal F_t$, so the constant process with value $X_0$
   is a martingale and may be added to, or subtracted from, each stopped
   process. The centering merely makes every localized process start at $0$;
   apart from the required integrability of $X_0$, no claim is made that $X$
   is integrable at a positive deterministic time, and no claim is made that
   $X$ has continuous paths.

5. **Path and integrability attributes.** A process has **continuous paths**
   when $t\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega$
   in an event of probability one; the usual almost-sure path conventions of
   [[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]] apply. A
   martingale $M$ is **square-integrable** when $EM_t^2<\infty$ for every
   $t\ge0$, and **$L^2$-bounded** when $\sup_{t\ge0}EM_t^2<\infty$. These are
   properties of the single process under consideration, not of its versions:
   a modification of a martingale need not be adapted, so every later statement
   names the adapted versions it uses.

The following remarks specify what follows directly from this vocabulary.

1. **A martingale is a local martingale.** If $M$ is a martingale, the constant
   sequence $\tau_n:=n$, $n\ge0$, localizes it: the stopped process $M^{n}-M_0$ is again
   a martingale by the martingale identity applied at the deterministic times
   $s\wedge n\le t\wedge n$. The converse fails; a local martingale need not be
   a martingale, and no such implication is used in this development.
2. **Localization after a separately justified stopping operation.** Suppose
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X$, $\sigma$ is a stopping time, $X^\sigma$ is
   adapted, and each $(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$ is a martingale. Then
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X^\sigma$. Indeed it still increases to infinity,
   $(X^\sigma)_0=X_0$, and the pathwise identity
   $$(X^\sigma)^{\tau_n}-(X^\sigma)_0=X^{\sigma\wedge\tau_n}-X_0=(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$$
   verifies exactly clause 4. The stopped-piece martingale assertion and
   adaptedness are hypotheses here, not consequences of the unrestricted
   all-pairs definition. They must be established in each application.
   The sequence $(\sigma\wedge\tau_n)$ is not a substitute for $(\tau_n)$:
   its almost-sure limit is $\sigma$, which need not be infinity.

Two processes with the same index set and corresponding target spaces have the
same **process law** if all corresponding finite-dimensional laws agree; their
source probability spaces need not be the same. Suppose in addition that

probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, take values in the same
measurable space at each $t$, and $\{X_t=Y_t\}$ is measurable for each $t$.

$\mathbb P(X_t=Y_t)=1$ for every fixed $t$. They are **indistinguishable**
when the event
$\{\omega:X_t(\omega)=Y_t(\omega)\text{ for every }t\in I\}$ is measurable
and has probability one. The latter has one exceptional null event; the former
may have a different null event at every time.

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

Work on the finite horizon $[0,T]$ of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]. For càdlàg
(right-continuous with left limits) finite-variation processes $X,Y$ starting
at zero, with $\Delta X_s:=X_s-X_{s-}$ and $\Delta Y_s:=Y_s-Y_{s-}$, define
their **optional quadratic covariation** by
$$[X,Y]_t:=\sum_{0<s\le t}\Delta X_s\,\Delta Y_s,$$
and write $[X]:=[X,X]$. The series is absolutely convergent because each path
has finite variation. This is the jump-sum convention for optional brackets
used on this page.

For a square-integrable model martingale $M=N-A$ from
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]], a **continuous
predictable bracket** $\langle M\rangle$ is a continuous, predictable,
increasing process $B$ with $B_0=0$, $\mathbb E[B_T]<\infty$, and $M^2-B$ a
martingale, when such a process exists. For two square-integrable model
martingales $M=N-A$ and $M'=N'-A'$ from that contract, a **continuous
predictable cross bracket** $\langle M,M'\rangle$ is a continuous, predictable
finite-variation process $C$ with $C_0=0$, $\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(C)_T
<\infty$, and $[M,M']-C$ a martingale, when such a process exists. The
uniqueness lemma below fixes the meaning of “the” bracket in this continuous
compensator class. No general bracket-existence theorem is asserted.
The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the model martingale's
conditional-expectation interface; this definition makes no further choice.

Let $a\le b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). If $a<b$ and
$P=(n,t)$ is a partition of $[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]), the
**variation of $f$ over $P$** is

$$V(f,P):=\sum_{i<n}|f(t_{i+1})-f(t_i)|.$$

The sum is finite ([[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]) and nonnegative
([[def-abs-value]]). The set of all such sums is nonempty, since $[a,b]$ has the
partition with point set $\{a,b\}$. The function $f$ has **bounded variation**
on $[a,b]$ when this set of sums is bounded above ([[def-bounded-set]]). In that
case its **total variation** is

$$\operatorname{Var}_{[a,b]}(f):=\sup_P V(f,P).$$

Completeness of $\mathbb R$ gives this supremum and [[lem-sup-unique]] makes it
unique ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). On a singleton interval, by convention,
$\operatorname{Var}_{[a,a]}(f):=0$; no partition from
[[def-partition-and-refinement]], whose standing hypothesis is $a<b$, is invoked.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$. Then the closed bounded interval
$[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) is compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]): every family of
open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ whose union contains $[a,b]$ has a finite subfamily
whose union already contains $[a,b]$.

The proof is by repeated bisection. Supposing some open cover admits no finite
subcover, one halves the interval, keeps a half that still admits none, and
iterates; the halves shrink to a point, which the cover does reach, and a single
member of the cover then swallows a whole late-stage half. **The halving rule is
canonical**, taking the left half whenever the left half works, so the recursion
uses [[thm-recursion]] and no choice principle.

Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]) and let
$f : K \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $K$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$
is uniformly continuous on $K$ ([[def-uniform-continuity-real]]).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], proved there from the cover machinery of
metric spaces; the proof below uses the open-cover definition of compactness
in $\mathbb{R}$ directly. That the two
statements are the same statement in two vocabularies is
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], clauses 1, 2 and 5, immediately above.

**Choice-free proof.** The argument below uses the open-cover definition of compactness directly. It considers every continuity neighbourhood at once and extracts only a finite subcover, so no countable or global choice function is selected.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

derivations.claim: For finitely many distinct jump times $0<s_1<\cdots<s_q\le T$, choose disjoint intervals $(u_i,s_i]$ with $u_i\uparrow s_i$. A partition containing all their endpoints has variation at least $\sum_i|x_{s_i}-x_{u_i}|$, so [F2] and the left limits give $\sum_i|\Delta x_{s_i}|\le\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(x)$. Hence each set of jumps of size at least $1/m$ is finite, in its canonical time order, and the nonzero jumps form a countable set with $\sum_{0<s\le T}|\Delta x_s|\le\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(x)$. Let $J_t=\sum_{0<s\le t}\Delta x_s$. Absolute convergence makes omitted jump tails uniformly small, so finite jump partial sums converge uniformly to a path $J$; right continuity passes by an $\varepsilon/3$ estimate, and their left limits are Cauchy under the uniform tail bound, so completeness of $\mathbb R$ gives left limits for $J$. Absolute convergence gives $\Delta J_s=\Delta x_s$. For any partition, each increment of $J$ is a subseries of its jumps, so $\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(J)\le\sum_{0<s\le T}|\Delta x_s|$; the same argument bounds the variation of any omitted jump tail by its absolute sum. Therefore $x^c:=x-J$ is continuous and of finite variation. Choose a finite retained jump sum $z$ with omitted tail $r:=J-z$ satisfying $\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(r)<\varepsilon$, and set $y=x-r=x^c+z$. By [F3] and [F4], the continuous part has squared-increment sum at most $\omega_{x^c}(\|\pi_n\|)\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(x^c)\to0$, where $\omega_{x^c}(\delta):=\sup_{|u-v|\le\delta}|x^c_u-x^c_v|$; sufficiently fine partitions separate the finitely many retained jump times, so $\sum_j(\Delta_j^n y(t))^2$ tends to the sum of their squared jumps, with cross terms between each retained jump and the continuous increment in its partition cell tending to zero by the same modulus.

For every partition, expansion of squares and [F5] give $|\sum_j(\Delta_j^n x(t))^2-\sum_j(\Delta_j^n y(t))^2|\le2\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(y)\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(r)+\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(r)^2\le2\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(x)\varepsilon+3\varepsilon^2$, since $\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(y)\le\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(x)+\varepsilon$. Also $x=y+r$ gives $\Delta x_s=\Delta y_s+\Delta r_s$; applying the same finite-list expansion and [F5] to the jump sums, then using their absolute convergence [F1], yields $|[x]_t-[y]_t|\le2\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(y)\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(r)+\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(r)^2\le2\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(x)\varepsilon+3\varepsilon^2$. Letting $\varepsilon\to0$ proves $\sum_j(\Delta_j^n x(t))^2\to\sum_{0<s\le t}(\Delta x_s)^2$.

For every finite partition, telescoping differences of squares gives $x_t^2-x_0^2=2\sum_jx_{t\wedge t_j^n}\Delta_j^n x(t)+\sum_j(\Delta_j^n x(t))^2$. Step 2.1 gives the limit of the second sum, and rearrangement gives the stated limit of the left-endpoint sums.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a finite horizon
$T>0$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
For this model and every nonnegative predictable process $G$, define the
pathwise energy integral by
$$\int_0^tG_s\,dA_s:=\int_0^tG_sY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires the defining
integral for $A$ to be finite pathwise, and requires $A$ to be continuous,
adapted and predictable with
$A_0=0$, and that $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$. Set $M_t:=N_t-A_t$. The model
contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

The displayed intensity density alone does **not** assert that $N-A$ is a
martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.

at zero, with $\Delta X_s:=X_s-X_{s-}$ and $\Delta Y_s:=Y_s-Y_{s-}$, define
their **optional quadratic covariation** by
$$[X,Y]_t:=\sum_{0<s\le t}\Delta X_s\,\Delta Y_s,$$
and write $[X]:=[X,X]$. The series is absolutely convergent because each path
has finite variation. This is the jump-sum convention for optional brackets
used on this page.

For a square-integrable model martingale $M=N-A$ from
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]], a **continuous
predictable bracket** $\langle M\rangle$ is a continuous, predictable,
increasing process $B$ with $B_0=0$, $\mathbb E[B_T]<\infty$, and $M^2-B$ a
martingale, when such a process exists. For two square-integrable model
martingales $M=N-A$ and $M'=N'-A'$ from that contract, a **continuous
predictable cross bracket** $\langle M,M'\rangle$ is a continuous, predictable
finite-variation process $C$ with $C_0=0$, $\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(C)_T
<\infty$, and $[M,M']-C$ a martingale, when such a process exists. The
uniqueness lemma below fixes the meaning of “the” bracket in this continuous
compensator class. No general bracket-existence theorem is asserted.
The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the model martingale's
conditional-expectation interface; this definition makes no further choice.

Let $M$ be any square-integrable martingale on $[0,T]$, and let $H$ be a
bounded predictable step integrand on a deterministic partition. The elementary integral
$(I_t(H))_{0\le t\le T}$ of
[[def-elementary-predictable-counting-process-integral]] is a
square-integrable martingale.

Let $x:[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be càdlàg (right-continuous with left limits) and of finite total variation. For any
deterministic partitions $\pi_n$ of $[0,T]$ with mesh tending to zero, and
each fixed $t\le T$, put $\Delta_j^n x(t)=x_{t\wedge t_{j+1}^n}-x_{t\wedge t_j^n}$.
Then
$$\sum_j(\Delta_j^n x(t))^2\longrightarrow [x]_t:=\sum_{0<s\le t}(\Delta x_s)^2,$$
and the left-endpoint sums satisfy
$$\sum_jx_{t\wedge t_j^n}\,\Delta_j^n x(t)\longrightarrow\frac{x_t^2-x_0^2-[x]_t}{2}.$$

Let $M=(M_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a square-integrable all-pairs martingale with
right-continuous paths with left limits for every $\omega$, and let $\tau\le T$
be a stopping time. Then the stopped process
$M^\tau_t:=M_{t\wedge\tau}$ is a square-integrable martingale on $[0,T]$.

Assume AC. Let $N\in\mathbb N_0$, $p>1$, and $q=p/(p-1)$. If $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a nonnegative submartingale and $X_N\in L^p$, then
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}X_k\right\|_p\le q\|X_N\|_p.$$
In particular, for a martingale $M$ with $M_N\in L^p$,
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}|M_k|\right\|_p\le q\|M_N\|_p.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Since $A$ is continuous, $\Delta M_s=\Delta N_s$; each jump of $N$ is zero or one, so the jump-square definition gives $[M]_t=\sum_{0<s\le t}(\Delta N_s)^2=N_t$, using $N_0=0$.

Let $S=N+A$ and $\tau_n=\inf\{t:S_t\ge n\}\wedge T$ for integers $n\ge1$. The adapted nondecreasing càdlàg process $S$ satisfies $\{\tau_n\le t\}=\{S_t\ge n\}$ for $t<T$, so $\tau_n$ is bounded stopping; at the first crossing, continuity of $A$ and unit jumps of $N$ give $S_{\tau_n}\le n+1$, hence $|M_{t\wedge\tau_n}|\le n+1$. By [F5], $M^{\tau_n}$ is a square-integrable martingale.

The variables $M_T$ and $A_T$ are integrable, so $N_T=M_T+A_T$ is integrable; since $M$ is a martingale starting at zero, $\mathbb E N_T=\mathbb E A_T<\infty$. The pathwise total variation of $M$ is at most $N_T+A_T$, hence is integrable.

Choose nested deterministic partitions $\pi_m=\{0=t_0^m<\cdots<t_{q_m}^m=T\}$ with mesh tending to zero. The coefficients $H_j^{n,m}=M_{t_j^m\wedge\tau_n}$ are $\mathcal F_{t_j^m}$-measurable and bounded by $n+1$, so [F3] makes the step integral against $M^{\tau_n}$ a martingale. The partition identity [F4] gives $(M_{t\wedge\tau_n})^2-\sum_j(M_{t\wedge t_{j+1}^m\wedge\tau_n}-M_{t\wedge t_j^m\wedge\tau_n})^2=2I_t(H^{n,m})$. The stopped process has the same unit jumps as $N^{\tau_n}$, so the squared-increment sum converges to $[M^{\tau_n}]_t=N_{t\wedge\tau_n}$ by [F4] and step 1.1. Also $\operatorname{Var}(M^{\tau_n})_T\le N_{T\wedge\tau_n}+A_{T\wedge\tau_n}\le n+1$, so the terms are bounded by a deterministic constant depending only on $n$; dominated convergence in the martingale event identities proves $(M_{t\wedge\tau_n})^2-N_{t\wedge\tau_n}$ is a martingale.

Since $S_T=N_T+A_T<\infty$ a.s., $\tau_n=T$ eventually on each path. On nested deterministic grids, [F6] gives $\mathbb E\max_{u\in\pi_m}|M_u|^2\le4\mathbb E|M_T|^2$; right continuity identifies the increasing grid limit with $\sup_{u\le T}|M_u|$, and [F8] gives $\mathbb E\sup_{u\le T}|M_u|^2<\infty$. Thus $R=\sup_{u\le T}|M_u|^2+N_T$ is integrable and dominates every stopped value $|(M_{t\wedge\tau_n})^2-N_{t\wedge\tau_n}|$. For $B\in\mathcal F_s$, [F7] and the event identities from step 2.2 let $n\to\infty$, proving $M^2-N$ is a martingale.

Since $N-A=M$ is a martingale, $M^2-A=(M^2-N)+M$ is a martingale by step 3.1 and linearity, so [F2] and [F1] make $A$ a scalar bracket candidate; uniqueness gives $\langle M\rangle=A$. Also $[M,M]=[M]=N$, so $[M,M]-A=N-A=M$ is a martingale, making $A$ a cross-bracket candidate too; uniqueness gives $\langle M,M\rangle=A$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a finite horizon
$T>0$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
For this model and every nonnegative predictable process $G$, define the
pathwise energy integral by
$$\int_0^tG_s\,dA_s:=\int_0^tG_sY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires the defining
integral for $A$ to be finite pathwise, and requires $A$ to be continuous,
adapted and predictable with
$A_0=0$, and that $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$. Set $M_t:=N_t-A_t$. The model
contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

The displayed intensity density alone does **not** assert that $N-A$ is a
martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.

Under the finite-horizon contract of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]], the optional
quadratic variation of $M=N-A$ is $[M]_t=N_t$, its continuous predictable
bracket is $\langle M\rangle_t=A_t$, its self-cross predictable bracket is
$\langle M,M\rangle_t=A_t$, and $M_t^2-A_t$ is a martingale on $[0,T]$.

Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale on a finite horizon $[0,T]$ in the
all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] (in particular, it may
be the compensated counting-process martingale of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]). Let
$$0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T$$

integrand** is $H_0=0$ at time $0$ and $H_s=H_j$ on $(t_j,t_{j+1}]$. For this
chosen step representation define, for $0\le t\le T$,

representation is part of the input; representation independence and the
isometry are established in
[[lem-elementary-counting-process-integral-isometry]].

conditional-expectation interface; the finite-sum definition makes no
additional choice.

bounded predictable step integrand on a deterministic partition. The elementary integral
$(I_t(H))_{0\le t\le T}$ of
[[def-elementary-predictable-counting-process-integral]] is a
square-integrable martingale.

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

derivations.claim: On each $(t_j,t_{j+1}]$, write $\Delta M_j=M_{t_{j+1}}-M_{t_j}$ and $\Delta A_j=A_{t_{j+1}}-A_{t_j}$. derivations.claim: By [F2], choose bounded predictable step processes $H_n$ with $\mathbb E\int_0^T|H_n-H|^2dA\to0$. For any $m,n$, [F1] gives $\mathbb E|I_T(H_n)-I_T(H_m)|^2=\mathbb E\int_0^T|H_n-H_m|^2dA$, so terminal integrals are Cauchy in $L^2(P)$; the same estimate on $[0,t]$ gives the Cauchy property at every $t\le T$. If $K_n$ is another step sequence converging to $H$, then $\mathbb E\int_0^T|H_n-K_n|^2dA\to0$. Applying [F1] to $H_n-K_n$ makes the terminal limits and each fixed-time limit equal in $L^2$, so the limits in [F5] are independent of approximation.

Norm continuity and [F1] give, for every $t\le T$, $\mathbb E|I_t(H)|^2=\lim_n\mathbb E|I_t(H_n)|^2=\lim_n\mathbb E\int_0^tH_{n,s}^2dA_s=\mathbb E\int_0^tH_s^2dA_s$. This proves square integrability and the isometry.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.

indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic

indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

On dyadic partitions, left-step processes with value $N_{t_j}$ on $(t_j,t_{j+1}]$ are predictable by [F1] and converge pointwise to $N_{t-}$ for each $t>0$, so the left-limit process on $(0,T]$ is predictable. Direct integration gives $A_t=\lambda((t-L)^+\wedge W)$, so $A$ is continuous and increasing, $A_0=0$, and $A_t\le\lambda T$. Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a finite horizon
$T>0$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
For this model and every nonnegative predictable process $G$, define the
pathwise energy integral by
$$\int_0^tG_s\,dA_s:=\int_0^tG_sY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires the defining
integral for $A$ to be finite pathwise, and requires $A$ to be continuous,
adapted and predictable with
$A_0=0$, and that $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$. Set $M_t:=N_t-A_t$. The model
contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

The displayed intensity density alone does **not** assert that $N-A$ is a
martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.

Under the finite-horizon contract of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]], the optional
quadratic variation of $M=N-A$ is $[M]_t=N_t$, its continuous predictable
bracket is $\langle M\rangle_t=A_t$, its self-cross predictable bracket is
$\langle M,M\rangle_t=A_t$, and $M_t^2-A_t$ is a martingale on $[0,T]$.

Work on the finite horizon $[0,T]$ of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]. For càdlàg
(right-continuous with left limits) finite-variation processes $X,Y$ starting
at zero, with $\Delta X_s:=X_s-X_{s-}$ and $\Delta Y_s:=Y_s-Y_{s-}$, define
their **optional quadratic covariation** by
$$[X,Y]_t:=\sum_{0<s\le t}\Delta X_s\,\Delta Y_s,$$
and write $[X]:=[X,X]$. The series is absolutely convergent because each path
has finite variation. This is the jump-sum convention for optional brackets
used on this page.

For a square-integrable model martingale $M=N-A$ from
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]], a **continuous
predictable bracket** $\langle M\rangle$ is a continuous, predictable,
increasing process $B$ with $B_0=0$, $\mathbb E[B_T]<\infty$, and $M^2-B$ a
martingale, when such a process exists. For two square-integrable model
martingales $M=N-A$ and $M'=N'-A'$ from that contract, a **continuous
predictable cross bracket** $\langle M,M'\rangle$ is a continuous, predictable
finite-variation process $C$ with $C_0=0$, $\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(C)_T
<\infty$, and $[M,M']-C$ a martingale, when such a process exists. The
uniqueness lemma below fixes the meaning of “the” bracket in this continuous
compensator class. No general bracket-existence theorem is asserted.
The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the model martingale's
conditional-expectation interface; this definition makes no further choice.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $I$ be an index
set, and let $(\mathcal C_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of classes of events
$\mathcal C_i\subseteq\mathcal F$.

The family $(\mathcal C_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when for every natural
number $n\ge1$, every choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}\in I$, and
every choice of events $A_k\in\mathcal C_{i_k}$, one has

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_k\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_k).$$

Thus independence is a finite-subfamily condition. In particular, the empty
family and every one-member family are independent.

Fix a law $P$ and an iid sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P$. For a measurable vector function $\varphi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$, write $P\varphi=E_P[\varphi(X)]$ and $P_n\varphi=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\varphi(X_i)$, where $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}$ is the empirical measure. For a vector remainder $R_n$, $R_n=o_P(n^{-1/2})$ means $\sqrt n R_n\to0$ in $P$-probability.

A measurable estimator sequence $\widehat\psi_n$ of $\psi(P)\in\mathbb R^k$ is **asymptotically linear at $P$** with **estimator influence function** $\varphi$ if

$$\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P)=(P_n-P)\varphi+o_P(n^{-1/2}),$$

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$

$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $I$ be an index
set, and let $(\mathcal C_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of classes of events
$\mathcal C_i\subseteq\mathcal F$.

The family $(\mathcal C_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when for every natural
number $n\ge1$, every choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}\in I$, and
every choice of events $A_k\in\mathcal C_{i_k}$, one has

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_k\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_k).$$

Thus independence is a finite-subfamily condition. In particular, the empty
family and every one-member family are independent.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a finite $G\ge2$ and $d\ge1$. For each total sample size $n$, let $n_1,\ldots,n_G$ be positive deterministic integers with $\sum_{g=1}^G n_g=n$, and suppose $n_g/n\to\rho_g\in(0,1)$ with $\sum_{g=1}^G\rho_g=1$. If a measurable estimator of fixed $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$ has the separately established expansion, with remainder on the same sample probability space as its group sums,

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)=\sum_{g=1}^G\sqrt{\frac n{n_g}}\frac1{\sqrt{n_g}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\phi_g(O_{gi})+R_n,\qquad R_n=o_P(1),$$

then

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\Rightarrow N_d\!\left(0,\sum_{g=1}^G\rho_g^{-1}\Sigma_g\right).$$

An **event time** is a measurable real-valued map $T$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. A **covariate** is a measurable map $Z$ into a specified standard-Borel space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal B)$, where standard Borel means measurably isomorphic to a Polish space ([[def-standard-borel-space]]). A **censoring or inspection time** is a measurable real-valued map $C$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. When conditional laws are used, they are probability kernels $K_T(z,\cdot)$ and $K_C(z,\cdot)$ in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]] and [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. They are part of the specified model; their existence for real-valued targets and factorization through standard-Borel $Z$ follow under [[def-axiom-of-choice]] from [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]].

The notation $T\perp\!\!\!\perp C\mid\sigma(Z)$ has the meaning in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: for bounded measurable $a,b$, $\mathbb E[a(T)b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]=\mathbb E[a(T)\mid\sigma(Z)]\mathbb E[b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]$ almost surely. It is a model assumption about the conditional observation law, not a consequence of adjusting for $Z$ and not an empirical conclusion.

Under **right censoring**, the recorded pair is $U=\min(T,C)$ and $\delta=1\{T\le C\}$. Thus $\delta=1$ records an event at $U=T$, including a tie, while $\delta=0$ records censoring at $U=C$ and implies $T>C$. **Left censoring** at a known threshold $L$ records only $T\le L$. **Interval censoring** at known endpoints $L<R$ records $L<T\le R$. **Current-status observation** at an inspection time $C$ records only $\delta_C=1\{T\le C\}$.

**Left truncation**, also called delayed entry at $L$, selects a unit into the sample only when $T>L$; observation begins after that selection. **Right truncation** at $R$ selects a unit only when $T<R$. These are selection rules before the observed sample is formed, whereas censoring coarsens an event time after sampling. The strict and weak inequalities in these definitions fix the endpoint conventions. A random observation endpoint is called noninformative here only when it is fixed by design or is generated independently of $T$ conditional on the stated covariates under a parameter-distinct law; otherwise its joint observation law must be modeled.

For a positive integer sample size $n$, let $(T_i,C_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be event and censoring times with right-censored observations $(U_i,\delta_i)$ as in [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]], so $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=\mathbf 1\{T_i\le C_i\}$. The subject counting process and at-risk process are $N_i(t)=\mathbf 1\{U_i\le t,\ \delta_i=1\}$ and $Y_i(t)=\mathbf 1\{U_i\ge t\}$.
The endpoint convention makes $Y_i$ left-continuous at $U_i$: a subject is still at risk at the observed time, including a tied event and censoring time. Set $N_n=\sum_{i=1}^nN_i$ and $Y_n=\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Let $dN_n$ be the finite counting measure of observed events on $[0,\infty)$, with atom $\Delta N_n(u):=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{U_i=u,\ \delta_i=1\}$ at each $u\ge0$; in particular, $\Delta N_n(0)=N_n(0)$. Tied failures at $u$ contribute their full count and censorings at $u$ do not contribute to $dN_n(u)$.

For $t\ge0$, the **Nelson–Aalen estimator** is $\widehat\Lambda_n(t)=\int_{[0,t]}\frac{\mathbf 1\{Y_n(u)>0\}}{Y_n(u)}\,dN_n(u)$, where the integrand is defined to be zero when $Y_n(u)=0$. The **Kaplan–Meier estimator** is $\widehat S_n(t)=\prod_{\substack{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N_n(u)>0}}\left(1-\frac{\Delta N_n(u)}{Y_n(u)}\right)$.
Each product is finite and a factor is zero if every subject at risk fails at that time. The target survival function is $S(t)=P(T>t)$. If $T$ has density $f$, $S$ is positive on the horizon, and $\lambda=f/S$, the continuous cumulative hazard is $\Lambda(t)=\int_0^t\lambda(u)\,du=-\log S(t)$.

These inclusive endpoint formulas reduce to the usual $(0,t]$ formulas whenever $\Delta N_n(0)=0$. If $T$ has finite support $0\le a_1<\cdots<a_m$, write $q_j=P(T=a_j\mid T\ge a_j)$; the corresponding discrete cumulative hazard is $\Lambda_d(t)=\sum_{a_j\le t}q_j$. Under IID sampling, independent censoring, and positive risk probability at the support points, the Nelson–Aalen increments estimate these $q_j$; in general this discrete cumulative hazard is not $-\log S(t)$.

An empty event product is $1$, and an empty Greenwood event sum is $0$.

They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

For a positive integer sample size $n$, let $(T_i,C_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be event and censoring times with right-censored observations $(U_i,\delta_i)$ as in [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]], so $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=\mathbf 1\{T_i\le C_i\}$. On each interval between successive support points, the estimators and their targets are constant, so the same limits hold at the given $t$. derivations.claim: Put $V_i=-U_i$, let $F(x)=P(V_i\le x)$, and let $F_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{V_i\le x\}$. Then $\bar Y_n(u)=F_n(-u)$ and $s_0(u)=F(-u)$. Thus both suprema are measurable. Fix $0<\varepsilon<1$. Choose the finitely many distinct quantiles $x_k=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge k\varepsilon\}$ for $1\le k<1/\varepsilon$, together with $x_0=-\infty$ and $x_{m+1}=+\infty$, where $m$ is the number of distinct finite cutpoints. Between consecutive distinct quantiles $x_j<x_{j+1}$, the quantile construction gives $F(x_{j+1}-)-F(x_j)\le\varepsilon$; any jump at a cutpoint is isolated as its singleton point. At each finite cutpoint, both $F_n(x_j)$ and $F_n(x_j-)$ converge in probability to their expectations by Chebyshev's inequality applied to the IID indicators $\mathbf 1\{V_i\le x_j\}$ and $\mathbf 1\{V_i<x_j\}$. For $x\in(x_j,x_{j+1})$, monotonicity gives $F_n(x_j)\le F_n(x)\le F_n(x_{j+1}-)$ and $F(x_j)\le F(x)\le F(x_{j+1}-)$; hence $|F_n(x)-F(x)|$ is at most the largest one-sided endpoint error plus $\varepsilon$. At singleton cutpoints, direct endpoint convergence applies. Taking the maximum over the finite partition, then $n\to\infty$ and $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, proves the first convergence.

Let $Z_n=\sup_{0\le u\le t}|\bar Y_n(u)-s_0(u)|$. Since $Z_n\le1$, for every $\eta>0$, $E[Z_n^2]\le\eta^2+P(Z_n>\eta)$. Step 1.1 makes the second term tend to zero; then letting $\eta\downarrow0$ proves the expected-square convergence.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,

$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$

pathwise energy integral by
$$\int_0^tG_s\,dA_s:=\int_0^tG_sY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad t\le T.$$
