$\sup_j|w_j|<\infty$, define the weighted logrank score and its conditional
variance estimate by
$$U_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j(O_j-E_j),\qquad \widehat V_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j^2V_j.$$
When $\widehat V_w>0$, set
$Z_w:=U_w/\sqrt{\widehat V_w}$. If $\widehat V_w=0$, this standardized
statistic is left undefined; the unstandardized score remains defined. The
normal calibration is only an approximation until the separate terminal
limit hypotheses are verified. It is not the finite-sample Fisher
randomization p-value.

For a fixed observed record, the displayed scores are statistics in the
measurable-map sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]: each risk count is a
finite sum of Borel indicator functions, and every denominator is positive
at an observed event time. A weight rule is fixed before assignments or
outcomes are inspected and is recomputed by the same rule for any candidate
assignment.

The risk-set table concerns one predeclared event type. If simultaneous
records contain distinct event causes that are not exchangeable, form
separate cause-specific counts $O_{jc}$ and $d_{jc}$ using the same
pre-event risk set; use the displayed hypergeometric variance only for a
cause whose failures are conditionally exchangeable. This definition does
not pool different causes or add their variances without a specified
cross-cause covariance model.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n_0,n_1$ be deterministic, $n=n_0+n_1$,
and let $Z_i=g$ for subject $i$ in group $g\in\{0,1\}$. On a common
finite-horizon filtration, each subject has the one-event process
$$N_{gi}(t)=1\{U_{gi}\le t,\ \delta_{gi}=1\},\qquad Y_{gi}(t)=1\{U_{gi}\ge t\},$$
and satisfies the separate counting-process contract
$$A_{gi}(t)=\int_0^tY_{gi}(s)\lambda(s)\,ds,\qquad M_{gi}=N_{gi}-A_{gi},$$
where $\lambda$ is a common deterministic nonnegative hazard density with
$\Lambda(\tau):=\int_0^\tau\lambda(s)\,ds<\infty$. Assume each $M_{gi}$ is
a square-integrable martingale under this contract, $Y_{gi}$ is predictable,
and no two subjects have simultaneous event jumps. Write $N_{g,n}$ and
$Y_{g,n}$ for the group sums, $N_n=N_{0,n}+N_{1,n}$, and
$p_n(t)=Y_{1,n}(t)/(Y_{0,n}(t)+Y_{1,n}(t))$, with $p_n(t)=0$ on an empty
pooled risk set.

Assume the observed-time and allocation hypotheses of
[[lem-logrank-risk-fraction-converges]]: within each group the observed
times are IID, $n\to\infty$, $n_g/n\to\rho_g\in(0,1)$, and, with
$y_g(t)=\rho_gP(U_{g1}\ge t)$ and $y=y_0+y_1$,
$\inf_{0\le t\le\tau}y(t)>0$. Set $\bar z(t)=y_1(t)/y(t)$. Let $w_n$ be a common predictable
weight process with $|w_n(t)|\le C$ and a measurable supremum satisfying
$\sup_{t\le\tau}|w_n(t)-w(t)|\to_P0$ for a deterministic bounded predictable
weight $w$. Then the weighted logrank score satisfies
$$\frac{U_{n,w_n}}{\sqrt n} =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{g=0}^1\sum_{i=1}^{n_g} \int_0^\tau w(t)\bigl(g-\bar z(t)\bigr)\,dM_{gi}(t)+o_P(1).$$
In particular, fixed deterministic bounded predictable weights are included
by taking $w_n=w$.

Assume the two-group common-hazard model with finite-horizon predictable
risk processes and the explicit square-integrable martingale contracts
$M_{gi}=N_{gi}-A_{gi}$, $A_{gi}(t)=\int_0^tY_{gi}(s)\lambda(s)\,ds$; assume
no simultaneous event jumps. Let $Y_{g,n}=\sum_iY_{gi}$,
$Y_n=Y_{0,n}+Y_{1,n}$, and assume the uniform risk-fraction convergence
$Y_n/n\to y$ and $p_n=Y_{1,n}/Y_n\to\bar z$ in probability on $[0,\tau]$,
with $p_n=0$ on an empty risk set (as proved in
[[lem-logrank-risk-fraction-converges]]). Let $w_n\to w$ uniformly in
probability, where the predictable weights are uniformly bounded and $w$
is deterministic. Suppose event times are continuous, so every observed
failure time has $d_j=1$ almost surely. Here $\widehat V_{n,w_n}$ is the
plug-in statistic defined in [[def-logrank-risk-set-score-and-test]]; the
claim is its asymptotic consistency and does not assert an exact finite-sample
conditional variance law. Here $y_0,y_1$ are deterministic nonnegative Borel functions,
$y=y_0+y_1$, $\inf_{0\le t\le\tau}y(t)>0$, and $\bar z=y_1/y$. Define
$$\sigma_w^2:=\int_0^\tau w(t)^2\frac{y_0(t)y_1(t)}{y(t)}\lambda(t)\,dt.$$
Then the weighted plug-in variance sum from
[[def-logrank-risk-set-score-and-test]] satisfies
$$\frac{\widehat V_{n,w_n}}n\longrightarrow_P\sigma_w^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a finite $G\ge2$ and $d\ge1$. For each total sample size $n$, let $n_1,\ldots,n_G$ be positive deterministic integers with $\sum_{g=1}^G n_g=n$, and suppose $n_g/n\to\rho_g\in(0,1)$ with $\sum_{g=1}^G\rho_g=1$. For group $g$, let $O_{g1},O_{g2},\ldots$ be IID with law $P_g$ on a measurable space; assume the subject families in distinct groups are independent. Let $\phi_g$ be measurable with $E_{P_g}\phi_g=0$, $E_{P_g}\|\phi_g\|_2^2<\infty$, and $\Sigma_g=E_{P_g}[\phi_g\phi_g^T]$. If a measurable estimator of fixed $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$ has the separately established expansion, with remainder on the same sample probability space as its group sums,

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)=\sum_{g=1}^G\sqrt{\frac n{n_g}}\frac1{\sqrt{n_g}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\phi_g(O_{gi})+R_n,\qquad R_n=o_P(1),$$

then

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\Rightarrow N_d\!\left(0,\sum_{g=1}^G\rho_g^{-1}\Sigma_g\right).$$

The group count $G$ is fixed; the laws $P_g$ may differ. The covariance may be singular. This is a terminal finite-dimensional result: it neither proves the estimator expansion nor supplies a continuous-time or functional martingale CLT.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a finite horizon
$T>0$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
For this model and every nonnegative predictable process $G$, define the
pathwise energy integral by
$$\int_0^tG_s\,dA_s:=\int_0^tG_sY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires the defining
integral for $A$ to be finite pathwise, and requires $A$ to be continuous,
adapted and predictable with
$A_0=0$, and that $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$. Set $M_t:=N_t-A_t$. The model
contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

The displayed intensity density alone does **not** assert that $N-A$ is a
martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.

For the compensator contract on $[0,T]$, let $H$ be a predictable real
process with
$$\mathbb E\int_0^T H_s^2\,dA_s<\infty.$$
When the elementary integrals of a sequence of bounded predictable step
processes converging to $H$ in this norm converge in $L^2(P)$, denote the
resulting $L^2(P)$ class at time $t$ by
$$\int_0^t H_s\,dM_s.$$
The definition is conditional on existence of the limit. The L²-extension
theorem below proves existence for every such predictable $H$, independence
from the approximating sequence, the martingale property, and the isometry.
The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the conditional-expectation and
$L^2$-completion interfaces used by that theorem.

For every predictable $H$ on $[0,T]$ with
$\mathbb E\int_0^T H_s^2\,dA_s<\infty$, the limit in
[[def-l2-counting-process-integral]] exists at each $t\le T$, is independent
of the approximating step sequence, and defines a square-integrable
martingale. It satisfies, for each $t\le T$,
$$\mathbb E\left(\int_0^tH_s\,dM_s\right)^2=\mathbb E\int_0^tH_s^2\,dA_s.$$

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

For a finite family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space,
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).$$
Equivalently, it is $\sum_{i,j\in I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$. The empty sum has variance zero, and the singleton formula is the identity.
The original finite-probability-space case is included, since every real random variable there is square-integrable and the covariance/variance definitions agree with the finite centered-product/square formulas.
In the first display, the second sum is over two-element subsets of $I$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $d,k,m\ge1$ be fixed. For each $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y_n\in\mathbb R^k$ be random vectors on one probability space; the probability space may vary with $n$. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ be a random vector on any probability space, and let $c\in\mathbb R^k$ be constant. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n-c=o_P(1)$, then
$$ (X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow(X,c). $$
Consequently, for every continuous $h:\mathbb R^{d+k}\to\mathbb R^m$, $h(X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow h(X,c)$. No independence between $X_n$ and $Y_n$ is required.

derivations.claim: Put $h_g(t)=w(t)(g-\bar z(t))$. For a subject record $(u,\delta)$, define the real map $ \phi_g(u,\delta)=1\{\delta=1,\ u\le\tau\}h_g(u) -\int_0^{u\wedge\tau}h_g(t)\lambda(t)\,dt. $ The deterministic integrand is bounded and Borel, so its indefinite integral is Borel and this map is measurable. From the definitions of $N_{gi}$, $Y_{gi}$ and $A_{gi}$, this is exactly $\int_0^\tau h_g(t)\,dM_{gi}(t)$. Its energy is at most $\|h_g\|_\infty^2\Lambda(\tau)$; [F8] and [F9] therefore make it square-integrable and centered. It is the same measurable function of each subject record within group $g$, so [F1] makes the transformed records IID within group and [F2] makes the two groups independent.

By [F9] and [F11], $ \mathbb E[\phi_g^2] =\int_0^\tau w(t)^2(g-\bar z(t))^2P(U_{g1}\ge t)\lambda(t)\,dt. $ Multiplying by $\rho_g$ and summing over $g=0,1$ gives $ \sum_{g=0}^1\rho_g\mathbb E[\phi_g^2] =\int_0^\tau w(t)^2\{y_1(t)(1-\bar z(t))^2+y_0(t)\bar z(t)^2\}\lambda(t)\,dt =\sigma_w^2, $ where the last equality follows by substituting $\bar z=y_1/(y_0+y_1)$. The integral is finite since $w$ is bounded, $0\le y_g\le1$, and $\Lambda(\tau)<\infty$.

Fix $\epsilon>0$. Since $n_g\to\infty$, the integrand $\phi_g^2 1\{|\phi_g|>\epsilon\sqrt{n_g}\}$ tends pointwise to zero and is bounded by the integrable $\phi_g^2$. [F15] gives $ n_gP(|\phi_g|>\epsilon\sqrt{n_g}) \le\epsilon^{-2}\mathbb E[\phi_g^2 1\{|\phi_g|>\epsilon\sqrt{n_g}\}] \longrightarrow0. $ Thus each group satisfies the finite-variance no-large-jump condition. Also, for $S_{g,n}=n_g^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\phi_g(U_{gi},\delta_{gi})$, [F1] and [F12] make the cross covariances zero, and [F13] gives $\mathbb E[S_{g,n}^2]=\mathbb E[\phi_g^2]$. Applying [F14] to $S_{g,n}^2$ yields $P(|S_{g,n}|>M)\le\mathbb E[\phi_g^2]/M^2$; hence $S_{g,n}=O_P(1)$ by [F16].

By [A2], the risk-fraction hypotheses used by [F4] hold. Let $\widehat\theta_n=U_{n,w_n}/n$ and set $\theta=0$. By [F4], $ \sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta) =n^{-1/2}\sum_{g=0}^1\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\phi_g(U_{gi},\delta_{gi})+o_P(1). $ Set $\psi_g=\rho_g\phi_g$. The group-sum term in [F6] is $ S_n^*=\sum_{g=0}^1\sqrt{\frac n{n_g}}\, \frac1{\sqrt{n_g}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\psi_g(U_{gi},\delta_{gi}). $ Its difference from $n^{-1/2}\sum_{g,i}\phi_g(U_{gi},\delta_{gi})$ equals $ \sum_{g=0}^1\sqrt{\frac n{n_g}}\left(\rho_g-\frac{n_g}n\right)S_{g,n}=o_P(1), $ because $S_{g,n}=O_P(1)$ by step 2.2, $n_g/n\to\rho_g>0$, and there are only two groups. Thus the expansion required by [F6] is established with centered group influences $\psi_g$.

Each $\psi_g$ is centered and square-integrable by step 1.1, and $\operatorname{Var}(\psi_g)=\rho_g^2\mathbb E[\phi_g^2]$ by [F10]. The covariance in [F6] is therefore $ \sum_{g=0}^1\rho_g^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(\psi_g) =\sum_{g=0}^1\rho_g\mathbb E[\phi_g^2]=\sigma_w^2 $ by step 2.1. Applying [F6] to the proved expansion in step 3.1 yields $U_{n,w_n}/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_w^2)$.

Suppose $\sigma_w^2>0$ and put $V_n=\widehat V_{n,w_n}/n$. By [A2] and [F5], $V_n\to_P\sigma_w^2$, so $P(V_n>\sigma_w^2/2)\to1$. The function $(x,v)\mapsto x/\sqrt{\max(v,\sigma_w^2/2)}$ is continuous everywhere. Apply [F18] and this map to the score limit and $V_n$; the result converges to $Z/\sigma_w$ for $Z\sim N(0,\sigma_w^2)$, which has law $N(0,1)$ by [F17]. On $\{V_n>\sigma_w^2/2\}$ this map equals the stated standardized statistic. Since the complement has probability tending to zero, changing the statistic there has no effect on weak convergence, including any fixed finite extension on the zero-denominator event. When $\sigma_w^2=0$, step 4.1 gives the degenerate score law and no standardized conclusion.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: The degenerate score law is covered when σ_w²=0; the positive-variance studentization is stated separately.
Step 5.1 uses a positive-variance event only when σ_w²>0 and makes no standardized claim at zero variance.
Statement: Interior allocation fractions imply n_g→∞ for both groups, as used in steps 2.2 and 3.1.
Step 5.1 allows the singular scalar normal N(0,0), and step 5.1 avoids division when σ_w²=0.
Statement: The theorem uses fixed finite τ, finite Λ(τ), and risk positivity through the closed horizon.

The Statement and A1 declare AC for the L2 integral and independent-group terminal-limit suppliers. Step 1.1 uses the finite-energy integral and step 4.1 uses the Gaussian group limit under that assumption. The finite two-group covariance and scaling manipulations select no new arbitrary family.

boundaries.reason: The Statement assumes two independent IID groups, positive allocation/risk limits and explicit finite-energy martingale premises. Steps 3.1 and 4.1 invoke the already-proved subject expansion and group terminal CLT; step5.1 standardizes only at positive variance. A Gaussian score limit is not claimed to imply that entire common-hazard model. The forward boundary therefore concerns the stated conditional calculation, not a two-way characterization.

The Statement assumes two independent IID groups, positive allocation/risk limits and explicit finite-energy martingale premises. Steps 3.1 and 4.1 invoke the already-proved subject expansion and group terminal CLT; step5.1 standardizes only at positive variance. A Gaussian score limit is not claimed to imply that entire common-hazard model. The reverse boundary would require inferring the model premises from that conclusion, which this item does not claim.

risk_review.notes: Read all six proof steps, all 21 direct supplier statements and the complete independent-groups terminal theorem proof. The truncated record is a measurable transformation of each IID pair and preserves group independence. Positive pooled support and interior allocation limits explicitly supply both repaired lemmas; no terminal source change is needed. The deterministic bounded Borel subject influence is its event term minus its absolutely continuous compensator integral, hence is a measurable function of one record. Isometry gives centering and finite variance; Tonelli gives sum rho_g E(phi_g^2)=integral w^2 y_0 y_1/y lambda. Finite second moments justify the tail/DCT and Markov O_P(1) bounds. Scaling psi_g=rho_g phi_g reconciles the independent-groups theorem expansion: the allocation mismatch times tight group sums is o_P(1), and covariance is sum rho_g^{-1}Var(psi_g). Slutsky with max(v,sigma^2/2) handles positive variance and negligible zero-estimate events; zero sigma^2 gives only a degenerate score law. Horizon events are counted inclusively; the continuous-time contract excludes baseline events and simultaneous jumps. AC is explicitly inherited from L2 and Gaussian-limit suppliers; no process CLT, iff or extra censoring inference is used. No finding/defect.

citations.quote:
Fix a follow-up horizon $\tau>0$ and a finite set of subjects
$\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. A right-censored record for subject $i$ is a
pair $(U_i,\delta_i)\in[0,\tau]\times\{0,1\}$, where
$U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ is the observed time and
$\delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\}$ records an event, including an event-censoring tie;
$\delta_i=0$ records right censoring. A two-group assignment is a map
$z:\mathcal I\to\{0,1\}$. These conventions are the right-censoring
observation scheme; the score below uses the observed record and does not
infer event or censoring laws from it.

Let $t_1<\cdots<t_K$ be the distinct observed failure times in $[0,\tau]$.
For $g\in\{0,1\}$ define the risk count and event count at $t_j$ by
$$Y_{gj}(z):=\#\{i:z_i=g,\ U_i\ge t_j\},\qquad d_{gj}(z):=\#\{i:z_i=g,\ U_i=t_j,\ \delta_i=1\}.$$
Write $Y_j=Y_{0j}+Y_{1j}$, $d_j=d_{0j}+d_{1j}>0$, and
$O_j=d_{1j}$. Since $t_j$ is an observed failure time,
$1\le d_j\le Y_j$. The expected group-1 count under the conditional
hypergeometric model is
$$E_j:=d_j\frac{Y_{1j}}{Y_j}.$$
Under that model the $d_j$ failing subjects are a uniform $d_j$-subset of the
$Y_j$ subjects at risk, conditional on the risk-set and event-count margins.
The corresponding conditional variance is
$$V_j:= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Y_{1j}Y_{0j}d_j(Y_j-d_j)} {Y_j^2(Y_j-1)},&Y_j>1,\\[6pt] 0,&Y_j=1. \end{cases}$$
If the study has no observed failures, all sums below are empty and equal zero.
The conditional hypergeometric model is an explicit finite risk-set
assumption; equality of survival laws with arbitrary censoring or subject
heterogeneity does not by itself assert this conditional allocation law.
The uniform law on the finite set of $d_j$-subsets is the uniform finite
probability space of [[def-uniform-finite-probability-space]].

A **weight rule** assigns a real value $w_j$ using only the predeclared time
and information available strictly before the failures at $t_j$; deterministic
bounded time weights are a special case. If
$\sup_j|w_j|<\infty$, define the weighted logrank score and its conditional
variance estimate by
$$U_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j(O_j-E_j),\qquad \widehat V_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j^2V_j.$$
When $\widehat V_w>0$, set
$Z_w:=U_w/\sqrt{\widehat V_w}$. If $\widehat V_w=0$, this standardized
statistic is left undefined; the unstandardized score remains defined. The
normal calibration is only an approximation until the separate terminal
limit hypotheses are verified. It is not the finite-sample Fisher
randomization p-value.

For a fixed observed record, the displayed scores are statistics in the
measurable-map sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]: each risk count is a
finite sum of Borel indicator functions, and every denominator is positive
at an observed event time. A weight rule is fixed before assignments or
outcomes are inspected and is recomputed by the same rule for any candidate
assignment.

The risk-set table concerns one predeclared event type. If simultaneous
records contain distinct event causes that are not exchangeable, form
separate cause-specific counts $O_{jc}$ and $d_{jc}$ using the same
pre-event risk set; use the displayed hypergeometric variance only for a
cause whose failures are conditionally exchangeable. This definition does
not pool different causes or add their variances without a specified
cross-cause covariance model.

For a positive integer sample size $n$, let $(T_i,C_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be event and censoring times with right-censored observations $(U_i,\delta_i)$ as in [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]], so $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=\mathbf 1\{T_i\le C_i\}$. The subject counting process and at-risk process are $N_i(t)=\mathbf 1\{U_i\le t,\ \delta_i=1\}$ and $Y_i(t)=\mathbf 1\{U_i\ge t\}$.
The endpoint convention makes $Y_i$ left-continuous at $U_i$: a subject is still at risk at the observed time, including a tied event and censoring time. Set $N_n=\sum_{i=1}^nN_i$ and $Y_n=\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Let $dN_n$ be the finite counting measure of observed events on $[0,\infty)$, with atom $\Delta N_n(u):=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{U_i=u,\ \delta_i=1\}$ at each $u\ge0$; in particular, $\Delta N_n(0)=N_n(0)$. Tied failures at $u$ contribute their full count and censorings at $u$ do not contribute to $dN_n(u)$.

For $t\ge0$, the **Nelson–Aalen estimator** is $\widehat\Lambda_n(t)=\int_{[0,t]}\frac{\mathbf 1\{Y_n(u)>0\}}{Y_n(u)}\,dN_n(u)$, where the integrand is defined to be zero when $Y_n(u)=0$. The **Kaplan–Meier estimator** is $\widehat S_n(t)=\prod_{\substack{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N_n(u)>0}}\left(1-\frac{\Delta N_n(u)}{Y_n(u)}\right)$.
Each product is finite and a factor is zero if every subject at risk fails at that time. The target survival function is $S(t)=P(T>t)$. If $T$ has density $f$, $S$ is positive on the horizon, and $\lambda=f/S$, the continuous cumulative hazard is $\Lambda(t)=\int_0^t\lambda(u)\,du=-\log S(t)$.

These inclusive endpoint formulas reduce to the usual $(0,t]$ formulas whenever $\Delta N_n(0)=0$. If $T$ has finite support $0\le a_1<\cdots<a_m$, write $q_j=P(T=a_j\mid T\ge a_j)$; the corresponding discrete cumulative hazard is $\Lambda_d(t)=\sum_{a_j\le t}q_j$. Under IID sampling, independent censoring, and positive risk probability at the support points, the Nelson–Aalen increments estimate these $q_j$; in general this discrete cumulative hazard is not $-\log S(t)$.

A baseline event is included at $u=0$; if it occurs then $N_i(0)=1$, so a model contract requiring $N_i(0)=0$ must exclude this case.

An empty event product is $1$, and an empty Greenwood event sum is $0$.

On a horizon where every event contribution has $Y_n(u)-\Delta N_n(u)>0$, the **Greenwood variance estimate** is $\widehat V_G(t)=\widehat S_n(t)^2\sum_{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N_n(u)>0}\frac{\Delta N_n(u)}{Y_n(u)\{Y_n(u)-\Delta N_n(u)\}}$.
Greenwood's formula is used as a first-order asymptotic variance estimate when the sampling and censoring assumptions justify that approximation; the formula alone asserts no asymptotic result and is not an exact finite-sample variance identity. It is undefined when a contributing denominator is zero.

For each fixed $t$, these are statistics of the observed sample in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. To express event-time sums and products as fixed finite operations, scan indices $i=1,\ldots,n$ and include only the first event observation at each distinct time; each inclusion condition uses finitely many Borel equalities and inequalities among the observed $U_i$ and $\delta_i$. Risk and event counts are finite Borel sums, and every division uses the stated positive-count branch. Greenwood is defined only on its positive-denominator domain.

derivations.claim: Integrating the hazards gives, for $t\ge1$, $S_1(t)=e^{-(t+1)}$ and $S_0(t)=e^{-(2t-1)}$; for $0\le t\le1$, $S_1(t)=e^{-2t}$ and $S_0(t)=e^{-t}$. On $[0,1]$, $S_1(t)<S_0(t)$ for $t>0$. For $t\ge1$ their ratio is $S_1(t)/S_0(t)=e^{t-2}$, so they meet at $t=2$ and reverse order after it. Each event-time interval $(0,1)$ and $(2,2.5)$ has positive probability, and the specified censor-time values have positive mass. For every subject required to be censored at $c\in\{1.5,2.5\}$, $P(T>c)=S_g(c)>0$ under its group hazard. Mutual independence of all event and censoring times therefore makes the finite intersection defining the sample pattern have positive probability.

At $t_1$, $(Y_{1},Y_{0},d,O)=(4,2,1,1)$, so the score contribution is $1-4/6=1/3$ and the plug-in variance contribution is $4\cdot2/6^2=2/9$. The two censorings at $1.5$ leave one group-1 subject at risk. At $t_2$, $(Y_{1},Y_{0},d,O)=(1,2,1,0)$, so the score contribution is $0-1/3=-1/3$ and the plug-in variance contribution is $1\cdot2/3^2=2/9$. Hence $U=0$ and $\widehat V=4/9>0$, giving standardized score zero. By [F2], $\widehat S_1(t)=1-1/4=3/4$ for $t_1\le t\le2.5$ because the only group-1 failure is at $t_1$; and $\widehat S_0(t)=1$ for $t<t_2$, then $1-1/2=1/2$ for $t_2\le t\le2.5$. The censorings contribute no product factors. Thus the empirical curves reverse order at $t_2$. The cancellation of the score and the crossing population hazards show why this one sample statistic does not establish equality of the survival laws.

citations.quote:
Fix a follow-up horizon $\tau>0$ and a finite set of subjects
$\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. A right-censored record for subject $i$ is a
pair $(U_i,\delta_i)\in[0,\tau]\times\{0,1\}$, where
$U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ is the observed time and
$\delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\}$ records an event, including an event-censoring tie;
$\delta_i=0$ records right censoring. A two-group assignment is a map
$z:\mathcal I\to\{0,1\}$. These conventions are the right-censoring
observation scheme; the score below uses the observed record and does not
infer event or censoring laws from it.

Let $t_1<\cdots<t_K$ be the distinct observed failure times in $[0,\tau]$.
For $g\in\{0,1\}$ define the risk count and event count at $t_j$ by
$$Y_{gj}(z):=\#\{i:z_i=g,\ U_i\ge t_j\},\qquad d_{gj}(z):=\#\{i:z_i=g,\ U_i=t_j,\ \delta_i=1\}.$$
Write $Y_j=Y_{0j}+Y_{1j}$, $d_j=d_{0j}+d_{1j}>0$, and
$O_j=d_{1j}$. Since $t_j$ is an observed failure time,
$1\le d_j\le Y_j$. The expected group-1 count under the conditional
hypergeometric model is
$$E_j:=d_j\frac{Y_{1j}}{Y_j}.$$
Under that model the $d_j$ failing subjects are a uniform $d_j$-subset of the
$Y_j$ subjects at risk, conditional on the risk-set and event-count margins.
The corresponding conditional variance is
$$V_j:= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Y_{1j}Y_{0j}d_j(Y_j-d_j)} {Y_j^2(Y_j-1)},&Y_j>1,\\[6pt] 0,&Y_j=1. \end{cases}$$
If the study has no observed failures, all sums below are empty and equal zero.
The conditional hypergeometric model is an explicit finite risk-set
assumption; equality of survival laws with arbitrary censoring or subject
heterogeneity does not by itself assert this conditional allocation law.
The uniform law on the finite set of $d_j$-subsets is the uniform finite
probability space of [[def-uniform-finite-probability-space]].

A **weight rule** assigns a real value $w_j$ using only the predeclared time
and information available strictly before the failures at $t_j$; deterministic
bounded time weights are a special case. If
$\sup_j|w_j|<\infty$, define the weighted logrank score and its conditional
variance estimate by
$$U_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j(O_j-E_j),\qquad \widehat V_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j^2V_j.$$
When $\widehat V_w>0$, set
$Z_w:=U_w/\sqrt{\widehat V_w}$. If $\widehat V_w=0$, this standardized
statistic is left undefined; the unstandardized score remains defined. The
normal calibration is only an approximation until the separate terminal
limit hypotheses are verified. It is not the finite-sample Fisher
randomization p-value.

For a fixed observed record, the displayed scores are statistics in the
measurable-map sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]: each risk count is a
finite sum of Borel indicator functions, and every denominator is positive
at an observed event time. A weight rule is fixed before assignments or
outcomes are inspected and is recomputed by the same rule for any candidate
assignment.

The risk-set table concerns one predeclared event type. If simultaneous
records contain distinct event causes that are not exchangeable, form
separate cause-specific counts $O_{jc}$ and $d_{jc}$ using the same
pre-event risk set; use the displayed hypergeometric variance only for a
cause whose failures are conditionally exchangeable. This definition does
not pool different causes or add their variances without a specified
cross-cause covariance model.

Fix a finite randomized treatment-assignment model with allowed assignments
$\mathcal Z$ and known law $p$, with unit set $\mathcal I$ as in
[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]]. Fix a map
$\gamma:\mathcal Z\to\{0,1\}^{\mathcal I}$ assigning each allowed assignment
a binary logrank group map. For each subject $i$, let
$(U_i(z),\delta_i(z))\in[0,\tau]\times\{0,1\}$ be the full right-censored
record under assignment $z$. Assume the **record sharp null**: for every $i$,
the pair $(U_i(z),\delta_i(z))$ is constant over all $z\in\mathcal Z$. Fix
before observing assignment or records a bounded logrank weight rule and the
two-sided ordering $T(z)=|U_w(\gamma(z);U,\delta)|$.

The inclusive assignment-tail p-value
$$p_{\rm rand}(z):=\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z') 1\{|U_w(\gamma(z');U,\delta)|\ge |U_w(\gamma(z);U,\delta)|\}$$
is superuniform under the assignment law, so it is a valid finite-sample
p-value for the record sharp null. If an auxiliary $V$ is independent of
the assignment and uniform on $[0,1]$, replacing the inclusive tail by the
strict-tail mass plus $V$ times the tied-score mass gives an exactly uniform
p-value. The result uses the actual assignment probabilities and asserts no
validity under a weak average-effect null or under an equal-hazard null alone.

Let $N\ge1$, and let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ index the fixed
experimental units at the actual treatment-assignment level. Let
$\mathcal Z$ be a nonempty finite set of allowed assignments. If treatment
is assigned to clusters, each cluster is one indexed unit; no separate
probability-sampling unit is present. The index $i$ identifies that unit,
and no visit or repeated-measurement index is modeled here.

A known assignment law is a function $p:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$ satisfying
$\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)=1$, so $(\mathcal Z,p)$ is a finite probability
space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]); assignments of probability
zero may remain in $\mathcal Z$. A **potential-outcome schedule** is a function
$\theta:\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, with
$Y_i(z):=\theta(i,z)$. The schedule and the units are fixed; the assignment
$Z$ is the only randomness supplied by the design, and the observed response
vector is $Y_\theta(Z)=(Y_i(Z))_{i\in\mathcal I}$. The schedule is defined
for every allowed assignment, including zero-probability assignments, and
may depend on the full assignment vector, so no no-interference assumption is
implicit. The scientific statistical model contract
[[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]] requires the observation space,
units, quantity status, observation mechanism, support, conditioning
convention, and adequacy assumptions to be recorded; this model specifies
those fields as follows.

To express this as a statistical experiment, take the data space
$\mathcal X=\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}$ with its full power-set
sigma-algebra, which is a sigma-algebra by [[def-sigma-algebra]] and makes
$\mathcal X$ a measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), and parameter
set $\Theta=\mathbb R^{\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z}$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$
let $P_\theta$ be the law
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]) of the deterministic
observation map $O_\theta(z)=(z,Y_\theta(z))$ from $(\mathcal Z,p)$. The map
is measurable because its domain has the full power set, in the preimage
sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], and its law
is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]. Thus
$((\mathcal X,2^{\mathcal X}),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ is an
experiment in the sense of [[def-statistical-experiment]]. The assignment
law asserts no response-error model, Gaussian law, superpopulation
randomization, or sampling representativeness beyond the stated finite
assignment mechanism. Its finite full-measure support set is
$$S_\theta:=\{(z,Y_\theta(z)):z\in\mathcal Z,\ p(z)>0\},$$
since $P_\theta(S_\theta)=\sum_{z:p(z)>0}p(z)=1$. The record contains the
assigned vector and every unit's response; missing or censored outcomes and
repeated visits require a separately declared observation mechanism. The
inferential target is the assignment-invariance hypothesis for these $N$
units, not an estimand for a wider population.

Inference in this page holds $\mathcal I$ and $\theta$ fixed and averages
over the declared law $p$; it does not condition on the realized assignment.
The status of the quantities is explicit: $\theta$ and all
$Y_i(z)$ are fixed, $Z$ is random, $(Z,Y_\theta(Z))$ is observed, and
potential responses under unassigned vectors are fixed but latent. The
assignment set, weights, and implemented randomization protocol are
design-controlled and should be checked against protocol records. Assignment
logs and response records are empirically assessable, but those checks do not
prove that the declared law generated the data. Potential outcomes under
unassigned vectors are fixed and latent in the realized record. This does
not imply nonidentifiability from the observed-data law: for each $z$ with
$p(z)>0$, the law assigns mass $p(z)$ to $(z,Y_\theta(z))$, and therefore
determines $Y_\theta(z)$. Assignment invariance on this positive-probability
set is **empirically assessable**, and the theorem tests the stronger
invariance hypothesis on all allowed assignments. Values at assignments
with $p(z)=0$, and restrictions on those values, are **substantively
untestable** from this law, since changing them leaves $P_\theta$ unchanged.
One realized assignment does not reveal responses at other assignments.
These classifications do not make the design or scientific model
empirically true.

derivations.claim: The prescribed full record for each subject is identical under all three allowed assignments, so the full-record sharp-null hypothesis in [F2] holds. Under the map $\gamma(e_1)$, the event at time 1 contributes $1-1/3=2/3$ and the later risk sets contain no treated subject, so $U(\gamma(e_1))=2/3$. Under $\gamma(e_2)$, time 1 contributes $-1/3$, and time 2 contributes $1-1/2=1/2$, giving $U(\gamma(e_2))=1/6$. Under $\gamma(e_3)$, time 1 contributes $-1/3$, time 2 contributes $-1/2$, and time 3 contributes zero, giving $U(\gamma(e_3))=-5/6$. These are the three distinct scores; their absolute values are $2/3,1/6,5/6$.

The inclusive absolute-tail probability at $e_1$ is $1/2+1/6=2/3$, at $e_2$ it is $1$, and at $e_3$ it is $1/6$, because the absolute scores are distinct and the assignment weights are $1/2,1/3,1/6$. Therefore the p-value takes $2/3,1,1/6$ with respective probabilities $1/2,1/3,1/6$.

Its distribution function is $0$ for $0\le u<1/6$, $1/6$ for $1/6\le u<2/3$, $2/3$ for $2/3\le u<1$, and $1$ at $u=1$. On each interval this is at most $u$, including the endpoints. Thus the exact finite assignment calculation is superuniform under the declared unequal-weight law, as in [F2].

citations.quote:
Fix a finite horizon $\tau>0$ and a fixed dimension $p\ge1$. Work on a probability space with an increasing filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le\tau}$ as in [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. For subject $i$, let $T_i$ be an event time, $C_i$ a censoring time, and $Z_i(t)\in\mathbb R^p$ a covariate process predictable relative to this filtration, in the sense of [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Use the right-censoring record convention of [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]]: $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\}$. For this vector covariate process, predictability means coordinatewise predictability: each real-valued coordinate is predictable in the sense of [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Define the history sigma-algebra $\mathcal G_i:=\sigma\{Z_i(t):0\le t\le\tau\}$. The conditional-independence assumption is $T_i\perp\!\!\!\perp C_i\mid\mathcal G_i$, meaning that for all bounded measurable real functions $a,b$, $E[a(T_i)b(C_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]=E[a(T_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]E[b(C_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]$ almost surely, as in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. This conditional-independence relation is a model assumption, not an empirical conclusion. No conditional-kernel representation given the entire covariate path is assumed here.

A Cox proportional-hazards specification fixes a coefficient $\beta_0\in\mathbb R^p$ and a baseline hazard density $\lambda_0:[0,\tau]\to[0,\infty)$ that is measurable and integrable. Its baseline cumulative hazard is the absolutely continuous function
$$\Lambda_0(t)=\int_0^t\lambda_0(u)\,du.$$
The conditional event intensity at time $t$ for subject $i$, while that subject is at risk, is
$$Y_i(t)\lambda_0(t)\exp\{\beta_0^T Z_i(t)\},\qquad Y_i(t):=1\{U_i\ge t\}.$$
These specify the conditional event-intensity component. The law of the covariate paths and the censoring law subject to the stated conditional-independence assumption remain nuisance components and are not fixed here. Thus this is a semiparametric model specification; $(\beta_0,\lambda_0)$ alone do not define a full parametric statistical experiment on the observed-data space.
For the counting-process arguments below, require $Y_i$ to be predictable as well; this is part of the stated observation model and is not inferred from the hazard formula alone.
For a constant covariate value $z$, the corresponding event survival function is
$$S(t\mid z)=\exp\{-e^{\beta_0^Tz}\Lambda_0(t)\}.$$
For fixed covariate values $z,z'\in\mathbb R^p$, at times with $\lambda_0(t)>0$ the hazard ratio is
$$\frac{\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta^Tz}}{\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta^Tz'}}=e^{\beta^T(z-z')}.$$
The relative hazard factor is $e^{\beta^T(z-z')}$ even at times when both baseline-scaled hazards vanish and their quotient is undefined. It is an instantaneous hazard ratio, not a ratio of cumulative event probabilities. For time-varying covariate paths $z(t),z'(t)$ the instantaneous relative hazard factor is $e^{\beta^T(z(t)-z'(t))}$ and may vary with time.

For a sample of $n$ subjects, put $R(t)=\{j:U_j\ge t\}$. When failures are untied, the Cox partial likelihood on $[0,\tau]$ is
$$L_p(\beta)=\prod_{i:\,\delta_i=1,\ U_i\le\tau} \frac{\exp\{\beta^TZ_i(U_i)\}}{\sum_{j\in R(U_i)}\exp\{\beta^TZ_j(U_i)\}}.$$
An empty product is $1$. This partial likelihood is built from risk-set contributions; it is not asserted to be the full likelihood of the censored observations.

Tied-event likelihoods require an explicit time-recording convention. Put $D(t)=\{i:U_i=t,\delta_i=1\}$ and $d_t=|D(t)|$. If a discrete or grouped-time model conditions on exactly $d_t$ failures from $D(t)\subseteq R(t)$ at recorded time $t$ with the risk set fixed for that time, additionally assume that, conditional on that risk set, its covariate weights, and $d_t=d$, the failure subset law assigns each size-$d$ set $A\subseteq R(t)$ probability proportional to $\prod_{j\in A}w_j(t)$. Under this explicit subset-law assumption, its exact conditional tie contribution is
$$\frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq R(t)\\|A|=d_t}}\ \prod_{j\in A}w_j(t)}, \qquad w_j(t):=\exp\{\beta^TZ_j(t)\}.$$
For the separate exact Cox tied-partial-likelihood convention obtained by coarsening a continuous-time ordering into one recorded tie interval, assume the risk set at the interval start is $R(t)$, its only within-interval departures are the $d_t$ failures in $D(t)$, and the covariates are fixed at the recorded time. Conditional on each successive failure, the next failure label is chosen from the remaining risk set with probability proportional to its weight. Summing these order contributions gives the ordered-risk-set conditional partial-likelihood contribution
$$\sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Perm}(D(t))} \prod_{k=1}^{d_t} \frac{w_{\pi_k}(t)} {\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)-\sum_{\ell<k}w_{\pi_\ell}(t)}.$$
Here $\operatorname{Perm}(D(t))$ is the set of bijections from $\{1,\ldots,d_t\}$ to $D(t)$.
The discrete subset expression is exact under its explicit subset-law convention, and the permutation expression is exact for its stated partial-likelihood ordering convention; the latter is not generally the full likelihood of interval-coarsened censored observations. These conventions are not interchangeable without a model relating them. The Breslow and Efron tie formulas are approximations, respectively
$$L_B(\beta)=\prod_{t:d_t>0} \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\left(\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)\right)^{d_t}}$$
and
$$L_E(\beta)=\prod_{t:d_t>0} \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\prod_{k=0}^{d_t-1}\left(\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)-\frac{k}{d_t}\sum_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)\right)}.$$
With an absolutely continuous event hazard and independent subjects, exact event-time ties have probability zero; grouped-time tie formulas describe additional observation/model conventions.

For a discrete event-time law, the survival relation $S(t\mid z)=S_0(t)^{e^{\beta^Tz}}$ describes proportional integrated hazards and is not equivalent in general to a hazard-ratio model. The proportional-hazards and proportional-integrated-hazards formulations agree under the continuity condition on the baseline survival; the hazard-density model above uses the absolutely continuous convention.

The counting-process martingale property used for inference is a separate model-contract assumption in the estimator theorem below. The hazard formula by itself does not assert that a compensated event count is a martingale. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the cited event-observation and predictability interfaces; this definition makes no further choice.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID random elements with law $P$. For a class $\mathcal F$ of measurable, integrable real-valued functions on $\mathcal X$, write

$$Pf:=\int f\,dP,\qquad P_nf:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(Z_i),\qquad \mathbb G_n(f):=\sqrt n\,(P_nf-Pf).$$

The map $f\mapsto P_nf-Pf$ is the centered empirical process, and $\mathbb G_n$ is its $\sqrt n$-scaled version. More generally, for independent processes $X_1(t),\ldots,X_n(t)$ whose marginal expectations are finite for each index $t\in T$, the centered process sum is

$$S_n(t):=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(X_i(t)-\mathbb E X_i(t)\bigr),\qquad t\in T.$$

On an auxiliary probability-space extension, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n$ be independent signs, each taking $+1$ and $-1$ with probability $1/2$, independent of the observations. The empirical Rademacher process is

$$R_n(f):=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i f(Z_i),\qquad f\in\mathcal F.$$

The centered Rademacher process $\sum_i\sigma_i(f(Z_i)-Pf)$ is a distinct process; no equality between it and $R_n$ is part of this definition.

For a countable class of measurable functions, each displayed supremum of measurable sample paths is measurable. For an uncountable class, ordinary probability or expectation is used only when a specified countable subclass has the same supremum almost surely for the process in question; this is the separable-version convention used here. Otherwise state results using outer probability

$$P^*(A):=\inf\{P(B):A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$$

and, for a nonnegative possibly nonmeasurable random quantity $Y$, outer expectation

$$\mathbb E^*Y:=\inf\{\mathbb E U: U\text{ is measurable, nonnegative, and }U\ge Y\}.$$

In particular, measurability of every $f$ separately does not by itself make an uncountable supremum measurable.

A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$ when the integral is finite, using the real-power convention, including $0^{1/r}=0$, of [[def-real-power]]. If the integral is $+\infty$, define $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=+\infty$ directly. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this nonnegative extended integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

Use the empirical-measure convention of [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]]: for iid observations $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ with common law $P$, $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)$ and $Pf=\int f\,dP$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable real-valued functions with a nonnegative measurable integrable envelope $F$, meaning $|f|\le F$ $P$-almost surely for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and $PF<\infty$. It is **pointwise measurable** if there is a countable subclass $\mathcal F_0$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ is the pointwise limit of a sequence from $\mathcal F_0$. For a pointwise-measurable class, dominated convergence [[thm-dominated-convergence]] gives $Pf_k\to Pf$ along the approximating sequence, and finite empirical averages converge pointwise, so the supremum defining the uniform law is determined by $\mathcal F_0$. The class is **$P$-Glivenko–Cantelli** if

$$\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\longrightarrow0$$

in probability. It is **strongly $P$-Glivenko–Cantelli** if the same convergence holds almost surely. For an uncountable class with a countable pointwise-dense subclass, the supremum is interpreted using outer probability unless the chosen version makes it measurable. For a pointwise-measurable class the supremum is determined by the countable subclass and is measurable. That subclass has a common conull envelope bound, so the supremum is finite almost surely; after choosing a real-valued version, almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability by [[thm-almost-sure-convergence-implies-convergence-in-probability]].

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty pointwise-measurable class of measurable real functions with a nonnegative integrable envelope $F$. Suppose $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^1(P))<\infty$ for every $\epsilon>0$. Then $\mathcal F$ is $P$-Glivenko–Cantelli: $\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\to0$ in probability. If Countable Choice is assumed, then the stronger conclusion holds that this convergence is almost sure. The terms $P_n$, $P$, and the outer-probability convention are those of [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]], and the class notion is [[def-glivenko-cantelli-class]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Put $R=\sup_{\beta\in B}\|\beta\|_2$ and $C=e^{KR}\max(1,K,K^2)$. Each risk coordinate is bounded by $C$ and is Lipschitz in $\beta$ with constant at most $KC$, since the segment between two points of $B$ lies in the radius-$R$ ball. By [F6]–[F7], the expectations are jointly measurable in time and parameter. Both empirical and population functions are continuous in parameter, so each parameter supremum equals the supremum over a fixed countable dense subset of $B$ and is measurable. Population ratios are deterministic Borel time functions and hence predictable.

For each fixed $t,\beta$ and coordinate $f$, independence and centering give $E[(P_nf-Pf)^2]=\operatorname{Var}(f)/n\le C^2/n$: the cross terms vanish by independence. On a finite $\varepsilon$-net of $B$, the squared maximum over its $m_\varepsilon$ points and the $d=1+p+p^2$ coordinates has expectation at most $dm_\varepsilon C^2/n$. Between a point and its nearest net point, the empirical-minus-population Lipschitz bound is $2KC\varepsilon$. Thus $\limsup_n E D_n(t)^2\le8K^2C^2\varepsilon^2$; let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The uniform bound $D_n\le2C$ and [F8] applied to $t\mapsto E D_n(t)^2$, followed by [F7], prove $E\int D_n^2d\nu\to0$.

Write $q=P(U_i\ge\tau)$. Since $c_0\le s^{(0)}(\tau,\beta_0)\le e^{K\|\beta_0\|_2}q$, $q>0$. For $Q_n=n^{-1}\sum_i1\{U_i\ge\tau\}$, independence gives $E(Q_n-q)^2=q(1-q)/n$, so $P(Q_n<q/2)\le4(1-q)/(nq)\to0$. Monotonicity of $Y_i$ and the weight bound give $S_n^{(0)}(t,\beta)\ge e^{-KR}Q_n$ for every $t,\beta$. Hence on the event $E_n=\{Q_n\ge q/2\}$ all sample denominators are at least $c=e^{-KR}q/2$, while all population denominators are at least $e^{-KR}q$.

On $E_n$, ratio subtraction and the bounds of steps 1.1 and 2.2 bound both $\sup_B\|\bar Z_n-\bar z\|_2$ and $\sup_B\|V_n-V\|_{\max}$ by a constant times $D_n(t)$. Off $E_n$, the weighted means have norm at most $K$ and the second-moment matrices have entries at most $K^2$, including the zero convention, so both errors remain bounded by constants depending only on $K,p$. Their expected squared errors are therefore at most $C_1E D_n(t)^2+C_2P(E_n^c)$. Steps 2.1–3.1 prove the fixed-time conclusions; integration against finite $\nu$, or [F7]–[F8], proves their integrated versions.

Under [A1], each coordinate class has the envelope from step 1.1 and the hypotheses of [F3]–[F5]. Apply only the probability branch of [F5] and take the finite union over coordinates to obtain $\sup_tD_n(t)\to_P0$. Step 3.1's ratio bound on $E_n$, whose probability tends to one, gives both uniform-in-time ratio conclusions. No such time-indexed class hypothesis was used in steps 1.1–4.1.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a finite horizon
$T>0$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires that this integral
be finite pathwise, that $A$ be continuous, adapted and predictable with
$A_0=0$, and that $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$. Set $M_t:=N_t-A_t$. The model
contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

The displayed intensity density alone does **not** assert that $N-A$ is a
martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.

$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

For the contract of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]], let
$\mathcal P_T$ be the predictable sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ and
define the finite measure
$$\mu(E):=\int_EY_s(\omega)\lambda_s(\omega)\,(ds\times P)(d(s,\omega)),\qquad E\in\mathcal P_T.$$
Then bounded predictable step processes are dense in $L^2(\mu)$. The time-zero
slice has $\mu$-measure zero.

Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale on a finite horizon $[0,T]$ in the
all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] (in particular, it may
be the compensated counting-process martingale of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]). Let
$$0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T$$
be a deterministic partition, and let each bounded random variable $H_j$ be
$\mathcal F_{t_j}$-measurable. The associated **bounded predictable step
integrand** is $H_0=0$ at time $0$ and $H_s=H_j$ on $(t_j,t_{j+1}]$. For this
chosen step representation define, for $0\le t\le T$,
$$I_t(H):=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}H_j\bigl(M_{t\wedge t_{j+1}}-M_{t\wedge t_j}\bigr).$$
This is a finite sum of square-integrable random variables. At this stage the
representation is part of the input; representation independence and the
isometry are established in
[[lem-elementary-counting-process-integral-isometry]].
The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the all-pairs martingale and
conditional-expectation interface; the finite-sum definition makes no
additional choice.

For every predictable $H$ on $[0,T]$ with
$\mathbb E\int_0^T H_s^2\,dA_s<\infty$, the limit in
[[def-l2-counting-process-integral]] exists at each $t\le T$, is independent
of the approximating step sequence, and defines a square-integrable
martingale. It satisfies, for each $t\le T$,
$$\mathbb E\left(\int_0^tH_s\,dM_s\right)^2=\mathbb E\int_0^tH_s^2\,dA_s.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The martingale property gives $EN_T=EA_T<\infty$. For a predictable set $E$, define $\mu_N(E)=E\int1_EdN$ and $\mu_A(E)=E\int1_EdA$. Measurability of the section integrals holds first for the generators in [F2] (their integrals are $1_B(N_t-N_s)$ and $1_B(A_t-A_s)$), then for all predictable sets: the sets with measurable section integrals form a lambda-system, using subtraction from finite terminal masses and increasing partial sums for disjoint unions. Apply [F3] to this generating pi-system. Pathwise countable additivity and [F4] now make $\mu_N,\mu_A$ finite measures. For an interval generator, $E[1_B(M_t-M_s)]=0$ by the martingale property, so their masses agree; time-zero masses are both zero and whole-space masses agree. [F3] gives $\mu_N=\mu_A$. Simple functions and [F4] yield the compensation identity for every nonnegative predictable $G$.

By [F5] choose bounded predictable steps $H_m$ with $E\int|H_m-H|^2dA\to0$. Step 1.1 and [F8] give $$E\int|H_m-H|\,d(N+A)=2E\int|H_m-H|\,dA\le2(EA_T)^{1/2}\left(E\int|H_m-H|^2dA\right)^{1/2}\longrightarrow0.$$ For steps, [F6] identifies the integral with the difference of its pathwise $N$ and $A$ integrals. The displayed bound makes those differences converge in L¹ to the stated pathwise expression. By [F7] the same step integrals converge in L², hence L¹ on the probability space, to the completed stochastic integral. Uniqueness of L¹ limits proves equality almost surely. Apply this argument separately to each fixed terminal time and each of the finitely many coordinates.

Step 1.1: N_0=A_0=0 makes both measures of time-zero generators zero. Step 2.1 uses the completed-integral isometry F7, so zero compensator energy gives zero L2 integral and the same zero pathwise expression.

Statement and steps 1.1, 2.1: scalar real integrands are included. The compensation and step-increment arguments allow any finite unit-jump count; for a path with one jump at t in (0,T], the N integral is H_t Delta N_t=H_t.

Steps 1.1, 2.1: if EA_T=0, EN_T=EA_T and nonnegativity imply A_T=N_T=0 almost surely. Monotonicity makes both integrators zero; the compensation measures and completed L2 integral vanish. The bound in step 2.1 remains valid with factor (EA_T)^(1/2)=0.

Statement and step 1.1: the generator (s,t] and terminal sum (0,T] retain the right endpoint. Both time-zero masses are zero since N_0=A_0=0. Step 2.1 applies at each fixed terminal time; at t=0 the jump sum is empty and both integrals are zero.
A1 and step 2.1 carry the inherited AC through the density approximation.

This worksheet direction has no separate hypothesis-to-criterion forward implication.

EN_T=EA_T follows from M0=0 and the martingale hypothesis; both compensation measures are finite. Generator section measurability extends by the lambda-system argument (whole space and zero-time masses included), and equality on predictable generators gives compensation for arbitrary nonnegative predictable G, including infinite expectations.
