citations.quote:
Fix a finite horizon $\tau>0$ and a fixed dimension $p\ge1$. Work on a probability space with an increasing filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le\tau}$ as in [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. For subject $i$, let $T_i$ be an event time, $C_i$ a censoring time, and $Z_i(t)\in\mathbb R^p$ a covariate process predictable relative to this filtration, in the sense of [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Use the right-censoring record convention of [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]]: $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\}$. For this vector covariate process, predictability means coordinatewise predictability: each real-valued coordinate is predictable in the sense of [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Define the history sigma-algebra $\mathcal G_i:=\sigma\{Z_i(t):0\le t\le\tau\}$. The conditional-independence assumption is $T_i\perp\!\!\!\perp C_i\mid\mathcal G_i$, meaning that for all bounded measurable real functions $a,b$, $E[a(T_i)b(C_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]=E[a(T_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]E[b(C_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]$ almost surely, as in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. This conditional-independence relation is a model assumption, not an empirical conclusion. No conditional-kernel representation given the entire covariate path is assumed here.

A Cox proportional-hazards specification fixes a coefficient $\beta_0\in\mathbb R^p$ and a baseline hazard density $\lambda_0:[0,\tau]\to[0,\infty)$ that is measurable and integrable. Its baseline cumulative hazard is the absolutely continuous function
$$\Lambda_0(t)=\int_0^t\lambda_0(u)\,du.$$
The conditional event intensity at time $t$ for subject $i$, while that subject is at risk, is
$$Y_i(t)\lambda_0(t)\exp\{\beta_0^T Z_i(t)\},\qquad Y_i(t):=1\{U_i\ge t\}.$$
These specify the conditional event-intensity component. The law of the covariate paths and the censoring law subject to the stated conditional-independence assumption remain nuisance components and are not fixed here. Thus this is a semiparametric model specification; $(\beta_0,\lambda_0)$ alone do not define a full parametric statistical experiment on the observed-data space.
For the counting-process arguments below, require $Y_i$ to be predictable as well; this is part of the stated observation model and is not inferred from the hazard formula alone.
For a constant covariate value $z$, the corresponding event survival function is
$$S(t\mid z)=\exp\{-e^{\beta_0^Tz}\Lambda_0(t)\}.$$
For fixed covariate values $z,z'\in\mathbb R^p$, at times with $\lambda_0(t)>0$ the hazard ratio is
$$\frac{\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta^Tz}}{\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta^Tz'}}=e^{\beta^T(z-z')}.$$
The relative hazard factor is $e^{\beta^T(z-z')}$ even at times when both baseline-scaled hazards vanish and their quotient is undefined. It is an instantaneous hazard ratio, not a ratio of cumulative event probabilities. For time-varying covariate paths $z(t),z'(t)$ the instantaneous relative hazard factor is $e^{\beta^T(z(t)-z'(t))}$ and may vary with time.

For a sample of $n$ subjects, put $R(t)=\{j:U_j\ge t\}$. When failures are untied, the Cox partial likelihood on $[0,\tau]$ is
$$L_p(\beta)=\prod_{i:\,\delta_i=1,\ U_i\le\tau} \frac{\exp\{\beta^TZ_i(U_i)\}}{\sum_{j\in R(U_i)}\exp\{\beta^TZ_j(U_i)\}}.$$
An empty product is $1$. This partial likelihood is built from risk-set contributions; it is not asserted to be the full likelihood of the censored observations.

Tied-event likelihoods require an explicit time-recording convention. Put $D(t)=\{i:U_i=t,\delta_i=1\}$ and $d_t=|D(t)|$. If a discrete or grouped-time model conditions on exactly $d_t$ failures from $D(t)\subseteq R(t)$ at recorded time $t$ with the risk set fixed for that time, additionally assume that, conditional on that risk set, its covariate weights, and $d_t=d$, the failure subset law assigns each size-$d$ set $A\subseteq R(t)$ probability proportional to $\prod_{j\in A}w_j(t)$. Under this explicit subset-law assumption, its exact conditional tie contribution is
$$\frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq R(t)\\|A|=d_t}}\ \prod_{j\in A}w_j(t)}, \qquad w_j(t):=\exp\{\beta^TZ_j(t)\}.$$
For the separate exact Cox tied-partial-likelihood convention obtained by coarsening a continuous-time ordering into one recorded tie interval, assume the risk set at the interval start is $R(t)$, its only within-interval departures are the $d_t$ failures in $D(t)$, and the covariates are fixed at the recorded time. Conditional on each successive failure, the next failure label is chosen from the remaining risk set with probability proportional to its weight. Summing these order contributions gives the ordered-risk-set conditional partial-likelihood contribution
$$\sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Perm}(D(t))} \prod_{k=1}^{d_t} \frac{w_{\pi_k}(t)} {\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)-\sum_{\ell<k}w_{\pi_\ell}(t)}.$$
Here $\operatorname{Perm}(D(t))$ is the set of bijections from $\{1,\ldots,d_t\}$ to $D(t)$.
The discrete subset expression is exact under its explicit subset-law convention, and the permutation expression is exact for its stated partial-likelihood ordering convention; the latter is not generally the full likelihood of interval-coarsened censored observations. These conventions are not interchangeable without a model relating them. The Breslow and Efron tie formulas are approximations, respectively
$$L_B(\beta)=\prod_{t:d_t>0} \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\left(\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)\right)^{d_t}}$$
and
$$L_E(\beta)=\prod_{t:d_t>0} \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\prod_{k=0}^{d_t-1}\left(\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)-\frac{k}{d_t}\sum_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)\right)}.$$
With an absolutely continuous event hazard and independent subjects, exact event-time ties have probability zero; grouped-time tie formulas describe additional observation/model conventions.

For a discrete event-time law, the survival relation $S(t\mid z)=S_0(t)^{e^{\beta^Tz}}$ describes proportional integrated hazards and is not equivalent in general to a hazard-ratio model. The proportional-hazards and proportional-integrated-hazards formulations agree under the continuity condition on the baseline survival; the hazard-density model above uses the absolutely continuous convention.

The counting-process martingale property used for inference is a separate model-contract assumption in the estimator theorem below. The hazard formula by itself does not assert that a compensated event count is a martingale. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the cited event-observation and predictability interfaces; this definition makes no further choice.

Let $O_i=(T_i,C_i,Z_i(\cdot))$, $i\ge1$, be IID subject records with law $P$, with jointly measurable predictable covariates, $p<\infty$, and $\|Z_i(t)\|_2\le K$ for all $i,t$ outside one null event. Let $B\subset\mathbb R^p$ be compact and contain $\beta_0$. With $Y_i(t)=1\{U_i\ge t\}$, define, for $r=0,1,2$,
$$S_n^{(r)}(t,\beta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i(t)Z_i(t)^{\otimes r}e^{\beta^TZ_i(t)},\qquad s^{(r)}(t,\beta)=E_P[Y_i(t)Z_i(t)^{\otimes r}e^{\beta^TZ_i(t)}],$$
where $Z^{\otimes0}=1$, $Z^{\otimes1}=Z$, and $Z^{\otimes2}=ZZ^T$. Suppose $c_0:=\inf_{t\le\tau}s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)>0$. For every finite deterministic measure $\nu(dt)=w(t)\,dt$ with nonnegative integrable density $w$, put
$$D_n(t)=\max_{r=0,1,2}\sup_{\beta\in B}\|S_n^{(r)}(t,\beta)-s^{(r)}(t,\beta)\|_{\max}.$$
Then for each fixed $t$, $E[D_n(t)^2]\to0$, and
$$E\int_0^\tau D_n(t)^2\,\nu(dt)\longrightarrow0.$$
There are measurable events $E_n$ with $P(E_n)\to1$ and a constant $c>0$ such that on $E_n$,
$$S_n^{(0)}(t,\beta)\ge c\qquad\text{for every }t\le\tau,\ \beta\in B.$$
Define $\bar Z_n=S_n^{(1)}/S_n^{(0)}$ and $V_n=S_n^{(2)}/S_n^{(0)}-\bar Z_n\bar Z_n^T$, setting each to zero at a zero denominator, and define $\bar z=s^{(1)}/s^{(0)}$, $V=s^{(2)}/s^{(0)}-\bar z\bar z^T$. Their fixed-time and integrated parameter-uniform errors satisfy
$$E\sup_{\beta\in B}\|\bar Z_n(t,\beta)-\bar z(t,\beta)\|_2^2\to0,\qquad E\sup_{\beta\in B}\|V_n(t,\beta)-V(t,\beta)\|_{\max}^2\to0,$$
$$E\int_0^\tau\sup_{\beta\in B}\!\left\{\|\bar Z_n-\bar z\|_2^2+\|V_n-V\|_{\max}^2\right\}\nu(dt)\longrightarrow0.$$
These conclusions require no regularity of the time-indexed covariate class beyond bounded predictability. In particular take $\nu(dt)=\lambda_0(t)\,dt$.

The stronger uniform-in-time conclusion remains valid under the following additional, sufficient condition: every scalar coordinate class $\mathcal F_{r,k}=\{O\mapsto[Y(t)Z(t)^{\otimes r}e^{\beta^TZ(t)}]_k:t\le\tau,\beta\in B\}$ is pointwise measurable and has finite $L^1(P)$ bracketing number at every positive width. Under that condition, $\sup_tD_n(t)\to_P0$, and both ratio errors converge uniformly on $[0,\tau]\times B$ in probability. This optional condition is not imposed by the Cox inference consumers.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a finite horizon
$T>0$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires that this integral
be finite pathwise, that $A$ be continuous, adapted and predictable with
$A_0=0$, and that $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$. Set $M_t:=N_t-A_t$. The model
contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

The displayed intensity density alone does **not** assert that $N-A$ is a
martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.

Under the finite-horizon contract of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]], the optional
quadratic variation of $M=N-A$ is $[M]_t=N_t$, its continuous predictable
bracket is $\langle M\rangle_t=A_t$, its self-cross predictable bracket is
$\langle M,M\rangle_t=A_t$, and $M_t^2-A_t$ is a martingale on $[0,T]$.

For every predictable $H$ on $[0,T]$ with
$\mathbb E\int_0^T H_s^2\,dA_s<\infty$, the limit in
[[def-l2-counting-process-integral]] exists at each $t\le T$, is independent
of the approximating step sequence, and defines a square-integrable
martingale. It satisfies, for each $t\le T$,
$$\mathbb E\left(\int_0^tH_s\,dM_s\right)^2=\mathbb E\int_0^tH_s^2\,dA_s.$$

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Under [[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]], for every nonnegative predictable $G$,
$$E\int_{(0,T]}G_t\,dN_t=E\int_0^T G_t\,dA_t.$$
For every bounded real predictable $H$, the L²-completed stochastic integral equals the pathwise finite-variation expression almost surely:
$$\int_0^T H_t\,dM_t=\sum_{0<t\le T}H_t\Delta N_t-\int_0^T H_t\,dA_t,\qquad M=N-A.$$
The identity holds at every fixed terminal time and coordinatewise for vector or matrix integrands. No left continuity of $H$ is assumed.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: At each recorded failure the risk set contains its failing subject, so its denominator is positive for every $\beta$, even if risk sets are empty at other times. Differentiate the finite sum defining $\log L_p$ to obtain $U_n(\beta)=\sum_i\int(Z_i-\bar Z_n(t,\beta))\,dN_i$ and $H_n(\beta)=-\int V_n(t,\beta)\,dN_\cdot$. Define $V_n=0$ on empty risk sets. It is predictable, its entries are bounded by $2K^2$, and [F5] permits the pathwise decomposition against $dN_\cdot=d\mathcal M+dA_\cdot$.

Since subjects have no simultaneous failures, $N_\cdot$ is simple; $\mathcal M=\sum_iM_i$ is square-integrable and has continuous compensator $A_\cdot=\sum_iA_i$. Its total compensator satisfies $A_\cdot(\tau)\le ne^{K\|\beta_0\|_2}\|\lambda_0\|_1$, and $EN_\cdot(\tau)=EA_\cdot(\tau)$ by [F5]. Thus the aggregate contract holds and [L2]–[L3] apply. For each fixed $\beta$, including the random predictable $V_n(t,\beta)$, their isometry bounds $E\|n^{-1}\int V_n(t,\beta)d\mathcal M\|_F^2\le C/n$.

The parameter maps $V_n(t,\beta)$ have a deterministic Lipschitz bound independent of $n,t$: on a nonempty risk set, differentiating a weighted expectation of a bounded coordinate $g(Z)$ gives $E_{n,\beta}[gZ]-E_{n,\beta}[g]E_{n,\beta}[Z]$, bounded by $2K\sup|g|$; apply this to $g=Z_j,Z_jZ_k$ and the covariance product. An empty risk set is empty for every parameter, so its zero convention also has this bound. The population maps satisfy the same bounds by differentiation under their bounded expectations and positive denominators. A finite $\varepsilon$-net of $B$ and step 2.1 control $n^{-1}\int V_n d\mathcal M$ on net points. Between points, [F5] bounds the difference by $C\varepsilon(N_\cdot(\tau)+A_\cdot(\tau))/n=O_P(\varepsilon)$; letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves its uniform parameter convergence to zero. The population Lipschitz bound and integrability of $s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)\lambda_0(t)$ also prove continuity of $J$.

The compensator term equals $\int V_n(t,\beta)S_n^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)\lambda_0(t)dt$. Its difference from $J(\beta)$ is bounded uniformly in parameter by $$C\int_0^\tau\left\{\sup_{\beta\in B}\|V_n(t,\beta)-V(t,\beta)\|_{\max}+|S_n^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)-s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)|\right\}\lambda_0(t)dt.$$ [F6] and [F2]'s expected integrated squared-error convergence make this bound tend to zero in L¹ and hence probability (if $\|\lambda_0\|_1=0$, the bound is zero directly). Combine this with step 3.1 and the Hessian identity in step 1.1 to prove the stated uniform parameter limit. Finally $J(\beta_0)=I$ by direct multiplication of $V(t,\beta_0)$ by $s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)$.

citations.quote:
Fix a finite horizon $\tau>0$ and a fixed dimension $p\ge1$. Work on a probability space with an increasing filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le\tau}$ as in [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. For subject $i$, let $T_i$ be an event time, $C_i$ a censoring time, and $Z_i(t)\in\mathbb R^p$ a covariate process predictable relative to this filtration, in the sense of [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Use the right-censoring record convention of [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]]: $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\}$. For this vector covariate process, predictability means coordinatewise predictability: each real-valued coordinate is predictable in the sense of [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Define the history sigma-algebra $\mathcal G_i:=\sigma\{Z_i(t):0\le t\le\tau\}$. The conditional-independence assumption is $T_i\perp\!\!\!\perp C_i\mid\mathcal G_i$, meaning that for all bounded measurable real functions $a,b$, $E[a(T_i)b(C_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]=E[a(T_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]E[b(C_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]$ almost surely, as in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. This conditional-independence relation is a model assumption, not an empirical conclusion. No conditional-kernel representation given the entire covariate path is assumed here.

A Cox proportional-hazards specification fixes a coefficient $\beta_0\in\mathbb R^p$ and a baseline hazard density $\lambda_0:[0,\tau]\to[0,\infty)$ that is measurable and integrable. Its baseline cumulative hazard is the absolutely continuous function
$$\Lambda_0(t)=\int_0^t\lambda_0(u)\,du.$$
The conditional event intensity at time $t$ for subject $i$, while that subject is at risk, is
$$Y_i(t)\lambda_0(t)\exp\{\beta_0^T Z_i(t)\},\qquad Y_i(t):=1\{U_i\ge t\}.$$
These specify the conditional event-intensity component. The law of the covariate paths and the censoring law subject to the stated conditional-independence assumption remain nuisance components and are not fixed here. Thus this is a semiparametric model specification; $(\beta_0,\lambda_0)$ alone do not define a full parametric statistical experiment on the observed-data space.
For the counting-process arguments below, require $Y_i$ to be predictable as well; this is part of the stated observation model and is not inferred from the hazard formula alone.
For a constant covariate value $z$, the corresponding event survival function is
$$S(t\mid z)=\exp\{-e^{\beta_0^Tz}\Lambda_0(t)\}.$$
For fixed covariate values $z,z'\in\mathbb R^p$, at times with $\lambda_0(t)>0$ the hazard ratio is
$$\frac{\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta^Tz}}{\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta^Tz'}}=e^{\beta^T(z-z')}.$$
The relative hazard factor is $e^{\beta^T(z-z')}$ even at times when both baseline-scaled hazards vanish and their quotient is undefined. It is an instantaneous hazard ratio, not a ratio of cumulative event probabilities. For time-varying covariate paths $z(t),z'(t)$ the instantaneous relative hazard factor is $e^{\beta^T(z(t)-z'(t))}$ and may vary with time.

For a sample of $n$ subjects, put $R(t)=\{j:U_j\ge t\}$. When failures are untied, the Cox partial likelihood on $[0,\tau]$ is
$$L_p(\beta)=\prod_{i:\,\delta_i=1,\ U_i\le\tau} \frac{\exp\{\beta^TZ_i(U_i)\}}{\sum_{j\in R(U_i)}\exp\{\beta^TZ_j(U_i)\}}.$$
An empty product is $1$. This partial likelihood is built from risk-set contributions; it is not asserted to be the full likelihood of the censored observations.

Tied-event likelihoods require an explicit time-recording convention. Put $D(t)=\{i:U_i=t,\delta_i=1\}$ and $d_t=|D(t)|$. If a discrete or grouped-time model conditions on exactly $d_t$ failures from $D(t)\subseteq R(t)$ at recorded time $t$ with the risk set fixed for that time, additionally assume that, conditional on that risk set, its covariate weights, and $d_t=d$, the failure subset law assigns each size-$d$ set $A\subseteq R(t)$ probability proportional to $\prod_{j\in A}w_j(t)$. Under this explicit subset-law assumption, its exact conditional tie contribution is
$$\frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq R(t)\\|A|=d_t}}\ \prod_{j\in A}w_j(t)}, \qquad w_j(t):=\exp\{\beta^TZ_j(t)\}.$$
For the separate exact Cox tied-partial-likelihood convention obtained by coarsening a continuous-time ordering into one recorded tie interval, assume the risk set at the interval start is $R(t)$, its only within-interval departures are the $d_t$ failures in $D(t)$, and the covariates are fixed at the recorded time. Conditional on each successive failure, the next failure label is chosen from the remaining risk set with probability proportional to its weight. Summing these order contributions gives the ordered-risk-set conditional partial-likelihood contribution
$$\sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Perm}(D(t))} \prod_{k=1}^{d_t} \frac{w_{\pi_k}(t)} {\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)-\sum_{\ell<k}w_{\pi_\ell}(t)}.$$
Here $\operatorname{Perm}(D(t))$ is the set of bijections from $\{1,\ldots,d_t\}$ to $D(t)$.
The discrete subset expression is exact under its explicit subset-law convention, and the permutation expression is exact for its stated partial-likelihood ordering convention; the latter is not generally the full likelihood of interval-coarsened censored observations. These conventions are not interchangeable without a model relating them. The Breslow and Efron tie formulas are approximations, respectively
$$L_B(\beta)=\prod_{t:d_t>0} \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\left(\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)\right)^{d_t}}$$
and
$$L_E(\beta)=\prod_{t:d_t>0} \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\prod_{k=0}^{d_t-1}\left(\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)-\frac{k}{d_t}\sum_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)\right)}.$$
With an absolutely continuous event hazard and independent subjects, exact event-time ties have probability zero; grouped-time tie formulas describe additional observation/model conventions.

For a discrete event-time law, the survival relation $S(t\mid z)=S_0(t)^{e^{\beta^Tz}}$ describes proportional integrated hazards and is not equivalent in general to a hazard-ratio model. The proportional-hazards and proportional-integrated-hazards formulations agree under the continuity condition on the baseline survival; the hazard-density model above uses the absolutely continuous convention.

The counting-process martingale property used for inference is a separate model-contract assumption in the estimator theorem below. The hazard formula by itself does not assert that a compensated event count is a martingale. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the cited event-observation and predictability interfaces; this definition makes no further choice.

Let $O_i=(T_i,C_i,Z_i(\cdot))$, $i\ge1$, be IID subject records with law $P$, with jointly measurable predictable covariates, $p<\infty$, and $\|Z_i(t)\|_2\le K$ for all $i,t$ outside one null event. Let $B\subset\mathbb R^p$ be compact and contain $\beta_0$. With $Y_i(t)=1\{U_i\ge t\}$, define, for $r=0,1,2$,
$$S_n^{(r)}(t,\beta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i(t)Z_i(t)^{\otimes r}e^{\beta^TZ_i(t)},\qquad s^{(r)}(t,\beta)=E_P[Y_i(t)Z_i(t)^{\otimes r}e^{\beta^TZ_i(t)}],$$
where $Z^{\otimes0}=1$, $Z^{\otimes1}=Z$, and $Z^{\otimes2}=ZZ^T$. Suppose $c_0:=\inf_{t\le\tau}s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)>0$. For every finite deterministic measure $\nu(dt)=w(t)\,dt$ with nonnegative integrable density $w$, put
$$D_n(t)=\max_{r=0,1,2}\sup_{\beta\in B}\|S_n^{(r)}(t,\beta)-s^{(r)}(t,\beta)\|_{\max}.$$
Then for each fixed $t$, $E[D_n(t)^2]\to0$, and
$$E\int_0^\tau D_n(t)^2\,\nu(dt)\longrightarrow0.$$
There are measurable events $E_n$ with $P(E_n)\to1$ and a constant $c>0$ such that on $E_n$,
$$S_n^{(0)}(t,\beta)\ge c\qquad\text{for every }t\le\tau,\ \beta\in B.$$
Define $\bar Z_n=S_n^{(1)}/S_n^{(0)}$ and $V_n=S_n^{(2)}/S_n^{(0)}-\bar Z_n\bar Z_n^T$, setting each to zero at a zero denominator, and define $\bar z=s^{(1)}/s^{(0)}$, $V=s^{(2)}/s^{(0)}-\bar z\bar z^T$. Their fixed-time and integrated parameter-uniform errors satisfy
$$E\sup_{\beta\in B}\|\bar Z_n(t,\beta)-\bar z(t,\beta)\|_2^2\to0,\qquad E\sup_{\beta\in B}\|V_n(t,\beta)-V(t,\beta)\|_{\max}^2\to0,$$
$$E\int_0^\tau\sup_{\beta\in B}\!\left\{\|\bar Z_n-\bar z\|_2^2+\|V_n-V\|_{\max}^2\right\}\nu(dt)\longrightarrow0.$$
These conclusions require no regularity of the time-indexed covariate class beyond bounded predictability. In particular take $\nu(dt)=\lambda_0(t)\,dt$.

The stronger uniform-in-time conclusion remains valid under the following additional, sufficient condition: every scalar coordinate class $\mathcal F_{r,k}=\{O\mapsto[Y(t)Z(t)^{\otimes r}e^{\beta^TZ(t)}]_k:t\le\tau,\beta\in B\}$ is pointwise measurable and has finite $L^1(P)$ bracketing number at every positive width. Under that condition, $\sup_tD_n(t)\to_P0$, and both ratio errors converge uniformly on $[0,\tau]\times B$ in probability. This optional condition is not imposed by the Cox inference consumers.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a finite horizon
$T>0$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires that this integral
be finite pathwise, that $A$ be continuous, adapted and predictable with
$A_0=0$, and that $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$. Set $M_t:=N_t-A_t$. The model
contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

The displayed intensity density alone does **not** assert that $N-A$ is a
martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.

Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale on a finite horizon $[0,T]$ in the
all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] (in particular, it may
be the compensated counting-process martingale of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]). Let
$$0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T$$
be a deterministic partition, and let each bounded random variable $H_j$ be
$\mathcal F_{t_j}$-measurable. The associated **bounded predictable step
integrand** is $H_0=0$ at time $0$ and $H_s=H_j$ on $(t_j,t_{j+1}]$. For this
chosen step representation define, for $0\le t\le T$,
$$I_t(H):=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}H_j\bigl(M_{t\wedge t_{j+1}}-M_{t\wedge t_j}\bigr).$$
This is a finite sum of square-integrable random variables. At this stage the
representation is part of the input; representation independence and the
isometry are established in
[[lem-elementary-counting-process-integral-isometry]].
The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the all-pairs martingale and
conditional-expectation interface; the finite-sum definition makes no
additional choice.

Under the finite-horizon contract of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]], the optional
quadratic variation of $M=N-A$ is $[M]_t=N_t$, its continuous predictable
bracket is $\langle M\rangle_t=A_t$, its self-cross predictable bracket is
$\langle M,M\rangle_t=A_t$, and $M_t^2-A_t$ is a martingale on $[0,T]$.

For every predictable $H$ on $[0,T]$ with
$\mathbb E\int_0^T H_s^2\,dA_s<\infty$, the limit in
[[def-l2-counting-process-integral]] exists at each $t\le T$, is independent
of the approximating step sequence, and defines a square-integrable
martingale. It satisfies, for each $t\le T$,
$$\mathbb E\left(\int_0^tH_s\,dM_s\right)^2=\mathbb E\int_0^tH_s^2\,dA_s.$$

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Under [[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]], for every nonnegative predictable $G$,
$$E\int_{(0,T]}G_t\,dN_t=E\int_0^T G_t\,dA_t.$$
For every bounded real predictable $H$, the L²-completed stochastic integral equals the pathwise finite-variation expression almost surely:
$$\int_0^T H_t\,dM_t=\sum_{0<t\le T}H_t\Delta N_t-\int_0^T H_t\,dA_t,\qquad M=N-A.$$
The identity holds at every fixed terminal time and coordinatewise for vector or matrix integrands. No left continuity of $H$ is assumed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Differentiating the finite product in [[def-cox-proportional-hazards-model-and-partial-likelihood]] gives $$U_n(\beta_0)=\sum_i\int_0^\tau\{Z_i(t)-\bar Z_n(t,\beta_0)\}\,dN_i(t).$$ By [F4], this pathwise integral can be decomposed as the L² stochastic integral and its compensator integral. Writing $dN_i=dM_i+Y_ie^{\beta_0^TZ_i}\lambda_0\,dt$, the compensator contribution is zero because $\sum_iY_i(t)e^{\beta_0^TZ_i(t)}\{Z_i(t)-\bar Z_n(t,\beta_0)\}=0$ whenever the risk denominator is positive; outside the risk set every summand is zero.

Set $\mathcal M=\sum_iM_i$ and $H_n(t)=\bar Z_n(t,\beta_0)-\bar z(t)$. The process $H_n$ is predictable by [F1]–[F3] and the deterministic measurability of $\bar z$. For bounded predictable step approximations, the finite-sum definition [L2] is linear in the integrator; the isometry [L4] and $A_\cdot=\sum_iA_i$ pass that identity to the L² limits. Thus $n^{-1/2}U_n(\beta_0)=n^{-1/2}\sum_i\xi_i-n^{-1/2}\int_0^\tau H_n(t)\,d\mathcal M(t)$. No simultaneous failures make $N_\cdot=\sum_iN_i$ a simple counting process, and the sum of the subject contracts is a square-integrable martingale contract with compensator $A_\cdot=\sum_iA_i$.

The predictable aggregate integrand $H_n$ is bounded by $2K$. Its compensator energy satisfies $$n^{-1}E\int_0^\tau\|H_n(t)\|_2^2\,dA_\cdot(t)=E\int_0^\tau\|H_n(t)\|_2^2S_n^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)\lambda_0(t)dt\le e^{K\|\beta_0\|_2}E\int_0^\tau\|H_n(t)\|_2^2\lambda_0(t)dt\longrightarrow0$$ by [F2]'s integrated squared-error conclusion, without a time supremum. Thus [L4] shows the aggregate correction in step 2.1 tends to zero in L² after division by $\sqrt n$, and therefore is $o_P(1)$.

By [F4], $\xi_i$ equals the event sum minus the compensator Lebesgue integral with integrand $Z_i-\bar z$. Both are measurable functions of the $i$th subject record and the deterministic function $\bar z$, so the $\xi_i$ are IID. The integral isometry gives mean zero. Applying its scalar form to each coordinate and polarizing the identity gives the cross-coordinate isometry, hence $E[\xi_i\xi_i^T]=\int_0^\tau E[Y_i(t)e^{\beta_0^TZ_i(t)}\{Z_i(t)-\bar z(t)\}^{\otimes2}]\lambda_0(t)\,dt=I$. The equality follows by expanding the outer product and using $\bar z=s^{(1)}/s^{(0)}$. Independence and centering give $E\|n^{-1/2}\sum_i\xi_i\|_2^2=\operatorname{tr}(I)$. For $M>0$, nonnegativity gives $M^2P(\|n^{-1/2}\sum_i\xi_i\|_2>M)\le E\|n^{-1/2}\sum_i\xi_i\|_2^2=\operatorname{tr}(I)$, so the normalized sum is $O_P(1)$ by [L5]. Combining this with step 3.1 proves the representation and the stated moment properties.

citations.quote:
Fix a finite horizon $\tau>0$ and a fixed dimension $p\ge1$. Work on a probability space with an increasing filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le\tau}$ as in [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. For subject $i$, let $T_i$ be an event time, $C_i$ a censoring time, and $Z_i(t)\in\mathbb R^p$ a covariate process predictable relative to this filtration, in the sense of [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Use the right-censoring record convention of [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]]: $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\}$. For this vector covariate process, predictability means coordinatewise predictability: each real-valued coordinate is predictable in the sense of [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Define the history sigma-algebra $\mathcal G_i:=\sigma\{Z_i(t):0\le t\le\tau\}$. The conditional-independence assumption is $T_i\perp\!\!\!\perp C_i\mid\mathcal G_i$, meaning that for all bounded measurable real functions $a,b$, $E[a(T_i)b(C_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]=E[a(T_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]E[b(C_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]$ almost surely, as in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. This conditional-independence relation is a model assumption, not an empirical conclusion. No conditional-kernel representation given the entire covariate path is assumed here.

A Cox proportional-hazards specification fixes a coefficient $\beta_0\in\mathbb R^p$ and a baseline hazard density $\lambda_0:[0,\tau]\to[0,\infty)$ that is measurable and integrable. Its baseline cumulative hazard is the absolutely continuous function
$$\Lambda_0(t)=\int_0^t\lambda_0(u)\,du.$$
The conditional event intensity at time $t$ for subject $i$, while that subject is at risk, is
$$Y_i(t)\lambda_0(t)\exp\{\beta_0^T Z_i(t)\},\qquad Y_i(t):=1\{U_i\ge t\}.$$
These specify the conditional event-intensity component. The law of the covariate paths and the censoring law subject to the stated conditional-independence assumption remain nuisance components and are not fixed here. Thus this is a semiparametric model specification; $(\beta_0,\lambda_0)$ alone do not define a full parametric statistical experiment on the observed-data space.
For the counting-process arguments below, require $Y_i$ to be predictable as well; this is part of the stated observation model and is not inferred from the hazard formula alone.
For a constant covariate value $z$, the corresponding event survival function is
$$S(t\mid z)=\exp\{-e^{\beta_0^Tz}\Lambda_0(t)\}.$$
For fixed covariate values $z,z'\in\mathbb R^p$, at times with $\lambda_0(t)>0$ the hazard ratio is
$$\frac{\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta^Tz}}{\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta^Tz'}}=e^{\beta^T(z-z')}.$$
The relative hazard factor is $e^{\beta^T(z-z')}$ even at times when both baseline-scaled hazards vanish and their quotient is undefined. It is an instantaneous hazard ratio, not a ratio of cumulative event probabilities. For time-varying covariate paths $z(t),z'(t)$ the instantaneous relative hazard factor is $e^{\beta^T(z(t)-z'(t))}$ and may vary with time.

For a sample of $n$ subjects, put $R(t)=\{j:U_j\ge t\}$. When failures are untied, the Cox partial likelihood on $[0,\tau]$ is
$$L_p(\beta)=\prod_{i:\,\delta_i=1,\ U_i\le\tau} \frac{\exp\{\beta^TZ_i(U_i)\}}{\sum_{j\in R(U_i)}\exp\{\beta^TZ_j(U_i)\}}.$$
An empty product is $1$. This partial likelihood is built from risk-set contributions; it is not asserted to be the full likelihood of the censored observations.

Tied-event likelihoods require an explicit time-recording convention. Put $D(t)=\{i:U_i=t,\delta_i=1\}$ and $d_t=|D(t)|$. If a discrete or grouped-time model conditions on exactly $d_t$ failures from $D(t)\subseteq R(t)$ at recorded time $t$ with the risk set fixed for that time, additionally assume that, conditional on that risk set, its covariate weights, and $d_t=d$, the failure subset law assigns each size-$d$ set $A\subseteq R(t)$ probability proportional to $\prod_{j\in A}w_j(t)$. Under this explicit subset-law assumption, its exact conditional tie contribution is
$$\frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq R(t)\\|A|=d_t}}\ \prod_{j\in A}w_j(t)}, \qquad w_j(t):=\exp\{\beta^TZ_j(t)\}.$$
For the separate exact Cox tied-partial-likelihood convention obtained by coarsening a continuous-time ordering into one recorded tie interval, assume the risk set at the interval start is $R(t)$, its only within-interval departures are the $d_t$ failures in $D(t)$, and the covariates are fixed at the recorded time. Conditional on each successive failure, the next failure label is chosen from the remaining risk set with probability proportional to its weight. Summing these order contributions gives the ordered-risk-set conditional partial-likelihood contribution
$$\sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Perm}(D(t))} \prod_{k=1}^{d_t} \frac{w_{\pi_k}(t)} {\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)-\sum_{\ell<k}w_{\pi_\ell}(t)}.$$
Here $\operatorname{Perm}(D(t))$ is the set of bijections from $\{1,\ldots,d_t\}$ to $D(t)$.
The discrete subset expression is exact under its explicit subset-law convention, and the permutation expression is exact for its stated partial-likelihood ordering convention; the latter is not generally the full likelihood of interval-coarsened censored observations. These conventions are not interchangeable without a model relating them. The Breslow and Efron tie formulas are approximations, respectively
$$L_B(\beta)=\prod_{t:d_t>0} \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\left(\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)\right)^{d_t}}$$
and
$$L_E(\beta)=\prod_{t:d_t>0} \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\prod_{k=0}^{d_t-1}\left(\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)-\frac{k}{d_t}\sum_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)\right)}.$$
With an absolutely continuous event hazard and independent subjects, exact event-time ties have probability zero; grouped-time tie formulas describe additional observation/model conventions.

For a discrete event-time law, the survival relation $S(t\mid z)=S_0(t)^{e^{\beta^Tz}}$ describes proportional integrated hazards and is not equivalent in general to a hazard-ratio model. The proportional-hazards and proportional-integrated-hazards formulations agree under the continuity condition on the baseline survival; the hazard-density model above uses the absolutely continuous convention.

The counting-process martingale property used for inference is a separate model-contract assumption in the estimator theorem below. The hazard formula by itself does not assert that a compensated event count is a martingale. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the cited event-observation and predictability interfaces; this definition makes no further choice.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Use the IID bounded-covariate setup and the risk-support and compact-set hypotheses of [[lem-cox-uniform-risk-set-convergence]]. For each subject let $N_i(t)=1\{U_i\le t,\delta_i=1\}$ and $A_i(t)=\int_0^tY_i(u)e^{\beta_0^TZ_i(u)}\lambda_0(u)\,du$. Assume the continuous counting-process contract of [[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]] for each $M_i=N_i-A_i$ on one common filtration, and assume no two subjects fail at the same time. Write $N_\cdot=\sum_iN_i$, $A_\cdot=\sum_iA_i$, and $\mathcal M=N_\cdot-A_\cdot$. For $\beta\in B$, let
$$V_n(t,\beta)=\frac{S_n^{(2)}(t,\beta)}{S_n^{(0)}(t,\beta)} -\bar Z_n(t,\beta)\bar Z_n(t,\beta)^T,\qquad V(t,\beta)=\frac{s^{(2)}(t,\beta)}{s^{(0)}(t,\beta)} -\bar z(t,\beta)\bar z(t,\beta)^T,$$
using zero values when a finite-sample denominator is zero. Let $U_n(\beta)=\partial_\beta\log L_p(\beta)$ and $H_n(\beta)=\partial_\beta U_n(\beta)^T$. Define
$$J(\beta)=\int_0^\tau V(t,\beta)s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)\lambda_0(t)\,dt.$$
Then the partial log-likelihood Hessian satisfies
$$\sup_{\beta\in B}\left\|n^{-1}H_n(\beta)+J(\beta)\right\|_{\max}\longrightarrow_P0.$$
The map $J:B\to\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ is continuous.
In particular, $J(\beta_0)=I$, where
$$I=\int_0^\tau\left\{s^{(2)}(t,\beta_0)- \frac{s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)^T}{s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)}\right\}\lambda_0(t)\,dt.$$

Use the IID bounded-covariate model, risk-support hypotheses of [[lem-cox-uniform-risk-set-convergence]], the no-tie event process, and the per-subject counting-process contracts of [[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]. Let
$$\bar z(t)=\frac{s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)}{s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)},\qquad I=\int_0^\tau\left\{s^{(2)}(t,\beta_0)- \frac{s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)^T}{s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)}\right\}\lambda_0(t)\,dt,\qquad \xi_i=\int_0^\tau\{Z_i(t)-\bar z(t)\}\,dM_i(t),$$
where each vector integral is defined coordinatewise in L². If $U_n(\beta)=\partial_\beta\log L_p(\beta)$ is the partial-likelihood score, then
$$n^{-1/2}U_n(\beta_0)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_i+o_P(1).$$
The $\xi_i$ are IID, centered, square-integrable vectors with covariance matrix $I$. In particular, $n^{-1/2}\sum_i\xi_i=O_P(1)$. The replacement of the random risk-set mean by $\bar z$ is part of the conclusion.

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Put $\Delta_n=\hat\beta_n-\beta_0$ and $G_n=\int_0^1n^{-1}H_n(\beta_0+s\Delta_n)\,ds$. Since $\Delta_n\to_P0$, the segment lies in $B$ with probability tending to one. The Hessian lemma gives uniform convergence to $-J(\beta)$, and $J$ is continuous at $\beta_0$ by bounded covariates, the positive risk denominator, and $\lambda_0\in L^1$. Therefore $G_n\to_P-I$.
Since $I$ is positive definite, it is invertible. Matrix inversion is continuous at the nonsingular matrix $-I$, so $G_n$ is invertible with probability tending to one and $G_n^{-1}\to_P-I^{-1}$.

On the event that $\hat\beta_n$ is a score root and the segment lies in $B$, the fundamental theorem of calculus applied to the continuously differentiable finite-sample score gives $0=U_n(\hat\beta_n)=U_n(\beta_0)+nG_n\Delta_n$. Thus $\sqrt n\Delta_n=-G_n^{-1}\{U_n(\beta_0)/\sqrt n\}$.

Substitute [F4]. Its normalized IID sum is $O_P(1)$, so the product of that sum with $G_n^{-1}+I^{-1}=o_P(1)$ is $o_P(1)$. Hence $\sqrt n\Delta_n=I^{-1}n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_i+o_P(1)=I^{-1}n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\int_0^\tau\{Z_i(t)-\bar z(t)\}\,dM_i(t)+o_P(1)$, which is the asserted expansion.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all four steps and eight actual prerequisites. The compact neighborhood contains a ball around beta0, so consistency places the whole line segment in B with probability tending to one even without convex B. Uniform Hessian convergence and continuous J imply the integrated Hessian tends to -I. Positive definite I gives eventual invertibility; score-root and segment events need only probability tending to one. Fundamental calculus uses the integral Hessian, avoiding an invalid multivariate single-intermediate-point assertion. The signs give -G_n^-1 tending to I^-1. The separately proved normalized influence sum is O_P(1), so multiplication by the vanishing inverse error gives o_P(1). Measurability and consistency of the score root are explicit assumptions; neither existence nor consistency is inferred from the likelihood. Degenerate information is excluded by I positive definite, and no-event finite samples are harmless on exceptional events. AC is declared and the optional time-bracketing hypothesis is not used. citations.quote:
Use the IID bounded-covariate model, risk-support hypotheses of [[lem-cox-uniform-risk-set-convergence]], the no-tie event process, and the per-subject counting-process contracts of [[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]. Let
$$\bar z(t)=\frac{s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)}{s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)},\qquad I=\int_0^\tau\left\{s^{(2)}(t,\beta_0)- \frac{s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)^T}{s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)}\right\}\lambda_0(t)\,dt,\qquad \xi_i=\int_0^\tau\{Z_i(t)-\bar z(t)\}\,dM_i(t),$$
where each vector integral is defined coordinatewise in L². If $U_n(\beta)=\partial_\beta\log L_p(\beta)$ is the partial-likelihood score, then
$$n^{-1/2}U_n(\beta_0)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_i+o_P(1).$$
The $\xi_i$ are IID, centered, square-integrable vectors with covariance matrix $I$. In particular, $n^{-1/2}\sum_i\xi_i=O_P(1)$. The replacement of the random risk-set mean by $\bar z$ is part of the conclusion.

Assume AC. Let $p<\infty$, $\tau>0$, and $\beta_0\in\mathbb R^p$. Let subjects $O_i=(T_i,C_i,Z_i(\cdot))$ be IID and independent. Assume the Cox model of [[def-cox-proportional-hazards-model-and-partial-likelihood]] with bounded predictable covariates $\|Z_i(t)\|_2\le K$, baseline $\lambda_0\in L^1[0,\tau]$, and no tied failures. Assume the positive population risk denominators of [[lem-cox-uniform-risk-set-convergence]] on a compact neighborhood $B$ of $\beta_0$. In one common filtration, assume the observed event counts $N_i(t)=1\{U_i\le t,\delta_i=1\}$ have compensators
$$A_i(t)=\int_0^tY_i(u)e^{\beta_0^TZ_i(u)}\lambda_0(u)\,du$$
and that $M_i=N_i-A_i$ satisfies the square-integrable counting-process contract of [[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]. This martingale contract is an explicit model assumption. No bracketing or time-class regularity is required: the risk-set lemma supplies the integrated parameter-uniform laws for these bounded predictable paths.

Let $I$ be the matrix in [[lem-cox-partial-likelihood-hessian-convergence]] and assume $I$ is positive definite. Let $\hat\beta_n$ be a measurable $\mathbb R^p$-valued estimator such that, with probability tending to one, it solves the partial-likelihood score equation $U_n(\hat\beta_n)=0$, and suppose $\hat\beta_n\to_P\beta_0$. Then
$$\sqrt n(\hat\beta_n-\beta_0) =I^{-1}\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n \int_0^\tau\{Z_i(t)-\bar z(t)\}\,dM_i(t)+o_P(1), \qquad \bar z(t)=\frac{s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)}{s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)}.$$
The proof establishes the partial-likelihood score representation locally; it does not treat the score summands with the random risk-set mean as IID.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $(\mathcal O,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, and let $O_1,O_2,\ldots$ be IID with law $P$. Let $\hat\theta_n$ be a measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued estimator based on $O_1,\ldots,O_n$ for a fixed $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Suppose $\phi:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable, $E_P\phi=0$, and $E_P\|\phi\|_2^2<\infty$, and set $\Sigma=E_P[\phi\phi^T]$. Assume the separately established expansion, with remainder $r_n$ on the sample probability space,

$$\hat\theta_n-\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(O_i)+r_n,\qquad r_n=o_P(n^{-1/2}),$$

Then

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$

The remainder notation means $\sqrt n\,r_n\to_P0$, as in [[def-asymptotically-linear-estimator-and-influence-function]]. Thus $\phi$ is the estimator influence function in the asymptotically linear sense: the theorem assumes the expansion and does not establish it. The covariance may be singular, including zero.

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Define $\phi(O_i)=I^{-1}\xi_i$. By [F1], $E\phi=0$ and $\phi$ is square-integrable. Since $I$ is symmetric positive definite, [F4] gives $\operatorname{Cov}(\phi)=I^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(\xi_i)(I^{-1})^T=I^{-1}II^{-1}=I^{-1}$. The map is a measurable function of one subject record because $M_i$, $Z_i$, and the compensator $A_i$ are subject-specific and $\bar z$ is deterministic.

By [F2], the expansion is $\hat\beta_n-\beta_0=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(O_i)+r_n$ with $r_n=o_P(n^{-1/2})$. Fix a finite horizon $\tau>0$ and a fixed dimension $p\ge1$. Work on a probability space with an increasing filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le\tau}$ as in [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. For subject $i$, let $T_i$ be an event time, $C_i$ a censoring time, and $Z_i(t)\in\mathbb R^p$ a covariate process predictable relative to this filtration, in the sense of [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Use the right-censoring record convention of [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]]: $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\}$. For this vector covariate process, predictability means coordinatewise predictability: each real-valued coordinate is predictable in the sense of [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Define the history sigma-algebra $\mathcal G_i:=\sigma\{Z_i(t):0\le t\le\tau\}$. The conditional-independence assumption is $T_i\perp\!\!\!\perp C_i\mid\mathcal G_i$, meaning that for all bounded measurable real functions $a,b$, $E[a(T_i)b(C_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]=E[a(T_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]E[b(C_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]$ almost surely, as in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. This conditional-independence relation is a model assumption, not an empirical conclusion. No conditional-kernel representation given the entire covariate path is assumed here.

A Cox proportional-hazards specification fixes a coefficient $\beta_0\in\mathbb R^p$ and a baseline hazard density $\lambda_0:[0,\tau]\to[0,\infty)$ that is measurable and integrable. Its baseline cumulative hazard is the absolutely continuous function
$$\Lambda_0(t)=\int_0^t\lambda_0(u)\,du.$$
The conditional event intensity at time $t$ for subject $i$, while that subject is at risk, is
$$Y_i(t)\lambda_0(t)\exp\{\beta_0^T Z_i(t)\},\qquad Y_i(t):=1\{U_i\ge t\}.$$
These specify the conditional event-intensity component. The law of the covariate paths and the censoring law subject to the stated conditional-independence assumption remain nuisance components and are not fixed here. Thus this is a semiparametric model specification; $(\beta_0,\lambda_0)$ alone do not define a full parametric statistical experiment on the observed-data space.
For the counting-process arguments below, require $Y_i$ to be predictable as well; this is part of the stated observation model and is not inferred from the hazard formula alone.
For a constant covariate value $z$, the corresponding event survival function is
$$S(t\mid z)=\exp\{-e^{\beta_0^Tz}\Lambda_0(t)\}.$$
For fixed covariate values $z,z'\in\mathbb R^p$, at times with $\lambda_0(t)>0$ the hazard ratio is
$$\frac{\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta^Tz}}{\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta^Tz'}}=e^{\beta^T(z-z')}.$$
The relative hazard factor is $e^{\beta^T(z-z')}$ even at times when both baseline-scaled hazards vanish and their quotient is undefined. It is an instantaneous hazard ratio, not a ratio of cumulative event probabilities. For time-varying covariate paths $z(t),z'(t)$ the instantaneous relative hazard factor is $e^{\beta^T(z(t)-z'(t))}$ and may vary with time.

For a sample of $n$ subjects, put $R(t)=\{j:U_j\ge t\}$. When failures are untied, the Cox partial likelihood on $[0,\tau]$ is
$$L_p(\beta)=\prod_{i:\,\delta_i=1,\ U_i\le\tau} \frac{\exp\{\beta^TZ_i(U_i)\}}{\sum_{j\in R(U_i)}\exp\{\beta^TZ_j(U_i)\}}.$$
An empty product is $1$. This partial likelihood is built from risk-set contributions; it is not asserted to be the full likelihood of the censored observations.

Tied-event likelihoods require an explicit time-recording convention. Put $D(t)=\{i:U_i=t,\delta_i=1\}$ and $d_t=|D(t)|$. If a discrete or grouped-time model conditions on exactly $d_t$ failures from $D(t)\subseteq R(t)$ at recorded time $t$ with the risk set fixed for that time, additionally assume that, conditional on that risk set, its covariate weights, and $d_t=d$, the failure subset law assigns each size-$d$ set $A\subseteq R(t)$ probability proportional to $\prod_{j\in A}w_j(t)$. Under this explicit subset-law assumption, its exact conditional tie contribution is
$$\frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq R(t)\\|A|=d_t}}\ \prod_{j\in A}w_j(t)}, \qquad w_j(t):=\exp\{\beta^TZ_j(t)\}.$$
For the separate exact Cox tied-partial-likelihood convention obtained by coarsening a continuous-time ordering into one recorded tie interval, assume the risk set at the interval start is $R(t)$, its only within-interval departures are the $d_t$ failures in $D(t)$, and the covariates are fixed at the recorded time. Conditional on each successive failure, the next failure label is chosen from the remaining risk set with probability proportional to its weight. Summing these order contributions gives the ordered-risk-set conditional partial-likelihood contribution
$$\sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Perm}(D(t))} \prod_{k=1}^{d_t} \frac{w_{\pi_k}(t)} {\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)-\sum_{\ell<k}w_{\pi_\ell}(t)}.$$
Here $\operatorname{Perm}(D(t))$ is the set of bijections from $\{1,\ldots,d_t\}$ to $D(t)$.
The discrete subset expression is exact under its explicit subset-law convention, and the permutation expression is exact for its stated partial-likelihood ordering convention; the latter is not generally the full likelihood of interval-coarsened censored observations. These conventions are not interchangeable without a model relating them. The Breslow and Efron tie formulas are approximations, respectively
$$L_B(\beta)=\prod_{t:d_t>0} \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\left(\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)\right)^{d_t}}$$
and
$$L_E(\beta)=\prod_{t:d_t>0} \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\prod_{k=0}^{d_t-1}\left(\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)-\frac{k}{d_t}\sum_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)\right)}.$$
With an absolutely continuous event hazard and independent subjects, exact event-time ties have probability zero; grouped-time tie formulas describe additional observation/model conventions.

For a discrete event-time law, the survival relation $S(t\mid z)=S_0(t)^{e^{\beta^Tz}}$ describes proportional integrated hazards and is not equivalent in general to a hazard-ratio model. The proportional-hazards and proportional-integrated-hazards formulations agree under the continuity condition on the baseline survival; the hazard-density model above uses the absolutely continuous convention.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because

Fix a finite number $K\ge1$ of causes on a probability space. Let
$T_1,\ldots,T_K$ be measurable event times with values in $[0,\infty)$, and
assume that the minimum is attained by a unique cause almost surely. The
**observed first failure time** and its **cause** are
$$T:=\min_{1\le j\le K}T_j,\qquad D:=\min\{j:T_j=T\}\in\{1,\ldots,K\},$$
so $D$ is the smallest label attaining the minimum. For each $k$,
$$\{D=k\}=\bigcap_{j<k}\{T_k<T_j\}\cap\bigcap_{j>k}\{T_k\le T_j\},$$
which is measurable; the assumed almost-sure uniqueness makes the tie-break
irrelevant except on a null set.
No independence among the latent times $T_j$ is assumed. When an external
right-censoring time $C$ is present, the observation is
$(U,\delta,D^{\mathrm{obs}})$, where $U=\min(T,C)$ and
$\delta=\mathbf 1\{T\le C\}$ as in
[[def-event-time-observation-schemes]], and $D^{\mathrm{obs}}=D$ when
$\delta=1$; the cause label is absent when $\delta=0$. Thus an event tied with
censoring is recorded as an event.

The **all-cause survival function** is $S(t):=\mathbb P(T>t)$ for $t\ge0$.
For $u>0$, write $S(u-):=\mathbb P(T\ge u)$; this is the left limit of $S$
by continuity from above for measures
([[thm-continuity-from-above-for-measures]]). Set $S(0-):=1$.

For each cause $k$, its **event subdistribution measure** and
**cause-specific cumulative-incidence function** are
$$\nu_k(B):=\mathbb P(T\in B,D=k),\qquad F_k(t):=\nu_k([0,t])=\mathbb P(T\le t,D=k).$$
for Borel $B\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and $t\ge0$. The **cause-specific hazard
measure** is the measure with density
$$w(u):=\begin{cases}1/S(u-),&S(u-)>0,\\0,&S(u-)=0\end{cases}$$
relative to $\nu_k$:
$$\Lambda_k(B):=\int_B w(u)\,\nu_k(du),\qquad d\Lambda_k(u)=w(u)\,\nu_k(du).$$
The extension of $u\mapsto S(u-)$ by the constant $1$ for $u<0$ is
nonincreasing on $\mathbb R$ and therefore Borel measurable
([[thm-monotone-real-functions-are-borel-measurable]]), so $w$ is a
nonnegative Borel function and this measure is defined by
[[def-measure-with-density]]. It may have infinite total mass; no finite-horizon
integrability is assumed in this definition.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Every monotone function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ in the sense of
[[def-monotone-function]] is Borel measurable.

The function $s(u):=S(u-)=\mathbb P(T\ge u)$ is nonincreasing, hence Borel by [F4]. Thus $R:=\{u:s(u)>0\}$ is Borel and $w=s^{-1}\mathbf 1_R$ is nonnegative Borel.

u_k(u)=\int_{[0,t]}\mathbf 1_R(u)\,d
u_k(u)=
u_k([0,t])=F_k(t)$. The penultimate equality uses step 3.1, so this proves the measure-valued identity, including atoms and $t=0$.

u_k$ has a Lebesgue density, so the point $0$ contributes nothing to either side of step 4.1; substituting the density on $(0,t]$ into that identity gives the stated formula, including $t=0$.
