risk_review.notes: Read all seven steps and exact dependency statements. Finite square expansion uses integrable centered products; n-|h| counts ordered pairs and preserves Fourier signs/2π. Substitution of a supplied finite spectral measure is a finite integral interchange without existence/choice claim. Orthogonality under explicit CC normalizes Φ_n; geometric cancellation and sine monotonicity bound its circular tail by [2π n sin²(δ/2)]^-1. citations.quote:
A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

For real random variables $X$ and $Y$ on one finite probability space, define
$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2],\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
The **standard deviation** of $X$ is $\sigma_X:=\operatorname{Var}(X)^{1/2}$, using the unique nonnegative square root supplied by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. Variance is nonnegative because its defining random variable is pointwise nonnegative and expectation is a sum with nonnegative weights.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be a finite mutually independent family of real random variables on a common probability space, with independence in the sense of [[def-independent-random-elements]].

1. If every $X_i$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i\in I}X_i$ is integrable and
   $$\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{i\in I}X_i\right]=\prod_{i\in I}\mathbb E[X_i]$$
   in $\mathbb R$.
2. If every $X_i$ is nonnegative, the same identity holds in $[0,+\infty]$. A zero factor on the right makes the product zero even if another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise the usual extended nonnegative product is used.

The original finite-probability-space case is included: for a finite family of finite-valued real random variables, mutual atom independence as in [[def-independence-of-finite-random-variables]] suffices, and all expectations are finite. For $I=\varnothing$, both sides equal $1$. The converse is not asserted.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real-valued stochastic process on one
probability space, so each $X_t$ is a real random variable and each finite
tuple has its pushforward law
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]],
[[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]],
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]).
We call $X$ a **time series** here because its index set is $\mathbb Z$.

The process is **strictly stationary** when for every integer $r\ge1$, every
$t_1,\ldots,t_r\in\mathbb Z$, and every shift $m\in\mathbb Z$,
$$\mathcal L(X_{t_1+m},\ldots,X_{t_r+m})=\mathcal L(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_r}).$$
This condition concerns the full finite-dimensional laws and imposes no moment
condition by itself.

The process is **weakly stationary** when $E[|X_t|^2]<\infty$ for every
$t\in\mathbb Z$, its mean $\mu:=E[X_t]$ is independent of $t$, and for every
$h\in\mathbb Z$ the covariance
$$\gamma(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t)$$
is independent of $t$. Expectation, variance, and covariance have the meanings
in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]] and
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Strict stationarity alone therefore
does not supply the moment hypotheses needed for covariance or sample-mean
claims.

For a weakly stationary real process $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$, its
**autocovariance function** (ACVF) is
$$\gamma(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t),\qquad h\in\mathbb Z,$$
which is independent of $t$ by [[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]].

For a finite data vector $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R$, where $n\ge1$, let
$$\bar x_n:=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n x_t.$$
Its **biased sample ACVF** is the zero-extended sequence on $\mathbb Z$ given by
$$\widehat\gamma_n(h):=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^{n-|h|}(x_{t+|h|}-\bar x_n)(x_t-\bar x_n),\qquad |h|<n,$$
and $\widehat\gamma_n(h):=0$ for $|h|\ge n$. The absolute lag makes
$\widehat\gamma_n(-h)=\widehat\gamma_n(h)$.

For comparison, define the **pair-count-normalized rescaling**
$$\widetilde\gamma_n(h):=\frac1{n-|h|}\sum_{t=1}^{n-|h|}(x_{t+|h|}-\bar x_n)(x_t-\bar x_n),\qquad |h|<n,$$
and set it to zero for $|h|\ge n$. Its denominator is positive on the stated
domain. The names specify the denominator convention; they assert no
unbiasedness formula.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the angular Lebesgue
measure clause below; under it $\lambda_1$ is a measure and intervals have
their usual lengths ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]],
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

Let $\mathbb T:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ be the multiplicative unit circle
with its subspace topology from $\mathbb C$
([[lem-unit-circle-is-a-compact-metrizable-topological-group]]), identified
with angular frequencies by $z=e^{i\lambda}$. Write $d\lambda$ for
the finite angular Lebesgue Borel measure obtained from ordinary Lebesgue
measure on $[-\pi,\pi)$; thus $d\lambda(\mathbb T)=2\pi$, and the endpoints
$-\pi$ and $\pi$ denote the same point. The characters of discrete additive
$\mathbb Z$ are $h\mapsto e^{ih\lambda}$ by
[[thm-discrete-integers-have-circle-dual]].

For angular representatives $\lambda,\theta\in\mathbb R$, define their
circular distance by
$$d_{\mathbb T}(\lambda,\theta):=\min_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\lambda-\theta+2\pi k|.$$
The minimum exists because the displayed absolute values tend to infinity
with $|k|$, and changing either representative by $2\pi$ leaves it unchanged.

Precisely, for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb T$ put
$$d\lambda(B):=\lambda_1\{\theta\in[-\pi,\pi):e^{i\theta}\in B\}.$$
The map $\theta\mapsto e^{i\theta}$ is continuous by
[[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]] and
[[cor-complex-differentiability-implies-continuity]], so the preimage is
Borel by [[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]. Preimages
preserve disjoint unions, so this is a finite Borel measure under the stated
Countable Choice premise. Integrating a Borel function of the circle angle
means integrating its periodic lift over this half-open interval.

Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real weakly stationary process with mean
$\mu$ and autocovariance $\gamma(h)=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t)$
([[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]],
[[def-autocovariance-and-sample-autocovariance]]). A **spectral measure** for
$X$ is a finite positive Radon Borel measure $F$ on $\mathbb T$
([[def-radon-measure-on-an-lch-space]]) satisfying
$$\gamma(h)=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{ih\lambda}\,F(d\lambda)\qquad(h\in\mathbb Z).$$
Putting $h=0$ gives $F(\mathbb T)=\gamma(0)$. A **spectral density** is a
nonnegative measurable function $f$ with
$$F(B)=\int_B f(\lambda)\,d\lambda$$
for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb T$; it exists only when $F$ is
absolutely continuous with respect to $d\lambda$ and is unique up to
$d\lambda$-null sets.

For a known mean $\mu$ and integer $n\ge1$, the **known-mean periodogram** is
the random function
$$I_n(\lambda):=\frac1{2\pi n}\left|\sum_{t=1}^n(X_t-\mu)e^{-it\lambda}\right|^2,\qquad\lambda\in\mathbb T.$$
The centering uses the population mean, not the sample mean. The finite sum is
square-integrable, so $I_n(\lambda)$ has finite expectation: for
$Y_t=X_t-\mu$, the pointwise inequality
$|\sum_{t=1}^nY_te^{-it\lambda}|^2\le n\sum_{t=1}^n|Y_t|^2$ bounds its
expectation by $n\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[Y_t^2]<\infty$
([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]).

Define the normalized finite-sample Fejér kernel
$$\Phi_n(x):=\frac1{2\pi n}\left|\sum_{t=1}^ne^{-itx}\right|^2,\qquad x\in\mathbb T.$$

For smoothing, let $K:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous with compact
support, $\int_{\mathbb R}K(u)\,du=1$, and $K(0)>0$. For bandwidth $b>0$,
periodize it on the circle by
$$K_b(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\frac1bK\!\left(\frac{x+2\pi k}{b}\right).$$
Compact support makes this a finite sum at each $x$, and changing variables
over the intervals that tile $\mathbb R$ gives
$\int_{\mathbb T}K_b(x)\,d\lambda(x)=1$. For the Fourier grid
$\lambda_{j,n}=2\pi j/n$ ($0\le j<n$) and target $\lambda_0\in\mathbb T$, when
the denominator is positive define
$$w_{n,j}(\lambda_0):=\frac{K_{b_n}(\lambda_0-\lambda_{j,n})}{\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}K_{b_n}(\lambda_0-\lambda_{\ell,n})},\qquad \widetilde f_n(\lambda_0):=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}w_{n,j}(\lambda_0)I_n(\lambda_{j,n}).$$
The weights are nonnegative and sum to one.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Dependent Choice. Let
$X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real weakly stationary process with mean
$\mu$ and autocovariance $\gamma(h)=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t)$. Then
there is a unique finite positive Radon measure $F$ on $\mathbb T$ such that
$$\gamma(h)=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{ih\lambda}\,F(d\lambda)\qquad(h\in\mathbb Z),$$
and $F(\mathbb T)=\gamma(0)$. This is the spectral measure in
[[def-time-series-spectral-measure-and-periodogram]].

If, in addition, $\sum_{h\in\mathbb Z}|\gamma(h)|<\infty$, then $F$ is
absolutely continuous with respect to angular Lebesgue measure $d\lambda$ and
has the continuous nonnegative density
$$f(\lambda)=\frac1{2\pi}\sum_{h\in\mathbb Z}\gamma(h)e^{-ih\lambda},\qquad\lambda\in\mathbb T.$$
No mixing, central limit theorem, raw-periodogram consistency, or interval
coverage follows from these conclusions.

Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real weakly stationary process with known
mean $\mu$ and autocovariance $\gamma$. For every $n\ge1$ and
$\lambda\in\mathbb T$, its known-mean periodogram from
[[def-time-series-spectral-measure-and-periodogram]] satisfies
$$\mathbb E[I_n(\lambda)] =\frac1{2\pi}\sum_{|h|<n}\left(1-\frac{|h|}{n}\right)\gamma(h)e^{-ih\lambda}.$$
If $F$ is any spectral measure for $X$, this is equivalently the finite-sample
Fejér convolution
$$\mathbb E[I_n(\lambda)]=\int_{\mathbb T}\Phi_n(\lambda-\theta)\,F(d\theta).$$
If $F(d\theta)=f(\theta)\,d\theta$, the right side is
$\int_{\mathbb T}\Phi_n(\lambda-\theta)f(\theta)\,d\theta$.

The finite expectation identity and the convolution identity for a supplied
spectral measure use no choice principle. Assume Countable Choice for the
angular Lebesgue measure and the smoothing conclusion below, as required by
the measure convention in
[[def-time-series-spectral-measure-and-periodogram]].

For the smoothing definition in
[[def-time-series-spectral-measure-and-periodogram]], suppose
$F(d\theta)=f(\theta)\,d\theta$, where $f\in L^1(\mathbb T,d\lambda)$ is
continuous at $\lambda_0$. Let $K$ be as defined there and let $b_n>0$ satisfy
$b_n\to0$ and $n b_n\to\infty$. Then the weights are defined for all
sufficiently large $n$, and
$$\mathbb E[\widetilde f_n(\lambda_0)]\longrightarrow f(\lambda_0).$$
This is a bias limit for the smoothed estimator; it asserts no variance
consistency, raw-periodogram consistency, central limit theorem, or interval
coverage.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

Let $\mathbb T:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ carry the subspace topology of
$\mathbb C$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]],
[[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]) and the multiplication of
$\mathbb C$, and let $\varepsilon:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb T$,
$\varepsilon([t]):=\exp(2\pi i t)$, for the published one-dimensional torus
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).
Then $\mathbb T$ is a compact metrizable topological abelian group
([[def-topological-group]]), $\varepsilon$ is an isomorphism of topological
groups, and
$$|zw-z|=|w-1|,\qquad |z^{-1}-w^{-1}|=|z-w|$$
for all $z,w\in\mathbb T$.

For this page, a Borel measure $\mu$ on a locally compact Hausdorff space is
**Radon** when $\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact $K$, and, for every Borel
$E$ and every open $U$,
$$\mu(E)=\inf_{E\subseteq V\text{ open}}\mu(V),\qquad \mu(U)=\sup_{K\subseteq U\text{ compact}}\mu(K).$$
Cohn calls this convention regular. It does not assert compact inner
approximation for arbitrary Borel $E$.

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $\mathbb Z$ have the discrete topology, let
$\mathbb T=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ have the subspace topology from $\mathbb C$,
and give
$\widehat{\mathbb Z}$ the compact-open topology of the Pontryagin dual. Then
$$\Psi:\mathbb T\longrightarrow\widehat{\mathbb Z},\qquad \Psi(z)(n):=z^n,$$
is a group isomorphism and a homeomorphism. Thus in the angular coordinate
$z=e^{i\lambda}$, the characters of $\mathbb Z$ are exactly
$n\mapsto e^{in\lambda}$, with $\lambda$ taken modulo $2\pi$.

Let $X$ be a discrete topological space ([[def-standard-topologies]]) and $Y$ a
topological space. Every compact subset of $X$ is finite
([[def-compact-space]]), and on $C(X,Y)$ the compact-open topology
([[def-compact-open-topology-for-topological-domains]]) coincides with the
topology of pointwise convergence ([[def-topology-of-pointwise-convergence]]);
hence on every $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Y)$ the compact-open subspace topology is
the subspace topology inherited from the product $Y^X$. In particular finite intersections of sets $\{f:f(x)\in V\}$, with $x\in X$ and $V\subseteq Y$ open, form a basis; these are open-coordinate constraints, not requirements that a coordinate equal a prescribed value.

Let $X$ be a set and let $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]). Write

$$Y^{X} \;:=\; \prod_{x \in X} Y ,$$

the product of the constant family whose factor at every index $x \in X$ is $Y$
([[def-product-topology]]). Unwinding that definition, an element of $Y^{X}$ is a
function with domain $X$ taking its value at each $x$ in $Y$; so $Y^{X}$ **is**
the set of all functions $X \to Y$, and the projection at $x$ is evaluation,

$$\pi_x : Y^{X} \to Y, \qquad \pi_x(f) = f(x) .$$

The **topology of pointwise convergence** on $Y^{X}$ is the product topology: the
initial topology of the family $(\pi_x)_{x \in X}$
([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]), that is the topology generated by the
subbasis

$$\mathcal{G} \;:=\; \{\, \pi_x^{-1}[V] \;:\; x \in X,\ V \in \mathcal{T}_Y \,\}, \qquad \pi_x^{-1}[V] = \{\, f \in Y^{X} : f(x) \in V \,\} .$$

By [[thm-basis-criterion]] the finite intersections of members of $\mathcal{G}$
form a basis for it ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]), so the basic open sets are
exactly the sets

$$\{\, f \in Y^{X} \;:\; f(x_j) \in V_j \text{ for every } j < n \,\} \qquad (n \in \mathbb{N},\ x_0, \dots, x_{n-1} \in X,\ V_0, \dots, V_{n-1} \in \mathcal{T}_Y),$$

the value $n = 0$ giving the empty intersection $Y^{X}$ itself. A basic open set
therefore constrains a member of $Y^{X}$ at **finitely many points only**, and
that is the whole content of the topology.

**The restriction to the continuous maps.** Suppose in addition that $X$ carries
a topology, and write

$$C(X,Y) \;:=\; \{\, f \in Y^{X} : f \text{ is continuous} \,\}$$

([[def-continuous-map-top]]). The **topology of pointwise convergence on
$C(X,Y)$** is the subspace topology inherited from $Y^{X}$
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]); its subbasic open sets are the traces
$\pi_x^{-1}[V] \cap C(X,Y)$, since tracing carries a subbasis to a subbasis
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Nothing on this page gives $C(X,Y)$ a default topology.** The set $C(X,Y)$
carries several different topologies below, and every statement names the one it
means at the point of use.

**The product set.** Let $I$ be a set and let $X_i$ be a set for each $i \in I$.
The **product** is

$$\prod_{i \in I} X_i \;:=\; \Big\{\, x : x \text{ is a function with domain } I \text{ and } x(i) \in X_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\Big\},$$

and we write $x_i := x(i)$, the $i$-th **coordinate** of $x$. Two elements of the
product are equal exactly when they agree at every index, functions being equal
when they have the same domain and the same values. For $j \in I$ the $j$-th
**projection** is

$$\pi_j : \prod_{i \in I} X_i \to X_j, \qquad \pi_j(x) := x_j .$$

**Notation for a finite product.** For $I = n$ a natural number, which is the set
$\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ of its predecessors, an element of $\prod_{k<n} X_k$ is a
function on $n$ and we write it $(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$. In particular $I = 2$
gives the **binary product**, written $X \times Y$ for $\prod_{i<2} X_i$ with
$X_0 = X$ and $X_1 = Y$, whose elements are written $(u,v)$ for the function
$0 \mapsto u$, $1 \mapsto v$. This is the only meaning the symbol $X \times Y$
carries on this page.

**Two facts about when the product is nonempty, stated because they are used and
because they cost something.** If some $X_{i_0}$ is empty then the product is
empty, since no function can take a value in $X_{i_0}$. Conversely, suppose every
$X_i$ is nonempty.

- For $I = n$ a natural number, the product is nonempty, and this is a theorem of
  ZF: [[lem-finite-choice]] applied to the function $i \mapsto X_i$ on $n$
  supplies a choice function $g$ for the family of values, and
  $x(i) := g(X_i)$ defines a member of $\prod_{k<n} X_k$.
- For an arbitrary $I$ the assertion "$\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \varnothing$
  whenever every $X_i$ is nonempty" **is** the Axiom of Choice: it is the
  formulation recorded in [[def-axiom-of-choice]], and the choice function of
  [[def-choice-function]] is exactly a point of the product of a family by
  itself. Every use of it below is flagged at the step that spends it.

**The box topology.** Now let each $X_i$ carry a topology $\mathcal{T}_i$
([[def-topological-space]]). Put

$$\mathcal{R} \;:=\; \Big\{\, \prod_{i \in I} U_i \;:\; U_i \in \mathcal{T}_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\Big\},$$

the family of **boxes**. $\mathcal{R}$ is a basis for a topology
([[thm-basis-criterion]]): it contains $\prod_i X_i$, so it covers the product,
and it is closed under binary intersections, since

$$\Big(\prod_i U_i\Big) \cap \Big(\prod_i V_i\Big) = \prod_i (U_i \cap V_i)$$

and each $U_i \cap V_i$ is open by (T3). The topology it generates is the **box
topology** $\mathcal{T}^{\square}$, and $\mathcal{R}$ is a basis for it
([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]).

**The product topology.** The **product topology** $\mathcal{T}^{\Pi}$ on
$\prod_i X_i$ is the initial topology of the family of projections
$(\pi_i)_{i \in I}$ ([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]): the topology generated
by the subbasis

$$\mathcal{G} \;:=\; \{\, \pi_i^{-1}[U] : i \in I,\ U \in \mathcal{T}_i \,\}, \qquad \pi_i^{-1}[U] = \prod_{j \in I} W_j \ \text{ with } W_i = U \text{ and } W_j = X_j \text{ for } j \ne i .$$

By [[thm-basis-criterion]] the finite intersections of members of $\mathcal{G}$
form a basis for $\mathcal{T}^{\Pi}$, and those finite intersections are exactly
the boxes with all but finitely many factors unrestricted:

$$\mathcal{R}^{\Pi} \;=\; \Big\{\, \prod_{i \in I} U_i \;:\; U_i \in \mathcal{T}_i \text{ for every } i, \text{ and } U_i = X_i \text{ for all but finitely many } i \,\Big\}.$$

Indeed the intersection of $\pi_{i_1}^{-1}[U_1], \dots, \pi_{i_n}^{-1}[U_n]$ is
the box whose factor at $i$ is the intersection of those $U_m$ with $i_m = i$ and
is $X_i$ when no $i_m$ equals $i$; and the intersection of no members is the
whole product, the box with every factor $X_i$. Conversely a box with
$U_i = X_i$ off a finite set is such an intersection. Members of
$\mathcal{R}^{\Pi}$ are called **basic product-open** sets, and members of
$\mathcal{R}$ **boxes**. So $\mathcal{R}^{\Pi} \subseteq \mathcal{R}$, with
equality when $I$ is a natural number.

**The empty product.** For $I = \varnothing$ there is exactly one function with
domain $\varnothing$, the empty function, so $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} X_i$ is a
one-point set. A one-point set carries exactly one topology, namely
$\{\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\}$, since a topology must contain the empty set
and the whole set and there is nothing else to contain
([[def-topological-space]]); so the box topology and the product topology agree
there, and both equal the discrete topology and the indiscrete topology
([[def-standard-topologies]]), which coincide on a one-point set. There are no
projections to speak of, and the initial topology of the empty family is indeed
the indiscrete one ([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]).

**Convention.** Unless the box topology is named explicitly, $\prod_i X_i$ always
carries the product topology in this library. That is not a matter of taste: the
product topology is the one with the characteristic property of the next item,
and the box topology has no such property.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Fix $z\in\mathbb C$. Apply [[thm-recursion]] to the set $\mathbb C$, the
initial value $1$, and the function $w\mapsto wz$. This defines the natural
powers uniquely by
$$ z^0=1,\qquad z^{n+1}=z^nz\quad(n\in\mathbb N). $$

Let $\jmath\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z$ be the embedding of
[[lem-nat-embeds-int]]. For an integer $r\ge0$, that lemma gives a unique
$n\in\mathbb N$ with $r=\jmath(n)$; define $z^r:=z^n$. If $r<0$ and $z\ne0$,
there is a unique $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $-r=\jmath(n)$; define
$$ z^r:=(z^n)^{-1}. $$
The inverse exists because $\mathbb C$ is a field by
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]. Thus nonnegative integer powers are
defined for every $z$, while negative integer powers are defined exactly when
$z\ne0$; in particular $0^0=1$ and no negative power of $0$ is defined. The
integer and its unique natural representative are never conflated.

A **complex sequence** is a function $a\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb C$. Since the
additive reduct $(\mathbb C,+,0)$ of the complex field is a commutative monoid,
the finite-list construction of [[def-monoid-finite-product]], read additively,
defines its complex partial sums by
$$ S_0=0,\qquad S_{N+1}=S_N+a_N,\qquad S_N=\sum_{n<N}^{\mathbb C}a_n. $$
The superscript is omitted when the summands already make the codomain clear.

The **complex series** $\sum a_n$ converges to $s\in\mathbb C$ when
$S_N\to s$ in the metric of
[[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]; then $s$ is its sum. This is
the same finite sum and convergence as the vector-series definition on
$\mathbb R^2$ in [[def-series-of-vectors-and-rearrangement]]. The series
**converges absolutely** when the real series $\sum |a_n|$ of [[def-series]]
converges. For a bijection $\sigma\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$, its
**rearrangement along $\sigma$** is the complex series $\sum a_{\sigma(n)}$.

Let $(c_n)$ be a complex sequence and $a\in\mathbb C$. The **complex power
series centered at $a$ with coefficients $(c_n)$** is
$$ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n(z-a)^n, $$
with powers from [[def-complex-integer-powers]] and the preceding complex
partial sums. To define its radius without ambiguity, form the specific real
power series
$$ Q(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}|c_n|x^n $$
centered at $0$. The **radius of convergence** of the complex power series is,
by definition, the radius of this $Q$ in
[[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Thus the coefficient
sequence, real variable, and center of the comparison series are all explicit.

For $z=x+iy$ and $w=u+iv$, put
$$ d_{\mathbb C}(z,w):=|z-w|=\sqrt{(x-u)^2+(y-v)^2}=\lVert(x-u,y-v)\rVert_2. $$
Under the identification $\mathbb C=\mathbb R^2$, this is exactly the metric
$d_2$ induced by the Euclidean norm of [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]. It is a metric by
[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], so the metric axioms
are established rather than assumed.

Convergence in $\mathbb C$, Cauchy sequences in $\mathbb C$, and continuity of
maps between subsets of $\mathbb C$ mean the notions of
[[def-metric-convergence]], [[def-cauchy-in-metric]], and
[[def-metric-continuity]] for $d_{\mathbb C}$ (and the restricted metric on a
subset). These uses are therefore licensed by the metric-space definition
[[def-metric-space]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim: On $\Omega=\{-1,1\}^2$ with weight $1/4$ at each outcome, let $A(a,b)=\sqrt v\,a$, $B(a,b)=\sqrt v\,b$, and define the sinusoid model $X_t^{(s)}=A\cos(t\lambda_s)+B\sin(t\lambda_s)$. Direct finite sums and [F15] give $\mathbb E[A]=\mathbb E[B]=\mathbb E[AB]=0$ and $\mathbb E[A^2]=\mathbb E[B^2]=v$. Thus $\mathbb E[X_t^{(s)}]=0$, and [F16] gives $\gamma_s(h)=\mathbb E[X_{t+h}^{(s)}X_t^{(s)}]=v\cos(h\lambda_s)$, independent of $t$; this model is weakly stationary by [F1]–[F3], [F10].

Let $S_{t,N}:=\sum_{j=0}^N\rho^j\varepsilon_{t-j}$. For $M>N$, independence and centering make all cross terms vanish, so $\|S_{t,M}-S_{t,N}\|_2^2 =\sigma^2\sum_{j=N+1}^M\rho^{2j}\longrightarrow0$ by convergence of the real geometric series [F17]. Thus $(S_{t,N})_N$ is Cauchy in $L^2$ for every $t$.

For a complex $z$ with $|z|<1$, put $C_N(z)=\sum_{j=0}^N z^j$. The field and power laws in [F28] give $zC_N(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{N+1}z^j$, so subtracting the two finite sums yields $(1-z)C_N(z)=1-z^{N+1}$. Since $|1|=1$, $z\ne1$ and this factor is invertible. Multiplicativity of modulus in [F18] gives $|z^{N+1}|=|z|^{N+1}$ by finite induction, hence $\left|C_N(z)-\frac1{1-z}\right|=\frac{|z|^{N+1}}{|1-z|}\longrightarrow0$ by [F17] applied to the real number $|z|<1$. The metric and partial-sum definition in [F28] therefore give $\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}z^j=(1-z)^{-1}$, and subtracting its first term gives $\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}z^j=z/(1-z)$. This proof includes $z=0$ with $z^0=1$.

Put $a=\lambda_s$, $b=-\lambda_s$, and $F_s=(v/2)(\delta_a+\delta_b)$. By [F20] this is a finite positive Borel measure. It satisfies the Radon regularity clauses [F21]: for a Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb T$, the open set $U=\mathbb T\setminus\{x\in\{a,b\}:x\notin E\}$ contains $E$ and has $F_s(U)=F_s(E)$; for an open $O\subseteq\mathbb T$, the finite set $K=O\cap\{a,b\}$ is compact and has $F_s(K)=F_s(O)$; finiteness on compact sets follows from $F_s(\mathbb T)=v$. For a nonnegative simple $q=\sum_jc_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$ with pairwise disjoint measurable $E_j$, its integral is $\int q\,dF_s=\sum_jc_j(v/2)(\mathbf 1_{a\in E_j}+\mathbf 1_{b\in E_j})=(v/2)(q(a)+q(b))$ by [F20] and [F24]. Increasing simple approximation [F24] and monotone convergence [F14] extend this formula to nonnegative measurable $q$, and decomposition into positive and negative real and imaginary parts extends it to bounded complex Borel $q$, which is integrable because $F_s$ is finite by [F25]. By [F26] the character $\lambda\mapsto e^{ih\lambda}$ is Borel, and its modulus is one by [F18], so it is integrable. The evaluation formula now gives $\int_{\mathbb T}e^{ih\lambda}F_s(d\lambda)=\frac v2(e^{ih\lambda_s}+e^{-ih\lambda_s})=v\cos(h\lambda_s)=\gamma_s(h)$. Thus $F_s$ is a spectral measure. Its two atoms are distinct because $0<\lambda_s<\pi$, and each has mass $v/2>0$. By [F22]–[F23], any density relative to $d\lambda$ assigns zero mass to $\{a\}$, whereas $F_s(\{a\})=v/2$; hence $F_s$ has no spectral density.

By [F6] and AC, for each $t$ the Cauchy sequence $S_{t,N}$ has an $L^2$ limit class represented by a real random variable $X_t^{(\rho)}$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F7] gives $\mathbb E|\varepsilon_0|\le\sqrt{\mathbb E\varepsilon_0^2}=\sqrt{\sigma^2}$. Monotone convergence [F14] and the real geometric series [F17] therefore give $\mathbb E[\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}|\rho|^j|\varepsilon_{t-j}|]=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}|\rho|^j\mathbb E|\varepsilon_0|\le\sqrt{\sigma^2}/(1-|\rho|)<\infty$. Let $A_{t,N}:=\sum_{j=0}^N|\rho|^j|\varepsilon_{t-j}|$ and $A_t:=\lim_NA_{t,N}$. For each $M>0$, $M\mathbf1_{\{A_t=\infty\}}\le A_t$, so monotonicity [F25] gives $M\mathbb P(A_t=\infty)\le\mathbb E A_t<\infty$; letting $M$ increase shows the absolute series is finite almost surely. Each $A_{t,N}$ and $S_{t,N}$ is measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_t:=\sigma(\varepsilon_s:s\le t)$, so [F19] makes $A_t$, $C_t:=\{A_t<\infty\}$, and $\limsup_NS_{t,N}$ measurable. On $C_t$ the absolute convergence implies $S_{t,N}$ has a finite limit. Define $Y_t$ to be $\limsup_NS_{t,N}$ on $C_t$ and $0$ off $C_t$; it is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable and equals the signed series with value $0$ on the null divergence set. Its absolute tail satisfies $\mathbb E|Y_t-S_{t,N}|\le\sqrt{\sigma^2}|\rho|^{N+1}/(1-|\rho|)\to0$. Since $S_{t,N}\to X_t^{(\rho)}$ in $L^2$, [F7] applied with the constant $1$ gives $\mathbb E|S_{t,N}-X_t^{(\rho)}|\to0$, and hence $\mathbb E|Y_t-X_t^{(\rho)}|\le\mathbb E|Y_t-S_{t,N}|+\mathbb E|S_{t,N}-X_t^{(\rho)}|\to0$. Hence $\mathbb E|Y_t-X_t^{(\rho)}|=0$, and [F27] implies $Y_t=X_t^{(\rho)}$ almost surely. Choose the causal version $X_t^{(\rho)}:=Y_t$. For $N\ge1$, $S_{t,N}=\varepsilon_t+\rho S_{t-1,N-1}$, and $\|\rho(S_{t-1,N-1}-X_{t-1}^{(\rho)})\|_2=|\rho|\|S_{t-1,N-1}-X_{t-1}^{(\rho)}\|_2\to0$, so uniqueness of $L^2$ limits gives $X_t^{(\rho)}=\varepsilon_t+\rho X_{t-1}^{(\rho)}$ in $L^2$. Finite partial sums have mean zero by [F8], and $|\mathbb E X_t^{(\rho)}|\le\|X_t^{(\rho)}-S_{t,N}\|_2\to0$ by [F7]; hence $\mathbb E X_t^{(\rho)}=0$.

Finite second moments make every $\varepsilon_t$ integrable by [F7], and its variance is as specified in [F9]. For $h\ge0$, the only nonzero terms in $\mathbb E[S_{t+h,N}S_{t,N}]$ pair the identical innovation indices; by [F4]–[F5], for $N\ge h$ this expectation equals $\sigma^2\sum_{k=0}^{N-h}\rho^{h+2k} \longrightarrow\frac{\sigma^2\rho^h}{1-\rho^2}$ by [F17]. For the passage to the limit, Cauchy–Schwarz [F7] gives $|\mathbb E[S_{a,N}S_{b,N}]-\mathbb E[X_a^{(\rho)}X_b^{(\rho)}]| \le\|S_{a,N}-X_a^{(\rho)}\|_2\|S_{b,N}\|_2 +\|X_a^{(\rho)}\|_2\|S_{b,N}-X_b^{(\rho)}\|_2\to0,$ because $\|S_{b,N}\|_2\le\|X_b^{(\rho)}\|_2+\|S_{b,N}-X_b^{(\rho)}\|_2$ is bounded by the $L^2$ convergence. Covariance symmetry for these mean-zero variables follows from commutativity of real products, so the formula for $h\ge0$ gives $\gamma_\rho(h)=\sigma^2\rho^{|h|}/(1-\rho^2)$ for every integer $h$, with $\rho^0:=1$. It is independent of $t$, so $X^{(\rho)}$ is weakly stationary by [F10].

Since $|\rho|<1$, the autocovariance is absolutely summable by its formula in step 3.1 and the real geometric series [F17]. Put $z_-=\rho e^{-i\lambda}$ and $z_+=\rho e^{i\lambda}$. By [F18], both have modulus $|\rho|<1$, so step 1.3 sums their series from index $1$ as $z_-/(1-z_-)$ and $z_+/(1-z_+)$. Applying [F12], these two sums and [F18] yield $f_\rho(\lambda)=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\pi(1-\rho^2)} \left(1+\sum_{h=1}^\infty\rho^h(e^{-ih\lambda}+e^{ih\lambda})\right) =\frac{\sigma^2}{2\pi(1-2\rho\cos\lambda+\rho^2)} =\frac{\sigma^2}{2\pi|1-\rho e^{-i\lambda}|^2}.$ The denominator is at least $(1-|\rho|)^2>0$, so this is a continuous nonnegative density.

Applying [F13] to the two spectral representations gives $\mathbb E[I_n^{(s)}(\lambda)] =\frac v2\{\Phi_n(\lambda-\lambda_s)+\Phi_n(\lambda+\lambda_s)\},\qquad \mathbb E[I_n^{(\rho)}(\lambda)] =\int_{\mathbb T}\Phi_n(\lambda-\theta)f_\rho(\theta)\,d\theta.$ The first expectation is a sum of two shifted kernels because the spectrum is atomic; the second averages a continuous density. These are exact finite-sample bias formulas and make no distributional or coverage claim.

citations.quote:
For a weakly stationary real process $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$, its
**autocovariance function** (ACVF) is
$$\gamma(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t),\qquad h\in\mathbb Z,$$
which is independent of $t$ by [[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]].
Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the
published finite identities.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and
For every double sequence $(a_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathbb N}$ in $[0,+\infty]$,

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then
$$\int \liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Weak stationarity makes $\mathbb E[Z_t^2]=\gamma(0)$ for every $t$. Applying [F3] to $Z_t$ and the constant one gives $\mathbb E|Z_t|\le\sqrt{\gamma(0)}$, while applying it to the centered variables $Z_{t+h},Z_t$ gives $|\gamma(h)|\le\gamma(0)$. Consequently $$\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\mathbb E\bigl[|c_jZ_{t-j}|\bigr] \le \sqrt{\gamma(0)}\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}|c_j|<\infty.$$ Tonelli [F5] on counting measure over $\mathbb Z$ times the probability measure shows that the random series of absolute values has finite expectation, hence is finite almost surely. Thus $Y_t$ is defined by an absolutely convergent sum.

For any finite $J\subset\mathbb Z$, the finite filter $Y_t^J=\sum_{j\in J}c_jZ_{t-j}$ satisfies, by [F4], $$\mathbb E[(Y_t^J)^2]=\sum_{j,k\in J}c_jc_k\gamma(k-j) \le \gamma(0)\left(\sum_{j\in J}|c_j|\right)^2.$$ The equality is a finite covariance expansion; the inequality follows from $|\gamma(k-j)|\le\gamma(0)$ from step 1.1. Applying the same bound to a finite tail $J$ gives $\|\sum_{j\in J}c_jZ_{t-j}\|_2\le\sqrt{\gamma(0)}\sum_{j\in J}|c_j|$.

Enumerate $\mathbb Z$ as $0,1,-1,2,-2,\ldots$ and let $Y_t^N$ be the partial sum through the first $N$ terms. The absolute almost-sure convergence from step 1.1 gives $Y_t-Y_t^N=\lim_{M\to\infty}(Y_t^M-Y_t^N)$ almost surely. Fatou [F7] and the finite-tail bound of step 2.1 therefore give $$\mathbb E|Y_t-Y_t^N|^2 \le \gamma(0)\left(\sum_{j\text{ omitted after }N}|c_j|\right)^2 \longrightarrow0.$$ Thus $Y_t^N\to Y_t$ in $L^2$ and $Y_t$ is square-integrable.

Each finite filter is centered. The $L^2$ convergence in step 3.1 implies $L^1$ convergence by [F3] applied to the difference and the constant one; hence $\mathbb E[Y_t]=0$. For finite $J$, covariance bilinearity [F4] gives $$\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{t+h}^J,Y_t^J) =\sum_{j,k\in J}c_jc_k\gamma(h-j+k).$$ As $J$ increases through the enumeration, the left side converges to $\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{t+h},Y_t)$ by $L^2$ convergence and [F3]. The right side converges absolutely because $$\sum_{j,k\in\mathbb Z}|c_jc_k\gamma(h-j+k)| \le\gamma(0)\left(\sum_j|c_j|\right)^2<\infty,$$ with order of summation justified by [F6]. Its limit is independent of $t$, so $Y$ is weakly stationary with the stated autocovariance.

Let $c,d\in\ell^1(\mathbb Z)$. The triangle inequality and [F6] give $$\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}|(c*d)_m| \le\sum_{j,k\in\mathbb Z}|c_j||d_k| =\left(\sum_j|c_j|\right)\left(\sum_k|d_k|\right)<\infty,$$ so $c*d\in\ell^1(\mathbb Z)$. Tonelli [F5] and the uniform bound from step 1.1 give $$\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{j,k\in\mathbb Z} |c_jd_kZ_{t-j-k}|\right] =\sum_{j,k\in\mathbb Z}|c_jd_k|\mathbb E|Z_{t-j-k}| \le\sqrt{\gamma(0)}\left(\sum_j|c_j|\right)\left(\sum_k|d_k|\right)<\infty.$$ Hence this double random series is absolutely convergent almost surely. Reindexing the absolutely convergent terms by $m=j+k$ gives $$\sum_jc_j\left(\sum_kd_kZ_{t-j-k}\right) =\sum_m\left(\sum_jc_jd_{m-j}\right)Z_{t-m} =\sum_m(c*d)_mZ_{t-m}.$$ Both sides are the filter limits defined in the Statement, and the equality holds almost surely and in $L^2$ by the bounds of steps 2.1 and 3.1. This proves the composition formula.

Weak stationarity gives only E[Z_s²]=gamma(0), so Cauchy–Schwarz supplies the uniform E|Z_s|<=sqrt(gamma(0)) bound, not equality of absolute moments. Counting measure on Z and Z² is sigma-finite; Tonelli gives almost-sure absolute sums. Explicit enumeration and Fatou prove L² convergence without a completeness or choice shortcut. Finite bilinearity, Cauchy–Schwarz and absolute double-sum domination give gamma(h-j+k). Convolution is l¹ by nonnegative Tonelli; the corrected double-series expectation bound justifies regrouping, and applying the same filter bound to d(B)Z justifies L² composition. [[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]] and

Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real-valued stochastic process on one
probability space, so each $X_t$ is a real random variable and each finite
tuple has its pushforward law
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]],

We call $X$ a **time series** here because its index set is $\mathbb Z$.

derivations.claim: Suppose a causal representation exists, with $\Psi(z)=\sum_{j\ge0}\psi_jz^j$ and $\sum_j|\psi_j|<\infty$. Applying the finite polynomial $\phi(B)$ and using the ARMA equation gives $$\bigl(\phi(B)\Psi(B)-\theta(B)\bigr)\epsilon_t=0.$$ The coefficient sequence $a$ of $\phi\Psi-\theta$ is in $\ell^1$ because $\phi,\theta$ are finite polynomials and $\psi\in\ell^1$. By [F3], the variance of this zero random variable is $\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge0}a_j^2$. Since $\sigma^2>0$, every $a_j=0$, so $\phi(z)\Psi(z)=\theta(z)$ on the closed unit disk; the series for $\Psi$ converges uniformly there because $\sum_j|\psi_j|<\infty$.

Suppose $\phi$ has degree $m\ge1$ and roots $r_1,\ldots,r_m$ counted with multiplicity. None is zero because $\phi(0)=1$. By [F4] and normalization, $$\phi(z)=\prod_{\ell=1}^m(1-z/r_\ell).$$ If every $|r_\ell|>1$, then for $|z|\le1$ each factor has the geometric expansion $$(1-z/r_\ell)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}r_\ell^{-k}z^k.$$ The coefficient of $z^j$ in $1/\phi(z)$ has absolute value at most $\binom{j+m-1}{m-1}r_*^{-j}$, where $r_*=\min_\ell|r_\ell|>1$, since there are $\binom{j+m-1}{m-1}$ nonnegative $m$-tuples summing to $j$. Choose $1<r<r_*$. The polynomial factor $\binom{j+m-1}{m-1}(r/r_*)^j$ is bounded in $j$, so these coefficients are bounded by $Cr^{-j}$. Multiplication by the finite polynomial $\theta$ preserves an exponential bound. If $m=0$, $\phi=1$ and $\theta/\phi$ is finite, which also has an exponential bound after enlarging $C$. Thus $\eta(z):=1/\phi(z)$ and $\Psi(z):=\eta(z)\theta(z)=\theta(z)/\phi(z)$ have absolutely summable one-sided coefficients, and those of $\Psi$ have the stated exponential decay.

Suppose an invertible representation exists, $\epsilon_t=\pi(B)(X_t-\mu)$ with $\pi\in\ell^1(\mathbb N_0)$. Apply the finite filter $\phi(B)$ and commute the absolutely summable and polynomial filters by [F3] on the weakly stationary process [F2]: $$\phi(B)\epsilon_t=\phi(B)\pi(B)(X_t-\mu) =\pi(B)\phi(B)(X_t-\mu)=\pi(B)\theta(B)\epsilon_t.$$ The coefficient sequence of $\phi-\pi\theta$ is in $\ell^1$. Its filter of white noise is zero, so [F3] and $\sigma^2>0$ imply every coefficient is zero. The absolutely summable series $\Pi$ converges uniformly on the closed unit disk, so the coefficient identity yields $\phi(z)=\Pi(z)\theta(z)$ for $|z|\le1$.

If $\phi(z_0)=0$ for some $|z_0|\le1$, step 1.1 gives $\theta(z_0)=\phi(z_0)\Psi(z_0)=0$. This is a common root, contrary to the coprime condition in [F1]. Therefore causality implies that $\phi$ has no zero in the closed unit disk.

Let $\eta(z)=1/\phi(z)$ be the absolutely summable causal series from step 1.2. Apply the filter $\eta(B)$ to the given equation. Since $X-\mu$ is weakly stationary, [F2] and [F3] justify composition and $\eta*\phi$ is the constant coefficient sequence $1$. Therefore $$X_t-\mu=\eta(B)\phi(B)(X_t-\mu) =\eta(B)\theta(B)\epsilon_t =\Psi(B)\epsilon_t.$$ This is the required causal representation of the given solution.
If $\theta(z_0)=0$ for some $|z_0|\le1$, step 1.3 gives $\phi(z_0)=\Pi(z_0)\theta(z_0)=0$, contradicting coprimality. Hence invertibility implies that $\theta$ has no zero in the closed unit disk.

If $\theta$ has no zero in $|z|\le1$, the same geometric-series argument as in step 1.2 applied to its roots gives an absolutely summable causal series $\eta(z)=1/\theta(z)$. Set $\Pi(z)=\eta(z)\phi(z)$; its coefficients are absolutely summable. Applying $\eta(B)$ to the ARMA equation and using filter composition [F3] on the weakly stationary process [F2] gives $$\Pi(B)(X_t-\mu)=\eta(B)\phi(B)(X_t-\mu) =\eta(B)\theta(B)\epsilon_t=\epsilon_t.$$ Thus the model is invertible.

Steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, and 2.2 prove both directions of the causal criterion and identify its coefficients; steps 1.3, 2.3, and 2.4 prove both directions of the invertibility criterion and identify its coefficients. The proof uses no choice axiom.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real process on one probability space.
The backshift is $(BX)_t:=X_{t-1}$, and for a polynomial
$a(z)=\sum_{j=0}^m a_jz^j$ set
$a(B)X_t:=\sum_{j=0}^m a_jX_{t-j}$. Weak stationarity and the covariance
convention are those of
[[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]] and
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

A real process $\epsilon=(\epsilon_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is **white noise**
with variance $\sigma^2$ when
$\mathbb E[\epsilon_t]=0$, $0<\sigma^2=\mathbb E[\epsilon_t^2]<\infty$,
and $\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon_t,\epsilon_s)=0$ for all $s\ne t$.
This definition requires only zero covariance at distinct times; it does not
require independence, identical distributions, or Gaussian laws.

For a real sequence $\psi=(\psi_j)_{j\ge0}$ with
$\sum_{j\ge0}|\psi_j|<\infty$, a **causal linear process** driven by white
noise is
$$X_t-\mu:=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\psi_j\epsilon_{t-j},\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where the series is its almost-sure and $L^2$ limit, established by
[[lem-absolutely-summable-linear-filters-preserve-weak-stationarity]].

An **ARMA$(p,q)$ model**, for nonnegative integers $p,q$, is an equation
$$\phi(B)(X_t-\mu)=\theta(B)\epsilon_t,\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where
$$\phi(z)=1-\sum_{j=1}^p\phi_jz^j,\qquad \theta(z)=1+\sum_{j=1}^q\theta_jz^j$$
have real coefficients and constant term one. If $p=0$ or $q=0$, the
corresponding polynomial is $1$. First cancel every common nonconstant factor
of $\phi$ and $\theta$ in $\mathbb C[z]$, then normalize both remaining
polynomials to have constant term one. Thus the model uses a **coprime
normalized pair**, meaning that the two polynomials have no common complex
root and both have constant term one.

For an AR$(p)$ model ($q=0$), expansion gives the regression form
$X_t=c+\sum_{j=1}^p\phi_jX_{t-j}+\epsilon_t$ with
$c=\mu(1-\sum_{j=1}^p\phi_j)$. Thus a fixed intercept in the AR regression
is the original mean parameter written in observation coordinates.

A **causal representation** of this model is a representation
$X_t-\mu=\sum_{j\ge0}\psi_j\epsilon_{t-j}$ with
$\sum_j|\psi_j|<\infty$. An **invertible representation** is
$\epsilon_t=\sum_{j\ge0}\pi_j(X_{t-j}-\mu)$ with
$\sum_j|\pi_j|<\infty$. These are properties of the displayed relation
between $X$ and $\epsilon$, not claims that white noise is iid.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the angular Lebesgue
measure clause below; under it $\lambda_1$ is a measure and intervals have
their usual lengths ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]],
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

Let $\mathbb T:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ be the multiplicative unit circle
with its subspace topology from $\mathbb C$
([[lem-unit-circle-is-a-compact-metrizable-topological-group]]), identified
with angular frequencies by $z=e^{i\lambda}$. Write $d\lambda$ for
the finite angular Lebesgue Borel measure obtained from ordinary Lebesgue
measure on $[-\pi,\pi)$; thus $d\lambda(\mathbb T)=2\pi$, and the endpoints
$-\pi$ and $\pi$ denote the same point. The characters of discrete additive
$\mathbb Z$ are $h\mapsto e^{ih\lambda}$ by
[[thm-discrete-integers-have-circle-dual]].

For angular representatives $\lambda,\theta\in\mathbb R$, define their
circular distance by
$$d_{\mathbb T}(\lambda,\theta):=\min_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\lambda-\theta+2\pi k|.$$
The minimum exists because the displayed absolute values tend to infinity
with $|k|$, and changing either representative by $2\pi$ leaves it unchanged.

Precisely, for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb T$ put
$$d\lambda(B):=\lambda_1\{\theta\in[-\pi,\pi):e^{i\theta}\in B\}.$$
The map $\theta\mapsto e^{i\theta}$ is continuous by
[[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]] and
[[cor-complex-differentiability-implies-continuity]], so the preimage is
Borel by [[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]. Preimages
preserve disjoint unions, so this is a finite Borel measure under the stated
Countable Choice premise. Integrating a Borel function of the circle angle
means integrating its periodic lift over this half-open interval.

Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real weakly stationary process with mean
$\mu$ and autocovariance $\gamma(h)=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t)$
([[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]],
[[def-autocovariance-and-sample-autocovariance]]). A **spectral measure** for
$X$ is a finite positive Radon Borel measure $F$ on $\mathbb T$
([[def-radon-measure-on-an-lch-space]]) satisfying
$$\gamma(h)=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{ih\lambda}\,F(d\lambda)\qquad(h\in\mathbb Z).$$
Putting $h=0$ gives $F(\mathbb T)=\gamma(0)$. A **spectral density** is a
nonnegative measurable function $f$ with
$$F(B)=\int_B f(\lambda)\,d\lambda$$
for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb T$; it exists only when $F$ is
absolutely continuous with respect to $d\lambda$ and is unique up to
$d\lambda$-null sets.

For a known mean $\mu$ and integer $n\ge1$, the **known-mean periodogram** is
the random function
$$I_n(\lambda):=\frac1{2\pi n}\left|\sum_{t=1}^n(X_t-\mu)e^{-it\lambda}\right|^2,\qquad\lambda\in\mathbb T.$$
The centering uses the population mean, not the sample mean. The finite sum is
square-integrable, so $I_n(\lambda)$ has finite expectation: for
$Y_t=X_t-\mu$, the pointwise inequality
$|\sum_{t=1}^nY_te^{-it\lambda}|^2\le n\sum_{t=1}^n|Y_t|^2$ bounds its
expectation by $n\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[Y_t^2]<\infty$
([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]).

Define the normalized finite-sample Fejér kernel
$$\Phi_n(x):=\frac1{2\pi n}\left|\sum_{t=1}^ne^{-itx}\right|^2,\qquad x\in\mathbb T.$$

For smoothing, let $K:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous with compact
support, $\int_{\mathbb R}K(u)\,du=1$, and $K(0)>0$. For bandwidth $b>0$,
periodize it on the circle by
$$K_b(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\frac1bK\!\left(\frac{x+2\pi k}{b}\right).$$
Compact support makes this a finite sum at each $x$, and changing variables
over the intervals that tile $\mathbb R$ gives
$\int_{\mathbb T}K_b(x)\,d\lambda(x)=1$. For the Fourier grid
$\lambda_{j,n}=2\pi j/n$ ($0\le j<n$) and target $\lambda_0\in\mathbb T$, when
the denominator is positive define
$$w_{n,j}(\lambda_0):=\frac{K_{b_n}(\lambda_0-\lambda_{j,n})}{\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}K_{b_n}(\lambda_0-\lambda_{\ell,n})},\qquad \widetilde f_n(\lambda_0):=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}w_{n,j}(\lambda_0)I_n(\lambda_{j,n}).$$
The weights are nonnegative and sum to one.

Let $Z=(Z_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered real weakly stationary process
with autocovariance $\gamma$. For a real two-sided sequence
$c=(c_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}\in\ell^1(\mathbb Z)$ define
$c(B)Z_t:=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}c_jZ_{t-j}$. Then this filter is well-defined
almost surely and in $L^2$, is centered and weakly stationary, and has
autocovariance
$$\gamma_Y(h)=\sum_{j,k\in\mathbb Z}c_jc_k\gamma(h-j+k),\qquad h\in\mathbb Z.$$
For $c,d\in\ell^1(\mathbb Z)$ their filter composition is the convolution
filter
$$(c*d)_m:=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}c_jd_{m-j},\qquad c(B)\bigl(d(B)Z\bigr)=(c*d)(B)Z.$$
All sums are absolutely convergent in the senses justified below. This
argument uses no choice axiom.

For this page, a Borel measure $\mu$ on a locally compact Hausdorff space is
**Radon** when $\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact $K$, and, for every Borel
$E$ and every open $U$,
$$\mu(E)=\inf_{E\subseteq V\text{ open}}\mu(V),\qquad \mu(U)=\sup_{K\subseteq U\text{ compact}}\mu(K).$$
Cohn calls this convention regular. It does not assert compact inner
approximation for arbitrary Borel $E$.

For every double sequence $(a_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathbb N}$ in $[0,+\infty]$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{ij}\right)=\sup_{m,n\in\mathbb N}\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}a_{ij}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}a_{ij}\right),$$

where every sum is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]. Thus the order of summation may be interchanged, even when the common value is $+\infty$.
Every nonconstant polynomial in $\mathbb C[x]$ splits over $\mathbb C$.

Let $\mathbb T:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ carry the subspace topology of
$\mathbb C$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]],
[[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]) and the multiplication of
$\mathbb C$, and let $\varepsilon:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb T$,
$\varepsilon([t]):=\exp(2\pi i t)$, for the published one-dimensional torus
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).
Then $\mathbb T$ is a compact metrizable topological abelian group
([[def-topological-group]]), $\varepsilon$ is an isomorphism of topological
groups, and
$$|zw-z|=|w-1|,\qquad |z^{-1}-w^{-1}|=|z-w|$$
for all $z,w\in\mathbb T$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{T}_d$ be
its metric topology ([[def-metric-topology]]), so that $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$ is a
topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and is metrizable
([[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. $(X,d)$ is a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]) **if and only
   if** $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$ is a compact topological space
   ([[def-compact-space]]).
2. For every $A \subseteq X$: $A$ is a compact subset of the metric space
   $(X,d)$ if and only if $A$ is a compact subset of the topological space
   $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$, the two readings of "compact subset" being the metric
   subspace $(A, d_A)$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]) and the topological
   subspace $(A, (\mathcal{T}_d)_A)$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Nothing here is a coincidence and nothing is transported.** The open-cover
condition of [[def-metric-compactness]] quantifies over families of subsets open
in $(X,d)$, and by [[def-metric-topology]] those are exactly the members of
$\mathcal{T}_d$; so the two conditions are not merely equivalent, they are the
same condition written twice. No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]). Then $(X,d)$ is totally bounded
([[def-totally-bounded]]) and complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).

**Both implications are theorems of ZF.** Completeness is obtained here from the
finite intersection characterisation ([[thm-compact-iff-finite-intersection-property]])
applied to the closures of the tails of a Cauchy sequence, and not from the
extraction of a convergent subsequence, which would route the argument through
sequential compactness. What matters for the ledger is that the route taken below
selects nothing at all; the first remark below says why the other route was not
taken.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(X,d)$
be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]], [[def-metric-space]]).
Then there is an at most countable set $D \subseteq X$ ([[def-countable]]) that
is dense in $X$, that is $\overline{D} = X$
([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

**Where the axiom is spent.** Once at step 2.1, to fix a finite $1/(n+1)$-net for
every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ at the same time; the family of sets chosen from is
written down before any selection and does not depend on the earlier ones. The
appeal to [[thm-countable-union-of-countable]] at step 4.1 carries the same
hypothesis $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and no more, so nothing further is spent there.
As always on this page the claim is an upper bound on the cost of this proof, not
an assertion that $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is necessary.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

derivations.claim: By [F6], factor $\phi$ over $\mathbb C$ as $\phi(z)=\prod_{\ell=1}^m(1-z/r_\ell)$, with multiplicities and $\phi(0)=1$; if $m=0$, take the empty product $1$. None of the roots satisfies $|r_\ell|=1$. For a root with $|r_\ell|>1$ use $(1-z/r_\ell)^{-1}=\sum_{j\ge0}r_\ell^{-j}z^j$ on the unit circle. For a root with $|r_\ell|<1$ use $(1-z/r_\ell)^{-1}=-\sum_{j\ge1}r_\ell^jz^{-j}$ there. Each coefficient sequence is in $\ell^1(\mathbb Z)$, so their finite convolution and multiplication by $\theta$ give a two-sided sequence $h\in\ell^1(\mathbb Z)$ with $$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}h_kz^k=\frac{\theta(z)}{\phi(z)},\qquad |z|=1.$$ Conjugate roots occur in pairs for real $\phi,\theta$. For each conjugate pair the finite convolution coefficient is unchanged by complex conjugation after reversing its summation index; real roots have real coefficients. Multiplication by real $\theta$ preserves reality.

The angular measure $d\lambda$ is a finite Borel measure of total mass $2\pi$ by [F2]. Normalize it to $P=d\lambda/(2\pi)$, a Borel probability by [F11]. By [F7], $\mathbb T$ is Polish, so [F8] gives compact inner approximations for every Borel set under $P$; scaling by $2\pi$ gives the same property for $d\lambda$. For any Borel $E$, apply this inner approximation to $\mathbb T\setminus E$: for every $\eta>0$ there is compact $K\subseteq\mathbb T\setminus E$ with $d\lambda((\mathbb T\setminus E)\setminus K)<\eta$. Then $U=\mathbb T\setminus K$ is open, contains $E$, and $d\lambda(U\setminus E)<\eta$. Thus $d\lambda$ is outer regular on Borel sets and inner regular on open sets; it is finite on compact sets because its total mass is finite. Hence $d\lambda$ is Radon by [F4].

Write $a(z)=1/\phi(z)$ for the two-sided absolutely convergent series constructed in step 1.1. Its product with $\phi$ is the constant series $1$. Applying filter composition [F3] to the ARMA equation gives $$X_t-\mu=a(B)\phi(B)(X_t-\mu)=a(B)\theta(B)\epsilon_t=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}h_k\epsilon_{t-k}.$$ Thus every weakly stationary solution under the stated root condition is the same two-sided filtered white-noise process.

Define $$f(\lambda):=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\pi}\left|\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}h_ke^{-ik\lambda}\right|^2=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\pi}\frac{|\theta(e^{-i\lambda})|^2}{|\phi(e^{-i\lambda})|^2}.$$ The series is uniformly convergent because $h\in\ell^1$, so $f$ is continuous, periodic, and nonnegative. It is bounded on the compact circle; therefore $F(E):=\int_Ef\,d\lambda$ is a finite positive Borel measure by [F9] and [F10]. For any Borel $E$ and $\varepsilon>0$, outer regularity of $d\lambda$ gives an open $U\supset E$ with $d\lambda(U\setminus E)<\varepsilon/(\|f\|_\infty+1)$. Since $F(U)=F(E)+F(U\setminus E)$ and $F(U\setminus E)\le\|f\|_\infty d\lambda(U\setminus E)$, this proves outer regularity of $F$. For any open $O$, inner regularity of $d\lambda$ gives a compact $K\subset O$ with $d\lambda(O\setminus K)<\varepsilon/(\|f\|_\infty+1)$; the same bound on $F(O\setminus K)$ proves inner regularity of $F$ on open sets. Thus $F$ is Radon by [F4].

Applying the covariance formula in [F3] to the representation in step 2.1 and using $\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon_s,\epsilon_t)=\sigma^2$ when $s=t$ and $0$ otherwise gives $$\gamma(h)=\sigma^2\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}h_{k+h}h_k.$$ The sum is absolutely convergent because $h\in\ell^1(\mathbb Z)$.

Put $H_N(\lambda):=\sum_{|k|\le N}h_ke^{-ik\lambda}$. Since $h\in\ell^1$, $H_N$ converges uniformly to $H(\lambda):=\sum_kh_ke^{-ik\lambda}$. The sequence $H_N$ is uniformly bounded, so $|H_N|^2$ converges uniformly to $|H|^2$. Expanding each finite square gives $|H_N(\lambda)|^2=\sum_{|j|,|k|\le N}h_jh_ke^{-i(j-k)\lambda}$, and [F5] gives $\sum_{j,k}|h_jh_k|=(\sum_k|h_k|)^2<\infty$. Hence the finite squares also converge uniformly to the full double series. Integration against $e^{ih\lambda}$ preserves this uniform limit because the circle has finite measure. For each integer $h$, $$\int_{\mathbb T}e^{ih\lambda}f(\lambda)\,d\lambda=\sigma^2\sum_{j,k}h_jh_k\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{i(h-j+k)\lambda}\,d\lambda=\sigma^2\sum_kh_{k+h}h_k=\gamma(h),$$ where the middle integral is $1$ when $h-j+k=0$ and $0$ otherwise, and the last equality is step 3.1. Hence $F$ represents the autocovariance and $f$ is a spectral density under [F2].
