Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume AC and Countable Choice as carried by the point-process supplier. Let $\eta$ be a Poisson point process on $\mathbb R^d$ with locally finite, sigma-finite intensity measure $\nu$. For every nonnegative function $h$ measurable on the product of the Borel and configuration evaluation sigma-algebras,

$$\mathbb E\int h(x,\eta-\delta_x)\,\eta(dx)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\mathbb E[h(x,\eta)]\,\nu(dx).$$

At each counted occurrence $x$, $\eta-\delta_x$ removes exactly one occurrence; coincident remaining occurrences stay. Equivalently, for every such nonnegative $f$,

$$\mathbb E\int f(x,\eta)\,\eta(dx)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\mathbb E[f(x,\eta+\delta_x)]\,\nu(dx).$$

Both sides are extended nonnegative integrals.

Assume AC and Countable Choice as carried by the point-process supplier. For every stationary locally finite point process $\eta$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite positive intensity $\rho$, there is a unique probability law $P^0$ on the configuration space satisfying

$$\mathbb E\int h(x,\theta_x\eta)\,\eta(dx)=\rho\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int h(x,\mu)\,P^0(d\mu)\,dx$$

for every nonnegative product-measurable $h$. Moreover, $P^0$-almost every configuration has at least one occurrence at the origin.

Let $\mu$ be a locally finite counting measure as in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]]. For $x\in\mathbb R^d$, its **recentering at $x$** is the counting measure $\theta_x\mu$ defined on Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ by

$$(\theta_x\mu)(B):=\mu(B+x).$$

Thus an occurrence at $x$ is moved to $0$, and in an occurrence representation $\mu=\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$ one has $\theta_x\mu=\sum_i\delta_{X_i-x}$. The action obeys $\theta_{x+y}=\theta_x\circ\theta_y$ and $\theta_0$ is the identity. Joint measurability in $(x,\mu)$ is proved in [[lem-joint-measurability-of-spatial-recentering]].

**Axiom convention.** The point-process supplier used for this definition has transitive dependencies on AC and Countable Choice; the recentering formula itself makes no selections.
The map $(x,\mu)\mapsto\theta_x\mu$ from $\mathbb R^d$ times the evaluation-measurable space of locally finite counting measures to that space is measurable.

Assume AC and Countable Choice, as carried by the random-point-process supplier. Let $\eta$ be a stationary locally finite point process on $\mathbb R^d$ with $0<\rho:=\mathbb E[\eta(Q)]<\infty$, where $Q=[0,1)^d$. Its mean measure $\nu(B):=\mathbb E[\eta(B)]$ is

$$\nu(B)=\rho\lambda_d(B)$$

for every Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$.

Assume AC and Countable Choice as carried by the point-process and Palm suppliers. Let $\eta$ be stationary and locally square integrable as in [[def-stationary-point-process-and-intensity]] and [[def-second-factorial-and-reduced-moment-measures]], with finite positive intensity $\rho$ and reduced second factorial moment measure $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}$.

A **pair-correlation density** exists exactly when $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Borel Lebesgue measure [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]. Local finiteness makes $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}$ sigma-finite, so [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives a density; positivity of the measure makes that density nonnegative almost everywhere, and replacing its values on the null exceptional set by zero gives a nonnegative Borel version. The density is unique up to Lebesgue-null sets. Normalize it by $\rho^2$ and call the resulting nonnegative Borel function $g$:

$$\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(D)=\rho^2\int_D g(u)\,du$$

for every Borel $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. The definition does not assume pair densities for all stationary processes.

For $r\ge0$, let $B[0,r]=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\|u\|_2\le r\}$ be the **closed** Euclidean ball. **Ripley's K-function** is

$$K(r):=\rho^{-1}\int(\mu-\delta_0)(B[0,r])\,P^0(d\mu),$$

where $P^0$ is the full Palm distribution from [[def-full-palm-distribution]] and $\delta_0$ removes one distinguished occurrence at the origin. The Palm law has an origin occurrence almost surely by [[thm-refined-campbell-formula-and-palm-law-existence]], and the reduced-measure identity [[thm-reduced-second-factorial-moment-palm-identity]] gives the equivalent expression $K(r)=\rho^{-2}\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(B[0,r])$. For a simple process as defined in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]], deleting $\delta_0$ is the same as excluding the origin location; for a multiplicity-bearing process other co-located occurrences remain.

**Axiom convention.** AC and Countable Choice are inherited through the point-process and Palm dependency closure; no further choice is used by these definitions.

Let $S$ be as in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]]. A
**Poisson point process with locally finite, sigma-finite intensity measure
$\nu$** is a point process $\eta$ such that for every finite pairwise-disjoint
family of Borel sets $B_1,\ldots,B_m$, the counts $\eta(B_i)$ are independent
random elements ([[def-independent-random-elements]]) and $\eta(B_i)$ has the
scalar Poisson law of mean $\nu(B_i)$
([[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]],
[[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]). If $\nu(B)=\infty$,
the extended count convention is $\eta(B)=+\infty$ almost surely.
Here sigma-finite means that $S$ is a countable union of Borel sets of finite
$\nu$-measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]); for the
stated $S$, local finiteness also implies sigma-finiteness by the compact
exhaustion in
[[lem-locally-compact-second-countable-spaces-have-compact-exhaustions]].

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the evaluation-measurable space of locally
finite Borel measures. A **Cox point process directed by a random measure
$\xi$** consists of a point process $\eta$, a random locally finite measure
$\xi$, and a supplied probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$
to $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ such that $K(\xi,\cdot)$ is a regular
conditional law of $\eta$ given $\xi$
([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]) and, for $P_\xi$-almost every
$\mu$, $K(\mu,\cdot)$ is the law of a Poisson point process of intensity
$\mu$. The kernel is part of the model data; this definition does not assert
that such a kernel exists for every $(\eta,\xi)$. The mean measure of $\xi$ is
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, a measure by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]].

Both definitions permit multiplicities. They do not assert that diffuse
directing measures yield simple processes or that a Cox law determines the law
of its directing measure.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

derivations.claim: For each compact $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, [F6] gives $\mathbb E[\eta(C)^2]=(\rho|C|)^2+\rho|C|<\infty$, so $\eta$ is locally square integrable and satisfies the second-order premise of the K definition [F5].

Fix a configuration event $A$. In [F1] use $$h_A(x,\mu)=\mathbf1_Q(x)\mathbf1_A(\theta_x(\mu+\delta_x)),$$ which is product measurable by [F3] and the evaluation formula for adding one atom. At each occurrence $x$ of $\eta$, deletion followed by addition restores $\eta$, so the left side is $\mathbb E\int\mathbf1_Q(x)\mathbf1_A(\theta_x\eta)\eta(dx)$.

The right side of that Mecke identity is $$\rho\int_Q\mathbb P(\theta_x(\eta+\delta_x)\in A)\,dx=\rho|Q|\mathbb P(\eta+\delta_0\in A),$$ because $\theta_x\delta_x=\delta_0$ and stationarity gives $\theta_x\eta\stackrel d=\eta$. The refined Palm identity [F2] applied to $\mathbf1_Q(x)\mathbf1_A(\mu)$ says that the left side in step 1.2 is $\rho|Q|P^0(A)$. Since $|Q|=1$ and $\rho>0$, $P^0(A)=\mathbb P(\eta+\delta_0\in A)$ for every $A$, proving the full-Palm law identity.

Under this Palm law, $\mu$ has the distribution of $\eta+\delta_0$. Removing the single distinguished occurrence gives $(\eta+\delta_0)-\delta_0=\eta$ even if $\eta$ has other occurrences at $0$. Therefore $$\mathbb E^0[(\mu-\delta_0)(B[0,r])]=\mathbb E[\eta(B[0,r])]=\rho|B[0,r]|$$ by [F4]. Substituting in the K definition [F5] yields $K(r)=|B[0,r]|$.

The endpoint $r=0$ is included: the closed ball is $\{0\}$ and the same calculation gives $K(0)=\rho^{-1}\mathbb E\eta(\{0\})=0=|\{0\}|$. The proof uses the one-occurrence deletion convention and asserts neither diffuse-intensity simplicity nor any other simplicity property. AC and Countable Choice [A1]–[A2] are inherited supplier assumptions.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume AC and Countable Choice as carried by the point-process and Palm suppliers. Let $\eta$ be stationary and locally square integrable as in [[def-stationary-point-process-and-intensity]] and [[def-second-factorial-and-reduced-moment-measures]], with finite positive intensity $\rho$ and reduced second factorial moment measure $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}$.

A **pair-correlation density** exists exactly when $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Borel Lebesgue measure [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]. Local finiteness makes $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}$ sigma-finite, so [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives a density; positivity of the measure makes that density nonnegative almost everywhere, and replacing its values on the null exceptional set by zero gives a nonnegative Borel version. The density is unique up to Lebesgue-null sets. Normalize it by $\rho^2$ and call the resulting nonnegative Borel function $g$:

$$\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(D)=\rho^2\int_D g(u)\,du$$

for every Borel $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. The definition does not assume pair densities for all stationary processes.

For $r\ge0$, let $B[0,r]=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\|u\|_2\le r\}$ be the **closed** Euclidean ball. **Ripley's K-function** is

$$K(r):=\rho^{-1}\int(\mu-\delta_0)(B[0,r])\,P^0(d\mu),$$

where $P^0$ is the full Palm distribution from [[def-full-palm-distribution]] and $\delta_0$ removes one distinguished occurrence at the origin. The Palm law has an origin occurrence almost surely by [[thm-refined-campbell-formula-and-palm-law-existence]], and the reduced-measure identity [[thm-reduced-second-factorial-moment-palm-identity]] gives the equivalent expression $K(r)=\rho^{-2}\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(B[0,r])$. For a simple process as defined in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]], deleting $\delta_0$ is the same as excluding the origin location; for a multiplicity-bearing process other co-located occurrences remain.

**Axiom convention.** AC and Countable Choice are inherited through the point-process and Palm dependency closure; no further choice is used by these definitions.

Assume AC and Countable Choice as carried by the point-process and Palm suppliers. Let $\eta$ be a stationary locally square-integrable point process on $\mathbb R^d$ with intensity $0<\rho<\infty$, let $P^0$ be its full Palm distribution, and let $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}$ use $Q=[0,1)^d$. For every Borel $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,

$$\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(D)=\rho\int (\mu-\delta_0)(D)\,P^0(d\mu).$$

The subtraction removes one distinguished occurrence at the origin; any other co-located occurrences remain.

Assume AC and Countable Choice as carried by the point-process supplier. For every stationary locally finite point process $\eta$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite positive intensity $\rho$, there is a unique probability law $P^0$ on the configuration space satisfying

$$\mathbb E\int h(x,\theta_x\eta)\,\eta(dx)=\rho\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int h(x,\mu)\,P^0(d\mu)\,dx$$

for every nonnegative product-measurable $h$. Moreover, $P^0$-almost every configuration has at least one occurrence at the origin.

Fix a locally compact, second-countable Hausdorff topological space $S$
([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-second-countable-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]). Here locally compact means that every point has a
compact neighbourhood; second countable means that the topology has an at most
countable basis; and Hausdorff means that distinct points have disjoint open
neighbourhoods. Let $\mathcal B(S)$ be the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the
open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A **counting measure** on $S$ is a Borel measure of the form
$\mu=\sum_{j\in J}\delta_{x_j}$ for a finite or countable index set $J$ and
points $x_j\in S$, where repetitions are allowed and the empty sum is zero.
Each $\delta_x$ is the unit point mass at $x$
([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), and
the countable sum is a measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]]. The **multiplicity** at $x$ is
$\mu(\{x\})$. The counting measure is **locally finite** if
$\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact subset $K\subseteq S$
([[def-compact-space]]).

Let $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of locally finite counting
measures, equipped with the sigma-algebra generated by the **evaluation maps**
$\mu\mapsto\mu(B)$ for $B\in\mathcal B(S)$. A **point process** on $S$ is a
measurable map $\eta:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to
(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$ from a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), with measurability in the sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Equivalently, every
count $\eta(B)$ is a measurable random variable, because the evaluation maps
generate $\mathcal E$. Its **law** is the probability measure
$\mathbb P_\eta(A)=\mathbb P(\eta^{-1}(A))$ on $(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]],
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]). The process is
classified by its realized configurations: a configuration $\mu$ is
**simple** if $\mu(\{x\})\le1$ for every $x$, and is **multiplicity-bearing**
if some singleton has mass greater than one. This is a pointwise distinction;
no almost-sure simplicity assertion is part of this definition.

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of all locally finite Borel
measures on $S$, with the sigma-algebra generated by their evaluation maps. A
**random locally finite measure** $\xi$ is a measurable map into this space.

For a nonnegative Borel function $f$, write
$\eta(f):=\int_S f\,d\eta$. Define the expected measure, or **intensity
measure**, by $\nu(B):=\mathbb E[\eta(B)]$. The expected-measure and
random-integral measurability assertions are justified by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]]. The measure
$\nu$ need not be locally finite; it is locally finite exactly when
$\mathbb E[\eta(K)]<\infty$ for each compact $K$.

The mean measure of a random locally finite measure is likewise
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, covered by the same expected-measure lemma. Local
finiteness of each realization does not by itself assert local finiteness of
$\nu$.

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] with $D=B[0,r]$ and divide by $\rho^2>0$. By the K definition [F1], $$K(r)=\rho^{-2}\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(B[0,r]).$$

Suppose $\eta$ is simple. The event $A_2=\{\mu:\mu(\{0\})\ge2\}$ is measurable by the evaluation sigma-algebra. In the refined Campbell identity [F3], take $h(x,\mu)=\mathbf1_Q(x)\mathbf1_{A_2}(\mu)$ with $Q=[0,1)^d$. On the probability-one event of simple realizations, every counted occurrence $x$ has $(\theta_x\eta)(\{0\})=\eta(\{x\})=1$, so the left side is zero. The right side is $\rho|Q|P^0(A_2)=\rho P^0(A_2)$, hence $P^0(A_2)=0$. Combining this with the at-least-one origin property in [F3] gives $\mu(\{0\})=1$ $P^0$-almost surely. Therefore $(\mu-\delta_0)(B[0,r])=\mu(B[0,r]\setminus\{0\})$ $P^0$-almost surely, and the definition [F1] gives the stated simple-process formula.
The density clause in [F1] applied to the same closed ball gives $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(B[0,r])=\rho^2\int_{B[0,r]}g(u)du$. Substitution in step 1.1 proves the asserted integral formula.

At the endpoint $r=0$, the closed-ball convention gives $B[0,0]=\{0\}$, so $K(0)=\rho^{-1}\mathbb E^0[\mu(\{0\})-1]$; this is $0$ for a simple process, while any other co-located occurrences contribute in the multiplicity-bearing case. The proof uses no density-existence claim beyond the stated hypothesis. AC and Countable Choice [A1]–[A2] are inherited supplier assumptions, not additional derivation steps.

The **translation-invariant sigma-algebra** is
$$\mathcal I_\eta:=\{A\text{ in the configuration sigma-algebra}: P_\eta(\theta_x^{-1}A\mathbin{\triangle}A)=0\text{ for every }x\in\mathbb R^d\}.$$
It is a sigma-algebra because symmetric-difference nullity is preserved by complements and countable unions. **Axiom convention.** The point-process supplier used for this definition has transitive dependencies on AC and Countable Choice; the recentering formula itself makes no selections.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

derivations.claim: For every Borel $B$, $u\mapsto\eta_u(B)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\mathbf1_B(k+u)$ is measurable as a countable sum of Borel functions; every compact set meets only finitely many points of each $\eta_u$, so this is a locally finite random counting measure. For fixed $x$, put $t=x-\lfloor x\rfloor\in[0,1)$. The map $u\mapsto\{u-x\}$ is a translation on each of $[0,t)$ and $[t,1)$, with the two image intervals partitioning $[0,1)$; by [F2] it preserves uniform probability. Reindexing $k\in\mathbb Z$ gives $\theta_x\eta_u=\eta_{\{u-x\}}$, so the process is stationary. Since exactly one $k+u$ lies in $Q=[0,1)$ for every $u\in[0,1)$, $\eta_U(Q)=1$ and $\rho=1$.

For every compact $C\subseteq\mathbb R$, choose an integer $m\ge1$ with $C\subseteq[-m,m]$. If $u\in[0,1)$ and $k+u\in C$, then $-m-1\le k\le m$, so $\eta_u(C)\le2m+2$ uniformly in $u$. Consequently $\mathbb E[\eta_U(C)^2]\le(2m+2)^2<\infty$ and $\mathbb E[(2\eta_U)(C)^2]\le4(2m+2)^2<\infty$. Both lattice processes satisfy the local square-integrability premise in the second-order and K definitions.

For every configuration event $A$, the unit-cube Palm construction in [F3] gives $$P^0(A)=\mathbb E\int_Q\mathbf1_A(\theta_x\eta_U)\eta_U(dx).$$ There is exactly one occurrence $x=U$ in $Q$, and $\theta_U\eta_U=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\delta_k=:\Lambda$. Therefore $P^0=\delta_\Lambda$. In particular, using the uncentered configuration in the indicator $\mathbf1_{\{\mu(\{0\})>0\}}$ would give $0$ on the left Campbell sum almost surely, whereas the Palm-side value is $1$; this is why recentering cannot be dropped.

For each selected lattice occurrence $X_i=k+U\in Q$, the displacements to all other occurrences are $\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$. Hence [F4] gives $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(D)=\#(D\cap(\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}))$ for bounded Borel $D$. In particular $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(\{1\})=1$ while $|\{1\}|=0$, so no measurable density $g$ can satisfy [F5].

Now put $\widetilde\eta_U=2\eta_U$, so every lattice site has two occurrence indices and $\widetilde\rho=2$. A selected occurrence has one other occurrence at the same site, so $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(\{0\})=2$. Equivalently, $P^0$ is concentrated on $2\Lambda$, and $\mu(\{0\})=2$, so [F6] gives $2=\widetilde\rho\mathbb E^0[(\mu-\delta_0)(\{0\})]=2\cdot1$. Thus $K(0)=1/2$; deleting both origin occurrences would incorrectly give zero.

Assume the point-process supplier's AC and Countable Choice convention. Let $\eta$ be the stationary locally square-integrable point process with finite positive intensity from [[def-pair-correlation-and-ripleys-k-function]]. Given a compact convex observation window $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ with $0<|W|<\infty$, where $|\cdot|$ is Borel Lebesgue measure as in [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]], let $\xi(A):=\eta(A\cap W)$ for Borel $A$ be the complete observed counting measure in $W$ as in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]], and fix a radius $r\ge0$. Define the **border window**

$$W_{-r}:=\{x\in W:\overline B[x,r]\subseteq W\},$$

where $\overline B[x,r]$ is the closed Euclidean ball under the Euclidean norm used in [[def-pair-correlation-and-ripleys-k-function]]. Since $W$ is closed, $W_{-r}=\bigcap_{\|z\|_2\le r}(W-z)$ is closed and hence Borel. Let $N_\xi(A)=\xi(A)$ count occurrences, including multiplicities, and put $\widehat\rho=N_\xi(W)/|W|$. The border anchor weight is $w_{W,r}(x)=1$ for $x\in W_{-r}$ and $0$ otherwise.

If $N_\xi(W_{-r})=0$, return **not defined**. Otherwise $N_\xi(W)>0$ because $W_{-r}\subseteq W$, so $\widehat\rho N_\xi(W_{-r})>0$. For an occurrence representation $\xi=\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$, return

$$\widehat K_{\rm border}(r):=\frac{1}{\widehat\rho\,N_\xi(W_{-r})}\sum_{i:X_i\in W_{-r}}\sum_{j\ne i}\mathbf1\{\|X_j-X_i\|_2\le r\}.$$

Every eligible anchor has its full closed radius-$r$ neighborhood inside $W$, so all its radius-$r$ partner occurrences are observed. This defines a finite-data procedure only; it asserts no unbiasedness, consistency, or asymptotic guarantee.

**Axiom convention.** The procedure itself makes no choices; AC and Countable Choice are inherited through its point-process and K dependencies.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

citations.quote: A topological space $X$ is **second countable** when its topology has a basis $\mathcal B$ that is at most countable ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]], [[def-countable]]). Thus every open set is a union of members of one at most countable family $\mathcal B$.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

**The product set.** Let $I$ be a set and let $X_i$ be a set for each $i \in I$.
The **product** is

$$\prod_{i \in I} X_i \;:=\; \Big\{\, x : x \text{ is a function with domain } I \text{ and } x(i) \in X_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\Big\},$$

and we write $x_i := x(i)$, the $i$-th **coordinate** of $x$. Two elements of the
product are equal exactly when they agree at every index, functions being equal
when they have the same domain and the same values. For $j \in I$ the $j$-th
**projection** is

$$\pi_j : \prod_{i \in I} X_i \to X_j, \qquad \pi_j(x) := x_j .$$

**Notation for a finite product.** For $I = n$ a natural number, which is the set
$\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ of its predecessors, an element of $\prod_{k<n} X_k$ is a
function on $n$ and we write it $(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$. In particular $I = 2$
gives the **binary product**, written $X \times Y$ for $\prod_{i<2} X_i$ with
$X_0 = X$ and $X_1 = Y$, whose elements are written $(u,v)$ for the function
$0 \mapsto u$, $1 \mapsto v$. This is the only meaning the symbol $X \times Y$
carries on this page.

**Two facts about when the product is nonempty, stated because they are used and
because they cost something.** If some $X_{i_0}$ is empty then the product is
empty, since no function can take a value in $X_{i_0}$. Conversely, suppose every
$X_i$ is nonempty.

- For $I = n$ a natural number, the product is nonempty, and this is a theorem of
  ZF: [[lem-finite-choice]] applied to the function $i \mapsto X_i$ on $n$
  supplies a choice function $g$ for the family of values, and
  $x(i) := g(X_i)$ defines a member of $\prod_{k<n} X_k$.
- For an arbitrary $I$ the assertion "$\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \varnothing$
  whenever every $X_i$ is nonempty" **is** the Axiom of Choice: it is the
  formulation recorded in [[def-axiom-of-choice]], and the choice function of
  [[def-choice-function]] is exactly a point of the product of a family by
  itself. Every use of it below is flagged at the step that spends it.

**The box topology.** Now let each $X_i$ carry a topology $\mathcal{T}_i$
([[def-topological-space]]). Put

$$\mathcal{R} \;:=\; \Big\{\, \prod_{i \in I} U_i \;:\; U_i \in \mathcal{T}_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\Big\},$$

the family of **boxes**. $\mathcal{R}$ is a basis for a topology
([[thm-basis-criterion]]): it contains $\prod_i X_i$, so it covers the product,
and it is closed under binary intersections, since

$$\Big(\prod_i U_i\Big) \cap \Big(\prod_i V_i\Big) = \prod_i (U_i \cap V_i)$$

and each $U_i \cap V_i$ is open by (T3). The topology it generates is the **box
topology** $\mathcal{T}^{\square}$, and $\mathcal{R}$ is a basis for it
([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]).

**The product topology.** The **product topology** $\mathcal{T}^{\Pi}$ on
$\prod_i X_i$ is the initial topology of the family of projections
$(\pi_i)_{i \in I}$ ([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]): the topology generated
by the subbasis

$$\mathcal{G} \;:=\; \{\, \pi_i^{-1}[U] : i \in I,\ U \in \mathcal{T}_i \,\}, \qquad \pi_i^{-1}[U] = \prod_{j \in I} W_j \ \text{ with } W_i = U \text{ and } W_j = X_j \text{ for } j \ne i .$$

By [[thm-basis-criterion]] the finite intersections of members of $\mathcal{G}$
form a basis for $\mathcal{T}^{\Pi}$, and those finite intersections are exactly
the boxes with all but finitely many factors unrestricted:

$$\mathcal{R}^{\Pi} \;=\; \Big\{\, \prod_{i \in I} U_i \;:\; U_i \in \mathcal{T}_i \text{ for every } i, \text{ and } U_i = X_i \text{ for all but finitely many } i \,\Big\}.$$

Indeed the intersection of $\pi_{i_1}^{-1}[U_1], \dots, \pi_{i_n}^{-1}[U_n]$ is
the box whose factor at $i$ is the intersection of those $U_m$ with $i_m = i$ and
is $X_i$ when no $i_m$ equals $i$; and the intersection of no members is the
whole product, the box with every factor $X_i$. Conversely a box with
$U_i = X_i$ off a finite set is such an intersection. Members of
$\mathcal{R}^{\Pi}$ are called **basic product-open** sets, and members of
$\mathcal{R}$ **boxes**. So $\mathcal{R}^{\Pi} \subseteq \mathcal{R}$, with
equality when $I$ is a natural number.

**The empty product.** For $I = \varnothing$ there is exactly one function with
domain $\varnothing$, the empty function, so $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} X_i$ is a
one-point set. A one-point set carries exactly one topology, namely
$\{\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\}$, since a topology must contain the empty set
and the whole set and there is nothing else to contain
([[def-topological-space]]); so the box topology and the product topology agree
there, and both equal the discrete topology and the indiscrete topology
([[def-standard-topologies]]), which coincide on a one-point set. There are no
projections to speak of, and the initial topology of the empty family is indeed
the indiscrete one ([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]).

**Convention.** Unless the box topology is named explicitly, $\prod_i X_i$ always
carries the product topology in this library. That is not a matter of taste: the
product topology is the one with the characteristic property of the next item,
and the box topology has no such property.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

derivations.claim: Choose at most countable bases $\mathcal U$ for $X$ and $\mathcal V$ for $Y$ using [F1]. Their product $\mathcal U\times\mathcal V$ is at most countable by [F2], and its members $U\times V$ form a basis for $X\times Y$ by [F3]. Each such rectangle lies in $\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y)$; every open subset of $X\times Y$ is a union of a subfamily of this countable basis, hence a countable union of those rectangles. By [F4], this proves $\mathcal B(X\times Y)\subseteq\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y)$.

The coordinate projections $\pi_X:X\times Y\to X$ and $\pi_Y:X\times Y\to Y$ are continuous by the definition of the product topology [F3]. For Borel $A\subseteq X$ and $C\subseteq Y$, $A\times C=\pi_X^{-1}(A)\cap\pi_Y^{-1}(C)$ is Borel in $X\times Y$. Thus every generator rectangle of the product sigma-algebra [F5] belongs to $\mathcal B(X\times Y)$, giving the reverse inclusion.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and a bounded Borel set $W\subset\mathbb R^d$. Under
Countable Choice every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^d$ is Lebesgue measurable
([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]), so Lebesgue measure $\ell_d$ is
defined on each such set. Write $|A|:=\ell_d(A)$ for Borel $A$, and
$\mathcal B_W:=\{W\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\}$ for the trace Borel
sigma-algebra on $W$. Every member of $\mathcal B_W$ is Borel in $\mathbb R^d$
because $W$ is Borel. Define $\ell_W:\mathcal B_W\to[0,+\infty]$ by
$\ell_W(A):=\ell_d(A)$. If $(A_k)$ is pairwise disjoint in $\mathcal B_W$,
then each $A_k$ and their union are Borel in $\mathbb R^d$, so countable
additivity of $\ell_d$ gives
$$\ell_W\!\left(\bigcup_k A_k\right)=\ell_d\!\left(\bigcup_k A_k\right)
=\sum_k\ell_d(A_k)=\sum_k\ell_W(A_k),$$
and $\ell_W(\varnothing)=0$. Thus $\ell_W$ is a measure on the trace sigma-
algebra. Since $W$ is bounded, $\ell_W(W)<\infty$
([[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]).
The only choice axiom used to regard $\ell_d$ as a measure in this library is
Countable Choice, as recorded in
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]].

The **finite configuration space on $W$**, denoted $\mathcal C(W)$, is the
measurable subspace of locally finite counting measures on $\mathbb R^d$
consisting of those $\eta$ with $\eta(W^c)=0$ and $\eta(\mathbb R^d)<\infty$.
It is measurable in the ambient evaluation sigma-algebra because both
$\eta\mapsto\eta(W^c)$ and $\eta\mapsto\eta(\mathbb R^d)$ are evaluation
maps for Borel sets.
Thus each $\eta\in\mathcal C(W)$ has a representation
$\eta=\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$ for a finite $n\ge0$ and $x_i\in W$; repeated
locations are allowed and represent multiplicity. Its sigma-algebra is the
trace of the evaluation sigma-algebra: it is generated by
$\eta\mapsto\eta(B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq W$.

For a finite ambient configuration $\widetilde\eta$, its observation in $W$
is $\eta=\widetilde\eta|_W$, where
$\eta(B)=\widetilde\eta(B\cap W)$. The observation includes precisely the
locations belonging to $W$: a boundary location is included when and only
when it belongs to $W$. This convention does not replace $W$ by its interior
or its closure.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]). Equip
$\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]) with its order topology and let
$\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ be the corresponding Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A function $f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **measurable** when
$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Equivalently, it is enough to require
$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$
because the rays $(a,+\infty]$ generate $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

derivations.claim: First suppose $f$ is simple, with value $c_j\ge0$ on each member $B_j$ of a finite Borel partition of $W$. Then $G_f(\eta)=\prod_j c_j^{\eta(B_j)}$, using $0^0=1$; every exponent is an evaluation map. For each fixed $c_j$, the map $m\mapsto c_j^m$ on $\mathbb N_0$ is measurable: the inverse image of any Borel set is a union of the countable level sets $\{\eta(B_j)=m\}$. This also covers $c_j=0$ with $0^0=1$. The finite product is measurable by [F3].

For general $f$, choose simple functions $s_m\uparrow f$ by [F2]. If $\eta=\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$, then $G_{s_m}(\eta)=\prod_{i=1}^n s_m(x_i)\uparrow\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i)=G_f(\eta)$; the limit holds because the product has finitely many nonnegative factors, and it also holds for the empty configuration. Thus $G_f$ is a pointwise limit of measurable functions from step 1.1 and is measurable.

measurable subspace of locally finite counting measures on $\mathbb R^d$
consisting of those $\eta$ with $\eta(W^c)=0$ and $\eta(\mathbb R^d)<\infty$.
It is measurable in the ambient evaluation sigma-algebra because both
$\eta\mapsto\eta(W^c)$ and $\eta\mapsto\eta(\mathbb R^d)$ are evaluation
maps for Borel sets.
Thus each $\eta\in\mathcal C(W)$ has a representation
$\eta=\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$ for a finite $n\ge0$ and $x_i\in W$; repeated
locations are allowed and represent multiplicity. Its sigma-algebra is the
trace of the evaluation sigma-algebra: it is generated by
$\eta\mapsto\eta(B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq W$.

For a finite ambient configuration $\widetilde\eta$, its observation in $W$
is $\eta=\widetilde\eta|_W$, where
$\eta(B)=\widetilde\eta(B\cap W)$. The observation includes precisely the
locations belonging to $W$: a boundary location is included when and only
when it belongs to $W$. This convention does not replace $W$ by its interior
or its closure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure

   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is

4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then

   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).

$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $n\ge1$. The set $\mathbb Q^n$ is countable and dense in $\mathbb R^n$. Moreover the rational open boxes

$$\prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i),\qquad a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Q,\quad a_i<b_i,$$

form a countable basis for the product topology on $\mathbb R^n$.

Let $X,Y$ be second-countable topological spaces and give $X\times Y$ the
product topology. Then
$$\mathcal B(X\times Y)=\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y).$$

Fix a locally compact, second-countable Hausdorff topological space $S$
([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-second-countable-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]). Here locally compact means that every point has a
compact neighbourhood; second countable means that the topology has an at most
countable basis; and Hausdorff means that distinct points have disjoint open
neighbourhoods. Let $\mathcal B(S)$ be the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the
open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A **counting measure** on $S$ is a Borel measure of the form
$\mu=\sum_{j\in J}\delta_{x_j}$ for a finite or countable index set $J$ and
points $x_j\in S$, where repetitions are allowed and the empty sum is zero.
Each $\delta_x$ is the unit point mass at $x$
([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), and
the countable sum is a measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]]. The **multiplicity** at $x$ is
$\mu(\{x\})$. The counting measure is **locally finite** if
$\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact subset $K\subseteq S$
([[def-compact-space]]).

Let $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of locally finite counting
measures, equipped with the sigma-algebra generated by the **evaluation maps**
$\mu\mapsto\mu(B)$ for $B\in\mathcal B(S)$. A **point process** on $S$ is a
measurable map $\eta:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to
(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$ from a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), with measurability in the sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Equivalently, every
count $\eta(B)$ is a measurable random variable, because the evaluation maps
generate $\mathcal E$. Its **law** is the probability measure
$\mathbb P_\eta(A)=\mathbb P(\eta^{-1}(A))$ on $(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]],
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]). The process is
classified by its realized configurations: a configuration $\mu$ is
**simple** if $\mu(\{x\})\le1$ for every $x$, and is **multiplicity-bearing**
if some singleton has mass greater than one. This is a pointwise distinction;
no almost-sure simplicity assertion is part of this definition.

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of all locally finite Borel
measures on $S$, with the sigma-algebra generated by their evaluation maps. A
**random locally finite measure** $\xi$ is a measurable map into this space.

For a nonnegative Borel function $f$, write
$\eta(f):=\int_S f\,d\eta$. Define the expected measure, or **intensity
measure**, by $\nu(B):=\mathbb E[\eta(B)]$. The expected-measure and
random-integral measurability assertions are justified by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]]. The measure
$\nu$ need not be locally finite; it is locally finite exactly when
$\mathbb E[\eta(K)]<\infty$ for each compact $K$.

The mean measure of a random locally finite measure is likewise
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, covered by the same expected-measure lemma. Local
finiteness of each realization does not by itself assert local finiteness of
$\nu$.

Let $\nu$ be a finite Borel measure on $S$
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and put $\lambda=\nu(S)$. A
Poisson point process of intensity $\nu$ exists. If $\lambda=0$ it is the zero
process. If $\lambda>0$, its law is the push-forward of
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!}\left(\frac{\nu}{\lambda}\right)^{\otimes n}$$
on the disjoint union $\coprod_{n\ge0}S^n$ under
$(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$. Every Poisson point
process of finite total intensity has this same law. This is the
**mixed-binomial representation**: the total count is Poisson and, in the
construction, the $n$ locations in component $S^n$ have product law
$(\nu/\lambda)^{\otimes n}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

$$\ell_W\!\left(\bigcup_k A_k\right)=\ell_d\!\left(\bigcup_k A_k\right)

and $\ell_W(\varnothing)=0$. Thus $\ell_W$ is a measure on the trace sigma-
algebra. Since $W$ is bounded, $\ell_W(W)<\infty$
([[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]).

with their multiplicities and taking the empty product to be $1$, define
$$G_f(\eta):=\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i).$$
Then $G_f:\mathcal C(W)\to[0,\infty)$ is measurable.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: The zero extension of $\lambda_\theta$ is Borel: for Borel $E\subseteq[0,\infty)$ its inverse image is $W\cap\lambda_\theta^{-1}(E)$ if $0\notin E$, and $W^c\cup(W\cap\lambda_\theta^{-1}(E))$ if $0\in E$; both are Borel because $W$ is Borel and $\lambda_\theta$ is Borel on $W$. Thus [F2] defines its finite measure of total mass $\Lambda_\theta$ on $\mathbb R^d$, supported on $W$. The unit-rate reference intensity $1_W\,d\ell_d$ has total mass $v$ by [F1]. Thus [F3] applies to both Poisson laws, and their finite-mixture tuple integrals are supported on $W^n$.
The product factor in $g_\theta$ is measurable by [F5], and the exponential factor is a finite nonnegative constant. Hence $g_\theta$ is a measurable nonnegative function on $\mathcal C(W)$.

Let $A\subseteq\mathcal C(W)$ be measurable. Expanding [F3] for $P_\theta$ on its support $W$ and using [F4] gives $P_\theta(A)=e^{-\Lambda_\theta}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac1{n!}\int_{W^n}1_A\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}\right)\prod_{i=1}^n\lambda_\theta(x_i)\,\ell_W^{\otimes n}(d(x_1,\ldots,x_n)).$ For $P_0$, the same formula holds with $\Lambda_\theta$ replaced by $v$ and every product factor replaced by $1$.

Expand $\int_Ag_\theta\,dP_0$ by the $P_0$ formula in step 2.1. On the $n$-tuple component, $g_\theta(\sum_i\delta_{x_i})= e^{v-\Lambda_\theta}\prod_i\lambda_\theta(x_i)$, including $n=0$ by the empty-product convention. Cancellation of $e^{-v}$ with $e^v$ yields exactly the series for $P_\theta(A)$ in step 2.1.

Since step 3.1 holds for every measurable $A$, $g_\theta$ is a Radon–Nikodym density of $P_\theta$ relative to $P_0$, and therefore $P_\theta\ll P_0$. The explicitly displayed $g_\theta$ supplies the density version for every $\theta$, so the arbitrary selector in [F6] is not used. Taking its logarithm gives the stated expression when all event factors are positive; a zero factor makes the finite product zero and the log likelihood $-\infty$.

Let $W\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $\mathcal C(W)$ be as in
[[def-finite-window-spatial-observation]], with volume $v=|W|<\infty$. For
each parameter $\theta$, let $\lambda_\theta:W\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued
Borel function and assume
$$\Lambda_\theta:=\int_W\lambda_\theta(x)\,\ell_W(dx)<\infty.$$
Extend $\lambda_\theta$ by zero off $W$ and let $P_\theta$ be the law on
$\mathcal C(W)$ of the Poisson process on $\mathbb R^d$ with intensity measure
$\nu_\theta=1_W\lambda_\theta\,d\ell_d$. Let $P_0$ be the unit-rate Poisson
law on $\mathcal C(W)$ obtained from intensity $1_W\,d\ell_d$. Then
$$\frac{dP_\theta}{dP_0}(\eta)=g_\theta(\eta):=\exp\{v-\Lambda_\theta\}\prod_{x\in\eta}\lambda_\theta(x).$$
where the product counts atom occurrences and the empty product is $1$. In
particular $P_\theta\ll P_0$. This formula explicitly chooses a common
parameter-indexed density version, so it requires no arbitrary simultaneous
selection of Radon–Nikodym representatives.

For an observed $\eta$, if every observed occurrence has positive intensity,
the log likelihood, up to the parameter-independent term $v$, is
$$\ell_\eta(\theta)=\sum_{x\in\eta}\log\lambda_\theta(x)-\Lambda_\theta.$$
If any observed occurrence has zero intensity, the likelihood is zero and its
log is $-\infty$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Suppose $n>0$ and put $\widehat\rho=n/v>0$. For $\rho>0$ set $t=\rho/\widehat\rho$. By [F1] and the logarithm quotient law [F2], the log-likelihood difference is $\ell(\rho)-\ell(\widehat\rho)=n(\log t-t+1)$.

Suppose $n=0$. For $\rho>0$, [F1] gives log likelihood $-v\rho$, which is strictly below $0$ and tends to $0$ as $\rho\downarrow0$. At $\rho=0$, the empty product is $1$ and the density in [[thm-finite-window-spatial-poisson-likelihood]] has log likelihood equal to its parameter-independent constant, so the normalized log likelihood value is $0$. Thus zero is the maximizer when admitted and is only a supremum when the parameter space is $(0,\infty)$.

Let $\psi(t)=\log t-t+1$. For each $s>0$, $\frac{\psi(s+h)-\psi(s)}{h}=\frac{\log(s+h)-\log s}{h}-1\longrightarrow\frac1s-1$ as $h\to0$, by [F2]; hence $\psi'(s)=1/s-1$. If $t>1$, apply [F3] on $[1,t]$: its intermediate point $c>1$ has $\psi'(c)<0$, so $\psi(t)<\psi(1)=0$. If $0<t<1$, apply [F3] on $[t,1]$: its intermediate point has $\psi'(c)>0$, so again $\psi(t)<\psi(1)=0$. Equality holds at $t=1$. Therefore [F1] and step 1.1 give the unique maximum at $\rho=\widehat\rho$ among positive rates; at $\rho=0$ the observed nonempty configuration has likelihood zero.
Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove the positive-count claim, and step 1.2 proves the zero-count boundary claim.

Let $\eta$ be a Poisson point process on $S$ with finite intensity measure
$\nu$ (so $\nu(S)<\infty$ under
[[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]), and let
$h:S\times\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)\to[0,\infty]$ be
measurable. Addition $(x,\mu)\mapsto\mu+\delta_x$ is interpreted as addition
of counting measures. Then
$$\mathbb E\left[\int_S h(x,\eta)\,\eta(dx)\right]=\int_S\mathbb E[h(x,\eta+\delta_x)]\,\nu(dx).$$
Both sides are well-defined extended nonnegative integrals.

Let
$$D:=\{(x,\mu)\in S\times\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S):\mu(\{x\})\ge1\}.$$
Then $D$ is measurable in the product evaluation sigma-algebra, and the map
$R:D\to\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ defined by $R(x,\mu)=\mu-\delta_x$ is
measurable. The subtraction removes one occurrence, so any other occurrences
at $x$ remain.

Let $W$, $\ell_W$, and $\mathcal C(W)$ be as in
[[def-finite-window-spatial-observation]]. Let $P_{\theta,b}$ be a specified
probability law on $\mathcal C(W)$; $b$ denotes a fixed exterior configuration
when the model uses a boundary condition, and is omitted when it does not. For
this fixed boundary convention, a jointly measurable function
$\lambda_\theta:W\times\mathcal C(W)\to[0,+\infty]$ is a
**Papangelou conditional intensity relative to $\ell_W$** for this law and
boundary convention; the notation $\lambda_\theta(u;\eta,b)$ displays the
fixed boundary label but $b$ is not an additional variable in its measurable
domain. Omit $b$ when there is no exterior condition or when the fixed
convention is clear from context. The defining identity holds when, for every
nonnegative product-measurable
$h:W\times\mathcal C(W)\to[0,\infty]$,
$$\mathbb E_{\theta,b}\left[\sum_{x\in\eta}h(x,\eta-\delta_x)\right]=\mathbb E_{\theta,b}\left[\int_W h(u,\eta)\lambda_\theta(u;\eta,b)\,\ell_W(du)\right].$$
The sum runs over atom occurrences, so $\eta-\delta_x$ deletes one
occurrence; if $b$ is used, it is fixed on both sides. The identity is the
definition of the Papangelou intensity used on this page. It does not assert
that every finite-window law has such a function.

The deletion operation and the resulting measurable random sum use
[[lem-deletion-of-one-point-is-measurable]]. On the occurrence domain, the
deletion-composition is measurable; extend it by zero off that measurable
domain and integrate against the evaluation kernel $K(\eta,B)=\eta(B)$. This
integral is the displayed sum, and its measurability follows from the
deletion map and [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]], as
used in the deletion lemma.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and a bounded Borel set $W\subset\mathbb R^d$. Under
Countable Choice every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^d$ is Lebesgue measurable
([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]), so Lebesgue measure $\ell_d$ is
defined on each such set. Write $|A|:=\ell_d(A)$ for Borel $A$, and
$\mathcal B_W:=\{W\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\}$ for the trace Borel
sigma-algebra on $W$. Every member of $\mathcal B_W$ is Borel in $\mathbb R^d$
because $W$ is Borel. Define $\ell_W:\mathcal B_W\to[0,+\infty]$ by
$\ell_W(A):=\ell_d(A)$. If $(A_k)$ is pairwise disjoint in $\mathcal B_W$,
then each $A_k$ and their union are Borel in $\mathbb R^d$, so countable
additivity of $\ell_d$ gives
$$\ell_W\!\left(\bigcup_k A_k\right)=\ell_d\!\left(\bigcup_k A_k\right)
=\sum_k\ell_d(A_k)=\sum_k\ell_W(A_k),$$
and $\ell_W(\varnothing)=0$. Thus $\ell_W$ is a measure on the trace sigma-
algebra. Since $W$ is bounded, $\ell_W(W)<\infty$
([[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]).
The only choice axiom used to regard $\ell_d$ as a measure in this library is
Countable Choice, as recorded in
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]].

The **finite configuration space on $W$**, denoted $\mathcal C(W)$, is the
measurable subspace of locally finite counting measures on $\mathbb R^d$
consisting of those $\eta$ with $\eta(W^c)=0$ and $\eta(\mathbb R^d)<\infty$.
It is measurable in the ambient evaluation sigma-algebra because both
$\eta\mapsto\eta(W^c)$ and $\eta\mapsto\eta(\mathbb R^d)$ are evaluation
maps for Borel sets.
Thus each $\eta\in\mathcal C(W)$ has a representation
$\eta=\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$ for a finite $n\ge0$ and $x_i\in W$; repeated
locations are allowed and represent multiplicity. Its sigma-algebra is the
trace of the evaluation sigma-algebra: it is generated by
$\eta\mapsto\eta(B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq W$.

For a finite ambient configuration $\widetilde\eta$, its observation in $W$
is $\eta=\widetilde\eta|_W$, where
$\eta(B)=\widetilde\eta(B\cap W)$. The observation includes precisely the
locations belonging to $W$: a boundary location is included when and only
when it belongs to $W$. This convention does not replace $W$ by its interior
or its closure.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].

Let $\nu$ be a finite Borel measure on $S$
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and put $\lambda=\nu(S)$. A
Poisson point process of intensity $\nu$ exists. If $\lambda=0$ it is the zero
process. If $\lambda>0$, its law is the push-forward of
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!}\left(\frac{\nu}{\lambda}\right)^{\otimes n}$$
on the disjoint union $\coprod_{n\ge0}S^n$ under
$(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$. Every Poisson point
process of finite total intensity has this same law. This is the
**mixed-binomial representation**: the total count is Poisson and, in the
construction, the $n$ locations in component $S^n$ have product law
$(\nu/\lambda)^{\otimes n}$.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and a bounded Borel set $W\subset\mathbb R^d$. Under
Countable Choice every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^d$ is Lebesgue measurable
([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]), so Lebesgue measure $\ell_d$ is
defined on each such set. Write $|A|:=\ell_d(A)$ for Borel $A$, and
$\mathcal B_W:=\{W\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\}$ for the trace Borel
sigma-algebra on $W$. Every member of $\mathcal B_W$ is Borel in $\mathbb R^d$
because $W$ is Borel. Define $\ell_W:\mathcal B_W\to[0,+\infty]$ by
$\ell_W(A):=\ell_d(A)$. If $(A_k)$ is pairwise disjoint in $\mathcal B_W$,
then each $A_k$ and their union are Borel in $\mathbb R^d$, so countable
additivity of $\ell_d$ gives
$$\ell_W\!\left(\bigcup_k A_k\right)=\ell_d\!\left(\bigcup_k A_k\right)
=\sum_k\ell_d(A_k)=\sum_k\ell_W(A_k),$$
and $\ell_W(\varnothing)=0$. Thus $\ell_W$ is a measure on the trace sigma-
algebra. Since $W$ is bounded, $\ell_W(W)<\infty$
([[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]).
The only choice axiom used to regard $\ell_d$ as a measure in this library is
Countable Choice, as recorded in
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]].

The **finite configuration space on $W$**, denoted $\mathcal C(W)$, is the
measurable subspace of locally finite counting measures on $\mathbb R^d$
consisting of those $\eta$ with $\eta(W^c)=0$ and $\eta(\mathbb R^d)<\infty$.
It is measurable in the ambient evaluation sigma-algebra because both
$\eta\mapsto\eta(W^c)$ and $\eta\mapsto\eta(\mathbb R^d)$ are evaluation
maps for Borel sets.
Thus each $\eta\in\mathcal C(W)$ has a representation
$\eta=\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$ for a finite $n\ge0$ and $x_i\in W$; repeated
locations are allowed and represent multiplicity. Its sigma-algebra is the
trace of the evaluation sigma-algebra: it is generated by
$\eta\mapsto\eta(B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq W$.

For a finite ambient configuration $\widetilde\eta$, its observation in $W$
is $\eta=\widetilde\eta|_W$, where
$\eta(B)=\widetilde\eta(B\cap W)$. The observation includes precisely the
locations belonging to $W$: a boundary location is included when and only
when it belongs to $W$. This convention does not replace $W$ by its interior
or its closure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Extend $g$ and $h$ by zero outside $\mathcal C(W)$ and $W\times\mathcal C(W)$, respectively; [F5] makes these measurable extensions. For a test function $h$ as in the Statement, define on the domain where $(x,\zeta)$ contains an occurrence at $x$ $k(x,\zeta):=g(\zeta)h(x,\zeta-\delta_x),$ and set $k=0$ off that domain. The domain and deletion map are measurable by [F2]; the extensions, addition operation, and $g,h$ are measurable by [F4, F5], so $k$ is a nonnegative measurable test function for [F1]. Also the addition map is measurable by [F4], and since $g$ is finite and strictly positive, its ratio $\lambda_g(u;\eta)=g(\eta+\delta_u)/g(\eta)$ is a measurable function on $W\times\mathcal C(W)$.

The left side of [F1] with this $k$ is $\mathbb E_Q\left[g(\xi)\sum_{x\in\xi}h(x,\xi-\delta_x)\right]=\mathbb E_P\sum_{x\in\eta}h(x,\eta-\delta_x).$ On the right side, $(u,\xi+\delta_u)$ is in the deletion domain and $(\xi+\delta_u)-\delta_u=\xi$, so the integrand is $g(\xi+\delta_u)h(u,\xi)=g(\xi)\lambda_g(u;\xi)h(u,\xi)$. Consequently [F1] gives, after Tonelli's interchange [F6], $\mathbb E_P\sum_{x\in\eta}h(x,\eta-\delta_x)=\mathbb E_P\int_W h(u,\eta)\lambda_g(u;\eta)\,\ell_W(du).$ which is the defining identity [F3].
Step 2.1 proves the claimed Papangelou identity for every admissible nonnegative $h$, hence proves the Statement.

Let $W$ be as in [[def-finite-window-spatial-observation]] and suppose
$v=|W|>0$. Consider the homogeneous family $\lambda_\rho(x)=\rho$ with
parameter space either $[0,\infty)$ or $(0,\infty)$. For an observed
