Let $S$ be as in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]]. A
**Poisson point process with locally finite, sigma-finite intensity measure
$\nu$** is a point process $\eta$ such that for every finite pairwise-disjoint
family of Borel sets $B_1,\ldots,B_m$, the counts $\eta(B_i)$ are independent
random elements ([[def-independent-random-elements]]) and $\eta(B_i)$ has the
scalar Poisson law of mean $\nu(B_i)$
([[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]],
[[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]). If $\nu(B)=\infty$,
the extended count convention is $\eta(B)=+\infty$ almost surely.
Here sigma-finite means that $S$ is a countable union of Borel sets of finite
$\nu$-measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]); for the
stated $S$, local finiteness also implies sigma-finiteness by the compact
exhaustion in
[[lem-locally-compact-second-countable-spaces-have-compact-exhaustions]].

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the evaluation-measurable space of locally
finite Borel measures. A **Cox point process directed by a random measure
$\xi$** consists of a point process $\eta$, a random locally finite measure
$\xi$, and a supplied probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$
to $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ such that $K(\xi,\cdot)$ is a regular
conditional law of $\eta$ given $\xi$
([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]) and, for $P_\xi$-almost every
$\mu$, $K(\mu,\cdot)$ is the law of a Poisson point process of intensity
$\mu$. The kernel is part of the model data; this definition does not assert
that such a kernel exists for every $(\eta,\xi)$. The mean measure of $\xi$ is
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, a measure by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]].

Both definitions permit multiplicities. They do not assert that diffuse
directing measures yield simple processes or that a Cox law determines the law
of its directing measure.

Let $T>0$, $\theta>0$, and let $S=(0,T]$ carry its subspace topology and
Borel sigma-algebra. This space is Hausdorff as a subspace of $\mathbb R$;
rational intervals give a countable base; and each $x\in S$ has a compact
neighborhood $[x-\delta,x+\delta]\cap S$ for some $0<\delta<x$. Let $\ell$
be Lebesgue measure restricted to $S$. There exists a Poisson point process
on $S$ with intensity measure $\nu_\theta(B)=\theta\ell(B)$. Its total
count is finite almost surely, its event times have no ties almost surely,
and for every integer $m\ge0$ the joint density of the ordered event times
$$0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T,\qquad N(S)=m,$$
with respect to $m$-dimensional Lebesgue measure on the ordered simplex is
$$e^{-\theta T}\theta^m.$$
For $m>0$, conditional on $N(S)=m$, the ordered event times have density
$m!/T^m$. For $m=0$ the empty-pattern probability is $e^{-\theta T}$.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Let $(\Pi_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of pi-systems in a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, and assume $\Omega\in\Pi_i$ for every $i$.
If the family $(\Pi_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent, then the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(\Pi_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a finite horizon
$T>0$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires that this integral
be finite pathwise, that $A$ be continuous, adapted and predictable with
$A_0=0$, and that $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$. Set $M_t:=N_t-A_t$. The model
contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

The displayed intensity density alone does **not** assert that $N-A$ is a
martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.

Fix a supplied event history $h$ at time $t$ in the model of
[[def-temporal-point-process-and-conditional-intensity]]. Let
$\lambda_h^*(u)$ be its nonnegative no-event conditional hazard, supplied as
a locally integrable version on every finite interval, and put
$$\Lambda_h(u):=\int_t^u\lambda_h^*(s)\,ds.$$
For each finite $U>t$, on $t\le u\le U$ the conditional survivor and finite-
time density of the next event are
$$S_h(u)=\exp(-\Lambda_h(u)),\qquad f_h(u)=\lambda_h^*(u)\exp(-\Lambda_h(u))\quad\text{for almost every }u.$$
If $\Lambda_h(u)\to\Lambda_h(\infty)<\infty$ as $u\to\infty$, then
$K_h(\{\infty\})=\exp(-\Lambda_h(\infty))$. If
$\Lambda_h(u)\to\infty$, this terminal mass is zero. These conclusions
concern one next-event law and do not prove non-explosion of an entire
process.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as in
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]. Fix a finite
horizon $T>0$, a probability space with an increasing filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]], and an adapted
càdlàg (right-continuous with left limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued
process $N$ with $N_0=0$, $N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and jumps
$\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ outside one null event. Such a process is **simple**:
its event times are strictly ordered,
$0<T_1<\cdots<T_{N_T}\le T$. It is **locally finite** when it has finitely
many events on every finite interval.

For conditional-law calculations, the model supplies a measurable history
space $(\mathsf H,\mathcal G)$, an adapted measurable history random element
$H_t$ recording the initial information and events observed through time $t$,
and a measurable update map $h\mapsto h\oplus u$ that appends an event at
time $u$. Write $\mathcal H_t:=\sigma(H_t)$ and let $H_{t-}$ record only
events strictly before $t$. Relevant exogenous covariates are included in
the supplied history. Measurability has the meaning of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Predictability is
measurability for the predictable sigma-algebra generated by
$(s,u]\times A$ with $A\in\mathcal F_s$ and the time-zero generators, as in
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]].

The model supplies a probability kernel $K_{t,h}$ on $(t,\infty]$ for the
next event time given history $h$ at time $t$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]],
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]); its finite-time density
versions are jointly measurable in $(t,h,u)$. The value $+\infty$ means that
no later event occurs. If the finite-time measure is absolutely continuous
with respect to Lebesgue measure
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]],
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]), let $f_{t,h}$ be its supplied
nonnegative Radon--Nikodym density
([[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]). Write
$S_{t,h}(u):=K_{t,h}((u,\infty])$ for its survivor and define its
**no-event conditional hazard** by
$$\lambda_{t,h}^*(u):=\frac{f_{t,h}(u)}{S_{t,h}(u)}\qquad\text{where }S_{t,h}(u)>0.$$
Assume these hazards are locally integrable on every finite interval. The
model also supplies a nonnegative predictable effective-intensity process
$\lambda^*$ compatible with these waiting-time hazards: for each history
$h$ at time $t$, on its supplied measurable no-event continuation up to
$u>t$, the pre-event intensity $\lambda^*(u\mid h_{u-})$ agrees with
$\lambda_{t,h}^*(u)$ for Lebesgue-almost every $u$. The jointly measurable
hazard representatives used in the event-density factors are these same
versions on their proper domains $u>t$. Compatibility with the predictable
process is a model requirement, not an evaluation of a waiting-time density
at its excluded left endpoint. This pre-event convention means the event
at $u$ does not change its own intensity.

The **temporal conditional-intensity model** requires both this
hazard-compatible conditional law and the separate counting-process
compensator contract of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]: if an at-risk
indicator $Y$ and intensity density $\lambda$ are separately specified, the
effective intensity is $\lambda^*=Y\lambda$; without an at-risk indicator,
it is $\lambda^*$. Then $A_t=\int_0^t\lambda^*(u)\,du$ is finite pathwise,
continuous, adapted and predictable, $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$, and $N-A$ is
a square-integrable martingale in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]. At-risk exposure, if
present, is part of the effective intensity. The compensator clause is a
model assumption: a displayed hazard formula alone proves neither that a
process with this law exists nor that the martingale contract holds. No
stationarity or non-explosion claim follows from writing an intensity
specification.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The extension by zero has unit jumps only at the simple event times of $\eta$, and $N_t$ is finite because $N_1$ is Poisson with mean $1$. The effective intensity $\lambda^*(t)=\mathbf1_{(0,1]}(t)$ is deterministic Borel and hence predictable by [F4]. Direct integration gives $A_t=\int_0^t\lambda^*(u)\,du=t\wedge1$, so $A$ is continuous, nondecreasing, and bounded by $1$.

Let $\mathsf H$ be the space of finite counting measures on $(0,\infty)$ with the sigma-algebra generated by its Borel-set evaluation maps. Define the history random element by $H_s(B):=\eta(B\cap(0,s\wedge1])$ for every Borel $B\subseteq(0,\infty)$. It is a finite counting measure, and it is measurable because each evaluation is a measurable count of the supplied point process; its generated sigma-algebra is the event-history filtration in the Given clause. For finite $u>0$, define $h\oplus u:=h+\delta_u$. For every Borel $B$, $(h\oplus u)(B)=h(B)+\mathbf1_B(u)$, so the update is jointly measurable in $h,u$ and appends exactly one event.

For $0\le s\le t$, the increment $N_t-N_s$ is the count on $(s,t]\cap(0,1]$, a Poisson variable of mean $\min(t,1)-\min(s,1)$. Refine a finite family of past Borel sets into the disjoint atoms of the finite Boolean algebra they generate. Every atom lies in $(0,s]$, so [F1] gives independence of its count vector from the future increment. These count cylinders generate the natural-history sigma-algebra, and [F5] extends independence to that sigma-algebra. Therefore $\mathbb E[N_t-N_s\mid\mathcal H_s]=\min(t,1)-\min(s,1)=A_t-A_s$. Thus $N-A$ is a martingale. Since $N_t$ has finite second moment by [F3] and $A_t\le1$, this martingale is square-integrable and meets [F6]; $\mathbb E[A_T]\le1$.

For $s\ge0$ and $h\in\mathsf H$, supply the next-event kernel, viewed on $[0,\infty]$ and supported on $(s,\infty]$, by $$K_{s,h}(C):=\int_{C\cap(s,1]}e^{-(u-s)}\,du+e^{-(1-s)_+}\mathbf1_{\{\infty\in C\}}$$ for Borel $C\subseteq[0,\infty]$, where $x_+:=\max(x,0)$. Its finite-time mass is $1-e^{-(1-s)_+}$, so each $K_{s,h}$ is a probability measure. For fixed $C$, the finite-time term is $e^s\int_{C\cap(s,1]}e^{-u}\,du$, a Borel function of $s$ because the tail integral is monotone on $[0,1]$ and zero for $s\ge1$; the atom mass is also Borel. The finite-time density $f_{s,h}(u)=\mathbf1_{\{s<u\le1\}}e^{-(u-s)}$ is jointly measurable in $(s,h,u)$. By independent future increments, this is the conditional next-event law given $H_s$: its survivor for $u>s$ is $S_{s,h}(u)=e^{-((u\wedge1)-s)_+}$, since the event of no point in $(s,u]\cap(0,1]$ has probability $e^{-((u\wedge1)-s)_+}$. Thus $f_{s,h}/S_{s,h}=1$ on $(s,1]$ and $0$ after $1$, agreeing almost everywhere with $\lambda^*(u\mid h_{u-})=\mathbf1_{(0,1]}(u)$; this also agrees with [F7]. In particular, $K_{0,h}(\{\infty\})=e^{-1}$ and $K_{s,h}(\{\infty\})=1$ for $s\ge1$.

Taking $u\to\infty$ in step 3.1 gives $\Pr(T_1=\infty)=e^{-1}$, also the zero-count probability $\Pr(N_1=0)$ by [F3]. No events occur after time $1$, and $N_1$ is finite almost surely, so the process terminates and is non-explosive.

Let $S$ be as in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]]. A
**Poisson point process with locally finite, sigma-finite intensity measure
$\nu$** is a point process $\eta$ such that for every finite pairwise-disjoint
family of Borel sets $B_1,\ldots,B_m$, the counts $\eta(B_i)$ are independent
random elements ([[def-independent-random-elements]]) and $\eta(B_i)$ has the
scalar Poisson law of mean $\nu(B_i)$
([[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]],
[[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]). If $\nu(B)=\infty$,
the extended count convention is $\eta(B)=+\infty$ almost surely.
Here sigma-finite means that $S$ is a countable union of Borel sets of finite
$\nu$-measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]); for the
stated $S$, local finiteness also implies sigma-finiteness by the compact
exhaustion in
[[lem-locally-compact-second-countable-spaces-have-compact-exhaustions]].

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the evaluation-measurable space of locally
finite Borel measures. A **Cox point process directed by a random measure
$\xi$** consists of a point process $\eta$, a random locally finite measure
$\xi$, and a supplied probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$
to $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ such that $K(\xi,\cdot)$ is a regular
conditional law of $\eta$ given $\xi$
([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]) and, for $P_\xi$-almost every
$\mu$, $K(\mu,\cdot)$ is the law of a Poisson point process of intensity
$\mu$. The kernel is part of the model data; this definition does not assert
that such a kernel exists for every $(\eta,\xi)$. The mean measure of $\xi$ is
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, a measure by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]].

Both definitions permit multiplicities. They do not assert that diffuse
directing measures yield simple processes or that a Cox law determines the law
of its directing measure.

Let $T>0$, $\theta>0$, and let $S=(0,T]$ carry its subspace topology and
Borel sigma-algebra. This space is Hausdorff as a subspace of $\mathbb R$;
rational intervals give a countable base; and each $x\in S$ has a compact
neighborhood $[x-\delta,x+\delta]\cap S$ for some $0<\delta<x$. Let $\ell$
be Lebesgue measure restricted to $S$. There exists a Poisson point process
on $S$ with intensity measure $\nu_\theta(B)=\theta\ell(B)$. Its total
count is finite almost surely, its event times have no ties almost surely,
and for every integer $m\ge0$ the joint density of the ordered event times
$$0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T,\qquad N(S)=m,$$
with respect to $m$-dimensional Lebesgue measure on the ordered simplex is
$$e^{-\theta T}\theta^m.$$
For $m>0$, conditional on $N(S)=m$, the ordered event times have density
$m!/T^m$. For $m=0$ the empty-pattern probability is $e^{-\theta T}$.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

Let $(\Pi_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of pi-systems in a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, and assume $\Omega\in\Pi_i$ for every $i$.
If the family $(\Pi_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent, then the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(\Pi_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent.

filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is

   $t\ge0$ the restricted map

   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero

   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at

   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable

   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a finite horizon
$T>0$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires that this integral
be finite pathwise, that $A$ be continuous, adapted and predictable with
$A_0=0$, and that $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$. Set $M_t:=N_t-A_t$. The model
contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

The displayed intensity density alone does **not** assert that $N-A$ is a
martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.

Assume AC, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice for the cited likelihood
and hazard-calculus interfaces. Fix $T>0$ and a common specified initial
history. Let $(P_\theta)$ be a supplied family of laws for actual simple,
non-explosive temporal point-process models on $(0,T]$ satisfying
[[def-temporal-point-process-and-conditional-intensity]], with jointly
measurable conditional history-update and waiting-time kernels. Let $P_0$
be the supplied unit-rate Poisson reference on the finite-pattern space
$$\mathsf X_T=\bigsqcup_{m\ge0}\Delta_m,\qquad \Delta_0=\{\varnothing\},\quad \Delta_m=\{(t_1,\ldots,t_m):0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T\},$$
equipped with the disjoint-union Borel sigma-algebra. For a pattern
$0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T$, let $h_{i-1}$ be the initial history updated by
$t_1,\ldots,t_{i-1}$. On each simplex, the laws are dominated by $P_0$ and
the following chosen density representative gives the Radon–Nikodym
derivative $P_0$-almost everywhere:
$$\frac{dP_\theta}{dP_0}(t_1,\ldots,t_m)=e^T\left(\prod_{i=1}^m\lambda_\theta^*(t_i\mid h_{i-1})\right)\exp\!\left(-\int_0^T\lambda_\theta^*(u\mid h_{u-})\,du\right).$$
Here $h_{u-}$ is the history immediately before $u$. Thus the likelihood as a
function of $\theta$ is proportional to the product of pre-event intensities
times the terminal integrated-hazard factor; $e^T$ is parameter-independent.
If an observed event has zero intensity, the density is zero; a finite
log-likelihood requires positive intensity at each observed event. For
$m=0$, the event product is the empty product $1$ and the terminal no-event
factor remains.

For marked patterns, let marks lie in a supplied measurable space with a
common mark probability measure $Q$. Here $h_i$ records all past event
times and marks, and the marked-history update is supplied and measurable.
Require that the supplied waiting-time kernels, conditioned on this full
marked history, satisfy the same temporal model; an unmarked marginal
waiting-time law alone is not this hypothesis. If each event also has a
supplied jointly measurable conditional mark density
$q_\theta(k_i\mid t_i,h_{i-1})$ relative to $Q$, and the reference uses
independent marks with law $Q$, evaluate the displayed intensity factors
on these marked histories and multiply the ratio by
$\prod_iq_\theta(k_i\mid t_i,h_{i-1})$. The ground intensity does not
determine a mark law.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as in
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]. Fix a finite
horizon $T>0$, a probability space with an increasing filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]], and an adapted
càdlàg (right-continuous with left limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued
process $N$ with $N_0=0$, $N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and jumps
$\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ outside one null event. Such a process is **simple**:
its event times are strictly ordered,
$0<T_1<\cdots<T_{N_T}\le T$. It is **locally finite** when it has finitely
many events on every finite interval.

For conditional-law calculations, the model supplies a measurable history
space $(\mathsf H,\mathcal G)$, an adapted measurable history random element
$H_t$ recording the initial information and events observed through time $t$,
and a measurable update map $h\mapsto h\oplus u$ that appends an event at
time $u$. Write $\mathcal H_t:=\sigma(H_t)$ and let $H_{t-}$ record only
events strictly before $t$. Relevant exogenous covariates are included in
the supplied history. Measurability has the meaning of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Predictability is
measurability for the predictable sigma-algebra generated by
$(s,u]\times A$ with $A\in\mathcal F_s$ and the time-zero generators, as in
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]].

The model supplies a probability kernel $K_{t,h}$ on $(t,\infty]$ for the
next event time given history $h$ at time $t$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]],
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]); its finite-time density
versions are jointly measurable in $(t,h,u)$. The value $+\infty$ means that
no later event occurs. If the finite-time measure is absolutely continuous
with respect to Lebesgue measure
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]],
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]), let $f_{t,h}$ be its supplied
nonnegative Radon--Nikodym density
([[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]). Write
$S_{t,h}(u):=K_{t,h}((u,\infty])$ for its survivor and define its
**no-event conditional hazard** by
$$\lambda_{t,h}^*(u):=\frac{f_{t,h}(u)}{S_{t,h}(u)}\qquad\text{where }S_{t,h}(u)>0.$$
Assume these hazards are locally integrable on every finite interval. The
model also supplies a nonnegative predictable effective-intensity process
$\lambda^*$ compatible with these waiting-time hazards: for each history
$h$ at time $t$, on its supplied measurable no-event continuation up to
$u>t$, the pre-event intensity $\lambda^*(u\mid h_{u-})$ agrees with
$\lambda_{t,h}^*(u)$ for Lebesgue-almost every $u$. The jointly measurable
hazard representatives used in the event-density factors are these same
versions on their proper domains $u>t$. Compatibility with the predictable
process is a model requirement, not an evaluation of a waiting-time density
at its excluded left endpoint. This pre-event convention means the event
at $u$ does not change its own intensity.

The **temporal conditional-intensity model** requires both this
hazard-compatible conditional law and the separate counting-process
compensator contract of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]: if an at-risk
indicator $Y$ and intensity density $\lambda$ are separately specified, the
effective intensity is $\lambda^*=Y\lambda$; without an at-risk indicator,
it is $\lambda^*$. Then $A_t=\int_0^t\lambda^*(u)\,du$ is finite pathwise,
continuous, adapted and predictable, $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$, and $N-A$ is
a square-integrable martingale in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]. At-risk exposure, if
present, is part of the effective intensity. The compensator clause is a
model assumption: a displayed hazard formula alone proves neither that a
process with this law exists nor that the martingale contract holds. No
stationarity or non-explosion claim follows from writing an intensity
specification.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For $\theta>0$, [F2] gives a simple finite-count Poisson process; for $\theta=0$, [F1] and the zero-rate count law make the process empty. Extend its count by $N_t=\eta((0,t\wedge T])$. For $0\le s<t$, $N_t-N_s$ is the count on $(s,t]\cap(0,T]$, independent of each finite cylinder of past Borel-set counts by [F1]. Indeed, refine any finite family of past Borel sets into the disjoint atoms of the finite Boolean algebra they generate. Each atom lies in $(0,s\wedge T]$ and is disjoint from $(s,t]\cap(0,T]$, so [F1] makes the atom-count vector independent of the future increment; the cylinder vector is a function of those atom counts. Such cylinders generate $\mathcal H_s$, so [F4] extends independence to the whole history sigma-algebra. Therefore $\mathbb E[N_t-N_s\mid\mathcal H_s]=\theta((t\wedge T)-(s\wedge T))$, and $N_t-A_t$ is a martingale for $A_t=\theta(t\wedge T)$. The effective intensity is $\lambda^*(t)=\theta\mathbf1_{(0,T]}(t)$, which is deterministic Borel and predictable by [F5]; its integral is $A_t$, continuous and bounded by $\theta T$. Also $N_t$ has finite second moment by [F3]. Thus $N-A$ is square-integrable and the Poisson process meets the compensator contract [F6].

Let $\mathsf H$ be the space of finite counting measures on $(0,\infty)$ with its evaluation sigma-algebra, and define $H_s(B):=\eta(B\cap(0,s\wedge T])$ for Borel $B\subseteq(0,\infty)$. Each $H_s$ is finite and measurable by the evaluation measurability of $\eta$, and $\sigma(H_s)=\mathcal H_s$. For finite $u>0$ put $h\oplus u=h+\delta_u$; the evaluation identity $(h\oplus u)(B)=h(B)+\mathbf1_B(u)$ shows that the update is jointly measurable and appends one event.

For a fixed finite pattern, its pre-event intensity at $t_i$ is $\mu+\alpha\sum_{j<i}e^{-\beta(t_i-t_j)}$. Integrating the baseline gives $\mu T$. For each event time $t_i$, the integral $\int_{t_i}^T e^{-\beta(u-t_i)}\,du$ equals $\frac{1-e^{-\beta(T-t_i)}}{\beta}$ by [F10], also when $t_i=T$, when both sides are zero. Summing these terms gives the displayed cumulative hazard.

For $s\ge0$ and $h\in\mathsf H$, supply the next-event kernel, supported on $(s,\infty]$, by $$K_{s,h}(C):=\int_{C\cap(s,T]}\theta e^{-\theta(u-s)}\,du+e^{-\theta(T-s)_+}\mathbf1_{\{\infty\in C\}}$$ for Borel $C\subseteq[0,\infty]$, where $x_+:=\max(x,0)$. Its finite-time mass is $1-e^{-\theta(T-s)_+}$, so each $K_{s,h}$ is a probability measure, including when $\theta=0$ or $s\ge T$. For fixed $C$, the finite-time term is $\theta e^{\theta s}\int_{C\cap(s,T]}e^{-\theta u}\,du$, a Borel function of $s$ because the tail integral is monotone on $[0,T]$ and zero for $s\ge T$; the atom mass is also Borel. The finite-time density $f_{s,h}(u)=\theta\mathbf1_{\{s<u\le T\}}e^{-\theta(u-s)}$ is jointly measurable in $(s,h,u)$. Independent increments give the same conditional survivor, $$S_{s,h}(u)=e^{-\theta((u\wedge T)-s)_+},\qquad u>s,$$ so the kernel is compatible with the observed finite-window Poisson law and supplies its terminal continuation after $T$. Its hazard is $\theta$ on $s<u\le T$ and $0$ for $u>T$, agreeing with $\lambda^*(u\mid h_{u-})=\theta\mathbf1_{(0,T]}(u)$ (and is identically zero at $\theta=0$). Thus the homogeneous survivor formula used in the likelihood is exactly $e^{-\theta(u-s)}$ for $s<u\le T$.

Substitute the Hawkes pre-event values and integrated hazard from step 1.3 into [F7]. This gives exactly the displayed Hawkes likelihood ratio. The calculation is conditional on a compatible process law and proves no existence, non-explosion, or stationarity property for the specification.

Within the observation window, $0\le s<u\le T$, the probability of no event in $(s,u]$ is $e^{-\theta(u-s)}$, so the no-event hazard is $\theta$ there. Applying [F7] to the $m$ events gives exact ratio $e^T\theta^m e^{-\theta T}$, including $m=0$ by the empty-product and terminal-survival conventions.

If $m>0$ and $\theta>0$, the log-likelihood is $\ell(\theta)=m\log\theta-\theta T$, with derivative $\ell'(\theta)=m/\theta-T$ by [F8]. It is positive for $0<\theta<m/T$ and negative for $\theta>m/T$. The mean value theorem [F9] therefore makes $\ell$ increase up to $m/T$ and decrease thereafter; at $\theta=0$ the likelihood is zero because $m>0$. Thus the unique maximum is $\widehat\theta=m/T$.

If $m=0$, the likelihood is $e^{-\theta T}$, which strictly decreases on $\theta\ge0$ because $T>0$ and the exponential is strictly increasing. Its maximum is attained at $\theta=0$. If zero were excluded from the parameter space, this case would have only a boundary supremum.

For theta>=0, the frozen-window Poisson process has independent future increments from the evaluation-history sigma-algebra by disjoint-cell refinement and the pi-system criterion, hence the required square-integrable martingale with A=theta(t min T). The history/update evaluations are measurable and the explicit kernel normalizes, is measurable, has the correct survivor and intensity, including theta=0 and s>=T. The ratio e^T theta^m exp(-theta T) follows from the reviewed likelihood theorem; 0^0=1 retains the empty pattern. For m>0 the log derivative m/theta-T has one sign change and MVT gives the unique maximum m/T; theta=0 has zero likelihood. For m=0 strict exponential monotonicity gives maximum zero (only a supremum if zero is excluded). citations.quote:
An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment as in [[def-statistical-experiment]], and assume
$\Theta\ne\varnothing$. A **confidence-set procedure** is a map
$C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$, where
$\mathcal P(\Theta):=\{A:A\subseteq\Theta\}$, such that, for every
$\eta\in\Theta$, its
membership section
$$C_\eta:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\eta\in C(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Its **coverage at $\theta$** is
$c_C(\theta):=P_\theta(C_\theta)$, and its **confidence level** is
$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}c_C(\theta)$, the greatest lower bound of those
coverage values. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, it has coverage
at least $1-\alpha$ if $P_\theta(C_\theta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every
$\theta\in\Theta$.

Only membership sections need to be measurable; no sigma-algebra on the
parameter set is assumed. The parameter is fixed in the repeated-sampling
coverage probability.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

derivations.claim: For each $i$, define the induced full-parameter confidence set $D_i(x):=\{\eta\in\Theta:\psi_i(\eta)\in C_i(x)\}$. Each membership section of $D_i$ is $A_i(\eta)$, measurable by [A1], so [F2] applies and its coverage at $\theta$ is $P_\theta(A_i(\theta))\ge1-\alpha_i$. The miss event $B_i(\theta):=A_i(\theta)^c$ is measurable and, by [F3], satisfies $P_\theta(B_i(\theta))=1-P_\theta(A_i(\theta))\le\alpha_i$.

Failure of simultaneous coverage is $\bigcup_{i=1}^m B_i(\theta)$. By finite subadditivity [F3] and step 1.1, its probability is at most $\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i\le\alpha$. Taking the complement gives the stated simultaneous coverage bound. This argument allows the membership events to be dependent.

boundaries.evidence: If every miss event is empty, the union has probability zero; step 2.1 still yields coverage one.
When alpha is zero, all nonnegative alpha_i are zero; steps 1.1 and 2.1 give zero total miss probability.
For m=1, step 2.1 is the single marginal coverage bound.
Step 2.1 permits identical or otherwise dependent miss events; no independence premise enters the union bound.
The assumptions include alpha_i in [0,1] and alpha in [0,1]; steps 1.1 and 2.1 also cover the endpoints.

boundaries.reason: The proof constructs induced sets from fixed maps and makes no choice from a family of nonempty sets.
The statement is a one-way coverage implication, not an equivalence.

citations.quote:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), and fix an integer $m\ge1$ before observing the data. Write $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. A **finite family of null hypotheses** is a fixed list $H_{01},\ldots,H_{0m}$ with each $H_{0i}\subseteq\Theta$. For each $i\in[m]$, let $p_i:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ be a p-value statistic ([[def-p-value]]). It is **valid for $H_{0i}$** when

$$P_\theta\{x:p_i(x)\le u\}\le u\qquad(\theta\in H_{0i},\ 0\le u\le1).$$

If $H_{0i}=\varnothing$, this universal condition is vacuous and $i$ never belongs to a true-null index set. For a nonempty null it agrees with the published valid-p-value definition. The family may have any joint dependence among its p-values. Validity is required only under the corresponding null laws; a p-value statistic alone does not imply validity.

For $\theta\in\Theta$, the **true-null index set** is
$$I_0(\theta):=\{i\in[m]:\theta\in H_{0i}\}.$$
A fixed deterministic multiple-testing rule is a family of measurable rejection events $D_i\in\mathcal A$, one for each $i\in[m]$. Its total number of rejections and number of false rejections at parameter $\theta$ are
$$R:=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1_{D_i},\qquad V_\theta:=\sum_{i\in I_0(\theta)}\mathbf1_{D_i}.$$
Its **familywise error rate (FWER)** at $\theta$ is $P_\theta(V_\theta\ge1)$, and its **false discovery rate (FDR)** at $\theta$ is
$$E_\theta\!\left[\frac{V_\theta}{R\vee1}\right],$$
where $R\vee1=\max\{R,1\}$. The random variable $V_\theta/(R\vee1)$ is the **false discovery proportion (FDP)**. Strong FWER control at level $\alpha$ means that this FWER is at most $\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$, including parameters for which only some of the null hypotheses are true. The denominator convention makes the FDP zero when no hypothesis is rejected.

If the testing rule uses auxiliary randomization, include that randomizer in the observation and its sigma-algebra before defining the rejection events $D_i$.

These quantities are well-defined: the finite sums of indicators are measurable, $0\le V_\theta\le R$, and $0\le V_\theta/(R\vee1)\le1$, so the ratio is integrable under each probability law ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

Let $p$ be a valid p-value for a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0$ in a
statistical experiment. For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, the deterministic test
with rejection function
$$\varphi_\alpha(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{p(x)\le\alpha\}}$$
satisfies
$$P_\theta(p(X)\le\alpha)=E_\theta[\varphi_\alpha(X)]\le\alpha \qquad(\theta\in\Theta_0).$$
Consequently, whenever a nonempty alternative hypothesis
$\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta\setminus\Theta_0$ is specified, this test has size
at most $\alpha$ and hence level $\alpha$ in the sense of
[[def-test-size-and-power]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,

parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment as in [[def-statistical-experiment]], and assume
$\Theta\ne\varnothing$. A **confidence-set procedure** is a map
$C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$, where
$\mathcal P(\Theta):=\{A:A\subseteq\Theta\}$, such that, for every
$\eta\in\Theta$, its
membership section
$$C_\eta:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\eta\in C(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Its **coverage at $\theta$** is
$c_C(\theta):=P_\theta(C_\theta)$, and its **confidence level** is
$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}c_C(\theta)$, the greatest lower bound of those
coverage values. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, it has coverage
at least $1-\alpha$ if $P_\theta(C_\theta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every
$\theta\in\Theta$.

Only membership sections need to be measurable; no sigma-algebra on the
parameter set is assumed. The parameter is fixed in the repeated-sampling
coverage probability.

For every $\theta\in\Theta$, suppose each membership event
$$A_i(\theta):=\{x\in\mathcal X:\psi_i(\theta)\in C_i(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$ and has marginal coverage
$$P_\theta(A_i(\theta))\ge1-\alpha_i,$$
where $0\le\alpha_i\le1$ and $\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i\le\alpha\le1$. Then, for every $\theta\in\Theta$,

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), and fix an integer $m\ge1$ before observing the data. Write $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. A **finite family of null hypotheses** is a fixed list $H_{01},\ldots,H_{0m}$ with each $H_{0i}\subseteq\Theta$. For each $i\in[m]$, let $p_i:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ be a p-value statistic ([[def-p-value]]). It is **valid for $H_{0i}$** when

$$P_\theta\{x:p_i(x)\le u\}\le u\qquad(\theta\in H_{0i},\ 0\le u\le1).$$

If $H_{0i}=\varnothing$, this universal condition is vacuous and $i$ never belongs to a true-null index set. For a nonempty null it agrees with the published valid-p-value definition. The family may have any joint dependence among its p-values. Validity is required only under the corresponding null laws; a p-value statistic alone does not imply validity.

For $\theta\in\Theta$, the **true-null index set** is
$$I_0(\theta):=\{i\in[m]:\theta\in H_{0i}\}.$$
A fixed deterministic multiple-testing rule is a family of measurable rejection events $D_i\in\mathcal A$, one for each $i\in[m]$. Its total number of rejections and number of false rejections at parameter $\theta$ are
$$R:=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1_{D_i},\qquad V_\theta:=\sum_{i\in I_0(\theta)}\mathbf1_{D_i}.$$
Its **familywise error rate (FWER)** at $\theta$ is $P_\theta(V_\theta\ge1)$, and its **false discovery rate (FDR)** at $\theta$ is
$$E_\theta\!\left[\frac{V_\theta}{R\vee1}\right],$$
where $R\vee1=\max\{R,1\}$. The random variable $V_\theta/(R\vee1)$ is the **false discovery proportion (FDP)**. Strong FWER control at level $\alpha$ means that this FWER is at most $\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$, including parameters for which only some of the null hypotheses are true. The denominator convention makes the FDP zero when no hypothesis is rejected.

If the testing rule uses auxiliary randomization, include that randomizer in the observation and its sigma-algebra before defining the rejection events $D_i$.

These quantities are well-defined: the finite sums of indicators are measurable, $0\le V_\theta\le R$, and $0\le V_\theta/(R\vee1)\le1$, so the ratio is integrable under each probability law ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

$$P_\theta\{\text{at least one true null is rejected}\}=P_\theta(V_\theta\ge1)\le\alpha.$$

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

For $m\ge1$, fix a finite family of null hypotheses $H_{0i}$, $1\le i\le m$, before observing the data, and let $p_i:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ be p-value statistics valid for their respective nulls in the sense of [[def-null-valid-p-value-and-fwer-fdr]]. Given $\alpha\in[0,1]$ and an observation $x\in\mathcal X$, order the indices by the pairs $(p_i(x),i)$ in lexicographic order. This gives a unique permutation $\pi$ with $p_{\pi(1)}(x)\le\cdots\le p_{\pi(m)}(x)$; ties are ordered by increasing index.

Set
$$r_\alpha(x)=\max\{k\in\{0,\ldots,m\}:p_{\pi(j)}(x)\le\alpha/(m-j+1)\text{ for every }1\le j\le k\}.$$
The rejected-index set is $R_\alpha(x)=\{\pi(j):1\le j\le r_\alpha(x)\}$. Reject $H_{0i}$ exactly when $i\in R_\alpha(x)$; equivalently, compare sequentially to $\alpha/(m-j+1)$, stop at the first failed comparison, and reject only the preceding ranks.

For $m=0$, extend the procedure to the empty input by returning the empty rejected set. For $m\ge1$, every denominator in a tested rank is positive. The ordering is a unique finite permutation, and the finite set defining $r_\alpha(x)$ contains $0$, so the output is well-defined.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], each $p_i$ is measurable into $[0,1]$ with its Borel trace. For indices $a,b$, the difference $p_a-p_b$ is measurable by [F4], so $\{p_a\le p_b\}$ and $\{p_a<p_b\}$ are measurable preimages by [F5] of the Borel half-lines $(-\infty,0]$ and $(-\infty,0)$. For each permutation $\pi$, its ordering cell $C_\pi$ is the finite intersection over positions $a<b$ of $\{p_{\pi(a)}\le p_{\pi(b)}\}$ if $\pi(a)<\pi(b)$ and $\{p_{\pi(a)}<p_{\pi(b)}\}$ otherwise. These cells are measurable by [F6], and every $x$ belongs to exactly one because lexicographic ordering with index tie-breaking gives a unique permutation by [F3]. For rank $j$, let $Q_{\pi,j}=\{p_{\pi(j)}\le\alpha/(m-j+1)\}$; this pass event and its failure event $Q_{\pi,j}^{c}$ are measurable preimages of Borel half-lines by [F1], [F2], and [F5]. For $k\in\{0,\ldots,m\}$, intersect $C_\pi$ with the pass events for $j\le k$ and, when $k<m$, the failure event at $k+1$. Empty intersections are omitted when $k=0$ or $k=m$. The resulting measurable cell is exactly the event that the order is $\pi$ and the returned prefix length is $k$, by [F3]; these finitely many cells partition $\mathcal X$.

The event $D_i(\alpha)$ is the union of the cells from step 1.1 over all permutations and prefix lengths $k$ with $i\in\{\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(k)\}$. This is a finite union because there are $m!$ permutations and $m+1$ prefix lengths. By [F6], $D_i(\alpha)\in\mathcal A$ for every $i$.

$$r_\alpha(x)=\max\{k\in\{0,\ldots,m\}:p_{\pi(j)}(x)\le\alpha/(m-j+1)\text{ for every }1\le j\le k\}.$$

Input $m\ge1$ p-values $p_1,\ldots,p_m\in[0,1]$ and a level $q\in(0,1)$.
Order the hypotheses by the keys $(p_i,i)$, so equal p-values are ordered by
their original index, and write the ordered values as
$p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}$. Set

$$R:=\max\bigl(\{k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:p_{(k)}\le kq/m\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).$$

Reject exactly the hypotheses at ranks $1,\ldots,R$. If the set in the
maximum is empty, then $R=0$ and no hypothesis is rejected. This is a
deterministic step-up rule for the supplied p-values; its FDR guarantee is a
separate theorem.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Each $A_k=\{P_{(k)}\le kq/m\}$ is measurable by step 1.1; its indicator and the simple function $k\mathbf 1_{A_k}$ are measurable by [F2], and the finite maximum of these functions and $0$ is measurable because its sublevel sets are finite intersections. The same construction with $P_{-i,(k)}$ and thresholds $(k+1)q/m$ shows each level set of $S_i$ lies in the sigma-algebra generated by the remaining coordinates.

If $R=0$, no $P_i$ is zero because then $P_{(1)}=0\le q/m$, so no value is at most $Rq/m=0$. If $0<R<m$, maximality gives $P_{(R)}\le Rq/m$ and $P_{(R+1)}>(R+1)q/m>Rq/m$, so exactly the first $R$ ranks have values at most $Rq/m$; if $R=m$, all values are at most $P_{(m)}\le q=mq/m$. Fix $i$ and write $s=S_i$. If $s\ge1$, then $P_{-i,(s)}\le(s+1)q/m$, and if $s=0$ there are no other values to check. When $P_i\le(s+1)q/m$, at least $s+1$ full-family values meet that threshold, so $R\ge s+1$. If $R\ge s+2$, the qualifying rank $R$ has $P_{(R)}\le Rq/m$; deleting $P_i$ leaves at least $R-1$ other values at most $Rq/m$, making $R-1\ge s+1$ qualify in the definition of $S_i$, a contradiction. Hence $R=s+1$, and step 3.1 shows that $i$ is rejected.

If $P_i>(s+1)q/m$ but $i$ is rejected, step 3.1 gives $P_i\le Rq/m$; write $r=R\ge1$. At least $r-1$ other values are at most $rq/m$, so $r-1$ qualifies in the definition of $S_i$ (with $0$ automatically qualifying when $r=1$). Thus $r-1\le s$, whence $P_i\le rq/m\le(s+1)q/m$, a contradiction; therefore $i$ is not rejected.

Let $m\ge1$ be a finite number of hypotheses and write
$[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Fix a probability law $P$ and a set
$I_0\subseteq[m]$ of indices whose null hypotheses are true under $P$. A
measurable rejection rule is a measurable map
$\mathcal R:\Omega\to2^{[m]}$, where the finite set $2^{[m]}$ has its discrete
sigma-algebra. Set

$$R=|\mathcal R|,\qquad V=|\mathcal R\cap I_0|.$$

The **false discovery proportion** is

$$\operatorname{FDP}:=\frac{V}{R\vee1},\qquad R\vee1:=\max(R,1),$$

and the **false discovery rate** is

$$\operatorname{FDR}:=\mathbb E_P\!\left[\frac{V}{R\vee1}\right].$$

The **family-wise error rate** is

$$\operatorname{FWER}:=P(V\ge1).$$

Since $V\le R$ whenever $R>0$ and $V=0$ when $R=0$, the FDP is a measurable
random variable in $[0,1]$ and its expectation is finite. These definitions
use the fixed true-null set for the specified law; they do not assert that FDR
and FWER are equal except in the global-null case.

Input $m\ge1$ p-values $p_1,\ldots,p_m\in[0,1]$ and a level $q\in(0,1)$.
Order the hypotheses by the keys $(p_i,i)$, so equal p-values are ordered by
their original index, and write the ordered values as
$p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}$. Set

$$R:=\max\bigl(\{k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:p_{(k)}\le kq/m\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).$$

Reject exactly the hypotheses at ranks $1,\ldots,R$. If the set in the
maximum is empty, then $R=0$ and no hypothesis is rejected. This is a
deterministic step-up rule for the supplied p-values; its FDR guarantee is a
separate theorem.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $m\ge1$, $q\in(0,1)$, and let $P_1,\ldots,P_m$ be measurable
$[0,1]$-valued functions on one measurable space. Apply the algorithm in
[[alg-benjamini-hochberg-step-up-procedure]]. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$
and vector $x_{-i}\in[0,1]^{m-1}$, order the remaining values as
$x_{-i,(1)}\le\cdots\le x_{-i,(m-1)}$ and define

$$s_i(x_{-i}):=\max\bigl(\{0\}\cup\{k\in\{1,\ldots,m-1\}:x_{-i,(k)}\le(k+1)q/m\}\bigr).$$

When $m=1$, set $s_i=0$. Let $S_i=s_i(P_{-i})$, let $R$ be the number of
rejections, and let $I_i$ be the indicator that hypothesis $i$ is rejected.
Then $S_i$ is measurable with respect to the sigma-algebra generated by the
other coordinates and, pointwise,

$$\frac{I_i}{R\vee1}=\frac{\mathbf 1\{P_i\le(S_i+1)q/m\}}{S_i+1}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

From [F2], the rejected indices are exactly $\{i:P_i\le Rq/m\}$: if $0<R<m$, maximality gives $P_{(R)}\le Rq/m<P_{(R+1)}$; the cases $R=0$ and $R=m$ follow directly. The finite-union formula for $\{P_i\le Rq/m\}$ then makes the BH rule measurable. For $i\in I_0(\theta)$, [A1] and [F4] give independence, [F5] groups $P_i$ with the remaining p-values, [F7] makes $S_i$ measurable with respect to that group, and [F6] gives the product joint law of $P_i$ and $S_i$.
For $r\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$, set $t_r=(r+1)q/m\le q<1$. By [A1], $P_\theta(P_i\le t_r)=t_r$; independence from step 1.1 and [F6] give $P_\theta(P_i\le t_r,S_i=r)=t_rP_\theta(S_i=r)$.

By [F7], partitioning on the finite-valued $S_i$ writes $I_i/(R\vee1)$ as $\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\mathbf 1\{P_i\le t_r,S_i=r\}/(r+1)$. Each event is measurable, and [F8] and [F10] give the absolute expectation of its summand as $P_\theta(P_i\le t_r,S_i=r)/(r+1)\le1$, so each summand is integrable. Then [F8], [F9], and step 2.1 give the expectation sum $\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}t_rP_\theta(S_i=r)/(r+1)=(q/m)\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}P_\theta(S_i=r)=q/m$.

The measurable BH rejection rule from step 1.1 lets us apply [F1] with $P=P_\theta$ and $I_0=I_0(\theta)$. Thus $V=\sum_{i\in I_0(\theta)}I_i$ and $\operatorname{FDR}_\theta=\mathbb E_\theta[V/(R\vee1)]$; repeated finite linearity [F9] and step 3.1 give $\operatorname{FDR}_\theta=\sum_{i\in I_0(\theta)}q/m=(m_0(\theta)/m)q\le q$, since $m_0(\theta)\le m$. This is the FDR defined in [F1], not an FWER conclusion.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

derivations.claim: For $1\le r\le m-1$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, $\{y_{(r)}\le t\}$ is the finite union over $r$-element index sets $J$ of $\bigcap_{j\in J}\{y_j\le t\}$, since at least $r$ remaining values are at most $t$ exactly when the $r$th ordered value is at most $t$. Each coordinate cylinder is measurable in the stated finite product structure by [F1] and [F3], so these sublevel sets are Borel. Since the closed left rays generate $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ by [F4], each order statistic is Borel by [F2]. The coordinate-deletion projection from $[0,1]^m$ to $[0,1]^{m-1}$ is measurable: preimages of measurable rectangles are finite intersections of coordinate cylinders, and the rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra by [F3]. Thus lifting a Borel set in the remaining-coordinate space gives a Borel set in the full product. If $y\le z$ coordinatewise, at least $r$ coordinates of $z$ are at most $z_{(r)}$; their corresponding coordinates of $y$ are also at most $z_{(r)}$, so $y_{(r)}\le z_{(r)}$. Every remaining-coordinate order statistic is therefore coordinatewise nondecreasing.

Fix $k$ and suppose $p_i\le c_k$. Rank $k$ passes exactly when at least $k-1$ other coordinates are at most $c_k$, which is $y_{(k-1)}\le c_k$; for $k=1$ this holds by $y_{(0)}=0$. For each $j>k$, since $p_i\le c_k\le c_j$, rank $j$ passes exactly when at least $j-1$ other coordinates are at most $c_j$, namely $y_{(j-1)}\le c_j$. Hence $R=k$ exactly when the first condition of $C_{i,k}$ holds and every higher rank fails, which is $p_{-i}\in C_{i,k}$. If $k=m$, $i$ is automatically among the first $k$ ranks. If $k<m$ and $i$ is not among the first $k$ ranks, then $p_{(k+1)}\le p_i\le c_k\le c_{k+1}$ would make rank $k+1$ pass. Conversely, if $R=k$ and $i$ is rejected, then $p_i\le p_{(k)}\le c_k$, rank $k$ passes and every higher rank fails, so the conditions defining $C_{i,k}$ hold.

For any remaining vector $y$, replace coordinate $i$ by $0$. Since $c_1>0$, rank one passes. Every rank occupied by a zero-valued coordinate also passes because all critical values are positive, so $R$ includes all zero-valued coordinates and rejects the inserted coordinate $i$. Thus the resulting rejection count is some $r\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. By step 2.1, $y\in C_{i,r}$; hence the sets cover the space. If $k<\ell$ and $y\in C_{i,k}$, its condition at $r=\ell-1$ gives $y_{(\ell-1)}>c_\ell$, while membership in $C_{i,\ell}$ would give $y_{(\ell-1)}\le c_\ell$. Thus the sets are disjoint. They are Borel by step 1.1 and their finite defining inequalities.

If $y\in C_{i,j}$ for some $j\le k<m$, the defining inequalities include $y_{(r)}>c_{r+1}$ for every $r\ge k$, so $D_{i,k}$ is contained in the displayed intersection. Conversely, suppose those inequalities hold and set $p_i=0$. Rank one passes, and by the zero-coordinate argument in step 3.1 the inserted coordinate $i$ is rejected. No rank $\ell\ge k+1$ can pass: that would require $y_{(\ell-1)}\le c_\ell$, contrary to the assumed condition at $r=\ell-1$. Thus the rejection count is some $j\le k$, and step 2.1 puts $y$ in $C_{i,j}$. This proves the formula; when $k=m$, step 3.1 gives $D_{i,m}$ equal to the whole space. The formula is a finite intersection of Borel order-statistic superlevel sets and is coordinatewise increasing by step 1.1.
